entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Sect.1. Introduction. I. 'fHE SALUTATION. 1. Paul and Timothy. (1) "Paul, apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God"-" not of men, nor by meu" (Gal. i. l; ii. 8; 1 Cor. xv. 9, 10; 1 Tim. ii. 7; Acts ix. 15), as every true minister of Christ is able to say, holding his office, not by his own seeking or scheming, nor by election of the Church alone, though that is needful in its place (Acts xiii. 1-3), but by a distinct Divine appointment (John xxi. 15-17; Acts xx. 28). (2) The apostle delights to honour his associates. With every right to speak simply in his own name, yet he adds that of" Timothy the brother" (" my fellow-worker," Rom. xvi. 21; "my true child in faith," 1 Tim. i. 1). Not as a matter of courtesy and kind feeling only, but in view of the future needs of the Church, its older and more responsible officers should duly recognize young brother Timothy. 2. Saints and faithful brethren. (1) All true Christians are saints by their very calling, as persons devoted to God and brought near to him (eh. iii. 12; 1 Pet. i.15, 16; ii. 5, 9; 1 John i. 3; Exod. xix. 3-6) through the blood of atonement (Titus ii. 14; Heh. ix. 14; x. 12, 14; Rev. i 5, 6), and by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit (2 Thess. ii. 13; Titus iii. 5), and the continued influence of the truth (2 Thess. ii. 13; John xv. 3, 4, 7 ; xvii. 17). A spotless moral life is the outcome of this inward sanctity, which belongs to body as well as soul-" as becometh saints" (Eph. v. 3; 2 'l'im. ii. 19-21; 2 Cor. vi. 17; 1 Thess. v. 23). (2) They are bretli,ren to each other" in Christ," having access through him" in one Spirit to the Father," and belonging to " the household of God" (Eph. ii. 18-22; iv. 1-4; eh. iii. ll-14; Gal. vi.10; 1 Thess. iv. 9, 10; John xiii.14; xv. 12-17; 1 Jobn ii. 7-11; iii. 23); and faithful to Chdst the Head and to the brotherhood, when their faith is assaulted and their unity endangered (eh. ii. 7, 19; iii.15; iv. 3, 15-17; Phil i 27). 3. Grace and peace. (1) All Divine blessing is matter of grace to us as dependent creatures, but especially as fallen and sinful. It is " the grace of God that brings salvation " (Titus ii. 11; Eph. ii. 5), which "superabounded where sin abounded" (Rom. v. 20), and is the source of e.11 good in me.n (1 Cor. xv. 10) and of all we hope for (2 Thess. ii. 16; 2 Tim. i. 9, 10; Acts xv. 11). It is the outflow of God's love, of his "kindness and philanthropy" (Titus iii. 4); e.nd has its supreme expression in" Jesus Christ and him c~·ucified" (Rom. v. 8; Heb. ii. 9; John i. 17; iii. 16; 1 John iv. 10). Our everlasting songs will resound "to the praise of the glory of his grace" (Eph. i. 6 ; Rev. i. 5, 6 ; v. 12, 13; vii. 10). (2) Peace, is the effect of grace within the soul-the end of its war with God in forgiveness of sin (vers. 14, 20; Eph. ii. 16; 2 Cor. v. 19; Rom. v. 1), the restoring of inward harmony and health (Rom. viii. 6), freedom from fear and trouble (eh. iii. 16; Phil. iv. 7; John xiv. 27), bearing fruit in mutual concord an.J. amity (Eph. ii. 14-16; Rom. xv. 7; 2 Thess. iii. 16). It is the gift, the legacy of Christ (Eph. i. 2; ii. 14, 17 ; John xiv. 27; xvi. 33; xx.19, 26). 'l'hese all-comprising gifts a.re primarily "from God our Father." Grace is the outgoing of the Father's love toward his rebel children (Acts xvii. 28; Eph. ii. 4, 6; Luke xv. 11-32), and peace the reuniting of the child to the Divine family (Eph. ii. 18, 19). ll. THE THANKSGIVING. 1. 7'he essentials of the Christia1i life. (Vers. 3-5.) "Fides, aruor, apes: summa Christianismi '' (Bengel). Compare the order and relation of the three graces here and in 1 'l'hess. i. 3; Eph. i. 15-18; with 1 Cor. xiii. 13; also Heh, :1, 22-25, Revised V crsion. (1) "'l'o hear of your faith in Cllrist J csus" is goo.i 20 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [oH, I, 1-29,

neWI! indeed. So in the case of a child or friend; how much more in thnt of a whole communit_y ! W~at boundless and end_less pos~\bilities of good are implied in this single fact! It 1s the birth of true, eternal life (eh. 11. 12, 13; Rom, vi. 1-11 • John i. 12 • iii. 36; vi. 4i, Si; xvii. 3), the entrance into a fellowship with Christ' (1 Cor. i. 9) _which brings a -~appiness and pow:er to whi~h ~here is no measure (1 Pet. i. 8; 1 ,John 1. 3, ~; John ni. 38; xv. 11; xvi. 22; Ph1L 1v. 13). (2) "Faith worketh by love" (CnL v. 6) ; hearing of the first, if it be genuine, one is sure to hear of the second. Love is the first "fruit of the Spirit " (Cnl. v. 22), the witness of a Divine life in the roul (1 John iii. 14; v. 1). This love is oot,lwlic-a family affection, goina out to all the children of God, tM saints everywhere and of all times, whenever we ~ee them or bear or read of them; o,erleaping every national, social, or (alas that we should have to add!) ecclesiastical barrier (eh. iiL 11; Cnl. iii. 28). (3) But the present state and character of Christians call for thanksgiving on their account, most of all, "because of the hope in store for them in heaven." Faith and love are unspeakable blessings even now ; but what "if in this life only we had hoped in Christ" (1 Cor. xv. 19)? It is the thought of what awaits the Colossian believers in heaven, the conviction that they ha..-e "Christ in them, the hope of glory" (ver. 27; eh. iii. 4), that fills the apostle's heart with joy (Phil. i. 6; 2 Thess. L 3-5; 1 Pet. i. 3-7; John xiv. 2, 3; xvii. 24). So in regard to himself (Phil. i. 21-23; 2 Cor. v. 1-8; 2 Tim. iv. 6-8). Finis coronat opus. It is the grand outlook, the glorious prospect beyond death, that gives security and di:!nity, a serene calmness and a buoyant energy, to the Christian life (Rom. v. 1-5; ,·iii. 18, 35-39; 1 Cor. xv. 58; 2 Cor. iv. 16-18; Phil. i. 20; 2 Tim. i. 12; Heb. xi. 13, 35; Rev. ii. 10). This hope will not deceive; it is fonnded on" the word of the truth of the gospel " (1 Cor. xv. 15 ; 2 Pet. i. 16). 2. The progress of the gospel. (Vers. 6-8.) (1) It spreads by its inherent fruitfulness, by the living energy with which it works in those who receive it, by the silent contagion of conviction and example, acting continuously as leaven on the surrounding mass of the world (Matt. xiii 33). The fruit it produces in the lives of those who receive it becomes seed in its turn for the soil around. Epaphras has heard the gospel from St. Paul ; he carries it home and teaches and practises it there, and the Church of Colossm springs up ( comp. 1 Thess. i. 8-10). (2) At the same time, it has its special mess6'Tlgers and advocates -" ser..-ants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Cor. iv. 1); "Ye learnt from Epaphras" { eh. iv. 12; Rom. xii. 5-8; 1 Cor. xii. 28; Eph. iv. 11, 12). " A faithful minister of Christ : " how honourable the title! how great the reward (1 Pet. v. 1-4) ! We note the care of the apostle to commend and support hisfellow-· servant, and the grateful and graceful way with which he refers to the love of the Colossians to himself. The progress of the gospel is not a little helped by mutual: recognition and confidence of this kind on the part of Christ's servants towards each other. III. TBE OPENING PBAYER. I. Christian knowledge. (Vers. 9, 10.) (l} We so often find knowledge divorced from action, the head and the heart at variance, that we are apt to exclaim, "Knowledge, alas! 'tis all in vain.'' But it is, nevertheless, a precondition of all saving faith and all right action. In it lies the beginning of the soul's life (ver. 6 b), the means of its growth and advancement (ver. 10, "by the knowledge of God"), and the end towards which it strives (eh. iii. 10; 1 Cor. xiii. 12; J~hn xvii. 3). True," we know in part," and are "rather ~nown by _God" t~an_ know him (Gal. iv. 9); and knowledge, therefore, must go hand-m-hand with _the faith that worketh l,y love." Otherwise it" puffeth up," and needs to be humbled beneath the supremacy c,r love (1 Cor. viii. 1-3; xiii; 1 John iv. 7, 8; John xiii. 17; xiv. 15-17; xvi. 13). But it is possible to exalt love in a one-sided, prejudicial way; and then the prayer of Phil i. ~ should be called to mind. (2) Knowledge in the form of a sound and manly wr.derstanding (1 Cor. xiv. 20), an instructed and well-ordered comprehension of the Eystem of Christian truth, is necessary for the Church, absolutely necessary for her teachers, and especially in times of mental conflict., such as that on which the Asiatic Churches were theo enterinl!, and such as that which is now reaching an acute stage in our mooern Christendom. In her contention with heresy and scepticism, the Church's strength depends on the amount of " spiritual wisdom and understanding" possessed by btr members. And the understanding is a spiritual faculty, that needs to bo illformed and guidr;d by the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of tr1Jth. (3) Yet Qhristi"n know• oh, I. 1-20.] 'rHE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSTANS. 21

ledge can never be merely abstract, terminating in the intellect; for it is "knowledge of God's will." All its doctrines bear on practice; its principles of truth are laws of life; its teachings, commands, It concentrates reason, feeling, will, in the unity of a spiritual life, where each predominates in turn, and every faculty sustains and quickens every other (comp. Eph. iv, 13-15; John vii. 17; xiv. 15-17). 2, Christian conduct. (Vera. 10-12.) (1) Advancing to a completer knowledge of God's will, the Christian man more and more "bears fruit in every good work." For he know~ that God's will is the well-being of men, and that he cannot please him better, or co-operate more effectually with his gracious purposes towards mankind, than by "doing good, as he has opportunity, to all men, and especially to those that a.re of the household of faith" (Gai. vi. 10; 1 'l'im. ii. 3, 4; Titus iii. 8; Heb. xiii. 16; 1 Pet. ii.12-15; Matt. v.14-16, 44-48; xxii. 36-40). (2) And in him" patience has its perfect work." "In all power he is strengthened, according to the might of God's glory ''-to what end? In order to do some great thing, one would suppose; but no, it is "unto all patience and long-suffering." Patience is the mark of strength. In suffering human nature is most receptive of the power of God. And on that lonely sick-bed, where some quiet sufferer lies, may oftentimes be witnessed a. display of "the might of his glory" which the grandest achievements of the Christian hero will scarcely equal (2 Cor. xii. 9, 10; Rom. v. 3; Heb. ii. 10; v. 7-9; xii. 1---3; Jas. i. 2-4; Rev. vii, 13-15). Perhaps imprisonment had helped to teach the ardent and restless spirit of the apostle this lesson. He endures "with joyfulness,'' not with a mere passive and dumb submission; for he suffers "by the will of God" (Acts ix. 16; v. 41; Heb. xii. 5-10; 1 Pet. iii. 17). "It was granted" him (Phil. i. 29, •xapl<T9?/, "made matter of grace and favour") "to suffer for Christ's sake;" and thus, at least, he can glorify him, if in no other way (1 Pet. ii. 19, 20). For whatever gifts or means for doing good may be wanting to us, we have at any rate the capacity of suffering. (3) And whether doing or bearing his Lord's will, the Christian's life will be a constant " thanksgiving to the Father." At the thought of the blessings of redemption (vers. 12-14), as he gains a deeper insight into all "the good and acceptable and perfect will of God," new songs of praise break forth ever and again from bis soul. He is a child and heir of God (Rom. viii. 14-17), joint-heir with Christ and with his saints (Eph. iii. 6; Titus iii. 7; Gal. iii. 29), in the realm of light where his soul already dwells, and whose light will shine for him "more and more unto the perfect day." He rejoices "in hope of the glory of God." How shall he not, therefore, give thanks! So God would have it (1 Thess. v. 16-18). (4) And so walking, he walks "worthy of the Lord unto a.ll pleasing" (Eph. v. 10; Rom, xii. 2). God's smile rests upon him from day to day. " The Lord taketh pleasure in his servants." Christ could say, " I do al ways the things that please him" (John viii, 29), and they who are "as he is in this world" can, in their measure and degree, humbly say the same. They abide in their Saviour's love (John xv. 9, 10). They have" confidence·towards God'' (1 John iii. 21, 22)-confidence even in the thought of the day of judgment (1 John iv. 17), Pleasing God now, they will be accepted then, 3. The nature of salvation, (Vers. 12-14, 21, 22.) For that inheritance for which the Christian praises God be was "made meet," and he is grateful for the means, as well as for the end, of bis salvation, He holds the title-deeds of his heritage in certain acts and transactions on the part of God which make him meet for it, and make it meet for the Divine Father to invest him with it. (1) His salvation is an act of rescue-a redemption by power. For men were captives, under a dark and cruel tyranny (Eph. ii. 2; vi. 12; 2 Cor. iv. 4; 2 Tim. ii. 26; Acts xxvi. 18; Heb. ii. H; John viii, 34; xii. 31; xiv, 30; xvi.11; Lnke iv. 6, 18), When we consider how inbred and inveterate is the power of evil over mankind, how allied with the disordered course of nature, and how its working in this world is a part of a vast, mysterious con- federacy of spiritual forces acting powerfully and insensibly upon and around us, we need not wonder that our salvation is represented as a mighty and glorious achievement of Divine power, one with that exhibited in Christ's victory over death (Epb. i. 19, 20; eh. ii. 12). Delivered, we are at the same time translated-carried over at once into the opposite camp as subjects and soldiers of Christ Jesus; whose kingdom is that where love rules, whose means nnd ends, counsels and agencies, are all the ministern of lovo. Light and love are one, as darkness and hate (1 John ii. 9-11; iv. 7-v. 5). (2) It is equally an net of ransom-redemption by price. God cannot deny hiwaelf. 22 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [oll, I, 1-29,

He is "ajnst God and" Saviour." His power works on tho linos Inid down by his right<-'onsness. He would have destroyed rather than saved us would hnve violated the human conscience, had he (conceivably) saved us without forgiveness; or without a forgiveness rationally grounded on some act of propitiation. that should make amends for the guilty past. 'l'his propitiation, ns it frees us from the power of Satan and of de~th, is our ransom._ The Son of ~D?-'s ~ove_, if he wo~ld redeem us, must pay tlis ,:,rice. w·hat. that price should be, D1vme Justice determines, while Divine love pro• ,ides it. He bought us with "his own blood" (Gal. iii. 13 ; Acts xx. 28; 1 Pet. i. 1S, 19); "gave his life a ransom" (Matt. xx. 28; Titus ii. 14). (3) And we may anticipat.e what follows in vers. 20, 21, by adding thl\t it is, finally, an act of reconciliation. God lays aside his holy resentment~gainst us as sinners, accepting the sacrifice of Christ which he himself bas provided, offered on earth and by our Representative, as a just and countervailing satisfaction "for the sins of the whole world" (Rom. iii. 25; John. i. 29; 1 John ii. 2); while men. thereupon, becoming aware of this (Luke ii. 14; Eph. ii. li), cease from their enmity a.nd strife against him (2 Cor. v. 19, 20). So" peace is made through the blood of the cross" (Eph. ii 16; Rom. v. 1, 10, 11). And meeting God in this peace-ma.king, men meet each other ; the broken unity of mankind is restored (Eph. ii. 13--16; eh. iii 11; John :x.i. 51, 52); and other worlcls, it may be, share with our own. in the "peace" established "on earth" (ver. 20).

entries.title: COL 1:15–23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
--8ect. 2. The redeeming &n and his kingdom. I. CHBIBT THE LORD OF m"IVEBSAL NATURE. (Vers. 15-17.) Colossiau error was undermining the Christian ,;:,stem by introducing into it a false, doalistic theory of nature; then widely prevalent in other quarters. And the leaders of Christian thought can never afford to be indifferent to the current philosophic views of their day. Indeed, in the contact of Christian teaching mth philosophy, and in the reflection of thoughtful men at all times, the question was sure to arise a.nd must constantly recur in new ·rorms, " What is the rela-- tion of Christ to the universe? At what point does he enter the scheme of things? He who died on. Calvary, who claims to save the souls of men, what has he to do with nature a.nd the common world?" If this question could not be answered, or if any inferior and limited position in the world of being must be assigned to him, then, as the Colossian heresy shows, his spiritual authority and the efficacy of his redemption become, in the same degree, limited and uncertain. Hence the teaching of the Epistles of this group (Colossians, Ephesians, Philippians) respecting the Person of Christ is the logical and theological sequel of that of the second (<r.llatians, Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians), respecting our salvation through him. We gather from the apostle's teaching here : L 1'hat in Olirut God becomes visible, and nature becomes intelligible. • To earnest philosophic thought, as to sound religious instinct, it has always been evident that "what is seen hath not been made out of things which do appear" (Heb. xi. 3). ~ "everlasting power and divinity are clearly seen from the creation of the w~rl_d" -but as " invisible things" (Rom. i. 20). Our latest Agnosticism is but a despamng echo of the cry of Job: "I go towards the east, but he is not there; and westward, but I cannot perceive him ; towa.rd the north, where he is workin~, b~t I c~!:'not see him ; where he veileth himself in the south, but I cannot find him (xxm. 8, 9). God effectually hides himself behind his works. All visfole point to invisible causes, all finite things lead up to the In.finite, all phenomena to the no~nal; but whith~r t~ey point we cannot follow. Some of the most profound and mmute of modem sc1ent1fic inquirers testify most strongly to this (e.q. M. Dumas and M. Pasteur, in their addresses at the French Academy, 1880, 1882). From that invisible, Christ comes forth to testify of him whom" no man hath seen nor can see" (John i. 14, 18; xiv. 9). We know now what the Maker of the universe is like. The world is no longer orphaned. The unknown God proves to be its Father, and his Son its elder Brother. Human thought has a visible centre around which to move, a sun which sheds light and warmth over e.ll its speculations. The incarnation and resurrection of Christ, with the whole course of his miracles (his signs), assure us that natural law is, and must prove itself ultimately to be, subservient to spiritual Jaw, the lower to the higher order, the material world to the moral being of man. His miracles and parables and his general teaching furnish many fruitful hints, some that lie on the surface, others that await our deeper searching or future need, respecting the meaning and use of the natural world. He is, after all, OH, I, 1-20,] 'l'IIE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 23

ile chief Interpreter, the Mnster of poets and philosophers of n:iture who often o·.vo most to him when they nre least aware of it, ns well as of religious thinkers and sncial reformers. While we hold fast this faith in the "Image of God the invisible," the "Firstborn of all creation," we may witness science and philosophy pursuing their inquil'ics without misgiving, and we rn11,y follow them, warily indeed, but without mistrust; for they can discover no truth which will not in the end support the '' trnth as it is in Jesus," and they labour, though they know it not, only to add their own to the "many crowns" that are pt'eparing for the head of our Immanuel. 2. All the relations which nat'll/l'e holds to God centre in Christ. (1) If the world rests on God, is grounded in him, refers secretly and everywhere to God as the immanent, perpetual Cause of its being and its energy; if in him "we live and move and are; "-then we 11.re to understand all this of Christ. "In him were created, in him consist aH things" (vers. 16, 17). "God was in Christ" creating the heavens and the earth; is "in Christ" sustaining, co-ordinating, directing the march of the circling worlds, the evolution of their teeming, endlessly varied forms of life. The " winds and the sea." that "obeyed him," disease and death and the mighty spirits of darkness that fled at his word, knew something of this secret, if men do not. (2) If through God the universe came to bu (Rom. xi. 36); if he supplied the agencies of creation, the matter and the force (nnlesa matter is really force) out of which it was generated, the laws which shaped its form and governed its development ;-then it appears that all this was done through Christ. (3) If the world moves towards God (Rom. xi. 36), in spite of all divergence and confusion; and if throughout the unmeasured cycles of its duration past and to come it advances towards the fulfilment of its destiny, "that God may be all in all" (1 Cor. xv. 28) ;-then its course is directed also unto Christ. The will of God respecting the kingdom of his Son was the secret of creation (Eph. iii. 9, 10). Man's sin did not give birth to that purpose. It called for its vindication in new forms of snpera.bound.ing grace; but from the beginning it was "the Father's will that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father" (John v. 23). He is "the Heir of all things" (Heb. i. 2), and it is "the glory of God the Father" "that every knee should bow,of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Phil. ii. 9-11). So far, therefore, as we can trace any Divine workin11: in the course of nature or history, we may refer it to Christ as truly as the forgiveness of sins or the resurrection of the dead. Nature and grace, body and spirit, history and revelation, the secular and sacred, are essentially one, are parts of the same scheme, each being the complement of the other (instance the inseparable connection of Christ's miracles of healing with his spiritual work), and are working under the same management (Matt. xxviii. 18), towards the same issue, that "purpose of the ages which God purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord, to sum up all things in Christ" (Eph. i. 10; iii. 9-11). II. CHRIST THE HEAD OF THE CHURCH. (Vers. 18-23.) 1. Into the world created to be " the kingdom of the Son of God'8 love," "sin entered, and death through sin; " and death became Icing, svn in death (Rom. v. 12, 13, 21), instead of "the Prince of life." Hatred was planted in the human breast, and with it came a darkness that "apprehended not the light of life" (vers. 13, 21; John i. 4, 5; 1 John iii. 8, 11, 12); and men fell under "the dominion of Satan" (Acts xxvi. 18; Eph. ii. 2, 3; Luke iv. 6; 1 John v. 19), the "murderer," the "father of lies;" till it cam,:, to pass that, though Christ ever "was in the world, the world knew him not" (John i. 10). Men were everywhere "cut off from Christ," "alienated," "children of wrath" (ver. 21; Eph. ii. 3, 12); how rebellious against him, his advent proved. Then, in their "wicked works," they not only denied the Son his pre-eminence, but even said, "Come, let us kill him" (Matt. xxi. 38; Luke xix. 14; Ps. ii.). 2. And he submits to die, that he may "put away sin by the sacrifice of himself." The Firstborn of all creation becomes Firstborn out of the dead. So high he was in his Divine, eternal birth, so low he stooped-to the Virgin's womb, to" a servant's form," and "unto death, yea, the death of the cross" (vers. 18, 20; Phil. ii. 7, 8; Rom. i. 3; ix. 5; 2 Cor. viii. 9; Gal. iv. 4; Heb. ii. 6-18), to restore his human brethren, to recover bis alii:nated kin"dom, "to reconcile all things unto himself" (vers. 18, 20; Rom. xiv. 9; Phil. ii. 10, 11; Rev. i. 5, 6, Revised 'l'ext). 3. So dying, he lives again that he may ~i,·e us life (Hom. vi. 4-11); descending, in turn he ascends and lifts us with him (Eph. 24 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [OD, L 1-29.

iv. 8-10; ii._ 5, ~; John xii. _32); em_ptying himself, he gains a new sovereign /ulness (,er. 19; Phil. 11. 8; Eph. 1v. 10; 1. 20-23) of all that the dark exiled broken miserable w_orld needs to ~tore it and build it up again (eh. ii. 9, io; Phii. iv. 19)'. 4. Round himself as the hvmg Oentre., he gathers a new ht1imanity and forms a new world, which u hu body, the Church (vers. 18, 24; eh. ii. 19; Eph. iv. 16; v. 23; John n. 1--S)-a body wider, and yet narrower, than the visible (Matt. xiii. 24-30 · John x. 16); "a spiritual house,'' built of those united as "living stones" to the ,: livincr Stone" (1 Pet.. ii. 4, 5), which "groweth unto a holy temple in the Lord" (Epb. ii. 21). So he is the Beginni11g (ver. 18) of an agelong, world-wide process of resurrection antl reconstruction. The life that is in him is an organic, formative, spiritual energy with a "mighty working" in it that is "able t.o subdue all things unto itself" (Phil. iii. ~1; Rom. ,iii. 2-11); a leaven destined to leaven the whole lump (Matt. xiii. 31-33). "The kingdom of this world" must "become the kingdom of our Lord and his Christ" (Re,. xi. 15; 1 Cor. xv. 25; Dan. ii. 34, 35; vii. 13, 14); "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus" must penetrate, transform, and dominate every sphere of human thought and activity; "the works of the devil" everywhere, and in every form and shape, must be "destroyed" (1 John iii. 8). Then only will he have "recon- ciled all things on the earth to himself." 5. For ourselves, as individuals, the design of Christ's reconciliation is the perfection of our personal character as approved by him- self at the day of f1ulgm.ent (vers. 22, 28). This is true also of the Church collectively (Eph. v. 2i). He is Judge as well as Saviour; and his justice is as inflexibie as his mercy is compassionate. "The King," for as King he will then appear, desires to be able to say to each of us, "Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom pre- pared for you;" "sit with me in my throne" (Matt. xxv. 34; Rev. iii. 21); but he will only say it to those who are worthy (Rev. iii. 4, 5). To this end he redeemed ns by his blood, bestowed on us his Spirit, brought us into his kingdom, subjects us to its discipline, employs us in its service, instructs us in its wisdom, enriches us with all its spiritual blessings-" to present us (on that day) holy and without biemish and unrepro,able before him" (Jude 24, 25; 1 Thess. iii.12, 13; v. 23, 24). 6. How far the influence of this recunciliation extends beyond the things upon the earth; and, if it does so extend, in what direction; whether or how it touches "the principalities and powers in heavenly places,"-we caunot tell, and dare not attempt t-0 guess. Origen, on the warrant of this passage (ver. 20), fondly thought that even Satan himself would be ultimately reconciled to God. At any rate, when he "through whom and unto whom all things have been created" is the sacrifice, and when the evil of this world is but a part of the realm of evil above and around us, we may not deny the possibility of others sharing with us, somehow, in the atoning virtue of his death. 7. But all this is so far stat.ed from the Divine side, as matter of Gocfs general purpose and plan in Christ (Eph. L 10; 1 'l'im. ii. 4; 2 Tim. i. 9; Acts iii. 21) ; and this plan will certainly be carried out; "all things," as a whole, will certainly be reconciled. But there is nothing here to contradict the possibility of a self-exclusion of individuals, belonging to this world or to other worlds, from the benedts of tbe Divine amnesty, and of their expulsion from a reconciled universe (2 These. L 9; Matt. xxv. 41; Luke xiii. 25; John xv. 6; Rev. x:riL 15). Ver. 23 intimates as much as this. "All this is yours," the Apostle virtually says, "if ye continue in the faith, not being moved away from the hope of the gospel;" but if not, what then? Contrast 2 Cor. v. 19 and 20; John x. 10 and v. 40. Still the distressing q nestion, "Lord, are there few that be saved?" presses on us, and our Lord's reply 6Jl8&ks in the same tones of stern and solemn warning (Luke xiii. 23---30). For us to whom the message of reconciliation is now addressed, it is clear that "now is the day of salvation " (2 Cor. vL 2). To be a minister of this reconciliation, and so a minister of the Church, a builder of the house of_ God, the Body of Christ, how high and respon~iblc the office (ve•e. 23-26; 1 Cor. iv. 1, 2; 2 Cor. v. 11-vi.10)! Yers. 24-29.-Sect. 3. Tl.e aposfle and hu mission. I. PAUL A MINISTER OF CHRTBT. (Yers. 24, 25, 28, 29.) In this passage the apostle draws a picture of himself which, taken wiLb the delineations furnished by him elsewhere, stands before the Church fol' all time as the ideal portrait of the" faithful minister" and the "good soldier of Chri8t Jesw,." The account he gives of himself here concerns ltis calling, liis aim, his work, OH, I, 1-29,] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 25

and his experience, 1. The apostle styles himself (1) mini.,ter of the gospel (ver. 23 b), of the glad tidings of salvation for all men, from all sin, in Jesus Christ (Matt. i. 21; Luke i. 68-79; Acts v. 31; xiii. 38, 39, 47; 1 Tim. ii, 3-7; Titus ii. 11-14), "the gospel of the grace of God" (Acts xx. 24). It is this that be hll.ll to serve-to publish, explain, apply it, to carry it everywhere and to aJI its practical issues. And in thus serving the gospel, he knows that he is best serving the interests of mankind (Titna iii. 3-8; 2 Cor. iv, 6; Eph. v. 9; Phil. iv. 8, 9). There is no charge so serious and responsible, requiring so high a character (1 Thess. ii. 4) or eo much boldness and power of utterance in its minister (Eph. vi. 19, 20). (2) He is also minister of the Ohurch (ver, 25), pastor and teacher as well as evangelist (Epb. iv. 11). And minister means "servant." The Church doP.H not exist for his sa.ke, but he for the Church's sa.ke: "We preach ourselves your servants [slaves] for Jesus' sake" (2 Cor. iv. 5; comp. ver. 24; 1 'l'hess. ii. 6-8 ; 1 Pet. v, 2, 3; John x. 9-15; Ezek. xxxiv.). He has authority, which he does not hesitate to use when need arises (1 Cor. iv. 19-v. 5; 2 Cor. x. 2-6); but it is that "which the Lord gave for edification" (2 Cor. x. 8; xiii. 10). To the Church he can say, "1 seek not yours, but you;" "whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, all are yours;" "I wiJI most gladly spend and be spent for yonr souls" (2 Cor. xii. 14, 15; 1 Cor, iii. 22 ; Phil. ii. 17 ; 1 Thess. ii. 8). And well may he do this, for he serves the Church for which the Lord Jesus" gave himself," which he" loves," which he" nourishes and cherishes as his own body" (ver. 24; Eph. v, 25, 29). He foJlows in the steps of "the good Shepherd," who" giveth his life for the sheep" (John x.11). (3) His ministry is a Divine trust, a stewardship of God (ver. 25; Eph. iii. 2, 9; 1 Cor. iv. 1; ix. 17). He was "separated from his mother's womb " (Gal. i. 15), was " sent" ( Acts xxii. 21), "was put to ministry" (1 Tim. i. 12), "appointed herald and apostle and teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth" (1 Tim. ii. 7). And in accordance with bis inward caJI, he was "separated" for his particular work by "the Holy Ghost," acting through the officers of the Church at Antioch (Acts xiii. 1-3). He is, therefore, a "minister of Christ," a "minister of God," and " steward of the mysteries of God" (~ Cor. ii. 23 ; vi, 4; 1 Cor. iv. 1). Hence the dignity and authority of his office (Gal. i. 1, 11, 12), and the power with which it invests him (ver, 29; 2 Cor. x. 4, 8; xii. 12; xiii. 3-6), and his responsibility for the final account (1 Cor. iv. 1-5; 2 Cor. v. 11 ; Phil. ii. 16; 1 Thess. ii. 19, 20; Heb, xiii.17). His business is to "serve the Church," but" to please God" (Gal. i. 10). 2. The aim of his ministry is twofold. (1) To fulfil the word of God (ver. 25}--to give it the widest possible extension (vers. 6, 23, Rom. xv. 17-21 ; 2 Thess. iii. 1), to carry it through every" open door" (eh.iv. 3; Epb. iii. 9; 1 Cor. xvi. 9; 2 Cor, ii. 12-14), and "manifest the savour of the knowledge of Christ in every place," and to co.rry it on to its full issue in the salvation and sanctification of all who hear it (ver, 28; Acts x.x. 27; 1 TheSil. ii. 11, 12 ; 2 Thess. ii.13-15). And so his aim is (2) to present every man perfect in Ghrist. (Ver. 28.) This is his endeavour and hope regarding every man to whom his ministry is addressed, unto which he toils hard and strives (ver. 29), His supreme reward "in the day of Christ," his "joy and crown of glorying" (1 Tbess. ii. 16 ; Phil. ii. 16), will be found in the saved souls, the perfected and ripened Christian characters, whom he will be able then to present as the fruit of" the grace of God that was with him" (1 Cor. xv. 10; Eph. iii. 2, 8; Rom. i. 13). 3, His work is (1) the preaching of Ohrist (ver. 29)-" Christ cruci- fied" (1 Cor. i. 23; ii. 2) and "risen again" (1 Cor. xv. 3, 4; Acts xvii. 18), "made unto us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor. i. 30); "Christ the Image of God" (ver. 15; 2 Cor. iv. 4), the" Firstborn of all creation" (ver, 15), "Head of the Church" (ver. 18), "Lord of both the dead and the living" (Rom. xiv. 0), "all and in all" (eh. iii.11). (2) The admonishing and teaching ef every man. (Ver. 28.) For "all have sinned" and need Christ (Rom. iii. 23-26), and. all have a claim on his salvation (1 Tim. iv. 10; ii. 3, 4; Rom. iii. 20, 30; i. lG; Heh. ii, 9; John iii, 16, etc.). He "admonishes every man," therefore, often "with tears (Acts xx. 31), of the nature and the penalties of sin, of the day of judgment and "the fear of the Lord" (2 Cor. v. 11), of the danger of falling from grace, of the special faults or errors he may discern in him (Gal. iii. 1-4, etc.; 1 Cor. i. 11, etc.). He teaches in all wisdom, supplying instruction apt for the simplest understanding :,nd for the weakest "babe in Christ," and also speaking "wisdom among the perfect" (1 Cor. ii. 6-iii. 2), seeking to meet every stage and state of the Christian lifo, and studying 26 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [on. 1. 1-29.

the r:~nl l~ncss 11nd ratience (2 Tim. ii. 24-20; 1 Thess. ii. 7), the sympathy Rnd 11da.p• th·eoess which the tl_l,11~,her's ~ork requires_(! Cor. ix. 20-22), "teaching publicly and from house to house,· . ke_epmg bnck 7:othmg that ~as _profitable," but everything thRt ""'~~ unprofitable ~l Tim n·. 6-8; vt. 3-5; ~ Tim. ii. 14-23; Titus iii. 8, 9), and rlymg every possible means to promote and to increase in all men" repentance toward God a1;1d faith ~~rd onr Lord ~esus Christ" (Acts u. ~8-21, 27). 4. In this work: (1) Hu; labour t-S intense and painful- (Ver. 29.) Work 1s in his eyes the one thing for ~hi~h the ,?hristian ministry is to be ~alued _and ?Ommended (1 Thess. v. 12, 13). Be is himself m labours more abund!l,llt, and m this respect chiefly is" more a minister of Christ" than some others (2 Cor. xi. 23; comp. 1 Cor. xv. 10). No kind of toil come5 amiss to him, for Christ's sake. Claiming his "right in the gospel" to "live of the gospel as the Lord ordained," yet on grounds of expediency he cheerfully foregoes it, and "brings himself into bondage to all,"" for the gospel's sake" (1 Oor. ix. 1-23). "These hands," as he holds them up hard and black with working at the coarse sailcloth, show how" in all things he gave us an example" of self-denying toil (Acts xx~ 34, 35). (2) .And vww his sufferings surpass even hi,s labours, yet they fill him with constant joy. (Ver. 24.) He is a prisoner, and his flesh rebels against" these bonds" (Acts x:xvi. 29). He cannot preach abroad, or visit the Churches (eh. iv. 3; Eph. vi.19, 20; Phil. i. 25, 26), whose "care" still "presses on him daily" (2 Cor. xi. 28). Many desert him ( eh. iv. 11), and some even who "preach Christ" do it to injure and not to help him (Phil i. 16). Yet even in this he can rejoice (Phil. i. 17, 18). He has learnt the secret of contentment (Phil. iv. 11). He is conscious of being "set for the defence of the gospel " (Phil i. 16). His sufferings are evidently tending to its furtherance (Phil. i 12-20). The cause of the Gentile Church is being effectually served by the sacrifice he has made (Eph. iii. 1, 13; Phil. ii. 17, 18). Above all, he feels that he is treading in the steps of Christ, su1fering in the same interest, carrying on the same cause; and he takes it as a gi~ of grace (Phil i 29) that he has thus assigned to him his special sh:i.re in that which Christ has been pleased to leave for his servants to su1fer after him. How shall he not rejoice to be "as his Master"! In the two words H01t1ii lryo,v,(oµe,as (v.er. 29), whose full force is untranslatable, the apostle paints himself to the life, as the spiritual athlete, the great Christian champion, never flagging in his effort.s nor shrin.ki.ng from the heavy blows that fall upon him, till the prize of victory is won· (comp. 1 Cor. iL 24-27 ; 2 Cor. ii. 14-17 ; iv. 7-18 ; xi. 23-33 ; Acts xx. 24; 2 Tim. iv. 7, 8). Bnt while we look at him with admiration, he cries out," It is not I, but Christ living in me; and in my poor efforts his mighty energy displays itself" (ver. 29; 1 Cor. xv. 10; 2 Cor. xii. 8, 9; Gal. ii. 20). II. CHRIST THE MYSTERY OF Gon. (Vers. 26, 27.) This is the glorious theme of St. Paul's ministry. 1. It is the burden of the old revelation, the secret of ancient .history. The great heroes of the Old Testament-patriarchs, lawgivers, prophets, kings -were fragmentary types of him, in their character, achievements, or sufferings (Heb. v. 10; Acui vii. 37, etc.). The highest aspirations and anticipations of "holy men of old, moved by the Holy Ghost," were directed mysteriously all along to him, to his birth, teaching, sufferings, resurrection, to "the glory that should fi;,llow," to "the preach in er of repentance and remission of sins to all nations in his name" (Luke xxiv. 2G, 27, 44---47). The Jewish system of worship and discipline, in its c~nstruction aod design, prefigured and prepared for his advent, who was hunself meanwhile secretly acting in it and speaking through it to his people (John i. 10, 11; 1 Cor. x. 4, 9; Heb. ii. 10--12; xi. 26). The whole history of Israel and the development of the Old Testament system unerrincrly O pointed to this goal, where it met the blindly groping, halfarticulate desire of all iaations. In Christ the lines of promise and of preparation, converging from the most, distant ages and widely separated peoples, meet 11nd are focussed, in this "fulness of the times." 2. But the goal 1vas hidden from the ages ar,d from the generations, who stood with straining sight seekiag to pierce the darkness of the future (1 Pet. i 10-12; '.Matt. xiii. 17). Seeing but a part of the promise, "afar off," and" at sundry times and in divers manners," they could not forecast it& issue, nor pitcc tocrether its scattered intimations. '!'he Gentiles knew that they needed a lJivine Saviour, and their need had become consciously extreme and desperate (1 Cor. i. l!:l-:!l; Epb. ii. 12; 1 These. iv. 13; Acts xvii. 23, 27). 'l'he Jews knew t)1at ho ...,,,uld come, but little suspected in what guise. 'l'hey knew not how great arid in wal'tl Oil, I, 1-29.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 27

WIIB thoir own need of him. Least of all did they expect or wish that he should be for "a light of the Gentiles, and for salvation unto the enrls of the earth" (Acts xiii. 4i). l'hose who know most of hie coming were least prepared to believe this. It is, alas! still a mystery to ·them (Eph. iii. 4-6; Rom. xi.; 2 Cor. iii. 12-16). 3. 1'his mystery brings to Gor£s saints, not only a Ohrist revealed to them, the open ser,ret of the Old Testament, but a Ohrist manifested in them (ver. 27; Gal. i. 16), Gentiles and Jew., alike (Acts xi. 17), which is a deeper secret stal. How" rich" is the Divine " glory" displayed in this ( With what "might" do our weak hearts need to be " strengthener] that Christ may dwell through faith" therein, that so we may be "filled with all this fulness of God" (Eph. iii. 16-19) I 4 . .And therefore this mystery of God is not finished yet. (Rev. x. 7; xxi. 1-8.) "Christ in you is the hope of glory" (ver. 27). Every saint of God is a new mystery to the world, and oven to himself (eh. iii. 3; 1 John iii. 1, 2). "'l'he manifestation of the sons of God" (Rom. viii. 19) has still to come, when their hidden life will be made visible. The soul united to Christ and like to him will be mated with "a spilitual body" (1 Cor. xv. 44), a "body of glory" (Phil.iii. 21). Then at last the inward and the outward, character and condition, will harmonize and be fitly matched, and" we shall be manifested with him in glory" (eh. iii. 3, 4). This is the Christian hope, of which "Christ in you" is the abiding pledge (eh. iii. 15, not-e; Eph. i. 13, 14; Rom. viii. 11).

-The apostle's thanksgiving for the spiritual progress of the Oolos,ia,ns. Notwithstanding the dangerous speculations of a Judreo-Gnostic philosophy which had sprung up at Colossre, threatening the integrity of their faith, the apostle is yet able to express his thankfulness for the faith and love which animated the Christian brotherhood in the valley of Lycus. He is thankful for their continned allegiance to the Lord Jesus Christ, who was the one satisfaction of all their yearnings, the one solution both of their speculative questionings and of their religious wants. J. THANKSGIVING I8 A CONSTANT EXERCISE OF THE CHRISTIAN HEART, AS IT IS ALSO A TRUE PART.OF PRAYER. "We give thanks to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you." 1. It ought to mingle with e:uery prayer. We never pray but we have cause ior thankfulness, and we never give thanks but we have cause to pray. And whatever may, be the subject of our rejoicing ought to be matter for thanksgiving. Prayer with thanksgiving was the apostle's constant recommendation (Phil. iv. 6). 2. It is to be addressed to God the Father in Ohrist. (1) Because we are commanded to "enter his gates with thanksgiving," "to be thankful to him and to bless his Name" (Ps. c. 4). (2) Because it is only from him that we have all good (Ja.s. i. 17). (3) Because it is only by him we are preserved from all sin (Ps. cxxi. 7). (4) Because he only is good in himself (Luke xviii. 19). 3. Reasons for thanksgiving. (1) It is the only requital God expects or we can make for bis mercies (Ps. 1. 10, 14; lxix. 30, 31). (2) We cannot expect a blessing nnless we are thankful for it. (3) The more thankful we are for mercies received, the more ground we have for expecting more of them. 4. We ought to be thank/ul as well as prayerful for others as well as ourselves. (Eph. vi. 18; 1 Tim. ii~l.) What a treasury of prayers belongs to the saints! II. THE SUBJECTS OF TIIE APOSTLE'S THANKSGIVING-THE FAITH AND LOVE OF THE CoLOSSIANB. "Having beard of your faith in Christ Jesus o.ndof the love which ye have toward all the saints." It is interesting to remark that the apostle, in the two Epistles written at the same time as this to Colossre, expresses thankfulness for similar blessings (Eph. i. 15; Philem. 5). 1. Their faith in Ghrist Jesus. (1) It was not merely faith resting npon him and finding its nurture and support in him. (2) But it centred in him as the sphere in which it had its due exercise. In this sense, Christ "dwells in the heart by faith" (Eph. iii. 17), and believers "rejoice in him" (Phil. iii. 3, 7). Such a faith is n. mercifui preservative against doctrinal errors. 2. Their love to all the saint.s. (1) The nature of this love. It includes: (a)" Doing good to all, especially to those of the household of faith" (Gal. vi. 10), and" distributing to the necessity of saints" (Rom. xii. 13). (b) Loving fellowship (Acts ii. 42). "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb. x. 25). ( c) Dearing with their infirmities. "Love coveroth 28 'l'B:E EPISTLE TO TB:E COLOSSIANS. [cu. I. l ..._29.

the multitude of sins" (1 Pet. iv. 8). We are not to grieve our brother with our meat else "we walk not charitably" (Rom. xiv. 16). (d) Cherishing R forgiving spirit (Eph'. iv. 31). (2) The manner of this love. (a) it is to be brotherly. We are" to love the brotherhood" (1 Pet. ii. 22). (b) It is to be sincere. "Without dissimulation" (Rom. xii. 9); "Not in word and in tongne, but in deed and in truth" (1 John iii. 18). (c) It is t.o be from" a pure heart" (1 Tim. i. 5). (d) It is to :t,e fervent. "Have fervent charity among yonrselves" (1 Pet. iv. 8). (e) It is to be full of labours (1 Thess. i. 3). (f) It is abc.e all to be catholic. " All the sa.ints," without distinction. (3) The reasons for this love. (a) Christ's example and command (John :xiii. 34). (b) It is a sism of l!TSCe. It is a t.oken that "we are translated from death to life" (1 John iii~ 14). David's delight was "in the sainb!" (Ps. xvi. 3), (c) It is the "fulfilling of the I.Aw" (Rom. xiii. 10). (d) There is comfort in it (Phil. ii. 1). (e) It commends the gospel to the world. We ought, therefore, to be " sound in love" (Titus ii. 2), and II to provoke one another to love and good works" (Heb. x. 24). 3. The relation between faith and urr,e. They are necessarily joined together; for: (1) Faith" worketh· by love" (Gal. v. 6) and ought never to work without it. (2) The grace of God abounds in "faith and love ,,hich is in Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. i. 14). Faith and love are the two members of the Christian religion. -4. The graces of the saints are easily known and heard of. The apostle heard of the faith and love of the Colossians. "Since the_day we heard of them." They ought, therefore, to be bright in their heavenly lustre. III. THE MOTIVE OB llllPULSIVE CAUSE OF THESE GRACES. " Because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens." 1. The nature of this hope. (1) The sense of the word oscilla.tes, it has been observed, between the subjective feeling and the objective realization; yet the thing hoped for is rather more prominent in the passage. It centres in the inheritance, in "the recompense of the reward," in "the good founda.tion against the time to come," in "the eternal life that God, who cannot lie, promised before the world began." (2) It is Divine in its origin, unlike the false hopes of men. We are"' begotten to a living hope" (1 Pet. i. 3). (3) Its true fulcrum, or point of support, is in the merits of Christ (1 Ti1n. L 2; Heh. vi. 19, 20). 2. The security ef this hope. "Which is laid up for you in the heavens." It is secure liecause: (I) It is la.id up in the country where onr Father dwells. And who can destroy it in such keeping? (:.!) It hi linked to "the two immutable things "-the oath and the promise of God, which are fastened within the veil by our Forerunner, even Jesus (Heh. vi. 19). (3) It is where the devil cannot come. (4) It is in heaven, not on earth, and therefore free from all the corruptions that the moth and rust of the world may inflict. 3. The quickening power of this hope. It has great influence upon our faith and love. God makes one grace cause another. " It is hope that plucks up the heart of man to a constant desire of union with God by faith, and of communion with man by lo.-e." Moses had respect to the recompense of the reward (Heh. xi. 25, 26). The saints will find that it is not in vain to serve the Almighty. They ought, therefore, to remember (1) that their hope is not in this world; (2) ~hat they should walk as "pil~ims and strangers," using the world as if they used 1t not; (3) that they should despise the scorn and hate of a world which "will always love his ?wn." 4. Buw i.s this hope to be increased, Though it cannot be made more secure, 1t may be more fully realized. To this end, we need (1) true grace, for we can only have" a good hope through grace" (2 Thess. ii. 16); (2) experience (Rom. v. 4); (3) patience and comfort of the Scriptures (Hom.xv. 4); (4) joy and peace in believing (Rom. xv. 13). IV. THE SO{;BCE OF OUR DIVINE BOPE. "Whereof ye heard before in the Word of the truth of the gospel, which is come unto yotL" 1. It is by the hearing of the Word we l.earn of (IU,r hope. ~'here is no other way of learning it. 'l'he Lord bas sent us the news of 63.lvation. Nature tells us nothing of a Divine hope. The importance of this hearinu is manifest because: (1) It is the source of faith. "Faith cometh by hearing, and h~ring by the' Word of God" (Rom. x. 14); "Hear, and your soul shall live" (Isa. Iv. 4). (2) It opens men's hearts (Acts xvi. 14). (3) It causes the stony h£:art to n,elt, and the proud heart to tremble (Isa. !xvi. 2). (4) 'l'he afflicted conscience is curtd by it (Ps. Ii. 8). Let us, therefore, thank God for it, love hie gospel, receive his coruma.nds, and submit to his guidance. 2. The preciousness of the Word. It is" tLE: Word of the truth of tbe gospel" As if to signify the contrast between the simI>le truth taught them by Epaphras and the errors of the false teachers. Ita OH, I, 1-29.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 29

preciousness lies in its truth. (1) It reveals to us the true mind or the Lord as to the way of salvation. "It is a true saying, and worthy of all acceptation" (I Tim. i. 12). (2) It exhibits to us Jesus Christ as the Truth, as" him that is true," as "the faithful and true Witness." (3) It reveals to us the gospel; for "it is the Word of the truth or the gospel." This gospel is (a) the power of God to salvation (Rom, i. 16). (b) It brings life and immortality to light (2 Tim. i. 10). (c) It brings abundance of blessings (Rom. xv. 14). (d) It is a witness to all nations (Matt. xxiv. 14). (4) It works truth in us by working knowledge in us and enabling us to do the truth (John iii. 22 ; Jas, iii. 17). Therefore believers ought to pray Gorl to give them the Spirit of truth, that "tht·y may come to the knowledge of the truth" (2 Tim. ii. 25), and never think of resting in the mere form of truth (Rom. ii. 20; John iii. 22). 3. The accessibility of the Word. It is" come unto you." It came without their seeking it or sending for it, 'l'he Colossians sat in darknes1,1 and the shadow of death, estranged "from the life of God through ignorance," till God caused the light to shine into their hearts. We ought, therefore, (1) to acknowledge the free grace of God in sending us such good tidings; (2) to rejoice in the gospel and walk by the light of it. V. THE FRUIT-BEARING POWER AND EXPANSIVENESS OF THE GOSPEL. "Even as it is also in all the world, bearing fruit and increasing." These words set forth at once the efficacy and the rapid growth of the gospel, its inner working and its outward expansion. 1. Its fruit-bearing power. (1) This was according to promise (Isa. lv. 10, 23). (2) It was its design-" to gather fruit which might abide to everlasting life" (John xv. 16). (3) It was to produce fruit "in all the world "-in all climates, among all races, in all ages of the world, as if to mark its universal adaptability to the wants of men. In this respect it differed from the false gospels, which were esoteric or limited in their application. It is the grand verification of the gospel that it continues to bear fruit age alter age (Ezek. x.lviii. 12). 2. Its expansiveness. lt-s rapid progress in the days of the apostles is one of the wonders of history; for "the Word of God grew and multiplied" in the face of the opposition of magistrates, the persecution of Jewish zealots, the perversions of false teachers, and the inconsistencies of Christian professors themselves. Though the Word was not yet announced to all nations, the whole world was the area of its increasing power. VI. THE EFFECTS OF THE GOSPEL, PARTICULARLY AT CoLOSS..£. "As it doth in you also, since the day ye heard and knew the grace of God in truth." 1. The hearing is necessary to the knowledge of the grace of God, yet there is a heal'ing that is resultless of all good. To hear with profit, we must (1) become fools that we may be wise (l Cor. iii. 18); (2) come with a purpose to be reformed by it (Ps. xxv. 14); (3) listen with a meek and humble spirit (Jas. i. 22); (4) hear with faith and assurance (Heb. iv. 1; 1 Thess. i. 5). 2. The true knowledge of the grace of God is fruitful in all the growths of righteousness. (1) 'l'he gospel as taught at Colossa, was an offer of free grace, as opposed to the false gospels, which were codes of rigorous prescription. We must, therefore, be careful (a) not to receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor. vi. 1); (b) to appreciate" the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, though he was rich, yet for your sakes became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor. viii. 9); (c) to avoid those who would" make void the grace of God" (Gal. ii. 21); (d) to find our constant standing in this grace (1 Pet. v, 2). (2) The gospel at Colossre had produced much spiritual fruit to the praise of God's glory, Epaphras makes special mention of their "love in the Spirit." It refers to all the love which is wrought in the heart by the Spirit. (a) This love is a chief gift of the Spirit (Gal. v. 22; Rom. xv. 30). (b) It is of necessity sincere (Rom, xii. 13), the outcome of a pure heart (1 Tim. i. 5), am! practical in its scope (1 John iii. 18). (c) It is inconsistent with the idea of working evil to a neighbour (Rom. xiii. 10) or of offending a brother in a thing indifferent (Rom. xiv. 15). 3. The early and continuous experience of this grace is a good sign of spiritual growth. "Since the day ye heard aud knew the grace of God in truth." This langua.ga implies that the work of God wrought speedily upon the Colossians, and that it continued to work. Their goodness was not as the morning dew. VII. THE FOUNDER OF CoLossrAN CHRISTUNITY-EPAPHRAS, ".As ye learned from Epaphrns, our beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf, who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit." 1. His character and position as a ,ninister, (1) '!'he apostle gives him the right hand of fellowship, and mentions him 30 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOBSIANS,,

with lo-.-ing reg1ml, that he may skC'n!Ithen his influence among the people of Colossm. He w0uld _thus be better b_eloved and more useful. (2) 'l'he commendation presents' Epaphrns m a twofold relation. (a) To the apostle himself (a.) as" our beloved fello\V- ser-.-ant.,'' working in the servioe of t.he sa.me Master and in loving relationship to all hiF ser-.-ants; (,6) as t.he representath·e particularly of the apostle himself being "a minister of Christ_ on our beh~ll~" preaching at Colo..~ instead ~r the apostle, ~ud, there- fore, not to he displaced by the new school of J ud8l0-Gnostio sectaries• (-y) perhaps nl5?, as "a ~ellow-prisoner," for Epaphrai:i appears in this light in the 'contemporary Epistle (Pb1lem. 23). (b) To the Coloss10.n Church. " Who is a faithful minister of Christ." (u) He was called a minister of the Colossians; for Christ is our true Master nnd _Epaphras is hi~ ~inister._ It is by h!s authority ministers act in the people'; sernce. (M His fa1th!ulness 1s to be specially noted. He was faithful to Christ to the truth, to the souls of men. It is "faithful men" who will be" able to teach others also" (2 Tim. ii. 2). It is necessary for "a steward of the mysteries" to be" found" faithful. 2. His continued interest in their welfare, (1) Epaphras tells the apostle rnmething that would tend to bind the flock at Colossre more closely together. "He declared unto us your love in the Spirit." A faithful minister is always glad to give a _good report of his people, and especially of what good things God has wrought by !nm. Ee has, no doubt, to make report of corruptions in opinion and worship at Colossre, but he is careful to make first mention of their spiritual graces. (2) He labours for them in prayer (eh. iv.12), that" they may stand fast, perfect and complete in the whole will of God."-T. C.

entries.title: COL 1:9
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
ll.-The apostle's prayer for the enlargemen,t and completion of their spiritual bfe. I. Tim URGE:!."'T SPIBIT OF THIS PB.AYER. " For this cause we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray and make request for you." 1. It is the duty as well as the <ksire of ministers, =t only to te,ach their flocks, but to pray for them. They must say, like Saniuel, "God forbid that I should . . . cease to pray for you" (2 Sam. xii. 23). The prayer of Moses was more influential against Amalek than all the weapons of Israel. "The prayer of a ri~hteous ma.n ave.ileth much" (Jas. v. 16). 2. They ou,ght tc be 11,nceasing in their mppli=tions. There must be "perseverance in supplication for all saints" (Ep_h. vi 18). We must give God no rest; for he often delays the answer to increase our importunity (Lnke xviii 3, 4; 2 Cor. xii. 8, 9). 3. The reason for conmmt s-un,licatwn.. "For this cause we also, since the day we beard it, do not cease to pray . . . for you." The apostle had heard of their faith and love, and was naturally concerned for their growth in grace, for the free course of the Word among t~em, and for their freedom from all error. He heard they were good, and he prayed that they might be better. • . . _ IL TBE SUBSTANCE 01' TEE APOSTLE'S PBAYEB. "That ye may be filled with. t"\l.E) knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding." 1. The Divif!6, will is the Eupreme rubJect of knowledge to a beUever. It is not mere speculations about God's nature or his counsels, but his will, that we are to study. This is God's will as it is made known to us either in Scripture or experience. (1) It is his determining will (Eph. L 5). (2) It is his prescribing will, including Law and gospel, and especially the nature of faith and repentance (Act.II :nil. 9; Eph. i 9; Rom. xii. 2.) (3) It is his will of approval (GaL i. 4; Matt. xvili. 14). (~) It is his _pr?vidential will (1 Cor. i. 1; Rom. i 10). We have much t,o learn concerrung God's will m these four respects. 2. TJ.e k-rwwledge 'TIULJlsary to 11,nder,tand it i• inatinct with "spiritool wisdom and wi.derstandimg." Knowledge is power, but it may work for evil as well as good. It must be regulated by wisdom and understanding. (1) Wisdom; not that which bas "a show of wisdom," and springs from vanity nurtured by the fleshly mind (eh ii. 18, 23); not fleshly wisdom (2 Cor. i. 12); much less that which is "earthly, sensual, devilish" (Jas. iii 17); but spiritual wisdom-the knowledge of the true end of liie, such as God gives to the simple (Ps. xix. 7), enabling them to penetrate the ~ysteries of Divine truth (1 Cor. ii. 6) and to understand__~heir dut! to God and man m all the relations of life. It is "from above" (Jas. m. 17); 1t presupposes the £:tisteuc(; of faith and love; it is a subject of Christian prayer. (2) Understanding is tLc faculty of spiritual insi"ht which takes in the bearings of things. It fits us for the ~crvice of God on earth and for the glory of God in heaven. As it is spiritual, it is OH. I. 1-29.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO 'l'llE COLOSSIANS.

touched with meekness and humility, 3. Tl1e measure., of this hnowled,7e. "That ye may be filled with the knowledge of his will." 'l'here is no limit assigner! to it. (1) We cannot rest with mere rudiments; we must be "filled with all knowledge" (Rom. xv. 14). (2) Thero will alwnys be something wanting in this life. "We know in part" (l Cor. xiii. 11). (3) Nothing but the knowledge of the will of God will ever satisfy the deep hunger of man's heart. 4. Motives to this fuller knowledge. (1) It is the glory of the saints to have it (Jer. ix. 24). (2) It is their special privilege to have iC (Mark iv. 11.) (3) To want it is a sin and a sorrow (Hosea. iv. 6). (4) It is the roost excellent of all knowledge; for it is eternal life itself (John xvii. 3). 5. Design of this lcnowledge. "'l'o walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, bearing fruit in every good work, and increasing by the knowledge of God; strengthened with all might, according to the power of his glory, unto all patience and long-suffering with joyfulness." 'l'he design is twofold as it bears respectively upon action and upon sufferjng. (1) The knowledge of God's will is to influence conduct. Its true end is practical obedience. We are "to walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing." (a) Walking worthy of the Lord. This is not (a) with a worthiness of merit, for we are all of us unprofitable servants (Luke xvii. 10); (fJ) but with a worthiness of meekness such as is becoming when we consider the dignity of our calling, the glory of the kingilom of God, the supplies of grace which the gospel affords, and the blessed hopes laid up for us in heaven. ("Y) It is a worthiness "unto all pleasing." We must "so serve God that we may please him" (Heb. xii. 28; 1 Cor. vii. 31). (i.) He that seeks not to please him in all things seeks not to please him in anything. (ii.) If we please him he will make our very" enemies at peace with us" (Prov. xvi. 7). (iii.) "Men-pleasing" is inconsistent with God-pleasing (eh. iii. 22). (iv.) It would be sinful and ungrateful to displease him. (v.) Pleasing God is the work of heaven (Ps. ciii. 20, 21). (b) A twofold aspect of worthy walking. (a) Christian fruitfulness. "Bearing fruit in every good work.'' (i.) The necessity of it. (a) It is for God's glory (John xv. 18). (b) As a proof of our faith (Jas. ii. 18, 26). (c) The edification of others (Matt. v. 16; 'l'itus iii. 8). (d) The increase.ofour final reward (2 John 8). (ii.) The means of it. (a) We must abide in the true Vine, Jesus Christ (John xv. 4; Phil. i.). (b) We must dwell beside the rivers of water (Ps. i. 3). (iii.) The extent of it-"in every good work." We must be harmoniously developed in our obedience as in our inward experience (Phil. iv. 8). (fJ) Increase in moral stature-" increasing by the knowledge of God.'' We grow in grace just as we grow in knowledge (2 Pet. iii. 18). There is a mutual interaction between knowledge and grace. We are to add to our faith virtue, and to our virtue knowledge (2 Pet. i. 5), just as we are to grow in all spiritual graces 'by knowledge. Knowledge promotes the sanctification of our callings and our food (1 'l'im. iv. 3), enables us to discern things that differ (Phil. i. 10), and keeps down corrupt affections (Isa. xi. 7, 9). (2) The knowledge of God's will tends to strengthen patience in suffering. (a) The need of abounding strength-" strengthened with all might." (a) 'l'he afflictions of life tend to weaken us. (fJ) Our adversaries are many. ("Y) Our faith is fitful. (6) We are often unsettled and tossed about by the wind of contrary doctrine (Eph. iv. 14). ( e) We are, perhaps," babes in Christ," and unskilful in the word of righteousness (Heb. v. 12, 13). (b) The source of our strength-" accord- ing to the power of his glory ; " his glory being the manifestation of his love to man (Eph. iii. 16). We "can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth us" (Phil. iv. 13). He "giveth strength to his people" and "strength is of the Lord" (Ps. lxii. 11). "They that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength" (Isa. xl. 31). "Glorious power will be victorious power." It is God's revelation of himself to us that gives us our greatest strength. It is his glory that sets his power to work, as it is by promise ,pledged to his people. Therefore: (a) Let us pray for knowledge and faith to discern God's promise and power (Eph. i. 8). (fJ) Let us hold fast the truth of the gospel, eschewing "winds of doctrine." Let us "follow the truth in love." ( c) The fruit of our strength-" unto • patience and long-suffering with joyfulness." (a) Patience or endurance. (i.) It is the grace which does not easily succumb under suffering, and is one of the most blessed fruits of the tree of life. It is the result of the bracing effect of affliction (Jas. v. 11), and is opposed to despondency or cowardice. (ii.) Our patience will grow (a) through the word of patience, for the comforts of tho Scriptures beget both patience and hopo (Rom. x.v. 4). (b) Wo must cultivate ;1 l:12 THE EPISTLE TO '.l'HE COLOSSIANS. [err. 1. 1-20,

humble and constant trust in the Lord (Ps. xxxvii. 3). (c) ,vo must continue insta~t. in prayer (Rom. xii. 12). (/J) _Long-su~ering is a temper of gentleness and self- restramt, closely connected with patience. (1.) It is the Lord's command that wo 6houhl suffer long (Matt. v. 21, 22). (ii.) There are injuries that befall us in Divine rrovidcnce (2 Sam. xvi. 10). (iii.) A revengeful spirit is a hindrance to prayer (1 Tim. i ,. S) and t.cdhe due power of the Word (Jas. i. 21), and it lets the devil into the heart (Eph. iv. 21). Therefore, let us practise this grace of long-sufferino-, (-,,) Joyfulness, "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." It is possible to be II s~rrowful yet al way rejoicing" (2 Cor. vi. 10). (i.) Our patience and long-suffering must be bal~nced with joy so as to sustain their true temper. (ii.) It is possible to be joyful in tribulations (Jas. i. 2). (iii.) It is commanded by Christ (Matt. v. 12) and enforced by his own example on the cross (Heb. xii. 2). (iv.) Its ground is our fello,vship with Christ in i,is sufferings (1 Pet. iv. 13), and the expectation of a heavenly inheritance (Heb, x:. H). (v.) It is one of the fruits of God's Spirit (Gal. v. 22).-T, C.

entries.title: COL 1:12
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Divine mutness of the saints for their inheritance, "Giving thanks to the Father, who made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light." I. Tm; NATURE AND GLORY OF THE Th'HERITANCE. Whether we understand by it heaven or the blessings of the kingdom is immaterial, but the original suggests the idea of a joint inheritance, of which each individual enjoys a part. 1. It is an ancient i,iherita11ce. For "it is a kingdom preps.red for you from the foundation of the world" (Matt. x:xv. 34). Its "Builder and Maker" is God himself (2 Cor. v. 1). 2. It is bound "I' tDiih the coheirship of Christ. (Rom. viii. 17, 18; Ps. ii.) God makes us "hein; and rich in faith" (Jas. ii. 5). By virtue of the coheirship, it is a free, sure, satisfying, durable inheritance. 3. It is a holy inheritance. It is "with the saints." Only saints enjoy it with one another. "The pure in heart shall see God" (Matt. v. 8). :Ko unclean thing shall enter into God's kingdom (Acts :u. 32; x:xvi. 18; 1 Thess. i. 10). 4. It i.s an inheritance "in li,ght." (1) The Lamb is the Light of heaven (Rev. x:ri. 23). (2) There will be clear vision in heaven's light. Whatever "makes manifest is light." "In thy light we shall see light." We shall" know even as we are known." We shall "see face to face." We shall dwell for ever "ill the light of God's coun- tenance." 'l'here will be no darkness there. II. THE MEETI-""EBI\ FOB. THE INHEB.IT.A.KCE. L It is implied that we have no na,tural ffll:dness for it. We could not merit it by our righteousness, and our spirits are out of harmony with its joys. There is nothing in us but" enmity against God" (Rom. viii. 7). The spirit which is in moral darkness cares not for the light. 2. The meetness is given to us. (1) We are made meet by our calling, by our justification, by our adoption. (2) We are made meet for it by our sanctification. The Father gives us; along with the kingdom, the disposition, inclination, behaviour of heirs, sons, kings, and priests. Ill. 'IRE AUTHOB OF TBl6 llEETNESS. "The Father." L It is he who hath begotten t1s to the inheritance. (1 Pet. i. 3.) 2. It is he <mly who can pardon us and accept us. 3. It is he who is the J,'wntain of all holiness. 4. It is he who is stronger than all to preserve TLS 'lo the end and crown fLS with final glory. (Jude 24; Eph. i. 17.) IV. TBE DUTY OF TRANKBGIVlll"G. "Giving thanks to the ]'a.ther.'' 1. A sanctified heart is ready to acknowledge the instrument 'by which good is received, yet more the .Authur of blessing. 2. It honours God to thank him. "Whoso offereth praise glorifi.eth me" (Ps. L 23). 3. A thankful heart u BUre of a gracious hearing. 'l'he more thankful we are for mercies received the more ground have we to expect more mercies,-T, 0.

entries.title: COL 1:13
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Translation into Ohrist', kingdom. The apostle now proceeds to show how the Father makes us meet for the inheritance of saints. "Who delivered us from the power of darkness, and translated us into the kingdom of the Son of his love." I. THE ORIGINAL OONDITlO!i OF ALL MEN. They are under "the power of darkness." 1. Coosider the =ni,ng ef this darknua. There is a darkness that is seasonable; which, in the economy of nature, brings rest and recovery to man. 'l'his darkness is far different. (1) It is the darkness of ignorance apart from "the light of life" (John vui. 12; Ei,h. v. 13). (2) It is the darkness ofsin (Rom. xiii. 12; 2 Cor. iil, 14), blindi!,g men against the truth. (3) lt iii the darkness of mi110ry (Isa. viii. 22). (4) on. r. 1-29.) 'fl-IE EPISTLE 'l'O 'rHE COLOSSIANS. 33

Hie the darkness of death (Pa, lxxxviii. 12). (5) It is the darkness of hell-'' utto,r darkness." 2. It is darkness organized for the ruin of men. It is " the power of rlark- ncss "-an arbitrary, usurped power, and not "a true kingdom." The prince of dark- ness is at the heacl of this dreary realm and strives to keep all his slaves in darkness, lest" the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus should shine into them" (2 Cor. iv. 4). II. 'l'HE BEB0UE FROM THIS POWER OF DARKNESS. "Who delivered us." None but God can do th'is work. The strong man will keep his own till the stronger come (Luke xi. 22). He delivers us iu our effectual calling. 1. He enlightens our mind~ in the knowledge of Ghrist, who is "the true Light." (,John viii. 12.) 2. He persuades and enables us to embrace Ghrist as offered in the ,gospel. (John vi. 44; Phil. ii. 13.) 3. He renews our wills and causes as to" wr1llc in the light as he is in the light." (1 John i. 7.) 4. Be clothes us "with tlie arm-0ur of light." (Rom. xiii. 12.) III. THE NEW KIKGD0M OF THE RESCUED CAPTIVES AND ITS NEW RELATI0~S. "And translated us into the kiugclom of the Son of his love." The word usually suggests the transplanting of races and the settlement of them in a new territor_v-. 1. The significance of the translation. (1) It implies separation (a) from the "·orlcl, (b) from sin, (c) from the devil. "Go out from among them, and be ye separate" (2 Cor. vi. 17). (2) It implies the assumption of entirely new relations. The believer is a member of a new society-" the kingdom of grace;" is "a. fellow-citizen with the saints;" is heir of the kingdom of glory. He has a new name, new hopes, new fdends, and works for a new heaven. 2. 'l'he new kingdom of the saints. '"!'he kingdom of the Son of hi;j love." (1) It is not the kingdom of inferior angels, as e1TOrists might fancy (eh. ii. 8), but that of God's own Son. (2) It is a kingdom already in existence. (3) It is a. kingdom that cannot be shaken like the kingdoms of earth (Heh. xii. 2d). (4) It is a kingdom that will endure to the end (Luke i. 33). (5) It is a kingdom in which the number of the possessors will not diminish the blessing~ enjoyed by each. (6) It is a kingdom in which Chl"ist now reigns by his Word and Spirit; the saints rejoicing to have him reigning over them. (7) All the subjects of this kingdom are kings (Rev. i. 6).-'l'. C.
