entries.title: COL 1:15–17
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0hrist's headship over nature. The Gnostic errorists at Colossre fa.ught that the gulf between the infinite God and finite man was bridged across by subordinate angelic agencies. 'l'he apostle teaches that the gulf is bridged by Jesus Christ, who, being both God nnd Man, touches both and is the Reconciler of God and man. He shows that Christ has a double sovereignty, a twofold mediatorial function -in relation to the universe and in relation to the Church. 'l'hus we have a most pregnant statement concerning the doctrine of the person of Christ with the view of showing that there is a real mediation between God and creation. I. His RELATION TO THE INVISIBLE FATHER. "\Vho is the Image of the invisible God." Christ i8 likewise called "the Brightness of the Father's glory, the express Image of his person" (Hcb. i. 3). 1. The meaning of this image. (1) Christ is not a. mere likeness of the Father, like the head of a sovereign stamped on a coin, or as a. son bears the features of his father. (2) But he is nn essential manifestation and embodiment of tbe Father. 'fhus the invisible God becomes visible to man, according to our Lord's own words, "No man bath seeu God nt any time; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, ho hath revcalecl him" (John i. 18). "lie th:\t hath seen me bath seen the Father" (John xiv. !l). (3) It implies his perfect equality with tho Father in respect to substance, nature, nod eternity. 'l'hc Son is the Father's Imngo except in rospcct that he is not tho Father. 2. Lessons to be drnwn from this representation of Christ's ylury. (1) If \\'O wonhl know ihc Father, wo must get into Christ by faith (2 Cor. iv. 4). (2) As it is Chri~t•s glory to be God's lma~e, bu it om honour to bo Chri~t•s imago, in knowlcd'.-!e (eh. iii. 10), in holinc8~, in ri·.'.litcuusnc~B (Eph. iv. il). We arc" pre,lestiualc,1 lo bo conf,,rmcd to the imagJ ut' bis :S,m" (rtom. viii. 2!l). (3) How great a sin it is lo turn llw t,;lury oI tl10 i1,c0,rq>libk Gud into tho image of corrnptible creatures" (!:urn. i. 23) ! COLOSSBNS, D 84 THE EPISTLE '1'0 THE COLOSSIANS. [oR, I, 1-29,

]I. Cm:r~T·s nF.T,ATION TO THE tTh,VF.RSE. He is "the Firstborn of nil creation," As his being God's Image implies his eternal uuity with God so his boing tho only b<-gottcn Son of God implies the distinctness of his Person. '11be apostle thus guards the tnith on one side against Arianism, on the other side against Sabellianism. Thero nrc two ideas involved in this statement. 1. Ghrist has a priority to all creation. Arians refer t.o the passage as implying that he is only one, thouah 0 the very first, of created beings. But (1) he is S.'lid here to be l'Cgotten, not created, (2) He is declared in the context to be "before all things," and therefore he is no part of them, (3) "All things" arc declared to be "made by him," but he is himself necessarily excepted from the number of the things he created. (4) The Scriptures elsewhere declare his eterunl pre-existence and Godhead. 2. Ghrist u sovereign Lord of creation by right of primo- geniture. The word " Firstborn" is used of the Me$Siah almost as bis technical designation (Ps. ii. 7), as we see by Heb. i. 6, "When he bringeth the First-begotten into the world." As such he is" Heir of all thinis" (Heb. i. 2; Rom. iv. 14). There is thus implied a meaiatorial function in the world as well as in the Church, 3. <Jhrist ,·s the actool, Oreaior of all things. " For in him were all things created, in the heavens and upon the earth, things visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers." These words justify the title of" Firstborn of all creation." They were all created " in him," not merely " by him "-as if the germ of all creative rower and wisdom lay in his infinite mind, as the sphere of their operation. The words impliedly c:i.:clude the Gnostic idea that Christ was nn inferior agent of the infinite God. He was the creative centre of the universe. Mark: (1) The extent of creation-" things in the heavens and things upon the earth." 'l'his includes all creation as described by locality. (2) The variety of the creation-" whether things visible or innsible." This division would include the sun, moon, stars, the earth with all its visible glories, in one class; the angels and the souls of men in the other class. (3). 'l'he ordera of creation, "whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers.' As Gnosticism placed Christ among the higher intelligences, the apostle places him far above all angelic intelligences of every order. It is not possible to say whether these names represent various grades of a celestial hierarchy, but it is probable that they do; " thrones and dominions" belonging to the first order, "principalities and powers" standing next, as including spirits both good and evil. Christ made the angels. 4. <Jhri.st is himself the End or final Cause of creatum. "All things have been created through him and for him." All things were created by him as well as for him-for the :wanifest.ation of his glory. "He that was the first Cause must be the last End." The final destination of the universe is referred to the Son, just as it is elscwbero ascribed to the Father (Rom. xi. 36). The Son is the Centre of the world's final unity. 6, Chri.st i.s the Sustainer of the universe. " And by him all things consist." The continued existence, as well as the creation, of all things, depends upon him. "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (John v. 17). He "upholds all things by the ,rnrd of his power" (Heb. i 3). The sustaining unity of the creation is in him (1) becauno he maintains its order, appointing all things to their respec~ive ends; (2) because he sustains the operation of all thincrs correlatincr means with ends; (3) because ho secures the co-operation of all thi;g;, so that all t~ings ,~ork toget~cr for_ his_ glory; (4) because he maintains the perpetuity of all things. rhus Chnst maintains the cohesion of the universe. JII. LESSONS TO llE DRAWN FBOll CHRIST'S RELATION TO HUI FATilER AND TO TRE VNIVEB6E. 1. We delight in tM doctrine of <Jhrist's divinity, which i~ the_ doctrine of C?,risumdom. 2. Jf he =de angels and men, they may weU worship l.im. 3. Bis relation to creation encourages us to hope that he will overrule all tM power of nature /or tM grc,wth of his Church. Even wicked men will have no power to. destroy his Church. The creation proves bis power, and his love proves his good will. 4. The kuowkdge of his glory ought to deter from all creature-worship. 5. We should ever 7,ray that he would direct the work of our hands continually. (Ps. xc. 7.) 6. We ought ,,,,t to fret at Divine providenr.,e. (l's, xxxvii. 2, 3.) The crcativo and administrative w,crk 0f Christ, in the natural order of things, is the comfort of all believers.-'!'. C.

V~r. 18.-Christ'~ headship of the Church. He is the l1ead of the new creation n9 "'ell ll.E 0f the natural creati0n. "And he is the Head of the bcdy, the Church: who

is tho Deginning, the Firstborn from the dee.<l; that in all things he might have the pre-eminence," I. CoNBIDER WHAT 1B INVOLVED IN THIS HEADSfllP OF THE CHURmf. There is a real essential union of the Hend nncl the members. 1. (Jhrist is the Centre of the Church'., life. Ho is its Life. "Because I live ye shall live also" (John xiv. 19). The union is strictly vital. "The second Adam is a quickening spirit" (1 Cor. xv. 45). 2. He is the Centre of its unity. Ilclievere are all one in Christ Jesus (1 Cor. xii. 12). We are haptized by the Spirit into one body (1 Cor. xii. 13). 3. He is the Source of all its blessings and comforts. (1) He loves it (Eph. v. 27). (2) lie sympathizes with its distresses (Matt. xviii. 5). (3) He supplies it with abundant grace. "Of his fulncss have we all received, even grace for grace" (John i. 16). 3. He is the Mainspring of all its holy activity. "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me" (Phil. iv. 13); "Without me ye can do nothing" (John xv. 5). I!. CONSIDER WHAT IS INVOLVED IN THE SUBJECTION OF THE BODY TO THE HEAD. 1. The (Jhurch must own no other Head than (Jhrist. There are under-currents of priestly domination in our day subversive of this headship. The Pope is not and cannot be the head of the Church in any sense. We can be in subjection to no other than Christ. 2. We must do nothing to dishonour our Head either in flesh or spirit. (2 Cor. vi. 15--18.) 3. We must use a-ll means to grow up into our He.ad in all things, that "there may bo increase of the body unto the building up of itself in love" (Eph. iv. 16). 4. We must dwell with our fellow-members in love and humility. "Keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Eph. iv. 3). The members must sympathize with one another (1 Cor. x. 24). III. 'l'm:: ORIGIN OF THE HEADSilIP OF CHRIST. " Who is the Beginning, the First• born from the dead." 1. Chi·ist is the Beginning of the new creation. Two ideas are implied in the expression. (1) Priority in time. He is "the Firstfruits of them that have fallen asleep" (1 Cor. xv. 20). (2) The origination of spiritual life. As be is "the Beginning of the creation of God" (Rev. iii. 14), he is the Beginning of the new creation. He is the "Prince of life" (A.cts iii. 14), the "Author of salvation" (Heb. ii. 10). 2. Christ is Head tlirough his resurrection. He is" the First-begotten from the dead." Consider: (1) That he was among the dead. Thus he made expia.tion for our sins. (2) That he was begotten from among the dead, because he was raised from death to life "for our justification" (Rom. iv. 23, 24). (3) That he was the first so begotten. (a) Others were translated or died again. (b) He rose to die no more (Rom. vi. 9). (c) His resurrection involves the resurrection of all his saints. (·l) His resurrection is his tHle to headship (Eph. i. 20-23). (5) Let us realize " the power of his resurrection" (Phil. iii. 10) in a holy life. IV. THE DESIGN OF THE FATilER WAS THAT ALIKE IN THE SPIRITUAL il'D THE NATURAL ORDER CHRIST MIGIIT HA VE THE PRE-EMINENCE. "That in all things he might have the pre-eminence." Both in nature and in the Church he is pre-eminent; aod the Father's d83ign will be yet more fully accomplished when all things are put under his feet and "the kingdoms of this world have become the kingdom of our Lord and his Christ" (Rev. xi. 15). Thus our Divine Redeemer is "Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the Ending, the First and the Last" (Rev. i. 8, 11, 17, 18).-T. C.

entries.content:
-The fulness of the Godhead in Jems Christ. "For it pleased the Father that in him should all fulness dwell." The apostle thus explains the headship alike of the Church nod of the universe, for he says the indwelling of Deity was the ground of both. I. THE NATURE OF TRIB FULNEss. 1. It is not the mere manifestation of Godhead. 2. It is Godhead itself in the totality of its powtTl"s and attrib1ttes. It is "the complete fnlnoss and oxhnustless perfection of the Divine essence." It is elsewhere described: "In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (eh. ii. 9). Christ is indeed "God manifest in the flesh" (l Tim. iii. 16). 'l'be Judmo-Gnostics taught that tho fulness of the Godhead was distribnt~d or dispensed among several spiritual. agencies- " thrones, dominations, princedoms, virtues, powers "-so as to introduce grades of angelic mediators between God and man. 'l'he apostle declares that. the fulness of the Gouhead rests, not in them, but in Christ as th~ Word of God. Thus he is no mere emanation from the Divine Dein~. 36 'l'HE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSI.ANS.

II. THERR rs A PERMA'KE1'TLT INDWELLING FULNESS IN nm. "That in him nil the fulness should have its permanent abode." This is the force of the ori"inal word which is very suggestive in the light of later Gnosti<l heresies. The false t~chers hoid that the ful~ess of the Godhead as dispel'8Cd among spiritual agencieR waa partial like a blurred image, an<l also temporary. The apostle teaches: 1. T/1.0,t the totality of Divine po~ abi.des i~ Ch~ 2. Th~t itabiius in him permanently and remains forever, not (mning and going lil.·e a tra,1sumt phenomenon. Therefore we have an inexhaustible supply for all the needs of the Church. 111. 'l'HE PRECIOUSSESS OF THIS INDWELLING FULNESS TO us. 1. Il was of tlu, Father's "good ple,wure " that it should abule in ht'$ ,:ncarnate Son for the welfare of the Church. 2. We are to receive "of his fulness and ,qrace Jor graC6." (John i. 16.) We arc to grow "unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ" (Eph. iv. 13). 'l'be st.andard is nothing short of the fulness of Christ. 3. The Church is his very ful- 11ess-" the fulness of him who filleth all in all," because his fulness is communiroted to her (Eph. i. 23). IV. LESSO!':S TO BE DRAWN FROM Tms TRUTH, 1. Great is the mystery of godliness. (1 Tim. iii. 16.) 2. Great is the comfort of the believer in virtue of this infinite fulness. There is fulness of wisdom to keep us from error, fulncss of grace to subdue our sin, fulncss of joy to keep us from despair, fulncss of mercy and pity to succour us in our distresses. "Therefore let no man take thy crown" (Rev. iii. 11); "Cast not away your confidence" (Heb. L 35). 3. Great is the security of the believer. It is a perma- nent fulncss.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 1:20
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.The reamciliation effeded by <Jhrist. "And, having made peace through the blood of tbe cross, by him to reconcile all things to himself." L Tm: NATURE OF THIS RECONCILIATION. 1. It implies a prior estrangement. Man "departed from the li\'ing God" (Heb. iii. 12). He is "alienated" from God (ver. 21). "The carnal mind is enmity against God" (Rom. viii. 7). Even God himself was an~ry with man (Ps. vii. 11). But this prior estrangement implies an antecedent friendship. 2. ThO'Ugh man was first in the breruh of this friendship, God was first in the reccnciliation. This blessed restoration of broken relations is traced to "the good pleasure" of the Father. It is a mistake to say that Christ is the cause of his Father ma.king to us the offer of reconciliation. The atonement is not the cause, but the effect, of God's love. 3. There was reconciliation on God's side as well as fflll,n's. 'l'here is a change in the Divine relation or mood of mind toward us; for he himself "made peace by the blood of the cross," and his reconciliation of all things to himself is represented as based upon the peace thus made. The death of Cluist wa.s a true satisfaction to Divine justice for sin, so that God could be "just and the Justifier of the ungodly." II. THE llEANB OF THIS BEOONCILUTION. "Having made peace through the blood of the cross." The reconciliation was not absolute or without mediation. It was "through the blood of the cross "-the :first term suggesting a comparison between Christ's death and the Old 'l'estament sacrifices; the second, the penal nature of the Redeemer's death as that of a cnrse-bea~ing Substitute. The apostle emphasizes this aspect of truth, because the errori.sts of his time denied alike a real incarnation and a real atonement. III. '.l'HE u:i.TVEBS.A.LITY oF TBIS BECONCILUTION. "By him to reconcile all things to b.imself; by him, whether they be things in earth or things in heaven. 1. " Things ir. earth" may i11clude more than man. (1) It may include the whole visible creation, which is "groaning and travailing together in pain until now," and "waiting for the manifestation of the sons of God" (Hom. viii. 19-21). 'l'he curse passed to the ground through man's sin; through man will the blessing reach it again. It is a z:;ignificant fact that Christianity in its purest form brings a happy change over those JJOrtions of 1.hc earth where it prevails. (2) But, definitely and primarily, "things in earth" refer to man. Man's reconciliation to God is based upon God's reconciliation to wan. It was iu virtue of Christ's death that the Holy Spirit came tu change the Ltans of wer, aud briua them into harmony with God. 2. " Things in heaven." l'i:ot aL;_.,c:,s, as ,-ome sup~usc, for they were never estranged from God and Christ, autl ll.e H~atl of augelc as well as men is never represented as the Modiator of angels. CII. I. 1-29.] nm EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSI ANS. 37

A mere increaso of knowledge or blessedness on their part, or the confirmation of them in their heavenly obedience, can hardly be covered by the term "reconcilif\tion. n The word must be used in its ordinary sense. The apostle has described 01,rist's mediatoria.l function as twofold: ns exercised in the natural creation and in the spiritual creationin the universe nnd in the Church. His object is not to show the extent either of the creation or of the reconciliation, but the person of the Creator and the Reconciler, arnl the Church marks the glorious sphere of the reconciliation as it is seen in its two great divisions of living and dead saints, The "things in heaven'' seem, therefore, to apply to the saints in glory.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 1:21–23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Application of the reconci?iation to the spedal case of the Colossians. I. THE NATURAL STATE OF THE COLOSSIANS. "And you, being in time past cstranaed and enemies in your mind in evil works, . . . bath lie reconciled." 1. They were ;stranged from God. The original term denotes that they had fallen from f\ prior relationship of amity. It points suggestively to the original innocence of nun in Eden, and to the deplorable effects of the Fall, as separating between God anci man (Isa. lix. 2). '!'hey had become strangers to God, (1) because strangers to the life of God (Eph. iv. 17); (2) because they followed strange gods (Deut. xxxii. 16; Rom. i. 25); (3) because they were "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel" (Eph. ii. 12). 2. They were hostile to God both in thought and deed. A strange thought that man should cherish a living enmity in a dead heart! It is enmity to God as Lawgiver and Punisher of sin. (1) Mark the reality of this enmity. (a) The threatening of the second command asserts it: "Them that hate me" (Ex:od. x.x. 5). (b) The friendship of the world involves it: "\Vhosoever will be a friend of the world will be an enemy of God" (Jas. iv. 4). (c) The carnal mind is full of it (Rom. viii. 7). (a) All scoffs and blasphemies manifest it (Ps. lxxiv. 18). (2) The seat of this enmity. "In your mind." It is an essentially carnal mind. The enmity lies deep down in the heart, which is a "chamber of imagery," full of all shapes of hatred to God and man. Strange that there should be hatred to him who is Author of our being and Fountain of our happiness I We need, indeed, in regeneration to be "renewed in our mind" (Eph. iv. ~3), that we may exchange our hatred for love. (3) The practical sphere of this enmity. "In evil works." The enmity is not caused by evil works, but is manifested through them (Matt. xv. 19). They whose "mind and conscience nre defiled" are "unto all good works reprobate" (Titus i. 16). II. THE RECONCILIATION OF TIIE CoLoss1ANs. "Yet now hath he reconciled in the body of his flesh through death." The reconciliation has been already explained. The means of it are here expressively set forth by the apostle. The passage su~gests: 1. That the atonement was a great liistoricfact; so that no person might conclllde that the reconciliation was effected apart from the person of the incarnate Son or after his return to glory. 2. That he was a real man in a human body, as if to refute Gnostic theories as to a phantom body or as to the bouy being essentially evil. It was a heresy to say that "Jesus Christ had not come in the flesh" (1 John iv. 2, 3). 3. That he carried about with him on earth a sin-bearing humanity. It was, therefore, a "weak, abased, and suffering humanity" (Rom. viii. 3). 4. Tltat his life was consummated by rkath, as the completion of his atoning sacrifice for sin. III. THE FRUIT OB EFFECT OF THE RECONCILIATION. "To preEent you holy and without blemish and unreprovable before him." 1. We see that sanctification follows reconciliation and does not precede it. It confounds the relations of things and perverts Christian doctrine to reverse the order. 2. The atonement provides for our sanctification. It purchased for us all the communications of Divine life. Christ is made to us at once "Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, and Redemption" (1 Cor. i. 30). 3. The nature of tliis sanctification. "Holy and without blemish and unreprovable." The words point, not to the relative standic.g before God, but to the externally observable advances in spiritual life. 'l'hese are ieprescnted, first-, positively-" holy;" nnd then negatively-" without blemish and unreprovable." 4. The end of this sanctijication. "'l'o present you holy nnd without blemish nnd unreprovable before him." Not, as somo allege, nt the day of judgment., but for his personal approbation, implying (1) that nll we do is in God's presence (Luke ii. 18; xiii. 26; Acts x. 33); l2) that Ood is the Witness cf nil our nets (Luke viii. 47; 2 Cor. vii. 12; Gal. i. 20); (3) that 38 'l'HE EPISTLE TO 'l'RE COLOSSIANS. [cu. 1. 1-29.

God not only accepts what is in any measure good (Luke i. 76), but highly esteems what is good in t.Jie saints (Luke i. 25; 2 Tim. ii. 2, 3; v. 4). IV. AN EXHORTATION TO PERSEVERANOE JN COID.'EOTION WITH THE PROVISION FOR THEIR RECONCILIATION. "If at 1811st ye continne in the faith !rl'Oundcd and steadfast and are not constantly shifting from the hope of the gospel, which ye heard which wa~ preached in all creation under heaven." I. The1·e is nothing strictly liypothetical in this passage, as the tense clearly indicates; yet warning is needed ns the divinely ordered means of averting failure. There were risks to faith in the presence of Judreo- Gnostic teachers. We need to be reminded that "he that endureth to the end shall be saved" (Matt. xxiv. 13); but God himself provides for us the grace of continuance. 2. The mode of this conti'nuanc.e. "Grounded and steadfast." (1) Marking its positive side. (a) We must be built on the true Foundation (Eph. ii. 20). We must be grounded in the doctrines of grace as well as "built as living stones" on "the precious Corner-stone" laid in Zion (1 Pet. ii. 6). Otherwise we shall be swept away in the rising floods of judgment (Luke vi. 48, 49). (b) We must be steadfast as the result of this grounding. An ungrounded Christian cannot be a growing Christian. It is well to be settled in the faith if we would make progress in Christian life. Suffering has its influence in increasing our stability. Therefore our apostle prays that the God of grace, "after tha.t ye have suffered a while," may "make you perfect, sta.blish, strengthen, settle you" (1 Pet. v. 10). (2) Marking its negative side. "And are not constantly shifting from the hope of the gospel, which ye heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven." (a) The apostle points to the danger of drifting. When the anchors are lifted, it is impossible to know where the ship may go on a dangerous ~bore. The false teachers were subtle and plausible and speculative. It may have been hard to resist their logic. But the end of their speculations was death-the sacrifice of the hope of the gospel (b) He points to a sure anchorage-" the hope of the gospel, which ye heard, which was preached in all creation under heaven." (a) 'l'his hope may have been tba.t of the resurrection, of which the false teachers said it "was past already" (2 Tim. ii. 18), and thus cut up by the roots the true expecta- tions of the Christian. (fJ) It was more probably the "hope of the gospel" generally, wliich is described in Eph. i. 18 as " the hope of our calling," including a.II the blessings of redemption with re.surrection itself. ('y) It was a hope (i.) ma.de known by the gospel; (ii.) imparted to them by Epaphras, the delegate of the apostle-" which ye heard ; " (iii.) and proclaimed as the uni verral hope of man to all creation. It was not, therefore, reserved for a select coterie of men. "Its universal tendency was already realized," and its wide publicity was not to be called in question. (3) Consider the importance of religious steadfastness. " We must hold fast the confidence and rejoicing of hope unto the end" (Heb. iii. G). Let us, therefore, bless God that "he has begotten us to a lively hope" (1 Pet. i. 3). (4) Seek wisdom from on high "to know what is the hope of our calling" (Eph. i. 18). (5) Let us read the Scriptures prayerfully, that "throuah patience and comfort of the Scriptures we may have hope" (Rom. xv. 4). (6)°Let u.s acknowledge that "truth that is acco1·ding to godliness" (Titus i. 1, 2).-'l'. C.

entries.title: COL 1:24–27
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.77.e mission, sufferings, gospel, and :preaching of the apostle. Re introduces here a somewhat abrupt reference to himself, not to vi_ndic~te ~is _authority as an apostle, which was not challenged at Colossre, but to emphasize his m1ss1on as the apostle of the Gentiles, and to draw the Colossians into closer relations of sympathy with himself. L THE .APOSTLE'S euFFEBINGS FOR THE CHURCH. " Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up that which is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body's sake, which is the Church." L The nature of his sufferings. 'l'hese are to be WJderatood by his frequent reference to the afflictions of Christ. (I) The afil.ictions of Christ are not (a) afflictions home on account of Christ; (b) nor afflictions impostd by CL.rist; (c) nor afflictions which resemble those of Christ; (d) nor the aflLctions which the apostle endures instead of Christ, as supplementing his afilictions; b11t the afilictions which Christ endures in his suffering Church. 'l'hc Messiah was "to be afllicted iu all their afil.ictions" (Isa. h:iii. ~). (2) How the apostle filled up that wLicL wa;, bocking of Chrui's afflictionij, Not as if Christ did not suffer all that on. 1. 1-29.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 30

wns necessary to the snlvation of men, but left something to be suffered by member8 like the apostle as o. means contributory to their own salvation. Roman Catholics baec upon this passage their doctrine of supererogatory mel'it and indulgences. Some Pro- testant divines think this position is to be met by distinguishing part of Christ's sufferings as vicariously satisfactory and part as merely edifying by way of example, and ropresent the apostle as supplementing, not the first, but the last kind of suffering. 'l'his view is subject to the grave objection that there were no sufferings of Christ that were not vicariously satisfactory, as there were none that were not likewise designed for edification, comfort, and example. The Roman Catholic view is unsountl, (") because it contradicts the whole tenor of Scripture (John xix. 30; Heh. x. 1-15); (f3) because it is absurd, for if the apostle supplied in his suffering what Christ failed to supply, nothing remains for other saints to supply by their sufferings. (3) The apostle shows in the context that bis work was not to redeem, but to edify the Church. What, then, is the meaning of the apostle's statement? That the sufferings of the members of Christ are the sufferings of Christ; for the Church is bis body, in which be exists, lives, and therefore suffers. All the tribulations of the body are Christ's tribulations. 2. TM design or intent of the apostle's sufferings. "For his body's sake, which is the Church." It was for the extension and edification of the Church. He suffers in his natural body-" in my flesh "-for the mystical body. He teaches us: (1) That we are to seelc the advancement of the cause of <Jhrist above our own personal comfort. (2) That we ought to endure sufferings because theiJ concern the good of others more than ourselves. (3) That we are not to take care for the flesh or serve the flesh. (Rom. xiii. 14 ; Gal. vi. 8.) 3. The spirit in which the apostle bore his varitd sufferings. " I now rejoice in my sufferings for you." (1) Because they were the means of nnspeakable blessing to the Gentiles; (2) because they would confirm the faith of the Colossians and encourage them to bear suffering with like patience; (3) because they would contribute to the apostle's own ultimate blessedness (Heb. x. 34 ; 1 Pet. i. 6, 7). IJ. THE SPECIAL DISPENSATION ASSIGNED TO THE APOSTLE FOB. THE BENEFIT OF THE GENTILES. "Whereof I was made a minister according to the dispei;sation of God which was given me to you-ward, to fulfil the Word of God; even the mystery which bath been hid from all ages and generations, but now bath it been manifested to his saints, to whom God was pleased to make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the Hope of glory." 1. The apostle's peculiar mission to the Gentiles. He calls himself here "a minister of the Church," as he bas just called himself "a minister of Christ." His commission is from God himself. "A dispensation of God is given to me." God is the Dispenser of nil good things to his Church. Hence we infer (a) that the efficacy of the Word depends much upon God's appointment of his servants; (b) that his servants ought to be regarded with confidence and love, because they are God's ambassadors and make the Word of God their sup!'eme r1:1le in dispensing the things of God; (c) that the commission ought to be executed with all faithfulness and diligence (2 'l'im. iv. 1, 2; 2 Cor. ii. 17; iv. 2). 2. The design of the dispensation given to the apostle. "To fulfil the Word of Go<l." 'l'hat is, to give its complete development to the Word of God-" to give its fullest amplitude to, to fill up the measures of, its foreordained universality." Every minister is bound "to fulfil the Word of God" in his ministry, (1) by preaching the whole counsel of God (Acts xx. 27); (2) by rightly dividing the Word of truth according to the wants of the hearers; (3) by the application of the promises of the Word (Luke iv. 21); (4) by bringing men to fulfil it in a gospel obedience (Rom. xv. 18). 3. 1'!1e long-hid but now revealed mystery of the gospel. (1) It is" Christ in you, the Hopo of glory." Here is the trne mystery of godliness. It is not Christ, but Christ freely given to the Gentiles. (a) Christianity is Christ in the heart. "He dwells in our hearts by faith" (Eph. iii. 18). Ho lives in us (Gal. ii. 20). Ho is in us (2 Cor. xiii. 6) if wo are not reprobates. If he is in us, then(") we must continue to live by faith (Gal. ii. 20); (f3) we may expect to receive "all the treasures of wisdom au,l knowledge" that are "hid in him" (eh. ii. 3); (-y) we may look for larger measure, of his love (Eph. iii. 18); (11) we must keep holy hearts, for he will not dwell in an "evil heart of unbelief"-" The heart is Christ's chamber of presence : shall we nut, therefore, keep it with all dili~enco?" ( ,) tho grace of Christ will be efficacious again,t all temptations (2 Cur. xii. 9). (b) Christ iu the heart is the Hope of gl0ry. (a.) Uc is 40 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cu. 1. 1-20.

express!~· cnll<'d "our Hope" (1 Tim. i_. 2; eh. i. 4, 23). (/3) He is the Hope of glory been use I!<' ha!', as our _Fororunner, ~amcd the anchor of our hope within the veil, nnd fat'reaed 1t to the two immutable things-the oath and the promise of God-in which it wns impossible that he should lie. (-y) 'l'he resurrection of Christ establishes this hope (1 Cor. xv. 19). We should be of" all men most miserable" without it. (3) W.o ~hould rea~ the Word, that ''. throug:i,. patie~ce and comfort of the Scriptures wo mnv have hope (Rom. xv. 4), seemg Chnst therein as the p;round of our hope for eternity. (•) There is no hope for man apart from Christ. (2) The mystery was long hid from the world. •• Hid from ages and from generations." (a) This does not mean that thr fut~ &.'llntion of ~.he Ge1;1tiles was unkno~vn in ancient times; for the prophets are ful of 1t (Isa. lx. 3; 1:rn. 2; liv. 1-3). (b) But the mystery was that the Gentiles shoula be admitted t-0 the blessings of salvation on equal terms with tho Jews. (3) The mystery was at last made known to the saints (a) by revelation to the apostle (Eph. iii. 5); (b) by preaching (eh. iv. 4; Titus L 3); (c) by prophetic exposition (Rom. xvi. 26); and (d) by the actual com-ersion of the Gentiles themselves without their conformity to Jewish usages.-T. C.

, ers. 2S, 29.-The manner in which tlu apostle discharged his divinely given trttSt. " 'Whom we proclaim, adruonisbing every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ: whcreunto I labour also, striving according to his working who worketh in me mightily." I. THE DUTY OF ll:IKfSTEns. It is to preach Christ. 1. It is not to preach morality. Though it is right and necessary to exhibit moral duties in the light of the cross. 2. It i,s not to preach a philosophy or a thauma.turgy. (1 Cor. i. 22-24.) 3. It is to preach Christ crucified. (1 Cor. ii. 3.) Some preach Christ's incarnation as the grand hope of man, but this is to present a broken hope, if it is not supplemented by the death of Christ. 4. It is to preach Christ as the only Saviour. "Neither is there salvation in any other" (Acts iv. 12). There is no salvation in ordinances, in ijaints, in angels, in images, in pictures, in works of righteousness. 5. Preachers must, likewise, rebuke sin (Isa. l viii. 1; 2 Tim. iii 17; Heh. ix. 10). (2) Preaching is to set forth examples of admonition {1 Cor. L 11). It impl_ies perfection in knowledge as well as holiness. entries.title: COL 1:1–8
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The hope laid up in J,eaven. This Epi3tle, written from Rome to m~et and overmaster tlie "Colossian heresy," begins with a salutatiou somewhat similar to those at the beginning of other Epistles. There is the assertion of Paul's apostleship as direct from Christ; there is the statement of the brotherhood of Timothy, an.:l the desire that grace and peace may be the constant portion of the saints and fa.ithl'nl brethren at Uolossre. llut, having thus started, Paul immediately passes to an account of their character as he had got it from Epaphras, and how this chuactcr had been produced. He is thankful for it, and he wish~s them to remember how it had been formed within them. And here we have to notice that- I. JESUS CIIBIST IS THE OBJECT OF THE CoLOSSIANB' FAITH. (Ver. 4.) They hau. happily been led to this-to trust in the personal Saviour. It is not the promises but the Promiser; not the proposition, but the Person pled;;jug himself to the fnlfilme~t of the proposition, in whom we believe. Now, the heresy, which will appear more clearly nfterwards, made a good deal of angelic and intermediate personages; there was, in fact, a tendency to a mystic peopling of the unseen with needless forms, explanatory, as the Colossiaus supposed, of the mysteries of creation. It was important in these circumstances to state with precision that Jesus Christ is the great Object of faith. Faith in such a Being becomes a glorious simplicity. It is a simple extension of that trust to him which we extend to our fellow-men. But his glorious personality, embracing a Divine as well as human nature, makes all the difference bet,r,;;en faith in men anu. faith in him. 'l'be latter is true saving faith. II. THE SAINTS WERE THE SPECIAL OBJECTS OF THE COLOSSIANS' LOVE. (Ver. 4.) While faith goes out to a personal Saviour, it worketh by love towards all the saints. lt'or it cannot but be that, in trusting and loving the perfect Saviour, we learn almost instinctively to love those in bis image. 'l'be saints, all the saints, are seen to have their claim upon the believe1·'s love. The love of good men is the note of a true Christian. Ill. Hl!AVEN WAS mDISPENSADLE TO THE CONSUMMATION OF TBEIB HOPE. (Ver. 5.) It is the characteristic of the Christian system to relegate a goodly portion of its promise to the world to come. It bas certainly a promise for the lifo that now is, but chiefly has it a promise for that which is to come. In heaven the hope is laid up. AnJ into this hope the Colossinns heartily entered. They looker! for more to follow- for a purity, for a power, for a perfection impossible in the present life. There is thus a faith, a love, and a hope characteristic of the saints at Colossro as well as elsewhere. IV. 'l'HIS ll0PE BAD DEEN COMMUNICATED THROUGH THE PilEACHED GOSPEL. (Vers. 6-8.) Had the Colossians not bad the gospel preached to them, they would never have entered into such glorious, heavenly hopes. 'l'he word of the gospel is fruit-bearing. It kindles the hopes of men. Everywhere it bas the same blessed effects in lifting men's hearts to heaven. It woultl seem that Epaphras bad been the iustrument in thu Lord's hand in evangelizing the Colossiaus. He had, as a faithful minister of Christ, preached the Word to them, and they had received it and become the loving disciples he represented them to be in bis report to Paul. "Love in the Spirit" was the leaJing ide,\ in their lives, All this was matter for profound gratitude to God, and so the apostl.i pours out his thanksgiving to God the Father (ver. 3) because of it. In such circum- stances it surely becomes us to see that we rise on tbe wings of hope to heaven and apprecio.te the glorious consummation which there awaits us. We need such a hope to complete the demands of our immortal being. We cannot be satisfied with the seen, with the present life, with the present world; we must have more. And this tho gospel gives us in that hope which is laid up for us in lieaven.-R. M. E.

entries.title: COL 1:9–14
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The_kingdom of God's dear Son. From the thanksgiving presenteu. because of the faith, hope, nnd love of the Colossil\us, Paul next proceeds to inter- THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cu. 1. 1-20.

cession for their spiritual r,rogrt•s~. There is considernblc similarity between the intercession he makes for the Ephc-sinns (Eph. iii. 14-21) nud the intercession he here makes for t.he (',0lossians. In both he appeals to the Father that tho most intimo.te and loving relations may be est.ablished between the persons prayed for nud "his dear :-on." He gives, however, in the case bcfoNI us a magnificence to his conception of Christ which is not found in the longer Epistle. Ju this way he could best meot and overcome the Gnostic tendency nt Colossre. Let us consider the trnth embodied in tho intercession in the following order:- I. WE SHALL CONSIDER THE KING HERE REFERRED TO. (Ver. 13.) Paul has already presented Jesus Christ as the Object of the Colossians' faith. But in the present section he presents him as "God's dear Son," or "the Son of his love" (uloii .-;js i&-yd7r71s a~.-ov), in posi;ession of a kingdom. This kingdom is the antithesis of "the power of darkness;" it is, in fact, a kingdom of light. The sphere of the inheritance of the saintly subjects is said to be light (ver. 12). Hence Jesus is brought before us in this prayer much as he is Lrougbt before us in the Apocalypse, as the light-giving Lamb (Rev. :xxi 23). "I am the Light of the world," he said; and as the greater light rules the day, so does Jesus rule in his kingdom (John viii. 12; Gen. i. 16). The sun is now known to be the source of all the light and heat enjoyed on the earth; to his genial beams we owe spring and summer and autumn, and all the precious fruits of the earth; so is it to Jesns Christ we owe all the procession of seasonable blessing which his kingdom affords. He is King, then, over such a realm a.1 Pilate could not appreciate-over a kingdom of truth, whose rigbt.s interfered not with the rights of ClBSar (John xviii. 33- 38; lfatt. x:rii. 21). The light in which our spirit.s are bathed is truth-the truth as it is in Jesus. From his glorions Person there radiates the benign and healing beams 1·.-hicb enable the recipients to grow even as the calves of the stall (Mal iv. 2). ll LET us OOXSIDER TllE SUDJECTS SECURED FOR THIS KING. (Vers. 13, 14.) Now, Paul in this prayer speaks of the Father providing subjects for his dear Son. And, s:r:i.nge to say, he finds them in the kingdom of darkness, and by translation he popu- latc.s the kingdom of his Son. He finds the raw material in sinners who need redemp- tion and pardon, and they become Christ's subjects through receiving at his hands these indispensable blessings. Truly it is a strange arrangement that the King, God's ciear Son, should, before entering upon his reign, first die and provide through the shedding of his blood the redemption and forgiveness the subjects need. Yet so it is. '.!.'he Father sent his Son to be the Sacrifice to take away sin, and from the altar he J.lllSSes to the throne. \Ve here can see how endeared the King must be to his subjects. Having lived and died to redeem us, we feel it to be only just that we should live, and, if need be, die for him. Hence the consecration of the blood of the Son of God is upon all the subjects. It is a kiugdom of redeemed and pardoned and blood-bought souls 01·er whom Jesus reigns. HL CoNSIDED NEXT THE OCCUP.A.TIO!.'B OF THIS KINGDOM. (Vers. 9-11.) We can now see clearly that the duty of the blood-bought subjects of King Jesus is,)n one word, to do his will. But, before we can do his will, we must know it.. H~nc~ Paul 1,rays that 1hese Colossians may be "filled with the knowledge of his '!ill Ill all 11 is<l.om and spiritual understanding." The cry of the blood~bought soul 1s ." Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" We place ourselves at the d1spos~l of our King ~nd ask him to show us his will. AB a rule, we shall not be left long 1n doubt regarding it. In the darkest hour tbe light ariseth for the upright (Ps. cxii. 4). If we straightforwardly want to know what Christ's will is, we shall soon find it. But this knowledge of Christ's will is that the Colossians may " walk worthy of the Lord unto nil pleasin" bdnu fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God." Jesus i~dicate'; his will that his blood-bought people may walk worthily. High moral principle is to characterize them constantly. And every good work will fi'-:d in the1;11 willing hands. '.!.'he servants of Christ Lave been always in the vo.n of ph1lant_hrop10 effort. And this morality and zeal will not be allowed to hinder progress 1n the kuc,wledg,; of God. Education is not withheld from any of Christ's subjects by reason of tLc IDultiplicity of other claims. The real education, which is in the knowledge of God-for the: world 2.nd all that it contains constitute in the last analysis simply a rt:ve\atiou of hi.a power aud Godhead (Rom. i. 20)-goes hand-in-hand with moral earubtne:,s and cff,,rt. Ilut yet again, the subjects of Christ's kingdom find the need Oil, I. 1-20.] 'l'HE EPISTLE 'fO THE COLOSSJANS. 43

of pntionce nnd long-sufl'~ring; they cannot get 11long without bearing a good deal from worldly people-sneers, rnsolence, persecution, and in extreme cases death. Yet the King strengthens his people with might according to his glorious power, so that they nre able "joyfully" to bear and suffer what is sent. It is here that the occupations of the kingdom constitute ll power. The world wonders at the saintR who can be so joyful in their King, in spite of the drawbacks and difficulties to which tl.cy arc exposed. IV. CoNSIDEil AGAIN THE COMPENSATIONS OF THE KINGDOM. (Ver. 12.) What is "the inheritllnce of the saints in light"? Does it mean a heavenly world where light, such as only shines on tropical lands shall bathe emancipated men, and they shall be enabled to lie like lotus-eaters amid the glory, and never further roam? It is to be feared that the current notions of heaven partake of the dreamy "sofa-religion," which to earnest worldly natures is so repulsive. Let us, on the contrary, remember that the doing of our Lord's will is its own reward. Heaven will afford no higher enjoyment than this. Our souls are not rightly balanee<l when they look for something elee or more. "We are saved," says Archer Butler, "that we may for eternity serve God; salvation itself would be misery if unaccompanied by a love for that service." In the pleasing of our King, therefore, all the compensations of the kingdom lie. The outward conditions and circumstances would be changed in vain if we were not animated by this loyal and loving spirit. May such meetness for the inheritance be our present experience, as it was that of the Colossians.-R. M. E. Vere. 15-2O.-The glories of King Jesw. The apostle, having in his prayer pleaded for the Colossians that they may be worthy members of the kingdom of Christ, proceeds to speak of the glories which belong to their King. His purpose, like that of every true preacher, is to make Christ pre-eminent. The central thought of the pa.~sage is that God is invisible, but Christ is the visible Manifestation of the Father's perfections. In him as the perfect "Image" we may "see God." I. JESUS AS TIIE GLORIOUS CREATOR REVEALED THE MIND OF Goo. (Vers. 15, 16.) We are apt to think of Christ's revelation of the Godhead solely in his incarnation. Doubtless it was the climax of the" exegesis" of the invisible God (cf. John L 18, 1!11-yijn.-o). But there were previous revelations, and this is Paul's idea here that creation is a revelation of God through the power of Christ. Now, one thing is certain about the creation, that it addresses itself to mind. If men imagined it was thO'Ughtless, they would not spend two minutes more in its investigation. All science proceeds on the postulate of creation being thinkable, intelligible, an appeal to ruind. li creation, then, embodies thought, we have further to notice that it is thongbt of the same order as human thought. .After all the weary investigation, therefore, which tries to blink the fact of creation being a revelation of God, we are reduced in the last analysi~ exactly to this idea. Of course, we have not succeeded in interpreting the revelation in nature with either accuracy or fulness ; but every year's honest work c:1rries us on towards the fuller understanding of the Divine Thinker who speaks to bis creatures in nil the work of his hands. The fascination of science lies in the fact that a <leeper Thinker than any of the investigators is behind the work, and is calling for interpreters. 'l'he wonderful creation is from end to end, in heaven above and in earth beneath, Christ's exposition of the mind of God. II. HISTORY IS ALSO AN EXPOSITION BY CHRIST OF THE DIVINE MIND. (Ver. 17.) For not only did Christ as Creator give the system a start, but as the Upholder of the system he makes it a continuous revelat-ion. 'l'he philosophy of history lies in the assurance of the great procession of facts being under the constant control and direction of Divinity. Of course, as in the forrncr case of the interpretation of nature, we may be o.nd are very far from n full grasp of the significance of history. Yet undoubtedly a 1·everentinl stu,ly of the course of events brings us daily nearer the understanding of tho whole. It adds to our interest to take with us this assurance-that Jesus Christ is at the back of o.ll being, upholding it, sustaining the system, and reducing it to an ordorly exposition of the Divine thought. A miu the o.pparently chaotic course of events, in consequence of the freedom and frailty of the creature, there is tho renll_v Ol'derly procession of the whole towar<ls that" one Divine event to which tbu whole creation moYos." III. CmnsT's ECCl,ESIASTICAI, IIEADSHIP IS A FURTHER Rl!:VELATION OF GoD. (Ver. THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. (011. I, 1-20,

18.) For not only has Christ been Creator, not only has he been and is the Preserver ?f the sy_stem, but he has also ?,Oen constih1~ Head of a. special class of beings, united rn what 1s called the Church. Many ot his creatures do not recognize either him or )1is relations to t.be universe. They a.et &s if he were not, and hiR control of them is without their leave a~d ill: spite oft<'ntimes of thP.ir opposition. Dut others hl\ppily h:n-e come to recognize him as Lord of all, a.nd consequently of themselves as well, Tielievers in him, adorers of him, they have learned to look on life as simply a longer or ~horter opportunity of doing his will or of suffering" his good pleasure." And ns Christ comes into tenderer 11nd closer relations to the believers of the world than he can come iut-0 towards the unbelievers, be is as closely bound to his believin"' people as the ruling and sovereign •·head" is to the subject and obedient" mem~rs "of the one body. And this headship of Christ is a re,elatiou unt-0 men of the mind of God. Of course, in this case, as in the previous cases, there is only an approximation to the understandin~ of God's mind and will as thus revealed. Dut we are progressing steadily towards the ideal of perfect light and perfect submission. 'l'he Churches may but imperfectly grasp what God in Christ means; they may be very wayward a.nd arbitrary in many of their interpretations; but the desire t-0 know and obey Christ brings them along the line of pri,ilege and duty with increasing appreciation and success. re h, CHRIST'S BECONCILUTION OF ALL THINGS U:STO GOD HE FURTHER REVEALS TO THE m.'IVEBSE TITE Mn.-» OF Go». (Vers.18-20.) Now, just as philosophy is the reduction of the multiform in fact to the uniform iu idea, so is there in the system administered by Christ provision made for the reconciliation of all thincrs to the Supreme, that the unity of all things may be the last thought of God. This is the meaning of the cross and the blood shed upon it, and all the redemptive system which centres around it. This is the purpose of Christ's resurrection to immortal life the first, that, as t!Je pre-eminent One, he might gather in his embrace a reconciled universe and lay it at the Father's feet. Of course, the prerogative of creaturely freedom is such a.s to refuse the reconciliation and to crystallize into hostility in some sad cases. It would be contrary to the Divine plan t-0 force the will and ride rough-shod over the determinations of the create.re. Some consequently, it would seem, are t-0 be allowed to take their own course and remain incorrigible ; yet in the unifying idea of God their discord, as in the music of the great masters, will be made t-0 contribute to and to emphasize the general harmony. Meanwhile, how grand the idea is of the unity of all things! Surely we should not allow ourselves to conflict consciously with it in our dealings with men. We should back it np as the goal and far-off Divine event to which all things are made to move. The blood of the crosa cries really for the reconciliation of the universe to God.-R. M. E.

entries.title: COL 1:21–29
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-771e indwelling <Jh:rut the believer's Hope of glory. The apostle now passes from the general idea of the reconciliation in Christ of all things, t-0 its particular application to the Colossians. We may allow the idea, by its very vastness and grandeur, to Lecome indefinite. We need, therefore, to see its application t-0 the individual soul. Paul consequently briD"'S the reconciliation home to every heart. And here we notice-- L THE Cor.ossuNs' ;ATUBAL STATE. (Yer. 21.) '!'hey were" alienated," and the alienation passed itito downright enmity, which manifested itself in "wicked works." Not only were they alienated from God, but from one another and even from themael ves. For sin is such a separating power that it not only cuts us off from God and from our fellow-men, but aleo from ourselves, so that we are divided and dissipated in the faculties and energies of our souls. Hence we find ourselves incurring, not only the Divine anger and the anger of our fellows, but we become angry with ourselves. It will be seen therefore, that the rP.Conciliation needed is a very wide one. IL 'IHEI~ GRACIOUS BEOONCILIATION. (Vers. 22-2i.) 'l'he reconciliation bas been brought about at no less a cost than the death of the Son of God. It must be precious. Alld now we are to notice how real it is. For just as the alienation and enmity have beelt towards God and men and self, so the reconciliation brings us into unity with God, unity with men, and unity with self. We are reconciled t-0 God; we are reconciled to our fellow-men; we are n,couciled to ourselves. 'l'his is secured by Christ's indwelling, so t1at he becomes our Hope of glory (ver. 27) and the Source of that holiness and bla:n..,ekssnei!il which are the characterii;tics of redeemed men. Let us look at this OU, I, l-2U.J 'l'JIE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. 15

roconcili11tion through 11tonement and indwelling. 1. We are reconciled to God by it. The Divine hatred to sin found fitUng outlet in the cross of Jesus, and in consequence Ohrist's Spirit comes and dwells in the believer as the Source and Fountain of a holy character. 'l'he inspired, Christ-inhabited soul becomes the object of restored fellow~hip ond complacency; God looks down in love, and he and man are one. 2. \Ve :1rc reconciled to our fellow-men by it, 'l'he indwelling Christ leads us to peace-makinf{, and we refuse to continue at war with those around us. \Ve rather rejoice in thu assurance thnt the atonement and inspiration of Christ are intended to bring abo11t peace and concord among men. 3. \Ve are reconciled to ourselves by it. For in si11, as we have seen, we are divided and dissipated; but grace comes and we are united fo fear God's Name. We doubtless battle with our sins, but we realize that this is tho way to regain our truCJ selves and put internal discord away. III. 'l'HEm EXPECTED PERSEVERANCE AND PERFECTION. (Vers. 23-28.) This faith in Christ, this body of truth through which we have been brought into such intimate relations to Christ, is that in which we are grounded and settle<l. We expect to con- tinue therein, and this is the meaning of our perseverance. Now, if Christ dwells within us by his Spirit, our progress is assured through his inspiration, and perfection in him is the goal we are to reach at last. This perfection which Paul aims at for the Colos- sians is not the imputed perfection which" completeness in him" implies, but the per- fection of sanctification which his inspiration secures in due season. Only thus are we brought into complete harmony with the universe of God. IV. THE APOSTLE'S PAINFUL MINISTRY IN SECURING THIS, (Vers. 24--29.) As the minister or servant of the Colossian Church, he had taken "pains " to instruct them properly. In this respect every good and noble work is painful; unless we take pains we cannot do it well. But over and above this, Paul was called upon to suffer special trials. He was a prisoner at this time at Rome. He was a suffering member in Christ's mystical body. Now, one member often suffers in the interests of other members. The atouement of Christ was the suffering of the Head in the'interests of all the members. In this none of the members can have any share. But Christ's afflictions had a wiuer meaning than simply atonement. He was perfected in experience by them, so as to be sympathetic in a degree impossible otherwise. In this department Paul could have fellowship with Christ in his sufferings (Phil. iii. 10). Now, the Colossiaos profited hy Paul's sufferings for them at Rome. All his pain, all his agonizings for them, all the devotedness of spirit he had manifesteu. for them durin!; many years, went to make up the needful basis for their spiritual progress. If he had not suffered as be did, he could not have composed these Epistles of the captivity. 'l'o this painful mini,try all earnest souls are called. It is part of our heritage, and the experiences found within it are altogether glorious.-R. M. E.

entries.title: COL 1:1
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Address and salutation. It is common to compare the Epistle to thCJ Colossians with the Epistle to the Ephesians. Written about the same time (both conveyed by 'l'ychicus), there are many coincidences in thought. But there is this difference--that the thought in this EpistlCJ does not centre round the Clmrch of Christ (the word occurs only twice, as compared with nine times in the Epistle to the Ephesians), but round the Person of Christ. '!'here is also this difference--that this Epistle has not the catholic form of the Epistle to the Ephesians, but has a certain controversial form, with reference to the peculiar state of the Colossian Church. In order to understand the Colossian heresy, it is necessary to bear in mind that the type of religion to which the Eastern mind was inclined was mysticism. One feature was the belief in a'good and a bad principle (Isaiah refers to them as light and darkness), the latter having its abode in matter. Another feature is the postulation of emanations, or intermediate agencies bCJtween heaven and earth. 'l'his mysticism seems to have had congenial soil in Phrygia, to which Colos."18 belonged. It had an ascetic side (communication with matter being to be oschowe<l), an<l, readily combining with Judaism, it formed Essenism. In the Galatian Churches it was Judnism that was strngglin,:; to modify Christianity. In the Colossiau Church it was rather this Essenism that was tLe modifying elemeut.. The modification of Christianity by Eastern philosophy (its fir.ding a place for redemption and the Person of Christ) was afterw.ird known as Gnosticism. L ADDREBB. 1. The writers. "Paul." He is the principal miter. The thou.;lit 46 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [err. 1. 1-29.

has n dislinrtivcly Panlino character. We cannot mistake its coming from tho writer of thC' E1•ist.le to the Ephesians. He hllS a relation to two personalities, who are yet one (Jesus being the Christ of God). (1) Bis relation to Christ. "An apostle of Christ Jesus." That gave him unquestionable authority in all matters which ho dis- cus.sod. He gave the mind of Christ. He was under tho infallible direction of the Spirit. And bis statements were to be accepted in the face of all statements lo the contrary. (2) Ht'~ ,·elation to God.. "Through the ,vill of God." It was not that ho had light in himself more tha.n any ordinary writer. It wns simply that God (Tmciously willed that he should communicate the mind of Christ to them and to oth~rs. And that 'ITTI.S his support in every word he dichted. "And Timothy." He is subordinated to Paul in the ·nitin~ of the Epistle; and his personality is, after a few introductory Yerses, lost sight of. He is brought into relation, not directly to Christ or God but to the brethren. "Our brother." A member of the Christia.n brotherhood 'l'imotby was. And that really contained more in it (title to everlastiug life) than "apostle" by itself. "Aposlle" would cease, but "brother" would remain. Apostle thouah Paul was io n brotherly way he consulted with Timothy regarding the Church of Colossre. Th: ground of his consulting with him would naturally be his acquaintance with that Church. That active brother, it may be presumed, bad ministered to them and had won their affection. entries.title: COL 1:3–8
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Pauline Soritcs. I. TrrAx1-:smv1xr., This forms a s11itable introduc- tion (in Ephesians tl10 apostle starts with a sublime but less pcrwnal doxology). 1. The facts of tl1anlcs_qivi11g, There may ho said to be two facts, but the other is subordinated to this (which accordingly is nssignecl the first place), "We give thanks to God the Father or om Lord Jesus Christ." In this exercise Timothy was conjoined with Paul. Ileing o. thing about which they were agreed, they could thank God, not only separately, but unitedly. This is a holy partnership on which God looks down with special pleasure. Where did they go to with their thanksgivings? It was to the First Source, through the Second Source. Ottr Lord as the Saviour anointed (Jesu., Olirist) dispenses blessings; but he has got them from the Father (" He has received gifts for men"), and therefore we trnce them up, in other3 as well as in ourselves, through Christ to his Father. "Praying always for you." This is stated to show the abundance of his opportunity for thanksgiving. He was always praying for the Colossian Ohurch as for other Churches. This was one form which his care for all the C'hurches (a daily care) took. And Timothy, it seems, was not behindhand, but was copying the comprehensiveness of his instructor. And as, in their like-mindedness, they had daily prayers together, when they came to thanksgiving ColosslB was never forgotten. 2. On what their thanksgiving iuas founded. "Having heard." He (Paul) was not (never had been) an eye-witness of the Church at Colossai, but his ear was open to all information from that quarter, by Colossian visitors, or by special deputy (from himselO, or through less direct channels. Timothy (with his many movements and, we may suppose, missions of inquiry) had probably been at Colossal, but his knowledge, too, had been added to by hearing. And, as the two talked over matters, they found subject for thanksgiving. It is one reason for our extending our knowledge of missionary operations (not confining them to one society or field) that, by doing so, we get a multiplicity of subjects for thanksgiving. 3. For what specially they thanked God. (1) Faith. "Of your faith in Christ Jesus." It was faith (subjectively) that made them a Church. When Paul and Timothy thanked God for the faith of the Colossians, they had in view the activity or their faith. It was not only there (that is supposed in their being addressed as "faithful brethren"), but it was strongly operating. The clement in which it operated, and in which it admitted of endless expansion, was Christ Jesus (a saving element being in him that was inexhaustibltl). (2) L6ve. "And of the love which ye have toward all the saints." Their love to be thus signalized must have been more than ordinarily active. There is a vague kind of love which does not amount to much. If it is really the Christian principle of love ( of the thirteenth chapter of 1 Corinthians) and if it is sufficiently active, it will show itself, not only in ihe absence of jealousy, but in the presence of positive interest. These Colossians did not confine their affections within their own circle, but let them go out toward all the saints. They acquainted themselves with the condition of other Churches, and in many ways were helpful to them. Faith and love are here referred to generally, but when Paul and Timothy gave thanl,s, they would be able to fix upon this and upon that as evidencing the reality and vitality of their faith and love. II. THE LOVE (wmcll FORMED MATTER OF THANKSGIVING) WAS CA.USED DY ROPE. "Because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens." This hope had a certain objective character. It wns something outside of them which was sately laid past for their future enjoyment. At the same time, it had a certain subjective character. Jt was something operating within their own breasts. 'l.'hey were kind to the saints of their day (without except.ion). Why? Because they looked beyond the present. The time would come when (removed from under earthly conditions) they would meet them in the heavens. They might get no reward here (their catholicity might bring them persecution), but it would be reward enough to see there those whom they had done their duty by, and to receive from Ohrist words of approval. It was because of this hope, then (so sure), that their love flourished. III. 'l'nE HOPE WAS COMMUNICATED IN THE GOSPEL. "Whereof ye heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel." We owe it to God that he has givcu us" the truth" (and the gifts of God are without repentance). We may well prize this gift of God when we think of the erroneous ideas which men (unaided by revelation) ha,e cntortained. This is the Promethean fire, not stolen, but, in in6nite love, sent down from henveD. Goel has 11laccd us under additional obligation by giving us tho truth iu THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [ell, I, 1-20,

the form of "tho Wor<l." Considering tho conditions of language and our el\rthly nC'cessitics, this form is perfect. "The Law of the Lord is porfoct." It is an abiding form. ThC're may be movements of thought away from" the Law and the testimony," but here always is the truth in the form in which God wishes us to have it, H only we can bring our minds up to it. The whole Word of tn1th is precious• but there is that which is to be regarded as singul~rly precious (being singled out hero), viz. tho gospel, or the good message, God's special mes.~ge (of a glad nature), to sinners in need of SP.lration. It was this gospel that the Colossi::.ns at a former period had heard. By this the burden of their sin had been remov,;-i, and the hope of immortality enkindled within them. IY. How THE GOSPEL (THROUGH V.iITCH THE HOP!< WAS COMMUNICATED) WAS PBE- SE?-."'l'ED. 1. There was a general gospel, movement. "Which is come unto you; even as it is also in all the world bearing fruit 1md increasing." The parting command of the Master was, "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to the whole creation [every creature]." And the command had been carried out (as time allowed) in its ,,ideness. The gospel-trumpet had been heard, not merely in Palestine, but had sounded out to all lands. And everywhere an efficacy had attended the preaching of the gospel. False forms of religion a.re limited by certain climatic conditions, by certain tempera- ments. Wba.t would do in Phrygia might not do in Rome. But the gospel (unmodi- fied) had been proved to be world-wide in its adaptation, adapted for Jew and Gentile, for Eastern and Western a.like. A.s the apostle represents it here, in all the world the gospel-tree had been bearing fruit and increasing. In a healthy fruit tree there is a double effort going on. There is an effort after f111it-producing, which is crowned when in autumn there a.re seen the ripe apples or rich clusters of grapes. But at the same time, there is a.n effort after the producing of more wood, which has a view to future fruit-producing. And so with regard to the gospel in the Church; if it is vital, then there will be produced the fruits of righteousness, the fruit of the Spirit (a rich cluster) 'A·hich is described in Galatians. And not only so, but there will at the same time be produced an increased sphere of fruit-producing. And the two processes can go on without their interfering with each other. The gospel in the Church may ba producing its rich clusters, and at the same time enlarging the sphere where such clusters may grow. 2. The movement in Oolossz partook of the characteristics of the general movement. " As it doth in you also." The gospel was as a tree ( on a small scale) in Colossre. And there, as in all the world, it was bearing fruit and increasin11:, Three fruits have already been mentioned, these the three Christian graces-faith, hope, and charity. And we may gather from the second word that the numbers of Christian converts were increasing at Colossre. And also Christians may have gone forth from Colossre to spread the gospel in other places. 3. This u·as to be accounted for by two cfrcumstances. (l) The gospel had been rightly presented to them. "Since the. day ye heard and knew the grace of God in truth." The movement is traced back to its very commencement. He (the writer, Timothy assenting) calls to mind the very day when the gospel was first preached to them. It was a red-letter day in the histo1y of Colossm (though viewed differently by some there), more famous than the da~ whe? Xerx:es halted there on his march a"ainst Greece1 or the day when Cyrus with l11s Greeks passtd through it on his march against his brother at Babylon .. It was really C~rist cnterin" the town., to take possession of those for whom he had died. And no spurious gospel had been preached to them. '!'here were spurious gospels, which cons!sted in cold moralities and riuorous prohibitions. Dut the gospel (the true gospel) which had been preached to the~ was the grar,e of God. It told of salvation wrought out, not in answer to ruan's call, but to satisfy tlie yearnings of Divine love. It was salvation offered, not to hwnan merit, but freely, on the ground of the infinite merits of the :Saviour. And this gospel (as evidence that it bad been rightly presented) they knew, from their own consciousness of salvation, to be the truth of God. (2) The gospel had ian rightly 1,resented to tl,em by Epaphras. " Even as ye learned of Epapbras." Hia cl,arnder more generaUy. "Our beloved follow-servant." He wa.s a servant of Christ (rea<ly to go anywhere at tLe Master's bidding). '!'hat was his f:(eneral fitness for ser- vic(:. 'l'L.al was what Paul and Timothy were as well as he. For he is called !h_cir "fellc,w-servant." Ar..d he was a fcllow-&errnnt whom they had learned to regard with fo,c ,·.-~rJL(:.;t aff,_cti 1Jn, His character with ~pecial i-eference to the Cl;urch at Colosue. OJI, I, 1-29,] THE EPIS'l'LE '1'0 nm COLOSSIANS. 49

"Who is n faithful minister of Christ on our behalf." He repregented Christ in ministering the gospel nt Colossro; ancl testimony is borne to his having faithfully represented him. lie bad not shrunk from declaring unto them the whole counsel of God. lie bml prrached unto them grace which, while free, bore good fruit. 'We may, therefore, rega.rd him (and not Paul directly) as the founder ef the Colossian ()hurch. At the samo time, he represented Paul (and bis coadjutors). He was acting on their boha.lf. There wero friendly relations between Coloss::e and Ephesus. In connection with the sojourn of the apostle for three years at that Asian centre, it is said tbat "all thoy which dwelt in Asia heard the Word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks." Among those who had occasion to visit Ephesus during that period, and were led to hear the Word, was probably Epaphras. Converted by the apostle, we can understand him charged by him to preach the gospel at his native Colossre. And thus, though Pan! had never visited Coloss::e, yet he claimed an interest in the Church as having led to Hs formation, in having given them Epaphras. V. EPAPHRAB CONVEYED TO ROME THE TIDINGS OF THEIR LOVE (FOR WHICH Goo WAS THANKED). "Who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit." He not only had conveyed the gospel from them to the Colossians, but had also conveyed to them now at Rome the tidings of their love. It was the love for which God was thanked, and it is here characterized as "in the Spirit" (one of the two references to the Spirit in an Epistle which is largely taken np with the Person of Christ). It was a love within that sphere in which the Spirit works (and wide as it), and sustained by the Spirit. Epaphras had acted a kindly part toward them. In giving an account of matLers relating to the Colossian Church, he had not concealed what was to their credit. The whole of the allusion to Epaphras (so honourable to him) was fitted and intended to establish his influence at Coloss::e, which may have been shaken by false teachers. 'l'his paragraph, so remarkable, bears a resemblance in form to the Sorites in logic. It is a series of propositions, in which the predicate of one becomes the subject of the next, and in which in the last there is a reference back to the first. The propositions are these: 1. We thank God especially for your love. 2. Your love, for which we thank God, was caused by hope. 3. 'l'he hope, which caused your love, was communicated in the gospel. 4. 'l'he gospel, which communicated the hope, was rightly presented by Epaphras. 5. Epaphras, who rightly presented the gospel, gave us tidings of your love (for which wo thank God). These propositions (if with some loss of clearness, yet with gain of force) are (with considerable detail) all compacted by the apostle into one unbroken paragraph.-R. F.

entries.content:
-Prayer leading up to the Person of Christ. L M.AKIXG REQUEST. 1. Impulse under which request was made /01· the Colossians. "For this cause we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray and make request for yo1L" It was formerly praying and giving thanks; it is now praying and making request. (1) It was an impulse with a sufficient cause, viz. the same which led to the thanksgiving. It was an impulse, not founded on fiction, but on matter of fact, on well-accredited testimony. Information received regarding the faith and love of the Colossians had led to praying and thanking God on their behalf. This information also (such is the force of "also," it is wrong to connect it with" we") led to praying and makin~ request on their behalf. (2) It was a united impulse. We; i.e. Paul and Timothy. So that here it is literally the carrying out of the Lord's words, "If two of you shall agree on earth, as touching anythin~ that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven." (3) It was a well-sustained impulse. It did not spend itself in a day (as is sometime3 thi> case); but, commencing with the clay when the first hearing ba.d taken place, it batl continued without interruption and was still operative. How much, then, did all this represent of availing prayer, of influence going forth on behalf of the Colossian Church I Illessed is the Church tha.t has two such men from da.y to clay mingling th(lir prayers together in its interest. 2. For what request was made. (1) For know- ledge. 'l'horo is the same notable 1)0tition in the Epistle to the Ephesians and in tht-> Epistle to the Philippianli. '!'here can be no doubt that the apostle was the friend of enlightenment. If ignornnco is the mother of superstition, then knowleuge is the mother of truo religion. (a) It ls a request for progressive knowledge, "'l'hat ye may bo filled with tho knowlcdgL·." \Vo nro not born with our minds full of knowledge. COLOSSI ANS. E 50 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS, [OH, I, 1-20,

Tiather a_rc our minds _like empty ~ssels that need to be filled. There is our capacity of kno,nng, o,·er agin_nst the_ Vl\.Stness of the knowable. 'l'his filling proce~s begine ~oon, nnd the prayer 1s that 1t may go on toward fulness. (b) It is a ,·equest for the tr°!'re~ive_ 1.-no_wledge of ~od's will. "OC his ·will." 'l'his is very wide as it stande. H 1s by his will that thmgs hllve been made as they are made. And, therefore, this !nay be t.nken ~ a prayer for the nd_vn.nce_ of_ sci?nco. It is not by his will that he 1s, or that be 1s love, or that there 1s 11, d1stmct1on between ri<>ht nnd wron"'. Dut it is his will thnt we should justly conceive of him, and that we should net in a bmnnner consi~tent ,vith his holy character. It is by his will that Christ became our Substituto and died for our sakation. And it is his will that we should believe on Christ and as we shall presently see, take after him in our characters. (c) It is a reg_uest for 'the 7,rogressive J."Mwl.edge of God's will within the spiritwil sphere. "In nil spiritual wisd~m. and ~n_dersta~ding." In Eph~ans "wisdom" is _c:mjoined with "prudence;" here 1t 1s conJomcd with "understandmg." We arc happily in the position of having exact definitions of these three words. Aristotle, in his • Nicomacbean Ethics,' treats of them at length. A.11 are characterized as intellectual virtues. "Wisdom" is conversant "·itb nniversals, or things eternal and immutable. "Prudence" and" understanding" are conver&nt with particulars, or dc:tails, or applications of principles or tbin"'s about which deliberation is needed. Prudence is :practi,caJ, (bas to do with lines of action, what is to be done or not to be done). Understanding is critical (has to do with processes of t,hought, how things are to be viewed or not to be viewed). 'l'his account of the three .vords is quit.e in accordance with Pauline usage. "Wisdom" has evidently with Paul to do with the everlasting verities-the character of God, the principles of his govern- ment, the mystery of redemption. And "understanding" has to do with subjects of thought which admit of doubt and which have to be presented in their relations to the great entities. .And his wisdom and understanding are of the spiritual kind, such as unspiritual men are stranger.. to. There must be a penetrating with the Spirit if we would rightly apprehend et.emal principles and understand their application to subjects that come up for consideration. .And it is this that is asked for the Colossians as necessary for the filling with the knowledge (the clenr, certain, experimental know- ledge) of God's will (2) For the Ohristian form of character. This is emphatically here the will of God., the knowledge of which is asked. (a) Generally. It is a request jar a worthy Ohristian walk. "To walk worthily of the Lord." Christ is Lord; we are his servants. And we are like those servants whose cars were bored, as bound to serve this Master for ever. He is no common Master; for (in connection with his doing of God's will) it is said that his ears were bored. Oonduct worthy of him, then, how shall we get the conception of it, and, when we have got the conception, put it into execution? "Unto all pleasing." It is implied in this language that be is uninterruptedly observant of our conduct, and that he forms an estimate of it as we proceed-an estimate which must be according to truth. It is implied also that, if we wonld bring our conduct up to what is worthy of Christ-, we must seek his universal approval, we must seek to please him in every moment that we live, in every step that we take. (b) Under a spe,ewl, aspect. (a) It is a request for progressive fruitfulness following "¥111- progressive knowl,ed,ge. "Bearing fruit in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God." It it better to read, "by the knowledge of God." The advantage of this translation (which is grammatically correct) is that "knowledge" is used a.s before, viz. as that which leads to good conduct as its fruit-. There is a taking up here of language which has already been employed. It was said that the ~ospel-tree was bearing fruit and increasing in Colossre as in all the world. Now, Uhristians are trees, whose fruit is every good work. A. work is good which has Christian principle in it. If for the sake of Christ we are industrious, eager to learn, contented, slow to anger, humble, ready to give up what is hurtful,-then we arc fruitful in good worb. Especially are we fruitful in good works if, after the example and for the sake of Christ, we live for the good of others, try to make all around us happy, are kind to the poor, pity the sinful. If a tree is in a healthy stal(,, it not only bears fruit, but increases (in wood) so that it bears more fruit another year.
