However our outward position may be altered, our inward position is to remain unaltered. Result. "Grounded." "My soul bath found the steadfast ground." ,v e try other foundations, only to find them insuffi- cient. ·when wo have got past our own doings and the services of the Church down to Christ, then we feel that we havo found the immovable Foundation, tbo steadfast ground for our being. ".A.nd steadfast." .A building even by its own weight getH steadied when it is upon a secure foundation. So by faith are we to get steadied upon the Foundation. We aro to become like the Foundation. The immovableness that is in Christ is to come up into us. (2) In hope. "And not moved away from the hope of the gospel." Believing in Christ we have hope toward God-we have hope in view of the future. We have hope of being presented holy and without blemish and unre- provable before God. 'l'his is the hope communicated in, evoked by, the gospel. From this hope we are not to be moved away (which is the negative corresponding to the positive connected with faith). We are not to be of two moods, hoping and desponding, but we aro to keep to the one mood, hoping. Circumstances may arise • in which we are tempted to despond or despair; but our hope is to partake of the immovableness of its object. The inexcusableness of being moved away from the hope of tl1e gospel. (a) From their having heard the gospel. " Which ye heard." Left to themselves, they would have been in heathenism and its hopelessness: "Having no hope, and without God in the world," as is said in Ephesians. Such had been their melau- choly state, but by the griico of God the gospel had been preached to them in Colossro. It bec~me them, then, to present a contrast to the hopelessness of heathenism, to be inspired with the hope of future presentation and everlasting continuance before God. (b) From the universality which characterized the gospel. "Which was preached in all creation under heaven." The form of the command was: " Go ye into all the world, and 1ireach the gospel to the whole creation." The apostle, writing not many years nfter the giving forth of the command, regards its universal character as already estab- lished. lt had already obtained this seal of its Divine authorship. It was not a partial provincial thing, but, preached in all creation under heaven, it had been proved to be adapted to the wants of men. They were not, then, to abandon its peculiar hope. (c) From Pau7!s pers011al relation to the gospel. "Whereof I Paul was made a lDinister." Of this gospel, the universal bope-briuger, he had the high privilege of being a minister. He had no claim to the position. He was only Paul, one who h:i.,l been a persecutor and had obtained mercy. But the gospel was dear to him, and, iu writing to them and in introducing his personal relation to them, he puts that forward as a reason for their not being moved away from their hope.-R. F.

entries.title: COL 1:24–29
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Paul's sujfel'ings. " Now." This is tho counecting word, and serves to bring down the time from the past (when he was made a minister) to the present wheu ho contemplates his sufferings. I. HE REJOICES IN ms SUFFERIN0S, BECAUSE THEY WERE FOR THE BE~EFIT OF THE CoLOSSIANB. "I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake." He adopts a triumphant key with regard to his sufferings. He is nut merely reconciled to them, but ho finds them a sphere in which be has occasion for rejoicing. He does not rejoice in them as suffer- ings, for they w~re no more pleasant to him than to others. Nor does he rejoice in them here because they were helpful to self-discipline. Dut he rejoices in them because they were beneficial to tho Colossians. Ile "·as suffering as a witness to the gospel. 1. His sufferings may have been as prayel's, 'l'he Lord looking down on them, in response to them, may have showered blessings on the Colossians. 2. His sufferings may have been as the sending of the gospel to them. Because he stood in the breach, others may have been left free to give them tho go,pcl. 3. ll-is sufferings may hcl"ve been as a ~timulus to them. Because he was courageous in enduring sufferings, th~ir courago may have been strengthened. !I. HE REJOICES IN HIS SUFFERINGS BECAUSE TIIEY WERE CONNECTED WITU THE AFFLICTIONS OF CHRIST, ".And fill up on my part that which is lacking of the afliic- tions of Christ in my flosh for his b<Xlv's sake.'' '!'he language employed is very remnrk- 58 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cu. I, 1-20.

ablC'. "Tiiat which is lacking" is properly "deficiencies." ThG word is distributive --{)DC cl,•ficicncy after another, The verb which governs "<lcfie.,cncics" is n doublG c0mr<>und. The simple verb would give this mcanina, "I fill the deficiencies of the ~mictions of Christ." The single compound would give this meanin::! "I fill up the deficiencies of the afflictions of Christ" (stress being laid on the fact tI;nt whnt the a_postle suppl!ed in suffering aft.er suffering ~et defi~iency a~er deficiency in the afflictions. of Chnst). T~e double compound gives th1~ mcanmg, "I on. 911 y part with snlfenng after suffenng meet deficiency aft.er deficiency on the part <if 0/lt'ist in his aftlictions" (stress being laid on the opposition of persons), Protestant commentators (with the exception of Dr. Lightfoot) seem to have settled down into regard.in"' the ajfficticns (!.f Ohrist as those endured by Christ in the sufferings of his people. It is quite script.urn! to identify Christ with the sufferin~s of his people (Matt. xxv. 31-46) • but the bringing in of this identification (with nothing in the language to point to it) hr.s the effect of obscuring the antithesis between the two persons to which the lo.no-uage i;i,cs prominence. It is more natural, then, with Dr. Lightfoot, to adopt the R~man Catholic exegesis, and to re,,<T&rd the afflict.ions of Christ, not as those which he endures mystically in the Church, but as those which he endured personally in his day, He did not complete these so as to preclude his people suffering after him; but Paul and others, with suffering after suffering, were meeting deficiency after deficiency in them. 'l'he Roman Catholic conclusion from this is that saints, by the merits of their sufferings, supplement the merits of the Saviour. But that is an utterly un-Pauline idea (coming in after Christ and making up the deficiencies of his merits), and certainly it is not borne out by the language which is employed here. 1. The sufferings of the apostle can be classed with the sufferings of Christ as aiftictive (not meritorious). In 2 Cor. i. 5 it is said that the su1ferings of Christ abounded to the Corinthians (or overflowed on them). If our snfferings are the overflo\\;ngs (or surplus) of the Master's snfterings, then they are in the same class, only, however, under the aspect in which they are presentea in that passage as sufferings for which consolation is provided. The exclusion of meritoriousness is secnred here by the use of the word "afflictions" (not '_'cross," or "ci.eath," or "snffering of death"). It is trae that in all his afflictions (and not merely in his ci.eatl,) l,e was accumulating merits for his people. Bnt it is qnite consistent with that to regard ti,em separately (compared with ours) as providentially appointed. 2. The sufft:rings of the apostle can be classed with the sufferings of Christ as edifying (not meritorious). There is a generalization of the previous thought. The sufferings Gf tbe apostle were edifying, not merely to the Colossians, bat to the body of Christ, which is the Church. They were as prayers, as the sending of the gospel, as stimulus fur the whole body of the faithful. Even we at this day are sharing in the benefit. And, though Christ by the meritoriousness of his sufferings actually gave rise to the Church, yet we can separate (for the sake of comparison) the edifying aspects of them. IIL HE REJOICES IN HIS BUFFEllINGS BECAUSE THEY WERE CONNECTED WITII HIS OFFICE. 1. He was a minister of the Ohurch. " Whereof I was made a minister." It is consonant to a Christian to suffer loss that others may be advantaged, It is cert.a.inly consonant to a minister of the Church to be afflicted (in soul and in body) that. othcr8 may rejoice. He is not so much the holder of a benefice as one who wears himself out for souls. It is said of the greatest Minister of the Church that he came uot to be miniskred. unto but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many. And Paul. in the B1Jirit of service, was closely assimilated to Christ, He was sowing that others might reap, labouring that others might enter on his labours. 2, He was ci,arged with tJ-.e ,,,,y6tery relating to the Gentiles. " According to the dispensation of God which was given me to yon-ward, to fulfil the Word of God, even the mystery which Lath been hid from all ages and generations: but now hath it been manifested tc Lis saints." .A.E, a minister of the Church, he held an office of trust. He was a. steward i[l tLe Louse of God. His office was of Divine appointment. It had reference to the Colossi.ans, but not to them exclusively, only to them as representatives of the Gentile wc,rl_d. fo this office be was charged. to fulfil (to complete the round of) a Divine dcehratiun. 'l'his was the mystery bid from the ages and from the generations (making up tl,e a~c:.,), but ruanifost.ed (brought into the clear light) to the saints of that day. 3. :I'i,i& r,,y&terv was a vlorwu., munifebta,tion. known wh(\t ie the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which i~ Christ in yon, the Hope ?f glory." '!'here is glory in nature; the sun is a glorio11s object. 'l'horo was glory In the Mosaic economy (with all its limitatior.1s). But in thi, mystery God was pleased, and had it in view, to make known the riches (the highest form, the greatest ailluence) of glory, This was a display such as was not given elsewhere. 'l'he sphere of this display was among the Gentiles. The darkness of the backgrouncl, therefore, added to the glory; but it was a glorious thing in itself. It is here described as "Christ in yot:, the Hope of glory." Stress is not to be laid on "in you." The first meaning is" among you," and" in you" only comes in under that. 'l'he stress of the thought is to be laid on this-that to them, in the hopelessness of heathenism, Christ came as the great Hope-bringer. In Christ ( not in his doctrine here, but in his Person) they had the forgiveness of sins, they had the beginning of redemption. Ilut what they had of Christ was only the earnest of what they would yet have. What they looked forward to in the future with hope was glory (differing from the glory previously mentioned only in that it respects persons and not things). This glory is to be thought of as the highest efflorescence of our being, from the Christ within, which is synonymous with full redemption. 4. The breadth of his duties !M charged with the mystery. "Whom we proclaim, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ.'' There was the broadest of all subjects, viz. Christ, who has already been presented as the First, the Midst, the Last, in the universe and in the Church. This Christ they spoke of, not in a whisper (or only to the initiated), bnt proclaimed that men widely might hear, This bold presentation of Christ was not one-sided. There was the preparing the way for Christ in admonishing (showing the need for repentance and urging to repentance), and then, as complementary to that, there was the building up in Christ in teaching (presenting Christ for faith in his qualifications and in his work). And in this they observed a universality; for it is said, with the emphasis of repetition, "admonishing every man and teaching every man.'' And having emphasized" every man," it is added (still having respect to universality)," with all wisdom." It was a point with the Gnostics that wisdom was to be kept back from the many. According to the apostle's teaching, there was no oligarchy of intellect (the few who had perception). There were no exclusive possessors of the Divine wisdom. 'l'here was universality in the Divine offer and intention. Another point with the Gnostics (as with others) was that only the few, the select spirits, could come to perfection; the many must be content with a lower attainment, a lower heaven. But the apostle did not go upon such principles. He saw perfection (the highest form of human existence) opened up for every roan in Christ (the ideal Man), and therefore he sought to present (under God, to whom pre-eminently it belongs to present) every man perfect in Christ. 5. The spirit in wliich he discharged his duties. "Wherennto I labour also, striving according to his working, which ·,rnrketh in me mightily." There is a recurrence from" we" to" I'' (with individualizing effect). '!'he apostle introduces a favourite metaphor of his. He painfully exercised himself in training for the conflict, and then he went down to the arena and engaged iu the conflict. Thus he comes back to the sufferings with which he started. The proclamation of the gospel (so broad) was a proceeding with painful accompaniments. But, iu the midst of all, he rejoiced because be was not left to his own strength, bnt was supernaturally supported. 'l'bere was an unseen Master beside him, nerving him as he laboured (in training) and strove (in the lists) ; and so he laboured and strove, not according to his own poor working, but according to his (Christ's) working that worked in him mightily,-R. l~.

Introduction. Throughout this Epiolle St. Paul is dealing with the twofold evil that had arisen in the Colossian Church-an error half Judaic, half Gnostic; an error that was theological and practical. It arose from the wrong conception of matter as inhHently evil, and as consequently demanding intervening me,liators between the material system of things and God, and as making abstinence from contact with material things, as far as might be possible, very incumbent on the godly. '!'his error has its modern analogies in sncerdotnlism and in pietism. To combat the error then and now the plenitude of Christ must be preached-Christ the Fulness; therefore the ailsufficient Mediator; therefore, too, the all-sufficient Consecralor of the matefril system. GO THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [OR, I, 1-29,

The errors of the ritualist and of the recluse are both met by this great fact of the }'lcnitude of Christ.-U. Il. T.

Vers. 1, ~.-The apostolic salutation, Pondering this salutation, we ask nbout it three questions. I. WHAT IT REVEALS ABOUT TRE APOSTLE. It indicates: 1. Hia dignity. 11 An npo_stle . . . by the will of God." This was a title (1) divinely derived ; (2) directly dcnved from God; (3) abundantly ;'usti,.fied, (a) by supero.atural visionsaud experiences, (b) by seals of success. This ti tie was used here, though not in his salutation to all the Churches, because here (1) he was dealing with error and erroneous teachers and so needed a claim of authority; (2) he was personally an entire strnncrer t~ the Colossians; (3) he writes from prison, and it was well he should remind himself and them or his trne dignity. He was a prisoner, yet none the less nn apostle, 2.. His condescension. " Timolheus our brother." He was no fellow-apostle, yet his brother ; he was his boyish, not to say childish, convert, yet his brother. Great souls never patronize; they elevate true men, of whatever station or a:ze, into brotherhood with them. The GrPatest said, " I have called you not servants, but friends." "Ho is not ashamed to call them brethren." II. WHAT IT rnPLIEs ABOUT THE CHURCH. It recalls to us: 1. Its locality and its associations. One of the historic Churches in the valley of the Lycus ; the town, too, had been famous, though its glory was waning. Xerxes and Cyrus had made it famous, but Paul's letter has made its name known where Xerxes and Cyrus have never been heard of. 2. Its character. This indeed ought to be the character of every Church. For its members were: (1) "Saints." The Old Testament description of Israel thus npplied to Christians to indicate their union with God. (2) "Faithful brethren." Indicating their union with each other. All free-masonries, guilds, etc., are but hints or what the Church is meant to be in this aspect of it. nr. "'HAT IT SUGGESTS .AllOUT TRUE DLESSEDNESS. "Grace and peace" is Panl's customary greeting; it is a blended Greek and Hebrew salutation. It expresses the Apostle's best wish for a Church. What is it? 1. " Grace." It is a Greek thought Christianized. It takes the conception of grace of Corm, of gesture, of tone, into the spiritual realm. It has on Paul's pen and lips two meanings. (1) It is to be enjoyed as the attitude of God in Christ towards men. It is thus the Divine pity, gentleness, favour, the bearing of a forgiving, condescending, loving God. That is infinite grace. (2) It is to be possessed as the spirit of a. Christian. It is thus "the grace of life"- moral beauty, spiritual loveliness. It is the indwelling in human character of more than all that the Greeks conceived in their "three Graces." 2. "Peace," It may include: (1) Freedom from persecution, then a great desideratum. (2) .Absence of internal dissemion. This was the one main purpose of his letter. (3) Inward calm of heart and quiet confidence in God. This is ideal peace. Christ's peace and the wish of Paul is the gift of Jesus; for he said, "My peace give I unto you."-U. R. T.

entries.title: COL 1:9–14
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The apostolic prayer. The maxims of the Church ns well as those of the world often throw a glamour round much that is worthless-a glamour that stirs our desire of possession. But neither the world nor a worldly Church can teach us what is really worth aiming at, struggling after, praying for. A man like Paul can. What he asks for it must be good to have. His prayer may well guide us. We ought to wish for what he sought for Christians; and, more than that, we are encouraged to hope for it. He prays- I. 'fHAT THEm KNOWLEDGE MAY mcnEASE. Partly because of the error by which many of the Colossian Church were being misled, but also because increase of knowledge is good for any Church, Paul here says he prays for it, and even at times afterwards urges it on them. No Greek had more veneration for the blue-eyed Athena, no Roman for wondrously equipped Minerva, than Paul had for knowledge. There are three expressions here to describe this knowledge, expressions that are very often used in combination both in the Old and New Testaments. They describe, generally, the science, the philosophy, and the art of religion. 1. Knowledge, which in the Greek is not the simple word for knowledge, but intensified, large, and thorough knowledge. In this case full acquaintance with the Law of God, the precepts of Christ, the doctrine of the apostles, which is essential as a beginning, a basis of Christian culture, but is only a beginning and a basis. 2. Wisdom, which is higher than knowledge and includes both knowledge and understanding. It is not mere additional information, the acquaintance with moro facts, or even more laws, or even more principles. Wisdom is digested knowledge, knowledge wrought into a system; or, as Cardinal Newman well puts it, "reason exercised upon knowledge." In this case it is the calm comprehensive view of the information attained-information about God's Law, Christ's precepts, the apostle's doctrine. 3. Spiritual understanding, using a word that denotes the application of knowledge to detail, following its processes as applied to daily life and separate actions. It means a keen, quick understanding of the bearing of God's will on aU their conduct, all their conversation, all their life. Such a knowledge, with wisdom and understanding, would not only save the Colossians, but save us. It is, thank God, a wisdom recorded for us in Scripture, incarnate in Jesus, interpreted by the Holy Spirit. But we must acquire it. Is half an hour a day too much to give? Is earnest study too much? Is persistent prayer too much? " Wisdom is the principal thing ; . , . with all thy getting get understanding." II. '1.'hat, as the result of their knowledge, THEIR CHARACTER MAY RIPEN. This we should expect from prayer for knowledge of the will of God; not His essence, nature, attributes, but will. Religion is not a system for speculation, but for the regufation of life. What the apostle here taught, viz. that the end of all knowledge is conduct, Jesus Christ mado gloriously clear in his words," If ye know these things, happy are ye if yo do them." No more than you would be satisfied if your vines year after year only "made wood," or your apple trees simply grew in height and in far-reaching branches, would St. Paul or Christ, the great Husbandman himself, have been satisfied if there had been only mental growth, intellectual growth-" cultllfe," as tho modern phrase isin this or any Church, Hence his prayer seeks blessing for character; he looks, as you on the vine, for clusters of the grape-for fruit.. In the description of character the apostle prays for, we notice: 1. A walking worthily of the Lord. A walk, a progress, an ac~ivity, worthy of tho follower of him who "bas left us an example that we should follow in his steps." 2. An increasing knowledge of God. So knowledge recurs, and this time it is more than a knowledge of God's will; it is a knowledge of God himself. THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cH. r. 1-29.

And all this is throucrh Cb_rist, onr !'l,ansom, our Rescuer; but now not a victo~ rescuing by force of nrm, but° a pl11lanthrop1st by payment of ransom. Thus Paul strikes the key-note of his messa"e to Colossre---Jcsu~ Chr:ist the King of the_ kingdom in which Christians already ar~; the Source of their deliverance from the gwlt and from the power of sin; Jesu1:1 Christ the Fulness, the Plenitude of God's presence and grace.-U. entries.title: COL 1:15–29
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0hrist all in all. The truth taught in our text is that Christ is all and in all, the one absolute Mediator between God and man, the only Heconciler of heaven and earth. We notice- · I. THE DIVINE PRE-EMINENCE OF CHRIST. This includes : 1. His supremacy in ,·elation to God. He is his Image, Likeness, Representation. Heathen idolatries utter the lon"- ing of the soul for him. To the prayer," Show us the Father," Christ answers," He th~t hath sren me bath seen the Father." 2. His supremacy in relation to nature. He is "the Firstborn." To all creation he stands as Heir. We notice: (1) His creative agency. Christ is the Wisdom of God; Christ is the Word of God; Christ is the Arm of God. (2) His sustaining energy. He binds all things together. (3) His consummating glory. llc is the End of creation, the Alpha. and the Omega.. As the bow of Ulysses could only be bent by its master, so creation only fully responds to the touch of Christ. 3. His supremacy in rel,ation to the Church. He is the Head. This implies sovereignty and sympath1·-vital union. We say that" the blood of the martyrs is .the seed of the Church." In an infinitely higher sense the blood of Christ is the seed of the Church. 4. HiB supremacy in relation to the Resurrection. He is "the Firstborn fron1 the dead." 'l'he risen Christ is the life of the Church. II. 'l.'HE EXPLANATION OF THIS DIVINE PRE-EMINENCE rs THE DIVINE PLENITUDE. Christ is as supreme as the apostle bas been describing because he is so full of God. He is the Ple'l"omr1. This, as Archdeacon Farrar shows, is the key-note of the Epistle. When we say this, we mean that_inJesus is found "the~totality of Divine attributes al)d powers." For in him there is: 1. Fulness of might. He is manifested in his miracles and in his own resurrection as the Lord of nature. Its forces are subject to him. 2. Fuluess of wisdom. He claims, and as far as can be these claims are verified, to reveal God and to know what is in man. He did not misinterpret the Divine nor misunderstand the human. 3. Fulness of love. God is love. But could there be an amplitude of love beyond that which is manifested in Jesus Christ? Where is the love of God and where the God of love, if not in Jesus? III. THE WOEK OF CHRIBT IN BIB PRE-EMINENCE AND PLENITUDE rs TBE WORK 01.1' RECONCILUTIO~. Our Lord is thus set forth as in his supremacy and fulness the !Treat Reconciler. This is God's purpose; nay, God's passion. But all words are faint in describin"' anv emotion in the infinite heart. The clr.ar teaching here is, not that God loves b;causc Christ died, but that Christ died because God loves. Reconciliation is the Father's desire, the Father's work. Much is left in necessary mystery, but Paul's words here answer for us two great questions. 1. What is God reconciling to himself through Christ? We must not be afraid of the assertion-" all things." By that I read all things (1) in this world's activities and institutions; (2) in human hearts aud mindi!. The whole universe of being is to find its lapsed harmony in Jesus Christ; to be set again in its riuht relation to the righteous Father. 2. How is God reconciling ali things to hirnselr"'through Jesus Christ? Such a work involves even Divine effort; such a work is worth accomplishing at e. tremendous cost, Hence "the blood of the cross," i.e. life poured out in a sacrifice ~f utmost pain and darkest shame. entries.title: COL 1:23–29
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The ministry of the mystery. In these words the apostle dwells on his own part in carrying out Christ's work of reconciling men to God. That he rloes this in no boastful spirit goes without Baying; but that he does so without any affectation of reserve or of modesty is equally plain. Indeed, he sets forth with unusual emphasis the glory of the Word the apostle has to proclaim, and the greatness of the work that proclamation involves: that Word, he shows, is a sublime mystery; that work a manifold ministry. !. THE WORK OF TRE MINISTRY IS THE PilOCLAU/llNG OF A BLESSED MYSTERY. The term "mystery," as P,tt1l here twice uses it, and often in this Epistle, does not describe what is essentially incomprehensible, but rather what was bidden but is now revealed. The gospel is a mystery, but a mystery that is to be preached fully, as Bishop Lightfoot renders the word" fulfil;" a mystery that is made manifest, a mystery into which (as the word borrowed from the ancient mysteries, in ver. 28, suggests) every man may be initiated. 1. The gospel a mystery. All religion deals with mystery. Genuine mystery is the stamp of a religious divinity; false mystery is the counterfeit superstition stamps. In its aspect towards the vast, the infinite, the Divine, religion must always have some mystery to man. 2. The gospel a mystery that was long secret from man. «Hidden things belong to God." 'l'here are hidden facts and laws in nature that science has only gradually discovered or is now only gradually discovering; hidden moral meanings in nature and history that poet's sight only can descry and poet's sonnonly describe. There were hidden things in religion that only holy men of old moved by the Holy Ghost could reveal. 3. The gospel is a mystery that is now fully rei·ealecl. ,vhatever may have been the guesses of nobler pagans, or the anticipations of patriarchs, or the predictions of prophets, all was only the pale light of very early dawn upon the bills of ancient time. It was noon when Christ lived, taught, died. The seal was broken, the secret was revealed. What secret? 4-. The gospel is the revealed secret of GoO:s.'IJITl,iversal redeeming love. Christ is fully proclaimed. And Christ is the Mystery. In him are all the treasures, all the wealth, of God stored away. (1) .All the mystery i~ revealed in Christ. As the rainbow has all possible colours in its wondrous arc, as the fabled music of the spheres has all possible tones in its chord, so in Christ is all the wisdom, all the righteousness, all the love, of God. (2) .All men may receive the blessings of this mystery. Christ, and Christ freely given to the Gentiles, and Christ freely given to be an indwelling Power in them, is the great Mystery, which, as Paul dwelt on it, made him proclaim it with newer and deepening joy. "Now," when I see the full extent of God's mercy-" now," when I ponder his mighty, all-sufficient, all-embracing love, I rejoice, not only to proclaim, but to suffer untold sacrifices in proclaiming it to men. Anything, Paul felt and said, was worth doing, anything was worth suffering, if he might but preach the whole gospel without reserve, to all men without restriction. This leads us to notice- II. THIS WORK INVOLVES COMPLETE CONSECRATION ON THE PART OF ITS MThTJ:STERS, 'rhis consecration may, indeed often does, involve: 1. Intensity of suffering. Very bold does tbo assertion of the apostle seem about "filling up what is behind of the sufferings of Christ." Were his sufferings incomplete, then? No and yes. Yes; for he left work to be done that involves suffering. There must be suffering sympathy, sufferin"' self-denial, sometimes suffering death, in carrying on the work of bringing men to G;d, This consecration will involve: 2. Mnnifoldness of labour. There is the three- fold function of the Christian worker denoted here. This consecration is the result of: 3. The highest constraint.-U. R. T.

'So had he (1 Cor. v. 3-5; ix. lG, 17; 2 Cor. ii. 10; xii. 12). We can hardly overrate the importan~e~ in the P:esent day, of maint.ai_ning the a'!-thority of all the apostles as inspired by the Spmt of Chnst to teach the doctrines of Christ, and of the authority of St. Paul among the rest. Such a consciousness of a Divine mission and authority on the part of any Christian "sent" "by the will of God" may be: I. Admonitory, '! What manner of persons ought we to be?" "It is scandalous to be compelled to say of ministers what Tacitus writes of Licinius, 'Such a torpor had invaded his mind that, unless others had reminded him that he was a prince, he would have forgotten it.'" Dr. Payson tells us that as he went about his work be could sometimes hardly restrain himself from shouting aloud from very joy, "I'm a minister of Christ; I'm a minister of Christ.'' 2. Encouraging. For if we are sent "by the will of God" to preach or teach that gospel which is "the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth," we may go and proclaim it, expecting it will be made a blessing, and making the watchword of the Crusaders our own, "God wills it." And we may emulate Paul's enthusiasm in preaching" the Word of reconciliation" (2 Cor. Y. 13-21). II. PAm's FELLOWSHIP WITH TrnoTHY. The relations of Timothy to Paul are described by various suggestive terms. 1. He was the apostle's spiritual child, his "own son in the faith" (1 Tim. i. 2; 2 Tim. i. 2). But here and in the inscriptions of oLher Epistles he recognizes him as : 2. A brother in the same "household of faith," the family of God, in which the Colossians too had their place, in which" one is your ll!aster, even Christ, and all ye are brethren." Elsewhere he recognizes him as: 3. A fellow-" steward of the mysteries of God." Well instructed from a child in the Scrip- tures, he preached the gospel at Corinth in company with Paul (2 Cor. i. 19), and .could be trusted to preach the same truth in his absence (1 Cor. iv. 17; 1 Thess. iii. 2). And he highly co=ends him a.s: 4. A devoted and most unselfish fellow-worker in the Church of Christ (1 Cor. xvi. 10, 11; Phil. ii. 19-22). Further illustrations may be found in the Epistles to Timothy. Such notices as these show the humility of the apostle. There is no pomp of office or pride of power. He acts in the spirit of bis own precept (Phil. ii. 3). He delights to honour a brother, though confessedly his inferior, by associating his name with his own, thus vouching for his fa.ith and commendi.ng him to the confidence of brethren who did not know him. IIL PA UL's ESTIMATE OF THE CoLOSSIANB, Here, as elsewhere, the ·apostle assumes that the Christian community he addresses is, in the main, worthy of the titles "saints and faithful brethren in Christ Jesus." These words imply that all who are members of a Church should be expected to be" saints," i.e. persons consecrated to the service of Christ; to be "brethren," adopted into the family of God and therefore "members one of another,'' and as brethren to be "faithful,'' to" show all good fidelity in all tbino-s" to "hold the beginnino- of their confidence steadfast unto the end." But such a cb;~ter can only be maintained "in Christ Jesus," by union with him. One of the Father5 tells us that a saint, sanctus, is so called from two words sanguinne tinctus, i.e. as it were tinged with blood, "because anciently they who wished to be purified were sprinkled with the blood of the sacrifice." The lesson suggested is valn,'\ble, though the etymology may not be correct (Heb. iL 14; x. 22). Augustine, commenting on Ps. lmvi. 2, says, "If thou shalt say that thou art holy of thyself, thou art proud; but being a believer in Christ and a member of Christ, if thou shalt not acknowledge thyself to be holy, thou art ungrateful. Say unto God,' I am holy; for thou hast sanclifi·,d n,e.'" Our names are a perpetual appeal to \lll to consecration, purity, and fidelity, co, I !-20,] THE EPISTLE ·ro THE COLOSSIANS. 65

or they o.re wHnoss against ue. H ie not enough to be called" faithful;" "it is req11ircd in stowards that a man befowndfaitliful" (Ps. cxxxix. 23, 24). IV. PAuL'B AFFECTIONATE anEETING To THEM, "Grace" is the initial good and· "pence" the final good, Grace is "the well-spring of all mercies, peace the crown of nil blessings." The old Hebrew salutation, "peace," expands under the Iio-ht and love of Christ to "grace o.nd peace" in many of Paul's Epistles, and to "gra.c~ mercy, and peace" in some of the later ones (1 Tim. i. 2; 2 'fim. i. 2; TituR i. 4). These blessings come from God our Father the Fountain (Ps. xxxvi. 9 ; Jas. i. 17); they aro treasured up in Christ the Reservoir, ever full of" living water" (ver. 19; John iv. 10, 14), and conveyed to us by the Holy Spirit as a channel; one yet manifold(" the seven Spirits," Hev. i. 4), because distributing to the necessities of each individual believer. We can wish fur one another no better blessings than God's grace and God's peace; for "in his favour is life;" "the peace of God passeth all understanding."-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 1:3–8
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-77ie thanlcsgiving. Good news from Colossre had been brought to Paul at Ilome by Epaphras. This devoted servant of Christ (eh. iv. 12) had probably been the first evangelist sent by Paul to Colossre, and the founder of the Church there (ver. 7, Revised Version). He brought also news which caused the apostle much anxiety (eh. ii. 1, 2, 8, etc.). But before he utters cautions he pours forth tbanks!siving3, We are thus reminded of two things. 1. Paul's largeness of heart. Love "rejoiceth in the truth" and" envieth not" those who have either more spiritual gifts or more temporal blessings (Rom. xii. 15). 'l'he fruit of Epaphras' ministry was a source of joy to him. He felt grateful for the gifts in money from the Philippians brought by Epaphroditus (Phil. iv. 17, 18), but more for "the love in the Spirit" of the Colossians reported by Epapbras. 2. Paul's sympathy with the mind of his Master. Christ also dictated Epistles. Wherever there is anything to commend in the Churches of Asia, the Lord mentions this before he utters a word of censure. The apostle, writing earlier, but taught by the same Spirit of Christ, pursues a similar course in nearly all his Epistles (Rom. i. 8; 1 Cor. i. 4; Eph. i. 16; Phil. i. 3; 1 Thess. i. 2; 2 Thess. i. 3). "The meeknens o.nd gentleness of Christ" enable him to praise and congratulate even the disorderly Church at Corinth. The apostle blends thanksgivings with his prayers, especially on account of that triad of graces, faith, love, hope, which elsewhere he rejoices in (1 Cor. xiii. 13; 1 'l'hess. i. 3). Their faith worked by love and was sustained by hope. Their permanent fruitfulness proved the reality of their spiritual life. We must, however, observe that the term "hope" is used here in a sense some- what different to that in the other passages quoted above. It is the object of hope (as in Gal. v. 5; Titus ii. 13; Heh. vi. 18), implying subjective hope. '!'hat "hope set before us" "we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast, and enter- ing into that which is within the veil." Following the suggestions of this figure, we may notice some of the links of the chain of spiritual blessings by which the souls of converts are connected with that anchor, and on account of which ministers may give thanks on behalf of Christians who in these respects resemble the Colossians. I. '\VE HAVE HEARD "TRI!: WORD OF THE TRUTH OF THE GOSPEL." No gospel, no hope (Eph. ii. 12). We did not come to the gospel; it " is come unto" us. The Physician. sought the patient, the Saviour the sinner (Isa. I.xv. 1; Luke xix. 10). The gospel in its triumphant progress throughout all the world reached Great Britain, an Dltima 77iule, brought by unknown missionaries who" for his Name's sake went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles." We ourselves have heard "the joyful sound," the genuine gospel, "the grace of God in truth" (Gal. ii. 6; 1 Pet. v. 12), the gospel of Christ which alone is "the power of God unto salvation." IL WE HAVE TRUSTED OURSELVES i·o CHRIST. "Your faith in Christ Jesus." We have not only heard, but we know, "the grace of God in truth." We know it because we have had a Divine Teacher. "In cmlo cathedram ho.bet qui corda docet" (Augus- tine). Our faith is the gift of God; it rests not" in the wisdom of man, but in the power of God." Thus we" know whom we have believed," etc. (2 Tim. i. 12; 1 John v. 13, 19, 20). Belief conducts to knowledge (John vi. 69). III. WE ARE BRINGING FORTH FBOIT. '\Vherever the gospel comes, i.e. comes home to men's consciences and hearts, it must be a fructifying power. "Even as it is also in o.11 the world bearing fruit," etc. Ours is not a faith whioh "ill dead in itself because it COLOSSIANS, F G6 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. ten. 1. t•-20.

hns not w<irk~;" "Can _tbnt ~-iith,s~v~ n 1~s ~J,,s. ii. 17, 11)? Ours is a II faith working thr0ngh lo,,·. The qmckcnrng :Spmt w1thm 11s will bring forth" fruit arLer his kind" (Gnl. v. 22, 23). One o_f th~ most cha~acteristic f11.1its is love. "The lo,e which yo hnve townrd all the sarnts. We chensh love toward them because in spito of nil their failings, they are bc.lo,ed children of our Father God (l John iv. 7; v. 1). IV. OUR FRUITS ARE VISIDLE AND PERMANENT. They are such as an Epnphras coulcl discern Rnrl re~o_rt. (?ur lig~1ts ~hine ; our good_ v,orks are seen ( cf. 1 'l'he~s. i. 7-!J ; 3 John 6). 'lh1s fru1t-beanng 1s prompt. "Since the day," etc. The fruit itself multiplies; the gospel is "healing fruit and increasing." Side by sido with the out- ,vard growth of the gospel (which may be illustrated by the notices of the increase of t.he Church in J udrea from the "about a hundred and twenty" to the" many myriads" of Acts xxi. 20; and from progress in our own days), there is tbo ripening of Cbristinn charncter (2 Thess. i. 8; Heb. vi. 10) and the leavening influence of the gospel on modem society. For all these things we thank God, but especially if our fruit is permanent. 'l'he gospel still u bearin_g fruit in us (Ps. i. 3). Our hearts are not tho ,;tony or thorny ground. Christ's object is being fulfilled (John xv. 16). We have not forgotten our first love; our last works are more than our first. "The past thingR perish if those things which were begun· cease to go on to perfection" (Cyprian). Growth and persistence are ea.uses for sincerest thanks. V. "TnE ITO!'E WHICH IS LAID UP m THE REA VENS" SUSTAms OUR FAITH AND LOVE. "Faith . . . and love •.. because of the hope." This hope laid up is itself one of the things "hoped for." It is a reserved blessing, part of that great goodness of Goel "laid up for them that fear thee" (Ps. xxxi. 19; 1 Pet. i. 4, 5). But the links in the chain of spiritual blessings we have examined unite our souls here to tho inheritance yonder (Rom. viii. 24, 25). Such hope maketh not ashamed (Rom. v, 5; Jude 20, 21). If our souls are not firmly moored to that object of hope "laid up for us in the heavens," let us ask-Which is the missing link ?-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 1:9–12
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Tlie intercession. The news brought by Epaphras had a further effect on the apostle. It prompted him, not only to thanksgivings, but to intercessions. In the Christian life some prayers receive definite answers and need not be repeated. But new subjects are perpetually coming before us. Thus there is a call on us to "pray (-rporr,0(.o,-) without ceasing" and to "make request (al-rloµa,)" with perseverance for definite blessings till they arc granted, and petitions are changed into· thanksgivings or are clearly refused. Note how Paul, while" in labours more abundant," fon.nd time for prayers "without ceasing" dso (Rom. i. 9; Phil. i. 4; 2 Tim. i. 3). As. a specimen of his intercessions take this prayer. The requests end with the words, "Giving thanks unto the Father," though the prayer may be said to include tho statements of sublime truth which follow (vers. 12-14), which suggest motives for seeking the blessings asked on their behalf. And the prayer itself comes to no definite end, but may be said to lose itself in adoration as the apostle unveils the mystery of the person and glory of Christ. The key to the somewhat involved clauses of the sentence is in ver. 10, "to walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing." And tho objects of the prayer are- L FULLER K};OW'LEDGE WITH A VIEW TO A MORE CONSISTENT ClIAnACTER, Paul prays that the Colossians may receive what they alreauy possess (vers. 6, !J; cf. Ps. cxvL 2; Matt. xiii. 12). The more God gives, the more we should ask of him. God's "will" includes doctrines to be believed and duties to be discharged _(cf. John vL 40; 1 'l'hcss. iv. 3). 'l'he two questions put by Paul on the day of his con version, " Who art thou, Lord ? " and "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" are the two great questions of the Christian life. An uneducated conscience is a more serious obstacle to growth in grace than an uneniightened intellect. Our "wisdom nnd understanding" need to be'' spiiitual" (Ps. xx:v. 9, 14; 1 Cor. ii. 9-12) as contrasted with " philosophy and vain deceit" and mere worldly policy ( eh. ii. 8, 18, 23). 'l'he Holy Spirit can make us discriminating as well as sensitive. The wisdom needed mo.y bo bad for the asking (Jas. i. 5). For all the knowledge gained is in order to enable us "to walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing." 'l'ho end of all knowledge is coridnct (John xiii. 17). II. A. CONSISTENT ClIARAOTEB JN ALL ITS VARIOUS ASPECTS. Three signs of Q full- OIi, I, 1-29,] 'J'JIF, EPIS'l'LE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 137 -•- - ----------------------------- orbed, consistent Christian character are mentioned in three clauses (see Greek, vers. 10-12). They nre comprehensive enough to describe a. completely sanctified life. 1. Fruitfulness. This is the natural, ns it is also the appointed, end of spiritual life (John. xv. 16); "fruit after its kind." Tittt whereas a fruit tree can bring forth only one vnriety of fruit, we are to be "bearing fruit in every good work "-all manner of fruit., like the tree of lifo in the Paradise of God. "Twelve manner of fruits" arP. said to be borne by that celestial tree. And no less than nine varieties of" the fruit of the Spirit" (note" fruit," not" fruits," unity in diversity) are enumerated in a single passage (Gal. v. 22, 23). Any manifestation of Christian consistency may be fruitful, though here the reference is chiefly to the active Christian life. While bearing fruit, we ourselves shall be "growing" and "increasing." A fruitful life is a healthy life. The "spiritual wisdom and understanding" already asked for will be means of grace and of growth, like rain and dew to the plant (Deut. xxxii. 2; Hos. xiv. 5). We shall increase "by the knowledge of God" (Revised Version, margin). Such spiritual fruitfulness and growth will be most "pleasing" to Go<l (John xv. 8). 2. Patience. (Ver. 11.) 'l'he reference here is to the passive virtues. "Patience and long-suffering" remind us of the heroic endurance and the superhuman self-restraint by which suffering Christians may glorify God. 'l'o enable us to suffer patiently and to suffer long, the omnipotence of God is put forth. His almighty and everlasting arms are placed beneath u& to prop up our poor feeble patience. So great are "the riches of his glory" and "the might of his glory," that he can enable us to endure, not only with patience, but even "with joy" (Rom. v. 3; 2 Cor. xii. 9, 10). Suffering may be as high a vocation as preaching. Notice bow our Lord, passing over all the active labours of Peter with a word (" Feed my sheep''), fixes attention on his last sufferings and death as the special means by which (in St. John's words)" he shou!tl glorify God" (John xxi.18, l!l). 3. Thanlcfulness. (Ver.12.) Some of the causes for thankfulness are brought before onr thoughts in the clauses that follow. But we need go no further than that nnme "the Father," for hallelujahs to rise to our lips. (Illustrate this from some of the Father's names," Father of mercies," "F2.ther of our Lord Jesus Christ," etc., and some of the statements respecting him-" The Father himself loveth you ; " "Your Father kncweth," etc.) Such thankfulness strengthens patience. (Illustrations: German Reformers, in times of special trouble, cheering one another by singing the forty-sixth psalm. Some Malagasy Christians, during the persecution, when meeting with the late Rev. W. Ellis and enjoying secret Christian fellowship, on one occasion said," We are so happy we must sing." Warned of the danger of being heard, they restrained themselves for a time, but soon said agaiu, "We must sing;" and they sang in a whisper. If this prayer is answered in our experience, we enjoy the three elements of a consistent and robust Christian life desc~ibed by our Lord in John xiiL 17, viz. knowing, doing, feeling : "If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them."-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 1:12–14
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The love of the Father. We have seen that the apostla's prayer loses itself in utterances of adorir.g gratitude to the Fountain of all good. In the work of our salvation we have proofs of the love of the Father (John iii. 16; Rom. viii. 32), the love of the Son (Gal. ii. 20; Eph. v. 2), and the love of the Spirit (Hom. xv. 30; Eph. iv. 30), of the one "God of our salvation." In vers. 12-H Paul reminds the ColosEians of the love of the Father, and that the blessings which this love secures to us are powerful moth•es for grntilude and for seeking to attain to that character for which he bas been praying. '!'he l>lessings which the Father's love procures for us includes four changes-a. change of place, of character, of kingdom, and of state. I. A ORANGE OF PLACE. There is an "inheritance" which bas been "prepared" and is "reserved" for us (Matt. xx_v. 34; 1 Pet. i. 5). It is not here, but "in heaven;" not here, nmid darkness ancl ignorance, "the shallow of death," and, what is worse, the stern realities of sin and of death itself; but "in light ''-note various uses of this figure (Isa. Ix. 19, 20; Eph. v. 8, 9; 1 John i. 5; ii. 8--10; Rev. xxi. 23; xxii. 5, otc.). 'l'hnt inheritance is possessed only by God's "saints," whether angelic or human. Tho sanctity needed for this inheritance is something more than that "eo11secrntion" of heart to God which even we sinrtil children of God mny cnj-oy as we 68 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [oH, I, 1-20,

render service in the lower sanctuary of" this present evil world." 'l'hc "saints in ,ight" are "without blemish," "faultless." God, who is himself" light," is our pledge, that in that mberitanee there shall be "no darkness at all," nothing "that defileth," etc, (Hcv. xxi. 27). II. A CHANGE OF CHARACTER. "Who made us meet," etc. The rtfercnce is not here to that growth in the elements of spiritual-mindedness by which we becorno increasingly filled for the employments and enjoyments of the heavenly inhoritnnco. Paul bus been praying for these (vers. 9-11); but l1ere he recognizes that tho new nature which God has bestowed on us has already qualified us "to be partakers," etc. A king's child is already, by his birth, capable of taking some part in the life and tho engagements of the palace. The penitent robber could talrn a place in Paradise on the day of his conversion. If we are partakers of the Divine nature wo are meet for the Divine inheritance. Already we are "children of the light." Our darkness is past, never to return; the light shineth, and when we change our pince it must needs be to an inheritance suited to our new natures and present characters (John xvii. 24). Without the new birth we shall be as unfit for our inheritance above as a boorish peasant, who had suddenly come to a peerage, for his new position, and as incapable of enjoying and really " inheriting" it as one who had no taste for art or sacred music would be if admitted to a picture-gallery or an oratorio; he could not "see the kingdom of God." ·what a glorious gift our new nature is I It is only by means of it we are made capable of receiving the blessings offered to us; as though a monarch could not only give us a high place in his service, but at the same time could endow us with power to discharge its duties, without which the mere position would be a bu1·dcn rather than a blessing. Thus God deals with us (2 Cor. v. 5 ; Eph. ii. 10). III. A CB.ANGE OF KINGDOMS. (Ver. 13.) 'l'he change of nature is accompanied by a twofold deliverance-we arc rescued from a lawless tyranny (ver. 13) and delivered from a lawful condemnation (vcr. 14). We speak of a change of kingdoms, for else- where we read of the "kingdom" of Satan who is "the prince of this world." But here the term suggests mere power (" the power of darkness," spoken of by Christ, Luke xxii. 53). 'l'he agents of Satan are described as "the powers, the world-rulers of this darkness" (Eph. vi. 12). We were under their power and under the tyranny of" the prince of I.he power of the air," who is at their head (Luke xi. 21; Eph. ii. 2). The mental anarchy of demoniacal possession is a fit symbol of the lawless tyranny of the kingdom of Satsn. From that tyranny the Father, with a strong band, rescued us, emancipated us, and transferred us into a Divine kingdom, of wbicl1 "the Son of his love" is the Head. LoYe is as much the essence of the only begotten Son as it is of the Father (1 John iv. 8-10). So that his kingdom is a kingdom where love is the ruling )JO'l"l"er, and where promises, privileges, and benedictions are the main motives for wearing bis easy yoke. We are made free citizens of that kingdom and shall share iu itti triumphs here and in its final glory. IV. A CHANGE OF STATE. (Ver. 14.) The kingdom which Christ established in our hearts is based on bis work as a Redeemer (Rom. xiv. 9; Phil. ii. 7-11). The pardon of sins and the translation into the kingdom are inseparable. Each blessing would be incomplete and insufficient without the other. Pardoned sinners left under the power of Satan can no more be thought of than subjects of Christ's kingdom still under wrath. We were under a lawful condemnation as well as a lawless tyranny. From that merited curse we have been ransomed by the Father's love through the redeeming work of Christ (Eph. i. 7; Titus iii. 5-,). The fundamental facts and doctrines of the gospel are all implied here (Rom. iv. 25; v. 1-11; 1 Cor. xv. 3, 4; Gal iii 10-13, etc.). We thus enjoy a change of state, being justified and no longer condemned. Note the words, "in whom," etc. Luther remarks that there is a good deal of divinity in the pronouns; so is there also in the prepositions. Christians not only receive hle~sings through Christ, but in Christ (ver. 19; 1 Cor. i. 30; 1 John v. 20, etc.); from whose fulness we receive (like the air, in which we live and move and draw our breath without limitation or restraint; not like water, supplied to us from time to time in a limited cistern). Notice too the necessity of all these four ~lcs~in~s tu us, and how absolutely dependent we are for them upon the love of God which 1s m Christ Jes\lil our Lord. Our enfranchisement in the kingdom of Christ includes free furgin[Jess, secures for Wl, by the work of the Spirit," the &anctificatiot1, without which C,11, J, 1-29.J THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSBIANS.

no mnn can seo tho Lord," nnrl ensures our admission to the heavenly inheritance. "Blessed aro they thnt wnsh their roLcs," etc. (Rev. xxii. 14; see also Acts xx. 32; xxvi. 17, 18; Rom. viii. 29, 30; Phil. iii. 20). \Vhat motives for "givina tha11k8 unto the Father" arise from the reception of such glorious gifts 1-E. 8. entries.title: COL 1:15–17
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-771e glory of tlte Son. The blessings which flow to us from the love of tho Father (vers. 12-14) are only enjoyed by union with "the Son of his love," "in whom" we are {l Cor. i. 30), and "in whom we ha.ve our redemption " and all its allied blessings. Who is this Son of God? In answering this question the npostle unfolds the true doctrine of the Christ, and meets one of the errors that was seeking o. home in the Colossian Church. The error of the heretical teachers was twofold-" They had a false conception in theology and a false basis of morals. These two were closely connected together and had their root in the same fundamental errorthe idea of matter as the abode of evil and thus antagonistic to God. As the two elements of the heretical doctrine were derived from the same source, so the reply to both was sought by the apostle in the same idea-the conception of the person of Christ as the one absolute Mediator between God and man, the true and only Reconciler of heaven and earth." The practical error is dealt with in the second chapter; the doctrinal heresy is refuted here. The false teachers seem to have believed in a variety of angelic or superhuman mediators who bad some place in the works of creation and redemption. Paul teaches that both in the universe and in the Church, in ereation aDtl redemption, Christ is the one and all-sufficient Mediatur. He alone could fill the voi,l between God and man; he alone could be the great Reconciler; and to him alone was due the homage which these false teachers were diverting to angels or other beings standing in the place which Goel claims for "the Son of his love." The apostle's teaching is "that in all things he might have the pre-eminence "-in relation to Gud; to the universe, the natural creation; and to the Church, the moral creation ( vers. 15-18). I. THE GLORY OF THE SoN IN RELATION TO Goo. "Who is the Image of the invisible God." The two chief ideas seem to be representation and revelation. Elsewhere the Son is called "the Elful~ence of his i:;lory [revelation], and the very Image of his substance [representation]" (Heb. i. 3). We may find an important application of this truth in the life and character of the Incarnate Word. Christ's words," He that bath seen me hath seen the Father," seem to require this. The Father's perfections were represented and reflected in the sinless character of the Man Christ Jesus, as the brightness of the midday sun, on which we cannot gaze, may be reflected in a lake or mirror, and under certain limitations its rays may be examined and analyze<l. Through the words and conduct of Jesus we may learn much concerning the truthfulness, the unselfishness, the indignation, and the Jove of God. But while this truth may have been a thought in Paul's mind, the truth he teaches here is part of the revel.i.tion which Scripture gives respecting the nature of the Triune Jehovah. That the term" Image" refers to the pre-incarnate Christ, we infer from (1) the creation being ascribed to him; and (2) the term "Firstborn," etc., being coupled with it-a term which includes both priority and supremacy. Notice: 1. There is that in the Divine nature v.,hich is both invisible and incomprehensible. (Exod. xxxiii. 20; John i. 18; 1 Tim. vi. 15, 16.) As we cannot see" the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" with mortal eyes, neither can we fully comprehend a Divine Being who is absolute, infinite, without beginning and without end. 2. Yet God hath been seen by mortal eyes. (Gen. xviii. 22-33; xxxii. 28-30; Exod. xxiv. 10, 11; xxxiii. 23; Josh. v. 13-15; vi. 2, etc.) And 'l:llen have learned to see God by the eye of faith, to know him as their own God. The doctrine of the Word of God, who is "the Image of God" (2 Cor. iv, 4), "the Life" and" the Light of men" (John i. 4; 1 John i. 2), is the reconciling truth. There is a glory in God which no creature can behold; but the Divine Word is a ray of that glory. There is a Divine personality which is invisible; but the Word is the express image of that Person. There is n Divine silence respecting mysLeries we cannot comprehend; but there is also a Divine" Word" which breaks the silence and reveals to us something of the infinite ano. incomprehensible (John i. 1, 14, 18). Every manifestation in time has been through liim who is "tho Imago of the invisible God." But" who by searching can find out God" eto, (Job xi. 7-<J)'t 70 nrn El'ISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. TO TIIE CREATION. This is unfol,lc,1 by f,,ur truths respecting him. 1. He is "the Firstborn qf all c1·eiltiun." In tho New 'l'estam~~1t the term." Firstbor~" is Rpplied five times !o Christ (vers. 15 aud 18; llo~1. nu. 29; Heb. 1. 6; ~~v._ 1. 5). Its use he:e figurati:cly reminds us of the place which the firstborn occupied Ji1 a lfohrew family. He is the means of all creation. 'l'he sixteenth verse confutes the notion of the Son of God being himself a creature, though the highest. He is the Creator, not of cc tho rest" of the universe, but of" all things." Who can adequately interpret that mysterious term "in him," etc.? We can only venture to snggest such truths as these: Apart from Christ there would have been no creation at all. He was the re:i.son for it. Ho was the First Cause and the Final Cause, the Alpha and the Omega of creation. The term cc in him" includes both the following truths "by him" and "for him," cc through him and unto him." 'l'he same preposition (iv), which the apostle so often uses to describe tho relations between the Saviour and his people, he here employs to teach us the relations between Christ the Creator and the universe. But these are but guesses towards an interpretation (Luke x. 21). \Ve are at any rate expressly faught that all things were created "through him" or" by him" (John i. 3); cc in the heavens" (revelations of the tele- scope, Isa. xl. 26) "and upon the earth" (revelations of the microscope, ma.king cc things invisible" become visible),-all were created by Christ. From the world of matter we turn to the world of spirits, t-0 things strictly" invisible." The false teachers may have indulged speculations as to the ranks and power and aulhority of angels. With• out discussing the subject, Paul teaches that, whoever they may be and whatsoever their authority, they arc all created by and subordinated to Christ, the "Firstborn of all creation." 3. He is tl,e ob}tct of all creation. We need not dissociate the human nature of our Lord in his present glory from the Divine nature when we reBe9t on the truth that all things were created cc for him," cc unto him." It is a sublime thought that everything in creaLlon anrl in history was planned for the glory of our blessed Redeemer. 'l'l.tio world with its mountains and lakes and cataracts, its flowers and fruits and birds, was made so beautiful because it was Christ's world. Other worlds, peopled by the heavenly hosts, "·ere created th,1t his glory might be revea!etl to them and through them. Man was created and the a:~es of history were all arranged fur him. Sin was pern,itted for him (like a dark cloud showing more clearly the glory of the rainb~w). The eternal purposes o_f redemµl}on_ and th_eir fulfilment_ in time were all for hun. What a proof of the Deity of Christ 1s supplied by comparing ver. 16 with Rom. xi. 36 ! 4-. He is the upholder of all creation. (Ver. 17.) Deing "before all tbinl7s" from the moment of creation. down to the present time, he ha<l. upheld all things by the word of hie power, and "in him all things consist," i.e. hold together. He is the Comer-stone of the uuiverse no less than of the Church. Dehind the laws of nature we sec the mind of Christ. If he were to cease to uphold things they could not "hold together;" their harmony, nay more, their very existeuce, would cease; for in him all things live and more and have their being. Dut "My Father worketh even until now, and I work" (John v. 17, 19; x. 30). All these truths respecting the glory of Christ remind us of the supreme claims over each one of us of that Divine Son who created us for his own glory and redeemed us by his own precious blood, that he mig,Lt reign over us for 0111· salvation (Acls v. 31; Rom. xiv. 7-9).-E. entries.title: COL 1:18–20
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Tli.e mpremaey of (Jhrist in the moral unii:erse. So supreme is the glory of Cli ri,t, tLat l,e cccupies a similar position in the morn! as he docs in thu

mnterial universe. We may linger on the exhnustlcss theme of the glory of Christ ns we sec further illustrations of it-- I. IN me nELATION TO THE CHURCH, 1. "He i3 tlie Ifead of the body, the OT,urch." For he is its Founder; the Church is his creation (Mau. xvi.18 • xviii.17-20). Havin" " 11II power m• h ea".en _an d earth" , h'1s glory and grace are so great ' that he ca.n sustaiu" '-l~o wh?lo ~hurch 1~ hfc, nnd rule and guide each member of it. Our life is bound up lnth his hfo; our interests nro mnde his own by the sympathy of our living Head. (Illustrate from Acts vii. 56; ix. 4; xviii. 0, 10; xxiii. 11; xxvii. 23, 24; 2 Tim. iv. 17, lt1.) 2." Wl10 is the Beginning "-the first in time and the first in power in relation to the Church. Because he is "the First and the La~t," "the Be!!innin"' of the creation of God," ho is nlso the Fountain," the Prince [or,' Author'] of life" (A~ts iii. 14) to bis Church. Every act of pardon granted, every shower of reviving grace bestowed, every interposition of Providence, is from him. (Illustrate from Jesus Christ's use of" I" ancl "mo" in John xiv.-xvi.) 3. "The Firstbornfrom the dead." He is the supreme Lord from among all who have entered the grave, by virtue of his being the first to rise to the new life from the dead. Note the contrast between the resurrection of Christ and of others. Dying voluntarily, though sinless (John x. 17, 18), he rose by his own power (John ii. 20), not to die again (R.om. vi. 9), in an immortal body (Rev. i. 18). 'l'hus he is the Cause, the Pledge, and the Pattern of our resurrection, and has supremacy over his Church in both worlds (Ilom. xiv. 0). Already we have seen that he is " Firstborn," and Lord of the mateiial creation ; and he has the same position in the spiritual creation, " that in all things he might have the pre-eminence." He is the Image and Manifestation of God, the First Cause and the Final Cause, the Creator and Preserver of the universe, the Head and Lord of the Church, the Author and Pattern of our glorious resurrection. Yes; and in all things he shall have the pre-eminence (Ps. lxxii. 17; 1 Cor. xv. 25). 'l'he day will come when commerce, science, art, literature, shall all be consecrated to him; when the minority shall become a majority, and an innumerable multitude shall "honour the Son even as they honour the Father" (John v. 23; Rev. vii. 9-17). II. IN HIS WORK As THE UNIVERSAL RECONCILER. Whichever of the alterndtive renderings of ver. 19 in the Revised Version we adopt, the precious pr::ictical truth is the same. 1'he pre-eminence of Christ is assured by "the fulness " that abicles in him. All the Divine perfections are bis (eh. ii. 9). We may take the term in its widest signification-a fulness of life and power and glory, of goodness and grace, without limit and without end. 1'hus the Man Christ Jeans, fnll of a Divine life (John iii. 34; v. 26), was qualified to be the Agent by which the great reconciliation in the universe should be accomplished (ver. 20). "'.!.'be well is deep;" the place is "holy ground." 'l'he reconciliation of "things npon the earth" is a mystery; how much more of" things in the heavens" I Notice: 1. Sin introduced discord into the universe, which spread to this earth. It not only separates men from God, but brings thereby calamities to "the whole creation." Sin left to itself works universal ruin ; "when it is full grown it bringeth forth death." God must stand in a different relation to sinners and to the unfallen. If the guilty are to be saved, a new relation must be established between them and God. This is" the reconciliation" (Rom. v. 11). 'l'he chauge in man's heart is a result, but the sequel of the change of relations established by "the reconciliation" (2 Uor. v. 18, 19). 2. To effect this reconcifri,tion a propitiatory sacrifice was nee,led. 'l'o show ~i~hteous _g_race to the guilty both the holiness and the love of God called for a D1nne sacrilice. No theory can fully clear up this myste1·y of Divine mercy; but faith accepts it and Christian experience attests it (Luke vii. 35). No sacrifice less than "the death," " the blood of the cross," could effect this reconciliation (Rom. v. 6-10; 2 Cor. v. 21). 0 paradox of mercy! 1'be shedding of human blood stirs up strife; Cbrist's blood briui~ down peace. Innocent blood cries for vengeance; the blood of the cross pleads for pardon (Heh. xii. 24). 3. But what is meant by the reconciliation of the things in the heavens Y It is not universal restoration of the devils and the damnc,I; for J:'aul is speaking of what God has already_ done by the ~)ood of t!1e cross, and i~ ver. 23 he speaks of the final salvation of believers as cond1t1o~al. 'I he passage winch best il\ustratos ours is Eph. i. 10. We can only throw out hmts as to the mcanrng. \Ve know that cmgols are iutcusely interested in the work of reLbnption (Eph. iii. 10; f2 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. ( CH, I, 1-29.

1 Pc-t. i. 12). The entrance of sin and its sprMd amona the human rnce mn.y hnve rrotlncc<l, t.hc,n~.h not distrust, yet something like dismay. Ilut tho death of Christ I:c1·cnlc<l the ml\Jesty and mercy of God as they had never been combined before. 'l'ho ,·ery fact. thl\t the lost sons of men could be "ma.de nioh" by the death of Christ brought these celestial sons of God still nenrer. 'l'he bonds which unite these unfallen yet finite creatures to God become firmer than ever, and thus the harmony of the universe becomes more complete. Such are some of the jewels in the crown of our Dh·"ine Mediator and Redeemer. , Learn: 1. The glory of the cross. Though "all the fulness" dwelt in Clirist even he could not effect a reconciliation except by death (Gal. vi. 14). 2. The eflfo~cy of the cross. Though erected on this tiny globe, its power extends throuahout 0 the universe. 3. The motives from the cross (2 Cor. v. 14, 15, 20).-E. S. P. Vcrs. 21-23.-Tlie apostle's comprehensive view of salvation. The work of Christ, though comprehensive enough_to affect the w~o\e universe, is so penetrative and personal that not a smgle human soul 1s overlooked In It. Note how Paul narrows his range of ,·icw from the universe to the individual: "To reconcile all things . . . you bath he reconciled . . . I was made a minister." But in his view of what the salvation of each individual was, there was no narrowness. In vers. 21-23 he gives us a com- prehensive Yiew of salvation. He speaks of the past, the present, and the future. I. WnAT wE WERE. "Alienated." True in an especial sense of the heathen Colossians (Eph. ii. 11, 12; iv. 17-19), we yet must not shrink from recognizing this as a description of the natural state of all sinful men who have not yet accepted the offer of reconciliation. It thus agTees with our Lord's verdict on humanity (John ill. 3). If we do not relish communion with God or conversation about him, and have no eager desire to do his will and enjoy his favour, these are clear signs of alienation, that there is a gulf between us and our Father. Such alienation does not end in mere indifference; it leads to positive enmity (Rom. viii. 7). This" hard saying" of Scripture can easily be justified in the court of conscience, and needs to be impressed on the hearts of the unconverted. They may feel a complacent regard towards a God of their own imagining, but a positive aversion to the living and true God, who hates iniquity and "is angry with the wicked every day." Are they subject to the Law of God ?-that is the test. They are not. Both hearts and acts are in antagonism to him; "enemies in your mind in your evil works." Not to speak of those sins of the flesh from which they may have been restrained, selfishness and all its kindred sins of the Spirit are sufficient proofs of the alienation and enmity of mind in its relations to God. The lamentable indifference of men to Christ and his salvation is the crowning proof of the enmity of the heart towards God (John iii. 18, lD). II. WnAT WE A.RE. "Reconciled." The work of reconciliation is twofold. Thero was a reconciliation effected on the cross (ver. 23; 2 Cor. v. HJ). There is a reconciliation still to be accomplished in the heart of every impenitent sinner (2 Cor. v. 20). For there are two obstacles in the way of complete reconciliation-the one is in the character of God; the other, in the character of man. The first arises from God's holiness; the second, from man's wilfulness. The first was removed by the work of Christ as a propitiatory sacrifice-" that he might himself be just, and the Justifier of him that bath faith in Jesus;" the second is taken away, immediately by the work of the Holy Spirit on man's heart, but mediately through the death and resurrection of Christ and all the spiritual powers that flow therefrom (John xvi. 7-11; Rom. v. 10). What a manifestation of" the riches of his grace which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence," thus to open a pathway by which a holy God might righteously make the first overtures of mercy to a reluctant rebel race I And was it not equally glorious to be able, without destroying man's freedom or doing any violence to his nature, to overcome his own unwillingness, and open a .rathway into his sinful heart for " the peace of God which passeth all understanding"? But at what a. cost this has been done! Paul never shrinks from " the offence of the cross." In the face of false teachers at Colossre and amongst ourselves, he affirms the reality of the sacrificial death of the Divine Son in whom" all the fulncss" dwelt. None but incarnate God could effect this reconciliation, and even he only "in the body of his flesh through death (Heb. i. 5-10). OJJ, L 1 -20.) 'l'HE EPIS'l'LE 'fO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS.

III. WrrAT WF: BJIALT, ~F:, "Presented fauH!ess." That the ~postle is lookin 6 forwnrd to the futuro we infer from ver. 23. He holds out before us the prospect of ntto.ining that perfection of character which we are striving to attain to, but which, as nn ideal, is perpetually risin:; and receding as we reach after it (Phil. iii. 12-14). We sbnll gain that holiness which we now" follow" (Heb. xii. 14; 1 Pet. i. 1.3--16). We sho.11 be "unblamable," or " without blemish" (a sacrificial term). The precept in Hom. xii. 1 will be perfectly fulfilled then. The confession in l Cor. iv. 3 will be needless then. We shall be" unreprovable." Now Christ must at least say," I have a few things against thee," and we confess Job ix. 20, etc. But then neither the accuser of the brethren, nor our own enlightened consciences, nor God himself, will reprove us (Rom. viii. 33, 34). And all this" before him." We shall be pure enough to bear the scrutiny and to be happy in the presence of that God whose holines~ is a consuming fire and whose presence would therefore be intolerable to a sinful soul (1 John iii, 1, 2; Jude 24, 25). But there is a condition attached. Paul describes it in terms of generous confidence:" If, as I would take for granted," etc. (cf. Phil. i. 6). There is a truth to be believed ('' the gospel"), a confidence to be maintained (your" faith," 2 Cor. i. 24), and an expectation to be cherished ("hope;" cf. Heb. iii. 14; vi. 11; 1 Pet. i. 3-5; Jude 20, 21). Learn: 1. Our steadfastness in Christ is the best evidence of our reconciliation by Christ, and our earnest of a presentation in glory. The loss of faith is the knell of hope. 2. Our assurance of reconciliation and our hope of final perfection are both bound up with the glorious gospel, and may be the privilege of all; ior that gospel ia a message of salvation for every creature under heaven.-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 1:24
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The privilege of suffering. Following the Revised Version, and omitting "who," we notice that there is an abrnptness in the way in which the apostle breaks forth into thanksgiving at the thought of bis sufferings. "Now I rejoice," etc. The underlying thought seems to be this : "If ever I have been disposed to repine at my lot, if ever I have felt my cross almost too heavy to bear, yet now, now when I contemplate the lavish wealth of God's mercy, now when I see all the glory of bearing a part in this magnificent work, my sorrow is turned into joy" (Lightfoot). In a measure every Christian labourer may enter into Paul's joy because be may share his motives also. \Ve note two reasons for regarding suffering as a privilege. I. WE MAY THUS KNOW THE FELLOWSHIP OF CmnsT's SUFFERINGS. "I fill up on my part that which is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh." The oneness of Christ and bis people is the key to these mysterious words. In 1 Cor. xii. 12 even the name " Christ" is given to the body as well as the Head. The sufferings which Christians endure are endured by Christ their Head in them; e.g. Matt. xx.v. 35, etc.; Acts ix. 4; 2 Cor. i. 5; Heb. xiii. 13. Jesus Christ during bis earthly life endurerl sufferings which were peculiar to himself. They were vicarious, propitiatory, and meritorious. They are "finished" (Rom. vi. 9, 10). But the time of suffering is not yet past (Rom. viii. 23). Till the period of education and probation is past, there are afflictions of Christ yet to be filled up (cf. Rev. xxi. 4, 5). They are needful for the accomplishment, not of the atoning, but of the saving work of Christ. And if he selects us to be members in whom he is pleased to fill up some of his sufferings, we may regard it as a privilege rather than as an infliction. The term for " fill up" is very emphatic. It suggests the thought of completing, in response to or in exchange for something else ; as though Paul meant" He suffered for my redemption ; shall I not in my turn suffer for bis glory and the good of his Church?''
