-St. Paul's view ef his ministry. In these verses we have a comprehensive view of the ministry of the apostle, which suggests truths respecting tlie nature, subject, and object of every ministry that claims to be apostolic in its spirit. lie teachts us the following truths : - . I. THAT ms JIIIKISTr.Y WAS A STEWARDSHIP OF THE WORD OF GOD. Twice we find the personal claim, " I;" "I Paul was made a minister." But far from the spil"it of egotism, we hear in these words the echo of such expressions of grateful huQJ.iHty as we find in 1 Cor. xv. 8-10; Eph. iii. 7, 8; 1 Tim. i. 12-14. For his ministry was, a "stewardship." He was entirely dependent for it on another. He went forth, not to. publish the thoughts excogitated in his own mind, but to "dollver" testimonies and doetrines which he had received (1 Cor. xv. 1-4). The "mysteries JI he had to dco.l with were not sacraments, but truths; and he was not a priest-, but a preacher "of tho gospel ... whereof I Paul was made a minister" (ver. 23). The stewardship was entrusted to him at his conversion (Acts xxvi 17, 18). From it he could not escape (1 Cor. iL 17). But he gloried in it (1 Cor. iv. 1, 2; Eph. iii. 8). Being a minister of Christ, he was a nrinister for the whole Church; "whereof," i.e. of which Church," I was made a minister." And as such he willingly recognized himself even as a bondservant of the Church as well as of Christ (506?1.or) "for Jesuij' sake" (2 Cor. iv. 5; see also 1 Cor. ix. 19-23). His one aim was to be faithful," to fulfil the Word of God" (Rom. xv. 19; 2 Tim. iv. 17). II. '!'HAT THE Worm ENTRUSTED TO BTM WAB A MYSTERY. A mystery, according to St. Paul, i;; a truth which was once hidden but is now revealed. It is not discovered Ly men, but revealed to men. This applies: 1. 'l'o the whole gospel (Eph. vi. 20). \Vho could have discovered or even conceived God's" way of salvation"? It was a mystery of mercy. But it is now an open secret, revealed by Christ's own lips and through his apostles and committed to our trust (1 Tiw. i. 11; Jude 3). 2. 'fo the wccious truth that was especiaUy entrnsted to St. Paul as the apostle of the Gentiles (Eph. iii. 1-7). The admission of us Gentiles to all the blessings of the gospel on terms of perfect equality with the Jews was a truth which, in spite of such predictions as Gen. xi.:ii. 18; Isa. lvL, lL, etc., was "hid from all ages and generations," eve11 f:·om the apostles of Christ during his earthly life (Matt. x. 5; xv. 24). Defore his conversion P,LUl would have been shocked at it as a blasphemous heresy. But God hnd n,vcalecl l,is Son in him (Gal. L Hi, lG). • ill. 'l'IIAT THIS )[YSTEilY FOUND ITS SOLUTION rn CllllIST. 1. When in the fulnees of tirue God, transcending the hopes of the most i;anguine antieipanta of a glorious future, "sent forth his Son," "his unspeakable gift,'' it would have been unlike God tu confine so great a blessing to such a fraction of humanity as the Jews. 2. '!'ho appeariug of Christ was the greatest vindication of God's dealings with tho heathen nations which iu time past were suffered" to walk iu their own ways" (Acts xiv. lCi). 0. 'l'he al0:.,e11,cut of Cbri,t explained the forgiveness of sins amonJ Gc1,Lilcs as well u:; Jew:; iu all ages (Hom. iii. 2a, W). 4. The resurrection of Chrbt brought life and OH, I, 1-20,] 'l'HE EPISTLE 'l'O THE UOLOSSIANS.

immortality to light in a world wliich sorrowed over its dead as having" no hope." 6. The ideCll hum[l[1it.y of Obrist(" the Son of man'') pointed him out as" the Way t•> the FC1ther" for nil men apart from the hedges and barriers of the Jewish fold (John x. lCl), 6. The reception of Christ in any soul brinas a new life and love and a new "hope of glory." No wonder, then, that here and els~hcre the apostle adrls term to term (" riches of.his glory,"" exceeding riches of his grace," etc.) to describe God's mystery of mercy for us Gentiles, "which is Christ in you the Hope of glory." IV. '!'llAT THE PilEA0HINO OF CHilIST AIMS AT THE PERFECTION OF MEN. (Vers. 28, 29.) We set before ourselves the highest standards. We aim to present men "perfect," in the manifold senses in which that won] is used in the New Testamentperfect in condition (Heh. v. 9), in knowledge (1 Cor. xiii. 12), in character (Jude 24), because perfect "in Christ Jesus" (1 Cor. i.30). But for this end: 1. We must preach "Christ" in all his fulncss, as our Immanuel, our atoning Priest, our Divine Head, our perfect Pattern, our final Judge, as " the Way and the Truth and the Life," as" all and in all." 2. W c must be discriminaLi vein our preaching-" warning" " teaching," "every man" "in all wisdom." 3. vVe must be earnest and "labour,'' "striving," etc. 4. We must be dependent, trusting to Christ's" working which worketh in me mightily."-E. S. P. Ver, G.-Tlie fruitfulness qf the gospel. I. THE GOSPEL IS FRUITFUL. It is not a barren doctrine. It is a living truth that produces effects in the hearts of men which are made manifest through the influence of them on external conduct. It is fruitful in two ways, 1. In increase. '!'he truth spreads like leaven; the mustard seed grows into a great tree; the two or three in an upper room multiply into the thousands of Pentecost and into the millions, the Churches of modern Christendom. 2. In good influences. The tree not only puts forth new shoots and so grows in size, it blossoms and bears fruit. The fruits of the gospel are the same graces as are elsewhere called "the fruits of the Spirit" (Gal. v. 22, 23). Christianity makes happier and better men of us. These fruits are as visible as the fact of the numerical increase of the Church. All modern history bears witness to them, especially in the elevation of woman, the abulition of Blavery, the recognition of national justice, the spread of a spirit of humanity, the creation of institutions of charity, and, better still, the doing of innumerable nameless deeds of ldndness. II. '£HE FIELD OF THE GOSPEL'S FRUITFULNESS IS THE WORLD. It was not preached in the whole world in St. Paul's day, nor is it even yet. But the process of bearing fruit thronghout the world then began and still continues. 1. The f n,it is seen in this world. The ripest fruit may not be perfected here, but if there is no fruit on earth there will be none in heaven. The gospel is first of all good news of peace on earth-it promises blessings for the present lifo (1 Tim. iv. 8). 2. The gospel brings blessings to the whole earth. It is suited to all kinds of men, of all nations and in all ages, because it speaks to the common heart of mankind, offerin_g the supply of universal wants and conferring graces that are universally good. 3. The gospel bears Jn.tit througlwut the worlcl by first of all bearing fruit in the Church. " As it doth in you also." We can only enjoy the fruits of the gospel by entering the kingdom of Christ. The fruitfulness of the Church is the direct cause of the spread of Christianity throughout tho world 'l'hus God is glorified in our fruitfulness (John xv. 8). Ill, THE SECilET OF THE GOSPEL'S FRUITFULNESS IS TD.E TRUE KNOWLEDGE OF TIIE ORA0E OF GOD OF WHICII IT IS THE DECLARATION. 1. The energy of fruit-bearing resides in the gi·ace of God. When men feel that grace they become new creatures. Tho constraining love of Christ works the miracle. 2. The receipt of this energy depends on the lcnowledge of Divine grace. It does not work by magic, b11t thro11gh an understanding or its truths. Therefore it is vain to pray for the increased fruitfulness of tlw gospel without also preaching the gospel. 3. A trne understanding of tlie grace of C0,l is necessary for its/1'1.1,iifulness. It must be kuown "in truth." Perversions of tlw gospel hinder the fruitfulness of Christianity. 'l'he gospel tells of facts. Let us see those facts clearly separated from the errors and imaginations of human theology. -W.F.A.

entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The knowledge of God's will. I. TnE i.NOWI,EDGE OF Gon's WILL IS 76 THE EPIS'l'LE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [en. 1. 1-29.

THE KNOWLEDClE wmoH rs MOST SUPREMELY IMT'ORTANT. 1. Tho knowled_qe of God is the most important knowledge attainable. Many are eager in pursuing the investi- gation of curious questions of human affairs who are quite indifferent to the truth nbout the Being who fills heaven and earth. Others are busily searchina into the mysteries of the works of God, while quite forgetful of the Maker or them~ nut to know God is to know the Highest and Best. 2. 'l'lrn knowledge of the will of God is the most important knowledge of God. (1) It is the highest knowledge of God• for the dis- rosition of the will is the chief characteristic of a spiritual being. (2) It' is the lrnow- Jedge of God with which we have most concern ; for, though there must be glories and wonders in all the great thoughts of God, for 11s it is most needful that we shoulJ. understand wbnt he is purposing to do and what he wishes us to do. (3) It is the most attainable knowledge of God. The abstract ideas of the mind of God are far above our reach. The practical thoughts and la"'s and commandment of his will o.re what he bas most clearly revealed. II. THE KNOWLEDGE OF Goo's WILL llAY BE ACQUIRED TIIIlOUGH SPIRITUAL WISDOM. 1. It may be acquired. This branch of theology is within our reach. In our darkest moments, when we cannot understand the thoughts and plans of God, we may discQvcr what God wills us to do. 2. It is to be got at through spiritual wisdom. We have it not by nature. We cannot reach it by efforts of bare human intelligence. Philosophy will not reveal it. A higher wisdom than the earthly, a purer wisdom than the carnal, heavenly and spiritual wisdom is necessary for this knowledge. 8. This spiritual wisdom is a Divine inspiration. ~t. Paul prays for it. It is not a product of experi- ence like our knowledge of the world. The man of the world learns much about evil by his experience, but little about goodness. Goodness and the will of God with which it is identical are only seen by a spiritual light which little children may have more clearly than learned men and experienced observers. It is an inward light, 11. spiritual inspiration. III. THE KNOWLEDGE OF Goo's WILL IS FRUITFUL IN GREAT 1':I.\OTI0AL RESULTS. This is not a barren knowledge acquired only for the satisfaction uf idle curiosity, nor even merely a worthy object of contemplation. 1. Vv e must know the will of Gou in order that our life may be worthy of Chri.~t. This is an important point not sufficiently considered by those people who slight tbe contemplative side of Christianity. The practical side will be a blundering failure without the due cultivation of the contemplative. A lame man with good eyes can walk more straightly than a man with sound limbs who is blind. To please God we must first of all know bis will. 2. This knowledge helps us to be fruitful in good works to men. We can never benefit men so much as by doing God's will. Our duty to God and our duty to men are mutually inclusive. We must study the will of God more carefully in order that our work amongst men mav be more wise and successful. We often fail in our conscientious efforts to benefit men because we do not work according to the method of God's will.-W. F. A.

entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-77,e inheritance ef the saints. I. CHBIBTIANS ARE HEIRS OF A RICII Th"HERITANCE. 1. The gospel offers Divine wealth. Its blessings are not confined to bare delive, ance from ruin. They include hidden treasures, pearls of great price, princely feasts, a whole kingdom of glory. 2. This wealth is, for the most part, pro- Hpective. It is an inheritance not yet possessed. 'l'be heir may be in severe straits before he comes into his property. We have foretastes of the future blessedness, but the chief part of this blessedness is yet to come. 3. The possession is to be bad with- QU,t any action of owrs in acquiring it. The heir docs not seize his estate and hold it by right of conquest; be does not purchase it; he does nothing t~ earn th~ worth of it; he simply receives it by bequest from another. We do nothmg to wm or earn our Christian hcritaae. Christ obtains it and bequeaths it, and as bis heirs we simply enter into possession" as the son of a great warrior peaceably takes possession of tho kingdom won by the sword of his father. 4. Still, the inheritance is received by rigltt. 'l'be heir has a right to Lis estate. Laws and documents secure it to him. 'l'he Divine covenant of grace is the Christian's title-deed, giving him no precarious hope, but a certain promise and right to his future blessedness. n. CHRISTI.ANS ARE BEING TRAINED FOR THEm GREAT INHERITAN'0E. The heir of II nobleman m1ll!t be educated so as to be fitted for his position in society. 'l'he heir of a on. L 1-20,J TllE EPl8TLE '1'0 THE COLOSSIANS. 77

throne needs o. special training in order that he may enter upon the duties as well as the privileges of royalty. H would be useless to bequeath a library to a man who had no interest in literature, or to leave an art collection to a man of boorish tastes. The heir must be suited to the inheritance. We hear much of the acqnisition of our inheritance, o.nd some seem to think that their great task is thus to secure it for thcmselve~. Dut we should remember that this thing is done, the kingdom won by the victory of Christ, the riches bought by his sacrifice of himself. Now, the solo requisite is that we should be ready to enter into possession. And this is a great ancl. essential requisite. An impure soul could not be admitted into heaven; but, if admitted, such a soul would find no joy there. Note: 1. God is making us meet for the great inheritance by the present discipline of life. 2. There are those who may be said to have been made thus ready, because, although not yet per[ect, they are new creatures and have characters and sympathies fitted for the enjoyments of the pure delights of heaven. 3. It may be remarked by the way that St. Paul knew of no purgatorial fires which were to keep Christians out of the joys of heaven for some intermediate period. !II. 'fnE REQUISITE FITNESS FOB THE CHRISTIAN 11-HERITANCE DEPENDS ON THE CHARACTER OF THAT mHEBITANCE. 1. The inheritance is in light. It lie~ in tl,e clearer realm of eternal trutli; it is characterized by the purity that excludes all. dark blots and stains of sin; it is radiant with the summer sunshine of heavenly joy. 2. Such an inheritance requires saintliness as a suitable condition of enjoyin:;; it. It is an inheritance of saints. Only those who are forgiven, cleansed, and purified can stancl. in the searching light of eternal truth; and they only can enjoy the blessings of a kingdom of holiness and find therein true gladness. Nevertheless, this is no reason for discouragement. St. Paul thanks God for accomplishing the necessary preparation. It is his work, and he will perfect it with all who trust to his grace and the power of his Spirit.-W. F . .A.

entries.title: COL 1:15
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0hrist in his relations to God and to the world. This Epistle to the Colossians is conspicuous among the writings of St. Paul for its enthusiastic assertion of the supreme glory and divinity of Jesus Christ. In opposition to an incipient Gnosticism which would lose the solitary rank of the Son of God in a crowded hierarchy of angels, it exalts that rank with a.n elevation and a distinctness not to be met with in any previously written portion of the New Testament. It is impossible to read the words of the apostle impartially without seeing that he taught the full divinity and pre-existence of Jesus Christ. The old unitarianism that appealed to scriptural authority for confirmation was simply blind with prejudice. Modern unitarianism is more consistent when it rejects the ioapiration of the book which plainly contains the doctrine it repudiates. It is true that the ideas of St. Paul are expressed in accordance with the notions of his times, especially in relation to the "Logos" doctrine of .Alexandrian philosophy, and therefore that if we interpret them into the language that fits our modern conception of things, they may appear to change their form. But however expressed, the truths taught by the great apostle concerning the Divine, pre-existent, and supreme Christ are essential to the gospel of the New Testament. I. CHRIST IN ms RELATION TO Goo. He" is the Image of the invisible God." This implies two facts. 1. Resemblance. 'l'he likeness is not external and accidental, "as one egg is like another "-the "homoiousion" of the semi-Arians. The image is produced by the prototype as the seal by the die; it is "the impress of his substance," as the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews describes it (Heb. i. 3). The language of the apostle refers to the Divine nature of Christ. Dut it remains true after the ·word has been made flesh. Thus we may sec that, as at the creation man was made iu the image of God, so in the Incarnation the pcrfeetion of humanity is identical with the exact likeness of God. Christ became no less human because he was the Image of Gou, but, on the contrary, just perfectly human. Our highest conception of divinity is our ideal of manhood. 2. Expression. Christ is the Image of the invisible God. "No ruau hath seen God at auy time," etc. (John i. 18). God is invisible because he is pure spirit. No change of, pla~e and n_o chan~e of state_w!ll _eve_r _enable us to see ~od with 011.r physical eyes. 'lhe hght which sufluses the air 1s 1nv1s1ble except where 1t sh,t111:1 78 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [en, L 1-20,

0n ~0~e object. nnd is r~flected to us. ~o'."1's nniversA!ly diffused presence requires such rcOcd1011 for us to 8ee 1t. ,ve h11ve this ln some degree in the works of natl\l'O-l!tar 8ea, and flower reflecting God's glory. But it is only in Christ the perfect Imacre thnt we can have the rerfoct manifestRtion of God. He only can say, "He that hath seen me bath seen the Father" (John xiv. 9), II. CHRIST m ms RELATIO~ TO THE WORLD. He is "the Firstborn of 1111 creation." That this expression refers, not to the Incarnatior., but to the Divine pre-existenco of Ch1ist, is rlain if only from the language of the following verse (ver. 16). It expres.cs two facts. 1. Pre-existence. We have no reason for thinking th&t the human soul of Christ existed before the Incarnation. But it is plainly taught by St. Paul that that which is Divine in him did so exist. Our Lord said the same of himself (John viii. 58). Without attempting to understand the mystery of the nature of God, we may gather this important lesson-that all those Divine characteristics which arc so beautifully revealed in Jesus of Nazareth were not l)roduced for the first time in the New Testa- ment days. Though kss knov.n, they were as really existing in the age of Moses and even at the first creation of the world. Therefore the very scheme of nature and the whole government of the world rnu~t be in accordance with what we know of Christ. As Christ will finally judge the world, and all that we know of his Spirit will lead us to be thankful that such a one is the Judge, so we may rejoice that the same Spirit of love and gentleness has been from the first eternally pervading all things. 2. Pre-eminence. The firstborn has the chief honour. Christ's rank is not only above that of the highest archangels; it is distinctive in kind. He is not the first creature of many creatures, but the first born of all creation, in the deepest sense the only begotten Son of the Father. (1) '!bus be who is most pure and good is most noble. (2) He who humbled himself and sacrificed himself the most was the most highly exalted. (3) All who trust in Christ may have the assurance that they could have no greater security fortheir confidence. (4) Christ is worthy of worship.-W. F. A,

entries.title: COL 1:18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -" The Firstborn from the dead." L IlEsunnECTION IS BIRTII. Christ rising the first from the dead is called the first born. Death looks ugly to us because we only see the earthly side. The experience of Christ should help us to look on to the other side and the issne of death in birth in the heavenly sphere. Thus the sunset of the east is the sunrise of the west. The Christian future is not merely rest; it is life. It is not a repetition of the old weary life of earth; it begins afresh in birth. IL CHllIBT INSTITUTES A 1mw ORDER OF LIFE. He is the new Adam. Mankind began its old life in the garden of Eden; it begins its new life in Joseph of Arimathma's i:arden. The sins, sorrows, and failures of the past are crucified with Christ, dead and buried. To the old weary earth Christ brings a new spring-time, and with it the birth of new hopes and energies. But the perfect development of this new order of things is only possible after death. Ch1ist has begun it, and as one by one his people follow him they too enter into its growing glories. • ill CHRIST IB SUPREME IN THE NEW LIFE. On earth be was lowly, despised, rejected, and slain. Proud enemies seemed to triumph over him. A Tiberius sat on the throne of the world and the Son of God was nailed to the cross. But in the new order he who was the Firstborn of all creation (ver. 15) resumes his rightfol rank and becomes the Firstborn from the dead. Therefore "he is the Head of the body, the Church." But the first step in the reconciliation began with Go,!, He desired it and prepared the way for it before men took any steps towarrls realizing it. For this reason he first of all srnt his Son into the world (John iii. 16), and is now sending ambassadors and beseeching us by them to be reconciled. We began the separation, for ours WlS the offence, but God begins the reconciliation. He doe~ not need to be reconciled to us. Ho waits to be gracious. The necessary reconcili].tion is on our side. ,vc need to be reconciled to God. 11. ALL THINGS IN EATITII AND HEAVEN ABE 'l'HE SUJlJECTS OF THE GREAT RF:CO~CILIA- TION, 1. The reconciliation i9 to be universal. It is God's good pleasure to reconcile all things. Nothing short of that complete restoration would satisfy him. If ninety and nine sheep are safe, the shepherd will not rest until he has found the hu □ dredth. Nevertheless, though this universal restitution is God's desire, there is a dark and difficult question as to how far the imperious will of man may stand out against it. 2. Though the laws of nature may not be altered, yet to us the wilderness will become a garden when we become reconciled to the God of nature. 3. The recon- ciliation reaches up to things in heaven. It unites earth to heaven. Through union with God all beings and all things become united among themselves. Thus peace is established on earth, heavenly mindedness becomes a sympathetic link between the toilers aud sufferers in this world and the angels and spirits of the just in tho higher -world. III. entries.title: COL 1:28
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The mission of Christian preaching. In describing bis own practice St. Paul describes the model mission of the Christian preacher. Nothing less than this great ideal should satisfy a Christian minister. But nothing outside it should be assumed by or expected of him. 'fbe apostle is but a preacher and teacher, not a. priestly authority. I. THE SUBJECT OF CHRISTIAN PBEACITTNO IS CHRIST. It does not consist in vague speculations on religion. It is clear, positive, definite, and concrete. The preacher is to uphold Christ. He is to tell the story of the life, death, and resurrectior:. of Christ; to draw the portrait of Christ (Gal. iii. 1); to proclaim the grace of Christ; to set forth the claims of Christ; and to show the relation of Christ to everything in life. 1. There is a unity in this preaching. It all centres in Christ. 2. '£here is a breadth in it. Christ has grace and authority in regard to all aspects of life. 3. There is power in it. The charm and spell of the gospel dwell in Christ himself. In proportion as he is lifted up does he draw all men to himself, and in proportion as the preacher wanders into side issues does he lose the secret of his influence. n;. THE FIELD OF CHRISTIAN PREACHING IS ALL MANKIND. Three times does the apostle express the universality of this truth as against the Jew who would limit the best treasures to his nation, and the Gnostic who would keep the higher truths for the more instructed. "Admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom." 1. Christ is for all; for (1) none are so good, or wise, or safe, or happy as to afford to do without him; and (2) none are so ignorant, or foolish, or guilty as to be beyond the reach of his blessings. 2. In Christ all wisdom is for all men. There is no reserve, at least of tha highest wisdom,-since the Christ who is preached to all men fr~ely is the Word and the Wisdom of God. Ill. THE METHOD OF CHRISTIAN PREACHING IS PRACTICAL INSTRUCTION. 1. Proclaiming Christ. The first requisite is information on the main points of the gospel. The Christian preacher is a herald and a witness (Acts ii. 32; iii. 15). 2. .Admonishing. Men must be charged with the guilt of their sins, as well as encouraged by the offers of the gospel. An earnest, faithful dealing with individuals according to their personal condition is a necessary though painful part of a minister's work. 3. Teaching. Thorough instruction must follow the general proclaiming of the gospel. Growth in grace depends largely on growth in knowledge. Neglect of this laborious, unexciting part of the preacher's mission, careful teaching, is sure to be avenged by ultimate weakness, if not by disastrous lapses into practical errors. IV. THE END OF CHRISTIAN PREACHING IS TO PRESENT MEN PERFECT IN CHRIST. We are not to be satisfied with such abstract teaching as simply informs the minds of people. The great work is most practical. It is to mould lives, to develop characters, to perfect souls. 1. It is to bring men into living ttnion with Christ. We preach Christ in order thnt men may live Christ. The great result is the effecting of a vital union with Christ. 2. It is also to lead men on to perfection in Christ. 'l'he preacher will be expected, at the return of his Master, to present, as the fruit of his life's work, not a crowd of raw converts, but a body of ripe Christians. 'l'he work is not finished in conversion. It only begins with that. Line upon line, and precept upon precept, often with sad iteration as old lessons unlearnt need to be repeated, characterizes the necessary task of the Christian preacher. And it is not done till perfection is reached. V. SUCCESS IN THIS !UBS\'.0:t'I l)EPJ;;NDB Ul'ON WOI\Kll\G H4RD l'.N T:aE fOWER OF Cmi1s·1•, 00L0SSIANB. G 82 TIIE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. -Sect 4. Tlie apostle's concern for the <Jolossian (Jhurc'A. Already the apostle has breathed ont his "hcnrt's desire and prayer to God" for thcso Colossi::ms (eh. i. !J-12), "unknown by face" to him (vers. 1, 6), ,md yet so dear b~cause of their faith and love (oh. i. 4, 8; ii. G, 11-13; iii. 1-3, !J, 10, 15), and the loyalty they b&ve hitherto maintained (ver. 6), and the objects of so much anxiety on nccount of DS THE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [cu. 11. 1-23.

the insi.Jio11s nn,l ,k1<lly nalnre of t~e assault being made upon their faith, of whose rcnl chnractrr they seem to have been httle aware. ,ve expect- therefore in this passage n re~urrence of !-he stra~n of thought pursued in_ tbe prayer'or the fi(st clrn.pter. Vve find a hke prominence given to knowledge, the cluef desideratum of this Church and to the need of a Christianly instnicted understanding as a safeguard acrainst the s~btletles an~ plausibiliti~s of error. At the &'lme time, the view now presented of this object has gamed greatly ID fulncss and depth by the development of the apostlo's araument in the interYcning paragraphs of his letter. 'l'he teaching of this section we m~y summarize in the words of 2 Pet. iii. 18, ns setting forth the nature and the elements of- I. GnOWTJI IN '!'IlE GRACE AND KNOWLEDGE OF OUR Lonn AND SAVIOUR JESUS OBRIST. (Vers. 2, 3, 6, 7.) 1. St. Paul has spoken of the Church as" the body of Christ" (eh. i. 18, 24), and so he must needs desire that its members may be knit together in love (ver. 19; Eph. iv. 16; 1 Cor. i. 10). Without such union the Church is no lon"er a body, and its members, broken and scattered, become an easy prey to error. The sal,;-ation of individual souls is but half the work of Christ. "He loved the Church and gave himself for her" (Eph. v. 25; Acts xx. 28). He seeks to builcl. the redeemed; regenerated units of mankind as" living stones" into "a holy temple" (Eph. ii. 20-22; l Cor. iii. 16, 17); to integrate them into the "one body" of which he is the Head and his Spirit is the Soul (Eph. iv. 3-6): colllp. sect. 2, II. 4 (homiletics). Of this union, love is tbe bond (eh. iii. 14; Epb. iv. 2; John xiii. 34, 35). In all true and lasting union amongst men some sympathetic affection must exist, either as a basis for the fellowship or as generated by it. Mere identity of beliefs or of interests will never hold men for long together. The heart must love or hate, must be attracted or repelled, in some degree, by every personality around it. And the union of souls in Christ, bein" the most deep and spiritual of any, must be thoroughly pervaded and determined by love. Moreover, the growth of Christian knowledge and the perfecting of personal character depend mnch more largely than we are apt to suppose, in this age of craggcrated individualism and selfish culture-seeking, on the soundness and complete- ness of our Church life, of our Christian social life. To St. Paul's mind the "pcrfoct man" and the perfect Church-the perrcction of the part and of the whole-are reciprocally dependent, and all but identical (Eph. iv. 11-16). 2. But love without lmowlcdge, beat without light, will not suffice. As "faith, being alone, is dead" (Jaa. ii. 17), so love in like condition is blind and easily falls into error. "I pray that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment" (Phil i. 9). The apostle declared that "God willed to make known to his saints the riches of the glory of his mystery" (eh. i. 27); accordingly he desires for them" all ricbes of the full assurance of the understanding," "unto the kuowledge of the mystery" (ver. 2). (1) The former is the 6llbjective counterpart of the latter. The understanding that is enlightened and informed in the truth belonging to the revelation of God in Obrist, that ranges freely, yet reverently, through" the breadth, and length, and height, and depth" of this mystery, and learns to comprel~nd it (Eph. iii. 18), is itself enriched, assured, and satisfied thereby. (2) The object which the mind contemplates, into which it seeks to penetrate ever more deeply, is Christ, the mystery of God. "To know him" is its supreme aspiration (Phil. iii. 10), in which intellectual inquiry is guided by spiritual sympathy and inspired by love (Pbil. iii. 7; John xiv. 21). 'fo know him as an historical Person is something; this knowled;.:c supplies the material and the basis for all other knowledge of Christ (Acts L 36-43). To know him as a living, present Saviour is the essential knowledge, the one thing needful (Phil. iii. 8---ll); it is to" gain Christ, and be found in him." But it is yet more than this to know him as the mystery of God -to discover his secret indwelling in nature and in history; to understand how" to him give all the prophets witness;" to hear the footfall of" the coming One" echoing along the silent chambers and winding corridors of the ages past (cb. i. 21); to find in him the cenlre of all life and law, uniting God and the world, eternity and time (eh. i. 15-17); to behold in" the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world," at the same time "the outbeaming of the Fatlz,,,', glory, the very Image of his substance, through whom also he ma<le the worlds, a.nd who upholds all things by the word of his power" (Heb. i. 2, 3), the "l!'irstborn of atl creation," the "Heir of all things." Here is knowledge indeed, and for him who is grounded in it, speculative theories of nature and of God and the mystic dreams of theosophy will have but little charm, 'l'hie OIi. II. 1-23.) 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 09

mystery of God surpasses nnd includes all others; for (Jhrist, in nature and in grace, in history o.nd personal experience, "is all and in all." In view of this Mystery, no wonder that t~e apostl~ says that we a.re" being renewed unto knowledge" (eh. iii. 10). We can conceive no obJect worthier of the pursuit of the loftiest and greatest minds than "the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus our Lord" (Phil. iii. 8; Eph. iii. 9-11; 1 Pet. i. 12). Dy it "the heart," the whole "inward man" (Eph. iii. 16), is "sto.blished" (ver, 7) and "encouraged" (ver. 2) by the "comfort of love" (Phil. ii. 1) and "the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (ver. 3) that a.re "in Christ." 3. Love and knowledge muae bear fruit in practical obedience. Christ Jesus was received by the Colossiaris as" the Lord" (ver. 6; eh. iii. 24; iv. 1). He is a Master to be obeyed (Rom. xiv. 9; John xiii. 13; xiv. 15), as well a.s a Mystery to be known and a. Saviour to be loved. In him we must walk. The whole conduct of life must be governed by his Spirit (Rom. viii. 14; Gal. v. 25) and directed toward his end1> (Phil. i. 20, 21; 2 Cor. v. 15). He "in all things" cla.irns to be "pre-eminent" (eh. i. 18; 1 Cor. xv. 25; 2 Cor. x. 5). Every desire, affection, pursuit, of the Christian must "acknowledge him to be the Lord." By such true obedience the soul grows in strength and security, and is ever being more completely "builded up in him" (ver. 7: comp. eh. i. 10). 4. And the root of this life of advancing knowledge and obedient love is faith. By this the soul is first "rooted in him" (vers. 5, 12; eh. i. 3, 23; Phil. iii. 9; Eph. ii. 8; Rom. v. 1, 2, etc.). From this root springs love (Gal. v. 6), obedience (Rom. vi.; viii. 3, 4), satisfying knowledge (Eph. iii. 17-19), every good word and work (1 Thess. i. 3; 2 Thess. i. 11; ii. 16, 17). If this fails, everything fails (Gal. iii. 1-5). Whatever strt!ngthens, comforts, and upbuilds the Christian, does so by ministering to his faith. A growing knowledge, a quickened love, a more steadfast obedience, enable bis faith to strike deeper root-stablish him in his faith (ver. 7). In this world he never ceases to "walk by faith" (2 Cor. iv. 18; v. 7); and his alx>unding in it is the greatest gain which the furthest advancement in the life of God can bring him. Yet faith, again, has its outward instrument and condition. It" comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God" (Rom. x. 17). The Colossians are to be "stablishcd in their faith," "even as they were tanght" (ver. 7: comp. eh. i. 5, 7). To that instruction they owe all they possess in Christ, even their own selves (Philem. 19). 5. And he who alx>imds in faith will abound in thanksgiving also. 'l'he more strongly the Christian believes in the Son of God and enters into the mysteries of his kingdom, the more joyfully and constantly will he offer his tribute of praise. This, too, is a fruit of faith-" the fruit of the lips" (Heb. xiii. 15; Hos. xiv. 2), the only fruit of all his mercies which we can directly render to the great Giver. Of such thanksgiving, called forth by the contemplation of the "mystery of God" in Christ, St. Paul's own act of praise in Eph. i. 3-14 is a noble example (comp. Rom. xi. 33-36; xvi. 25--27; 1 Tim. i. 12-17; 1 Pet. i. 3-5; Rev. i. 5-7; Matt. xi. 25-28. See sect. 1, III. 2, homiletics). II. A DANGER AND A BAFEGUA.l!D. (Vers. 4, 5.) 1. There was one thing that specially endangered Chiistian life and the well-being of the Church at Colossai. It was the charm of perverted eloquence (ver. 4). A clever tongue and o. popular style are gifts by no means incompatible with the faithful and spiritual pre3ching of Christ; but they have their peculiar dangers for their possessor, and for the Church in which they are exercised. St. Paul appears to have admired gifts of this kiud in Apollos, but he felt that a plainer and severer method became himself, in which the sheer might and majesty of the truth should stand forth without adornment of rhetoric or drapery of graceful diction that might distract attention from the all-important theme of his address (1 Cor. ii. 1-5). The possession of such powers ma.de the men whom he is denouncing at Colossle so formidable. Perhaps their very gifts had proved a snare to them; and there are indications in St. Po.ul's description of thern (vers. 8, 16, 18, 23: comp. Acts xx. 29, 30) of the arrogance and self-seeking spirit, and the intellectual dishonesty, into which men of popular powers are liable to fall. 2. On the other hand, there was one specially hopeful feature in tho state of this Church-the good orde:r which it had maintained (vcr. 5); contrast with 1 Cor. i. 11, 12; xi. 2-18; :xiv. 40. So far, these•• deceitful workers" had not succeeded in disturbing the Church's unity or stirring up insubordinntion against its officers. In every organized body it is o. first condition of strencrth and safety that its members should "obey them that have the rule" (Hcb. xiii. 17), should "all of them be subicct one to unother" (Et>h. v. 21 ; THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE COLOSSIANS. [OH, U, 1-28,

1 Pel v. 5), each in his place and rank keeping step and time with tbo movement or the whole.

Vcrs. 8-15.-Scct.. 5, The <Jh'l"istian's comp7eteness in <Jhr-ist I. A FALSE PBILO- FClrHY OF RELIGION. (Yers. 4-, 8, 11, 16-23.) "Not according to Christ" (ver. 8) is the fatal sentence which the apostle pronounces upon the system of doctrine that was finding l'ntrance at Colossro. However 11lausible in argument (ver. 4) or lofty in its intellectual pretensions ( vers. 8, 23 ), however skilfully it may avail itself of the venerable rites of :rncient faith or of the popular predilections and tendencies of the day (vers.11 16 18)1 nnd what~ver the apparent sanctity and austerity of its professors (vers. 18, 2~23) the religious system which sets him aside and professes to lead men into communio~ "·ith God and to the moral perfection of their nature otherwise than "in him," must n ftcr all be, at the heart of it," a vain deceit." For he is "the Way, the Truth, and the Life," the Lord and Life of nature and the Light of men (eh. i. 15-17; John i. 3, 4), the "Beginning" of the "new heavens and the new earth wherein dwelleth righteous- llPSS;" he is simply" all things and in all" to the Church of God. All true philosophy, though standing on natural grounds and drawing its premisses from natural experience and intuition, yet, rightly understood, must needs harmonize with the Christian faith, and "·ill be "according to Christ.~ For no two truths, however differently grounded or expressed, can really be contradictory. And the facts on which philosophy rests, the mental and material constitution of things concerning which it theorizes, "were crented" and "consist in him" (eh. i. 16, 17). "In Christ" must lie, therefore, the ultimate rationale of the finite universe, • The Colossian error presented itself as i,1,ilosophy, advanced on rational grounds, and claiming the attention of men of thought and culture within the Church. It inculcated the religious traditions of the Jew under the forms and methods of the Greek intellect, seeking to reanimate both by the aid of the new spiritual fervour and lofty moral aspirations of the Christian faith. There was nothing in itself blameworthy in such an attempt. Endeavours must be con- tinually made, though they can never be final, to harmonize the current philosophy of the age with the Divine revelation as received in the Church. St. Paul himself makes large contributions in this direction. But those who take this work in hand should understand both sides of the question. This the Colossian errorists failed to do. They tried to fit Christ into some plaoo in their preconceived philosophy, instead of allowing themselves to be led, a.s St. Paul would have taught them (eh. i. 15-20), through Christ to a deeper and more sound philosophy. Hence their teaching, put forward as Christian truth and claiming to be the Christian theory of life, is condemned as "philosophy and empty deceit." 1. It was according to tlle tradition of men. It could claim only human authority for its principles. They were not found in Christ's doc- trine, and bad received no authentication from his lips (Gal. i. 11, 12), no Divine attestation or proof of their being "from heaven" (Matt. xxi. 25, 26; Heb. i. 4). And anv scheme of religion, whether calling itself "philosophy" or not, that is in this position, stands self-condemned. "The world by wisdom knew not God" (1 Cor. i. 21). \Vbat he is how he is disposed towards the children of men, it is for him to say. They know' full well that they have lost his favour and defaced his image in their souls· but how their recovery is possible is to them" past finding out," And therefore, to fix'and measure the nature of God and the relations he may assume to us," accordincr to the tradition of men," is the height of ignorance and presumption. But Christ 1s 'i', the faithful Witness,"" the Word who was in the beginning with God" (Rev. i. 5; ,J olm i. 2); and an authentic voioo from heaven declares, "Thii; is my Son, my chosen: hear ye l,im" (Luke iL 35 ; John i. 18). 2. And such systems, leaving the clear and firm ground of obedienoo to the supremacy of Christ, are compelled to fall back, in rnme form or other, on the rudiments of the world, '!'heir advocates discover that the iufiuenoo of human names and the force of general reasoning do not command the <leferenoo of the conscienoo or stir the spiritual emotions, are indeed without that. "power of God" (1 Cor. i. 24, 25; 1 Thess. i. 5) which attends the word of Christ. 'l'hey_ret~rn, therefore, to the dead forms of old religio,~s, putting,_ as they s~ppose, a new meaning rnto them. They are at once "advanced, ~nd rea~t1onary. 'I hoy dress _up the newest rationalism in the cast-off garments of faith's ch1ldhood, They combmc a puerile ·itlinlism, borrowing its forms and practioos from the mere rudiments of an OH, II, 1-23.] THE EPIS'l'LE 'l'O THE COLOSSIANS. 101

age of sensuous "feeling 11fter God," with the most bare and abstract, the most arid an,l joyless, conceptions of his nature, or of a nature that is their substitute for him. The combination of" philosophy" and "circumcision" (vers. 8, 11), of eloquent and subtle reasonings with minute and arbitrary rules as to "ea.Un" and drinkinO'" and the physical c1;1lture of the soul (vers. 4, 16, 20-23), is after all not unnatural~• and is apt to repeat itself, to a greater or less extent, in every attempt at religion that is not essentially spiritual, 11nd that departs from the "one foundation, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Cor. iii. 11). 3. We must also mark the arrogant and overbearing temper of the new teachers at Colossm, their exclusiveness and their endeavour to form a personal party within the Church. They are "men speaking perverse things, to draw away ihe disciples after them" (Acts xx. 30). They would make simple Christians their "booty (ver. 8). They set up to judge their brethren in matters of diet and outward observance (ver. 16). They assume, in this character of judges in the Church, to deny to Christian men, walking in faith and love (eh. i. 4) and having Christ's peace within their heartg (eh. iii. 15), "the prize of their calling" (ver. 18), because they will not accept their notions and practices. 'l.'hey issue their decrees, "'rouch not, taste not," etc., as if they were the very law of God (vers. 22, 14). They are "humble" before the powers of the invisible world, and zealous to offer them a worship which they repudiate and abhor (ver. 15; Rev. xix. 10; xxii. 9); but rob Christ of his honour (vers. 18, 19, 23), and are proud and self-willed towards their brethren "whom they have seen." They heap upon the body invented and misdirected severities (ver. 23), while they are governed by "the mind of the flesh" (ver.18). 'l'hey aggrandize themselves, while they destroy the Church of God (ver. 19). II. THE COMPLETE CHRIST OUR COMPLETENESS, (Vers. 9-13.) For the Christian everything depends on what luJ thinks of Christ and malces him to be. Christ's glory is his security. His greatness and the greatness of our interest in him are commensurate. For" he gave himself for us" (Gal. ii. 20). Our salvation is not merely a u·ork of Christ, a something wrought out for us, and (externally) conferred upon us; it is "Christ in us" (eh. i. 2; Eph. iii. 17; Gal. i. 16; John xiv. 20; xvii. 26). A.nd St. Paul virtually says, "In robbing Christ of his glory, your new teachers nre robbing you of your salvation. By so much as his position is lowered, his fulness diminished, by so much is your spiritual life imperilled and impaired. Whatever is taken away from the completeness of his Person 2.nd the sufficiency of his mediation, is taken away at the same time from yom assurance of pardon (ver. 13; eh. i. 14) and your motives for holiness (eh. iii. 1, 2), from the ground of your faith (vers. 6, 7), and the certainty of your heavenly prize (ver. 18; eh. i. 23; iii. 15). Whatever touches his person touches the centre and vital spring of your life in God, the anchor of your immortal hopes, ancl the foundation on which rests the whole fabric of the Church" (ver. 19; Eph. ii. 20-22; Matt. xvi.15-18). 1. (1) In him dwells all thefulness of the Godhead. Then he is not a partial, or e.n approximate, or temporary manifestation of God-like previous theophanies-a mere phase of the Infinite. He does not rank and share with angels and the various orders of created being in mirroring by scattered, broken rays the glory of God. A.s the Son, he stands at an infinite distance from, and holds an absolute supremacy over, all creation (eh. i. 15; Heb. i. 2-4; iii. 6). God is what he shows himself to be in Christ, and no other. There, if we could but behold and receive it, is" all the fuluess of the Divine nature." In him we know the only true, the real, veritable God (John xvii. 3). A.t last we grasp the substance of truth and no longer chase its shadows (ver. 17). Here is nothing transient, to be displaced by further evolution: this fulness dwells in him; we reach finality, truth absolute, determinate; and ho who knows and has Christ may say, "This is the true God and eternal life" (1 John v. 20). (2) And this fulness dwells in liiin bodily. For the Divine Word" became flesh," ancl in a human body" made his tabcrnaclo amongst us" (John i. 14). Ila was" born of a woman, born under the law" (Gal. iv. 4), su!Tered our bodily ills and temptations, wrought with human hands, looked through human eyes, a.nd spoke in the languag<J of men; snt as a friendly guest at our tables, and stood as a mourner by our gravesides; died a human death, "in the body of his flesh" (eh. i. 22), by the hands of men, and was laid in an earthly grave; he rose, "the same Jesus," in that same body, and nscendcd into heaven ( eh. i. 18, 19; iii. 1-4), "far above all principality and power" (ver. 10; Eph. i 20-23), where ho sits a radiant body, "appeariug in tho presence of 102 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'IlE OOLOSSIANS. [ Cll, 11, 1-23,

God for us'.' (Heh. ix. 24), ~?d whom o?c dlly we shall sec (eh. iii. 1-4; Phil. Ill. 20, 21; 1 Pet. 1. 8, 9; 1 John 111. 2; Acts 1. 11)-" the Man Christ Jt'slls" "who is over nil, God blessed for ever" (Rom. ix. 5). This was the vision that dying' Stephen beheld in the presence of Saul of Tarsus (Acts vii. 05-60), which ere long appeared to himself (Acts ix. 3-6) and was henceforth evermore before his eyes. And since he has assumed it Christ's humanity is also pe,manent. The fulnessof the Godhead still dwells in him bodily'. He will not cease to be man any more thau he can cease to be (ft)d. His relationship to his human brethren, and the remembrance of his earthly sorrows, of" the wounds that he received in the house of his friends," are too precious to him for that. He is still "the Lamb, in the midst of the throne," who is" the Shepherd" of his heavenly flock (Rev. vii. 17), the "Firstbom out of the dead" among the "many brethren" that have eternal life in him (eh. i. 18; Rom. viii. 29). And heaven for us is "to be where he is," "to see him as be is" ( eh. iii. 4; Phil. i. 23 ; 2 Cor. v. 8; John xii. 26; xvi i. 24 • l John iii. 2)-" the Man Christ Jesus,"" the Lord of glory"! "All the fulness of th~ Godhead, in bodily form! "-a mystery compared with which the contradictions that so often baffle and vex us are trifles indeed; and yet an indubitable fact, that astonishes heaven (Eph. iii. 10; 1 Pet. i. 12) and glorifies the earth, and that fills struggling, sinful mortals "'ith a sense of Divine sympathy, an assurnuce of forgiveness and help that make all things possible. 2. But Christ's fulness does not ~imply "dwell in him," terminating in himself; it is an active, outjlowing fulness, that seelcs to make us in turn complete in him (ver. 10; Eph. i. 23; iii. 19; iv. 8-13; John i. 14, 16; xvii. 22, 23, 26). The Judaizers of Colossre, as we understand their position, were urging on their Gentile disciples that they should complete their imperfect Christian state by circnmcision and ibe adoption of various ritual observances (including worship of the angels along with Chri~t) and bodily austerities (vers. 16-23). These requirements they enforced by philosophical reasoning, under considerations of the symbolic meaning of ancient rites and the beneficial effect upon the soul of the regimen prescribed as cleansing and elevating to its proper level man's spiritual nature. St. Paul acknow- ledges by implication that, to a certain extent (but see ver. 23 b), the aim of this teach- ing is right; but the means it inculcates he utterly disallows, being "not according to Christ." The whole tendency of the system was to draw away attention and trust from Christ. Other objections, such as might easily present themselves, he does not care to argue. (1) In him ye were circumcised. "The inward reality of which this rite was the imperfect and prophetic symbol, the consecration of the present life to God, the putting off of the old sinful nature, the body of the flesh, bas already taken place in yo1L This is the circumcision of Christ, the change from sin to holiness, from moral filthiness to pnrity; and you know that you hnve passed through it, if yon are in Mm (1 Cor. vi. 11; GaL iii. 27; v. 24; Rom. xiii. 14). Do not grasp at the shadow when you have the BUbstance. De content to believe that in this, the 'one thing needful,' you are complete in him." (2) From this point the apostle goes a step further back, exactly on the line of his previous teaching in Rom. vi., respecting the connection of sanctification with justification, when be adds, "having been buried with him in your baptism 1 wherein also ye were raised with him." For a state of sinfulness is a state of death. The sinner lies immediately under the wrath of God (eh. i. 21; iii. 6; Eph. ii. 3; Rom. v. 10); and that anger, with the sense of alienation it brings and the shadow of condemnation it casts upon the conscience, is virtually death, is the c.eath of death (comp. Rom. vii. 24, 25 _and viii. 1, 2). 'fhere is no clea~isiog _of the soul of a_ de~d sinner till this sentence JS repealed, and" the love of God" 1s agarn "shed abroad rn bis heart" (Rom. v. 5). Christ gi,ves life that he may give purity (eh. i. 21, 22; Rom. vi. 13 • 'l'itus ii. 14; 1 Pet. ii. 24}-purity with life. And life comes through his resurrection· by the same law, the same power, which "raised Jesus our Lord from the dead," ~re our souls also raised from their death of sin. 'l'he operation in both cases is equaUy supernatural and Divine. The first event is the warrant and the 11ledge of the second. The return of our Surety and Champion from the grave assures us that his sacrifice is accepted and his victory complete (eh. i. 18; Rom. iv. 25; Acts ii. 32-36; xiii. 34-39 • John :n.19, 20). On this fact our faith in him as Lord and Saviour rests (Rom. iv. 24; vi. 7-11; x. 9; 2 Cor. iv. 14); it is a "faith in the working of God who raised him from the dead." Through this faith we are justified-forgiveness becomes onrs (ver, 13; eh. i. 14; Rom. v.1); and in this consciousness of pardon sinful man first OIJ, 11. 1-23.] 'fHE EPISTLE ·ro THE COLOSSIANS. 103

comes to know tho lifo of God (Eph. ii. 1-5; Rom. vi. 7-11); he is 1·econci1ed, and a now existence of peace nncl purity is born wilhin him (2 Cor. v. 17-21), to culminate in his final presentation perfect in O/irist (eh. i. 21, 22, 28). (3) Of this passing from death to life, not circumcision, but baptism, i.~ the appointed and proper Cfhristian symbol. Therein tbo believer is "buried with Chri~t" in his ~rave (ver. 12; Rom. vi.3, 5); his old self, his former condemned existence, is put off and washed away for ever. He emerges from the cleansing stream, "a now creature in Christ Jesus." .A.11 this baptism sets forth and sets forward, so far as the picturing and outward acting of the matter may. And being the authoritative public sign of the grace of a new life, it seals that life on the consciousness and memory of the believing and understanding recipient, and biuds its obligations upon him before God and man; so that henceforth he can only "reckon himself to be dead unto sin, but living unto God in ChriHt Jesus" ( Rom. vi. 11). III. TnE DAR REMOVED: THE VEIL LIFTED. (Vers. 14, 15.) What the individual Christian now realizes for himself in Christ-his new life in God and the cleansing and sanctifying of his nature-is but the personal appropriation of that which was reve:iled to the whole world and addresses itself to the wants of human nature everywhere. It meets the conditions brought about by God's previous dealings with mankind (eh. i. 23, 26-28; Rom. i. 2-5; xvi. 25-27; Acts xiv. 15-17; xvii. 26-31; Heh. i. 1, 2). In two respects the apostle signalizes the earlier relations of men to God as imperfect: two hindrances there were lo that "access to the Father" now secured ( l<:ph. ii. 18; Rom. v. 2; Hcb. vii. 19; x.19-22)-hindrances congruou.~ in nature and c1Tect, felt in the quick and instructed religious consciousness of Judaism more keenly than elsewherethat are "t.aken out of the way" in Christ. There was the law with its condemning voice for the conscience, and the angelic mediation with its terrors and its mysteries for the heart and understanding. The first guilty pair" hid themselves from the presence of the Lord among the trees of the garden" (Gen. iii. 8); and a sinful, weak-hearted people, chosen to be brought near unto him, said, "Let not God speak with us lest we die" (Exod. xx. 19). And God in mercy and in justice heard their prayer. He veiled himself behind his laws and his providence, behind the forms of nature, and the oracles of prophecy, and the progress of history, and the flashing forth of liis glory in the angels of his presence, until Law, the ..-cuaa,-oryos, "ordained through angels," shonld have done its work, "and the fulnass o(the times should be come" (Gal. iii. 19-24; Rom. v. 20). 1. Till then it was increasingly felt that the law with its decrees was aqainst "8. It" wrought wrath" (Rom. iv. 15). It brought us" under a curse" (Gal. iii. 10). It stirred up and brought to its crisis in an agony of self-despair the conflict between the better nature and tbe worse in man (Rom. vii. 7-25). It invoked death with its anticipatory terrors as the sral to its authority and the witness to our guilt (Rom. v. 12-14, 21; vii. 24; 1 Cor. xv. 56). The list of its commandments is but a catalogue of our offences, a tale of debts, not one of which we are prepared to meet, and yet which must be discharged "to the uttermost farthing." In Christ's cross, God has, at a stroke, wiped out the whole bill of oitr o.{frnces. lle has removed it from between us and himself, and nailed it, with CbrisL's body, to the cross, where he bids us read, "'!'hero is now no condemnation to them who are in Christ Jestis" (Rom. viii. 1; iii. 26). This the apostle had taught already, and it is the glory of his earlier Epistles, addressed to Churches infested with Pharisaic Judaism and its teaching of salvation by works of law, to havo established this truth in the understandin~ and the faith of the Church for e.11 time. 2. But the philosophic Judaism with which he has now to deal requires him to insist more strongly on the immediate revelation of God himself to the world that is made in Christ. Now that One be.s been "manifested at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself" (Heh. ix. 26; Isa. !ix. 2), it is po3sible to behold God by e. nearer vision. With the revelation of his pardoning mercy and sin-avenging justice in Christ, "the Son of his love" (Eph. ii. 4:; Rom. iii. 26), he makes known his inmost name and nature. 'l'o Israel, in comparison with ot_her nations," God was nigh" (Deut. iv. 7; Lev. xx. 26); and yet even Israe! complams, "Verily thou art e. Guel tbe.t hidest thyself'' (Isa. xiv. 15). He" came with ten thousand of his holy ones, and from bis right band went e. fiery law for them" (Deut. xxxiii. 2); and "the earth shook, the heavens also dropped e.t the presence of God" (Ps. Ixviii. 8). "He made the clouds his chariot;" his" way was in the se,,, and his path in the great waters, and his footsteps were not known" (Ps. lxxvii. 19, 20). 'l'he mystic 104 THE EPISTLE TO TUE COLOSSIANS. [ell, II, 1-23,

veil that screened his presence was ~s splendid as the law by which he ruled the con- sciences ~f men was stern and tern~le. Dut in Christ, he "laid his glory by.'' God appeared rn the Dabe of Dethlebcm, lD the Man of sorrows, in Chri 8 t crucified, ae tl,o Father of the children of men. He bids all his angels worship and wait upon tho lowly form of the Son of man, and the elements of nature (more closely linked with the angelic powers, perhaps, than we can imagine) are mado to do his bidding "that all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father" (John v. 23). "'l'b;y shall call his name Immanuel, God with us" (Matt. i. 23). None had "seen God at nny time;" the angels that had been his ministers, the glories of tho created world iu which he robed himself (Ps. cii. 2G; civ. 2), these could not utter his Namo: "the onlybegotten Son which is in the bosom of the Father, the Word made flesh, he declared him" (Jolm i. 14, 18). "The veil is done away in Christ." llut" the same veil," which in St. Paul's day bung between the Jewish ruiud and the true knowledge of God "remaineth unlifted" for those who will not behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Uor. iii. 14; iv. 3-6). God at ouce "reconciled the world unto himself" and unveiled himself to the world in him. 'l'his is the sum of these two verses.
