-Scct. 6. The claims of thefalse teacher. The Colossian error is the earliest Chriftian l,eresy, understanding the word in its stricter sense as denoting a move- ment in the direction ol e1Tor, originating within the Church itself. Itfirst answers to the terms of St. Paul's prediction in Acts xx. 29--31. 'l'he powerful J udaizina reaction with which St. Paul and the Gentile Church had previously to struggle, and which drew from him the Galatian and Roman Epistles, was negative and retrograde in its character, originating from without rather than from within the Church, and stimulated by the increasing violence and desperation of Jewish national feeling. Dut here we discern the rise of a heterodox school of thought within Christianity itself. At this point, first of all, were those elements. of error introduced, those seeds of division sown, which ripened into the wild and disastrous Gnostic apostasy of the second century ; and that may be said to have persisted to the present day. For our inveterate and multiplied ecclesi- astical divisions and our deeply rooted doctrinal differences, with the animosities and prejudices that attend them, show too plainly that the rents which then began to open in the Chnrch's unity are far from being closed. Accordingly, the Colossian error presents heresy in its germinal form. It contains and combined in itself the root- principles and incipient forms of those errors which have most widely prevailed in after ages. It unites evil tendencies which afterwards parted asunder and became oppofed to each other, which seem indeed to b6 radically inconsistent. Dut this was an age of eclecticism and amalgamation. Moreover, there is a latent contradiction inherent in falsehood and error. It must needs be inconsisteut and witnesses against itself. Its principles, when car1ied forward and pushed to their issues in logic and practice, become mutually destructive; and the system built upon them and the party which has espoused them of themselves break up into contending fragments. Hence the shifting phases and combinations of religious error-Protean, many-headed-under which the same elements constantly reappear, identical in essence, incessantly varying in form. "The truth as it is in Jesus" is alone self-consistent, harmonious, and enduring. Dut who will assure himself that he has in all things, so far as he might, truly ascertained aod followed it? Tm: FIRST HERESY. We have distinguished in the Colossian heresy four elements of error, which may be roughly designated under the names of rationalism, ceremonialism, mysticism, and asceticism. They are the heresies, respectively, of the intellect, of the religious instinct, of the spiritual consciousness, and of the moral will,-aberrations, each of them, of functions belonging to the highest and divinest part of man's nature. 1. The false teachers are evidently rnl ionalists. It is this characteristic which the apoEtle first expressly specifies (vcrs. 8, :.!3), and to which the whole tenor of the Epistle bears witness (see, especially, eh ) 9, 28; ii. 2-4; iii. 10, 16; and compare the introductory remarks in our homiletic~, 110ct, 2, I. and sect. 5, I.). 'l'hcy construed Christianity in terms of their preconceived pnilosophic theory. 'l'hey were philosophers first, and Christians afterwards, or only Chn~tiane so far as their philosophy permitted, Clirist waa not the centre of their thoughts, the Master of their intellect and heart (cL. ii. HI; iii. 11); but they made au idol of their intellectual B!fBltm, and ho must C1ll, II. 1-23.] 'l'IIB EPIS'l'LE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. 10:3

perforce bo mado to pay homago to it and fit himself into some limited and vacant 11pace where it '!light be nbl_e _tu mako room for him l Not in Christ, it appears, but in themselves and m "the tracht10n of men," were "the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," out of whic~ the Cliristian teaching, in its uncultured crudeness and poverty of thought, must havo its errors corrected and its deficiencies supplied l But the philosophy of theso Colossian illuminati was clearly wrong in its views both of the world and of human naturo; and no one woulcl be found now to advocate it. Their attempts to recast and rationalize Christianity proved an utter failure, and bore fruit in the next age only in_ immorality and schism. Their wisdom was but a "wisdom of words" (vers. 2, 3); they were "ever learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth" (2 Tim. iii. 7). Every system of philosophy, every scheme of human life, which aUempts to patronize and to pervert to its own purposes the Christian teachirw, has, we may be sure, a like doom awaiting it. St. Paul does not seek to check the rat.ionalistic movement at Colossro by mere repression, by discouraging intellectual inquiry. On the contrary, he impresses on his readers again and again the necessity of a better understanding, a deeper knowledge of" the mystery of God" (eh. i. 6, 9, 10, 25-28; ii. 1-4; iii. 10, lG). It was their slight and imperfect Christian education which laitl them open to the attacks of sophistry and a shallow philosophy. The letter is one that appeals to and stimulates Christian thought in an extraordinary degree, and is itself a theological discipline. The spurious and plausible gnosis, " the knowledge falsely so called" (1 'l'im. vi. 20), which was fascinating the Colossians, could be cast out only by the epignosis, the advanced and peifect knowledge (compare homiletics, sects, 1, III. and 4, I., II.). What Lord Bacon said of atheism may apply with equal trnth to heresy: "A little philosophy inclineth men's mind to atheism; but depth in philosophy bringeth men's minds about to religion." 2. \Vitlt their philosophical, a priori interpretation of Christianity, the false teachers of Colossre combined a love of ceremonialism and a devotion to the externals of worship. Here we note the Jewish element in their training, while their Greek sympathies aud habits of thought betray themselves in their fundamental philosophic bias. 'Ihe motive of their religiousness was, however, radically different from that of the traditional Jewish legalism, and St.. Paul deals with it in quite another method from that which he follows in Galatians. 'l'he "philosophers" of Colossre valued Jewish ritual for its expressiveness and symbolic truth, and practised it as a means of spiritual self-culture rather than in mere obedience to law. Hence they iusisted much on the sacred seasons and feasts, on the distinctions of meats (vers. 16, 17), on circumcision ( ver. 11), and studic,l greatly the·art of worship (vers. 18, 23); while, like the Essenes, they attached little importance to the sacrificial system of Judaism. So, at least, 'l·e should infer from the apostle's silence on these latter topics, as contrasted with the leading part they play in the Epistle to the Hebrews. '!'heir system was Jewish in its materials, but wholly different from the Jewish in spirit and tendency. But their piety was wanting in spiritual depth and reality, or they could scarcely have failed to recognize in Christ "the Image of God" (eh. i. 15), and the" new and living way" to the Father. Gou was to them so far off that they would not seek to approach him directly in the Persou of his Son, but supposed a whole hierarchy of mediators necessary, to make worship possible. He was, in their view, a great abstract Infinitude, no "living Father," no listening, answering Presence. Their religion was an elaborate arti6ce, beneficial chiefly in its reaction on themselves; and their God was shrouded, like an Oriental monarch, behind a multitude of vague and fugitive mediators, whom practically they worshipped instead of him. A like result ensues wherever the idea of a personal God is obscured an<l weakened in the minds of men, whether by philosophical reflection making him a formula, or by superstitious ignomnce treating him ns a fetish. For true worship is the converse-'' in spirit and in truth" (John iv. 23, 24), of the human children with their living Father in heaven, And this cannot well bo maintained where an ornate ceremouia.lism overpowers the senses and fills the imagination with its external pomp; or where the living God "in whom we live," and Christ the "one Mediator" (1 'l'im. ii. 5), arc so distant from tho realizations of faith, that angels, or departed saints, or the blessed virgin-mother, or ca.rthly priests and confessors, are thrust in to fill tho void, e.nd arc made in rcnlity to intercept tho soul'~ reverence aud devotion. Thtro ruo.y be o. sincere "zcnl for worship" in the anxious stu,ly of ecclesiastical dress an,l 106 TIIE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cu. n. 1-23.

decoration, and under the sensuous impressiveness of a eplendid and elaborate rltuallem, But thi_s is no~ wha_t "the Father s~eketl~" (John iv. 23, 24), and such aids to devotion often hrnder his children from seekmg hnn. Our worship must. indeed havo ite forms• and order and propriety (1 Oor. xiv. 4.0) must be studied in 'their r~crulatiou and i~ all the apP?intme~ts of the house of God. And men of varying tc~peram~nt and mental habit arc aided by a greater or less degree, and by different kinds of outward expression in their worship. Dut when the form is cultivated for its o~ sake and the s~ns~1ous ~nd the artistic predomin~te over and displace tho spiritual, the e'nd of "·orsh1p itself 1s frustrated, and the service that professes to be rendered to the Most High becomes a mockery to him, and a blind to his worshippers that eITectuo.lly hides him from them. Yet this tendency has often a strong attraction for devout and humble spirits," delighting in humility" (vcrs. 18, 23); who love to worship, and readily bow before any superior influence, but are not so anxious to" worship what they know" (John iv. 22). A multiplying of the objects of worship (vcr. 18) very commonly attends the excessive elaborntiou of its forms; for both are due to the samo cause, and are the manifestations of a religion weak in spiritual faith in God. The dissatisfaction and emptiness of soul which ensue on seeking God thus, lead to our making still more cumbrous and exacting the forms of devotion, and to our resorting to new mediators and new methods of approach to Lim, till Christian worship sinks into a round of ritual performance and semi-idolatry, and becomes an imposture iu itself and an aversion to thoughtful, truth-seeking men. 3. There was, in the third place, a strong vein of false mysticism in tlte Oolossian heresy. This element, in the nature of the case, is more difficult to distinguish and to delineate than those already set forth. The mysticism of Greece was chiefly derived and fo<l from Oriental sources. Pythagoras, in the latter half of the sixth century B.c., founded a school of mystical and ascetic philosophy, whose principles were largely adopted in the comprehensive system of Plato. 'l'he Pythagorean and Platonic mysticism was at this time greatly in vogue, especially in· Asia Minor and in Egypt, where it found a congenial soil. Tile Alcxandrine school of Philo imported its principles into Judaism. Tue Neo-Platonism, in which, in the fourth and fifth centuries A.D., pagan philosophy made a last splendid struggle for existence, and which bas left deep marks of its influence on the development of ()hrisLian thought, was a revival of Greek mysticism in a more intense and religious form. The Montanism of the second century, a product of the same Pbrygian soil on which the Colossian heresy sprang up, attested the persistence of the mystic tendency within the Church. Its later manifestations, as allied no,v with pantheistic rationalism, now with devout ceremonialism, now with rigid asceticism, we cannot endeavour here to follow. 'l'hertl bas always been in the Church a mystical school, side by side with the rationalistic, and the ritualistic or sacerdotal. And, within certain limits, the mystic principle has its rights, and must be recognized as essential to spiritual religiou. To mysticism, tbo spiritual consciousness of the individual is the source and the test of truth, God is to l,e reached by intuition. Meditative contemplation, aided by suitable init!ato~y and disciplinary symbolic rites, is the way of salvation, whose goal is absorption m the Divine nature. Such was the teachin" of ancient mystics geuerally; and the esoteric doctrines introduced at Colossre were, doubtless, of the same stamp. '!'hut God, iudced, reveals himself by his Spirit to the individual consciousness, is the teaching of St. Paul, and, as we believe, of the whole Bible (Rom. viii. 16; Gal. i. 1G; Ps. cxxxix., etc.). But when the inner consciousness, the spilitual reason, is regarded as in itself the primary source oi revelation, then error begins and hallucination supervenes. The mind turns itself in upon its own self-generated phantasies, inskad of fixing its gaze on the historical revelation of God and setking to comprehend and mirror its glory (2 Cor. iii. 18; iv. 6; Rom. i. 20; Ps. x.ix., etc.). The Colossian errorist, walking in the light of bis self-confident, self-contemplating reason, saw visions of angels as be imagined, and beard messages and teachings that were but the echo of his own speculations. With these deceived and deccivino- subjective imaginings the apostle confronts the actual historic Person and work of Christ, as the supreme Object of contemplation and of trust (eh. i. 13-15, 21, 22, 27-29; ii. 6, 7; iii. 11, 15-17). Only through "belief of the truth" come the testifying and sanctifying visitations of "the Spirit of the truth" (2 'l'hess. ii. 9-14; Eph. i. 13, 14; Acts ii. 38; xix. 1-7). The objective revelation of God to the soul and the subjective attestation and experience of its power OB. D, 1-23.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO 'flIE COLOSSIANS. lOi

nre rociprocnlly linked together, and advance pari passu. Compare the teaching of Christ in promising the Holy Spirit to his discipl(ls (,John xiv. 15-24). The cloctrine of the Holy Spirit was indirectly but vitally affected by the Colossian error; and this topic, though not brought forward in this Epistle, is prominent in the Ephesian letter, which is in many respects a complement to this and, in our belief, is "the letter'' to be sent" from Lnodicea" for the perusal of the Colossi an Church (eh. iv. 16). "Christ the Mystery of God," "Chtist in you tl,e hope of glory,"-this is the apostle's mysticism, the true mystery that is to expel the false, unhallowed mysteries, that seek by self-directed intuitions and self-invented lustrations and incantations to penetrate the secrets of the spiritual world and to enter into union with the Infinite. 4. Jn the sphere of morals and practical life, the Colossian errorists inculcated a strict a.1ceticism. 'l'his part of their system is consistent with each of the other three, though it pro- ·eeded rather from its philosophical and mystical than from its Judaistic and ceremonial constituent factor. In the early Christian ages, asceticism was frequently associated with theoretic rationalism; in later times, it bas been more frequently the ally of a sacerdotal type of Christianity. Asceticism was a thing foreign to Judaism. It was a religion too healthy and practical for that. Ps. cxxviii. expresses what bas always been the true religious feeling of Israel in regard to the blessings of this life. 'l'be Pharisaic yoke was indeed "grievous to be borne," and pressed on the externals of life with the weight of a slavery; but, after all, it concerned matters which habit makes comparatively easy, and its spirit was that of a formal legalism, aiming at precision in the performance of all external acts, and by no means valuing hai·d treatment of the body in itself. Dut the latter was the distinguishing feature of the new Colossian ethics, as of the ethics of Eastern mysticism and of Chlistian monachism, and, in some sort, of Puritanism too. (1) Asceticism is the perversion of a true and noble impulse. In it the maxim, Corruptio optimi pessima, has its saddest illustration. How natural it is for an earnest soul, striving after purity and fellowship with God, to fall into a hatred of the body and the material world! How all but irresistible must this tendency have been in the midst of the reeking impurities and the social dissolution of the pagan and barbarian worlds! (2) Moreover, the very nature of religious language, with its necessities of figurative expression, lends itself to misconstruction of scriptural truth in this direction. ·witness the interpretations still prevalent of St. Paul's own te11ninology. It is difficult, both in thought and in practice, to distinguish always between the body, which Christ raised, which becomes the temple of bis Spirit, whose members are to be instruments of righteousness, which is the symbol of the Church the bride of Christ, which nature itself teaches every man to nourish and to cherish (1 Cor. vi. 12-20; Rom. vi. 12-14; viii. 11; Eph. v. 22-30), and the flesh, which has to be stripped off, to be put to death, to be crucified with its affections and lust~, by all who are'' of Christ Jesus" (eh. ii.11; iii. 5; Gal. v. 24). (3) With the Colo;;sian errorist-, as in the Alexandrine theosophy, the body was the source of sin, the prison ic. which the soul is shut up and severed from God. 'l'o break the chains of scn~e, to cast off the bmden of the flesh and become pure spirit, and thus to rise towards God,-this was the aspiration of the ancient mystics. Matter and spirit were the two opposite poles of being; and the distinction between moral good and evil, for them, merged itself in this. They declared indiscriminate war against the physical life and natu,ral enjoyment as itself sinful or tending to sin. Their conception of holiness it was, of course, impossible absolutely to realize; but he woulcl npproximate to it the most nearly who maintained himself in as feeble and impoverished a bodily condition as was consistent with active thought. (4) Such doctrine was, we may be sure, more often preached than practised. But it took effect, within a little time, in the denunciation of marriage (1 'fim. iv. 3; Heb. xiii. 4), as among tho Jewish Essenes, with the dis- honouring of the family life and the weakening of social bonds which necessarily ensue. 'l'o this source we trace that false ideal of Christian purity which, before many centuries, became pr~valent in the Church Catholic, and the rise of the gigantic and baleful institution of monasticism and the celibate priesthood, which, hy withdrawing from the world the most powerfnl elements of Christian character and influence, and by the immorality and social disorganization which it engendered, has blighted the Church's history and delayed indefinitdy the conversion of mankind to the faith of Christ. (5) Let us Iistqu to Olli' heavenly Intercessor, who asks the Father," :::,.,'vt that thou shouldcst ins 'l'HE EPIS'l'LE TO THE COLOSSI.ANS, [ell, 11, 1-23,

t:lkc them out of tho world, but that thou sbouldest keep them from its e'l"il I" who bids his disciples be" the salt of tbti earth,"" the light of the world" (John xvii. 16; Matt. v. 1:~, 14). Let us have faith in the power of his Spirit, who can so sanctify our mortal body that "sin shall not reign in it" (Rom. vi. 12 ; 1 Cor. vi. 19, 20); and can so hallow the temperate and grateful use of the natural blessiugs God bestows upon us (1 Tim. iv. 3-5; eh. iii. 21, 22) that, "whether we cat or drink or whatsoever we do," we shall" do all to the glory of God" (1 Cor. x. 31; eh. iii. 17), Let us hear St. Paul, while he teaches us to "make not provision for the flesh to fulfil its lusts" (Rom. xiii. 14), yet to "abide with God," each in that secular state "wherein he was called" (1 Cor. vii. 24). (6) God's Law regulates, does not suppress, the natural life. 'l'he home, the field, the mart, the senate, all that belongs to the natural fabric and constitution of human life, is bis creation, the arena for the exercise of his superintend- ing providence, and the field of probation in .which he trains his children for their spiritual manhood. He sent bis Son to be the Saviour of the world, not of the indi- vidual soul alone, but of human society in its widest sense, including business and politiCJ, 11·t and science, all the public interests and constituent elements of collective human life, which are to find their sanctification, that is, their perfection and their unity, as they are penetrated and ruled by "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus." So "the kingdom of the world" shall "become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ" (Rev. xi.15). (7) The Gospel puts high honour on the human body. The fact that Christ was "born of a woman" redeems its birth from dishonour and contempt. The Incarnation is fatal to all theosophy l>ased on the hostility of the material to the spiritual, and to the false spiritualism which would seek God by fleeing from the body. Christ has incorporated our flesh with his own Divinity, aud in the body of his flesh (eh. i. 22) he redeemed us, and reconciled the world to God. To the meanest human person there belongs an unspeakable dignity and sacredness as partaking of that "blood and flesh" in which he shared (Bcb. ii, H), and through which he "poured out bis soul unto death" (Isa. liii. 12). Christ's work will be completed and" the travail of his soul satisfied" only by "the redemption of our body," which will consummate our "adoption "and will bring with it the deliverance of "the creation itself" from "the bondage of corruption" (Rom. viii. 18-25). For this end, we still" wait for a. Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ," descending from heaven (Phil. iii. 20, 21). So waiting, we shall keep pare and clean this "earthly house of our tabernacle" (2 Cor. v. 1; 1 John iii. 3). Nothing that belongs to it can we "call common or unclean" (Acts x. 15 ), "body of humiliatiou" though it is (Phil. iii. 21). We occupy it for Christ our ::Masler. It is the "temple of the Holy Spirit "-the Spirit of delicate purity, the Spirit of order and of beauty, the Spirit of health and unity, whose" communion" is the Church's breath of life, and the secret, perrnsive atmosphere and inspiration that brings all that is pure and healthful into the society of men.

entries.title: COL 2:8
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.A warning against speculative deceiv(fl's. "Take heed lest there shall be any one that maketh spoil of you through his philosophy nnd vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ." Mark- I. 'l'nE NATURE OF TllE PHILOSOPHY HERE CONDEMNED. It is philosophy inseparably connected with "vaiu deceit." '!'here is a philosophy which is highly serviceable to religion, as it is the noblest exercise of our ratiollal faculties; but there is a philosophy prejudicial to religion, because it sets up the wisdom of man in opposition to the wisdom of God. 1. The apostle refers to the Judreo-Gnostics who regarded Ohristianity mainly as a philosophy-that is, as a search after speculative truth, and not as n revelation of Christ and a. life of faith and love in him. The apostle claims for the gospel that it is thus "the wisdom of God." 2. He refers to the speculative result of such a philosophy. It tends to "vain deceit;" it is hollow, sophistical, disappointing, misleading. It is the "science falsely so called" which "puffs up" a.nl cannot edify. It always tends to undermine man's faith in the Word or God. II. TnE ORIGIN OF THIS PHILOSOPHY. "After the tradition of men." H had its source in mere human speculation, nnd could not appeal to inspired books. Our Lord condemned the Pharisaic attachmant to traditions ,(Matt. xv. 2, 3, 6; Mark vii. 8, 9). '!'hie later mystical tendency was strong in its traditions, which it reserved for the exclusive use of the initiated. III. THI!: SUIJJECT-JlfATTER OF THIS PIIIL0S0PHY. "After the rudiments of the world." '!'his seems to point to ritualistic observances worthy only of children, but not adapted to grown men. They belonged "to the world "-to the sphere of external and visible things. These rudiments were "beggarly elements," done away in Christ. IV. lTs NEGATIVE WORTHLESSNESS. "And not after Christ." 1. It harl, nol Christ for its ~utltor; for it followed "the tradition of men." 2. It had not Christ for lts Subject; for it displaced him to make way for ritualistic ordinances and angalic mediotors. No philosophy is wortl1y of the nome that cannot find a place for him who is the highest Wisdom (1 Cor. i. 30). V. THE DANGERS OF TIIIB PlllLOS0PHY. "Take heed lest there shall bo any ono that maketh spoil of you," It would have an enslaving effect, partly by its ritualistic drudgeries aud partly by its false teaching. There a.re worse losses than the loss of 112 THE EPIS'l'LE 'l'O THE COLOSSIANS. [on. H, 1-23,

property or c-ven children. This false philosophy would involve: 1. The loss of Ch1·i.,- tian liberty. (Gal. v. 1.) 2. The loss of much of the good seed sown in 0/wiseian hearf.s. (lllatt. xiii. 19.) ~- T~~ los.s qf what Christian~ had wrought. (2 John 10.) 4-. The loss of first love. (hcv. 11. 1.) 6, TM loss of the Joys of salvation, (Ps, li, 12.) -T.C.

. V~rs. 9, 10.- Christ tl1e Fulness of the Godhead, and our relationship to him, "For Ill !nm dwellcth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily; and in him ye ere made full who is the Head of all prindpality and power." The apostle is here condemninc, on~ of the false principles that underlay the teaching of the Gnostics-the substituti~n of angelic mediators for Christ. I. CHRIST'S TilUE DEITY AND TRUE RUMANTT,·. 1. He is '110 mere emanation from the supreme God, but" al,l the fulness of the Godhead." All the infinite perfections of the essential being of God are in him. The Gnostics taught that the fulness of the Godhead was distributed among many spiritual agencies. The apostle teaches that it is in Christ as the eternal \Vord. "The Word was with God,and was God." 2. This fulness "dwells" in him now and for ever, It is a blessedly abiding fact. It is a per- manent indwelling. 3. It dwells " bodily;" that is, with a bodily manifestation. The false teachers, imagining that matter was essentially evil, could not brook the thought of the Divine Redeemer linking himself for ever with a human body, and they, after Docetic theory, either denied the reality of his body or its inseparable connection with him for c-ver. But" the ,vord was made flesh" (John i. 14), and" The Rpirit which confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh,. , • is the spirit of anticbrist" (1 John iv. 3). II. Oun RELATI0NSITIP TO THE FULNESS OF CHRIST, "And in him ye aro made full, who is the Head of all principality and power." 1, Christian life is union with Christ. (l) We can obtain nothing from Christ till we are in Christ (1 John v. 20). "In him we have life" (1 John v.11), as in him we are chosen (Eph. i. 4). (2) We cannot, therefore, look for life from subordinate mediators. 2. Christian life is tlie enjoyment of hisfulness. (1) Therefore nothing is to be looked for from angelic mediators. "Out of bis fulness have we all received, and grace for grace" (John i. 16). His fulness is not finite, hut infinite. There can never, therefore, be lack of supply. (2) It ought to be our prayer to receive more largely of this fulncss. 'l'he apostle prayed for the Ephesians that they might be "filled up to all the fulness of God," and "grow unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ" (Epb. iii. 19; iv. 13). (3) To share in this fulness is no privilege of an esoteric few, but is that of all who are united to Christ by faith. Ill THE EXPLANATION OF TfilS RELATIONSHIP OF CHBIST'B FULNESS TO OUR FULNESB. "Who is the Head of all principality and power.'' He is more than Sovereign over. the powers. He is the SoW'ce of their life and activity. This headship over angels is asserted elsewhere (Heb. i. 1-14). Angels are not, therefore, mediators for man, dis- 1,lacing "the one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. ii, 5). They are but fellow-servants under the same Head (Rev. xxii. 8, 9). Therefore we do not seek our fulness in them, but ill OW' Head.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 2:11
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-11.e true circumcision. The Colossians did not need the rite of circumcision to make them complete, for they had received the spiritual circumcision, of which the rite was only a type. "In whom ye were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ." The apostle censures the ritualistic ideas of the false teachers by showing what is the natUI'e and effect of the true circumcision. L lTs NATURE. It is not external, but internal, wrought by the Spirit and not by the hands of men. It is "of the heart in the spirit, and not in the letter " (Rom. ii. 29). lt is "the circumcision of the heart,'' 60 often spoken of even in Old Testament times (Deut. L 16; l'.XL 6; Ezek. xliv. 7; Acts vii. 51), which ought to have accompauied the external rite. The Colossians, as Gentiles, were circumcised in this spiritual _881168 on the day of their conversion. II. lTs EXTENT. "In the putting off the body of the flesh;" not in the mere"cutting off of a part of the body, as in the external rite of Judaism, This language marks the OH. ll. 1-23.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 113

completeness of the spiritual cba.nge and its effects upon both body and soul. 1. The body of flesh is more than the mere body, which is not" put off," for it is not evil, but becomes "the temple of the Holy Ghost" (1 Cor. iii. 16; vi. 19). It is the body in ile fleshliness, regarded as the seat of the lusts which war against the soul and bring forth fruit unto death. The expression is similar to "the old man which is corrupt" (Eph. iv. 22), "the body of sin" (Rom. vi. 6), and" sinful flesh," or, literally," the flesh of sin" (Rom. viii. 3). The spiritual circumcision implies, not the mere putting off of one form of sin, but the putting off the whole of the power of the flesh. 2. The pulling off of the body of flesh implies deliverance from the domini® of sin-dying to sin ae a controlling and regulating power, so that the body, hitherto "the instru~ ment of unrighteousness," becomes "an instrument of righteousness unto God" (Rom. vi. 13). III. ITS AuTHon. "In the circumcision of Christ;" that is, the circumcision wrought by Christ through his Spirit. Its Author is not Moses or Abraham, bnt Christ himself, by virtue of our union with him. The formation of Christ in the soul as the Author of a new spiritual life is " the circumcision of Christ;" it is the new birth, which, under the power of the Holy Spirit, casts off the power of corruption. It is wrought by the Lord the Spirit (2 Cor. iii. 18), and is the result of Christ dwelling in us by faith (Gal. ii. 20; Eph. ii. 5--8). '!'his is the true circumcision, "whose praise is not of man, but of God."-T. C.

entries.title: COL 2:12
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The import of Christian baptism. Circumcision has passed away, something has come in its place in Christian times. The two ordinances ofcircumcision and baptism have e. correlative significance. "Having been buried with him in baptism, wherein ye were also raised with him through faith in the working of Go,!, who raised him from the dead." I. THE IMPORT AND DESIGN OF BAPTISM. It solemnly attests that fellowship with Christ in his death and resurrection on which all personal interest in the blessings of his salvation depends. " Baptism is the grave of the old man and the birth of the new." The whole process of spiritual renovation-the death of the corruption of nature and the rise to newness of life-is practically represented and scaled in baptism. We are identified with Christ : 1. In his death. "Buried with him in baptism" unto death. Our baptism unites us to him, so that we died with him. We are" planted in the likeness of death;" but here the apostle asserts a participation in bis death. 2. In his burial. After "he died for our sins according to the Scriptures" (1 Cor. xv. 3), "he descended into the lower parts of the earth" (Eph. iv. 9). So "we are buried with him," shut off f-tom the kingdom of Satan, as the dead in their graves are shut off from the living wor1".; and thus we have with him severed our connection with the old world of sin. 3. In his resurrecti®. For "we rose with him," that we might henceforth "walk in new1iess of life." We must share in his death, that we may share in bis life. Justification is in order to sanctification. Union with Christ in the one carries with it participation in the other. II. THE •INSTRUMENT THDOUGH WHICH WE ENJOY THE BLESSINGS SIGNIFIED IN BAPTISM. "'l'hrough faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead." 'rhis shows how the outward is based on the inward, and bow it derives from it whatever vitality it possesses. Faith appropriates the act of God's mighty power in Christ when be raised him from the dead, as an act that imparts its virtue to e.11 who in faith realize it. 'l'he physical power in raising Christ is the guarantee and assurance of the spiritual power which is exerted in us in regeneration. Faith is necessary to the effect of baptism as it is to salvation. "If thou bclievest in thy heart that God raised him from the dead, thou sbalt be saved" (Hom. x. 9). It is by faith we obtain the benefits of the spiritual resurrection and come to et know the power of his resurrection." The gmco is received through faith. In New 'l'estament times faith preceded baptism-a proof that baptism is not regeneration. The earliest cases were naturally those of adult baptism, in which there was e. profession of faith in Christ. III. 'rHE PLEDGE OF THE SPIRITUAL RESURI\ECTION. "The working of God, who raised him from the dead." '!'his power to us is made possible and actual by his resurrection; for" in that he liveth, he liveth unto God," Ilis resurrection involves both our bodily and ow· spiritual rcsurreciion,~T. C, C0J.0SSIANS. I lH 'l'IIE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSL\NS, [cH, II, 1-23,

V crs. 13-15.-Tlie atoneme_nt and_ i~s blessed i·esults. "And you, being dead through your tres~ssos. and t~e nncir~umc1S1on of your flesh, you, I say, did he quicken to_s:ether with lum, havmg forgiven us all our trespasses." 'l'heso words add no new thoughts to the passage, but are a more detailed explanation of the matters inv0lrcd in I h~ work of Christ in the soul. I. CONSIDER TIIE PERSONAL QUICKENING OUT OF A STATE OF DEATH AND DEFll,E:.rni-·r. 1. The condition <if all men by nature-.spiritual death, This death is viowod in I wo aspects: (1) lu r~lation to deliuite acts ?f transgression, as showing the power of sin nm!. ihe frmt of an evil nature. (2) In relation to the root of the evil-" the uncircumcision <•f your flesh;" your unsnncti6.ed, fleshly nature marked by alienation from God (see l,omiletical hints on Eph. ii. 1). 2. The quickening energy of God. "You did he q'.iickcn toge_ther with h!m." Spiritual_ death is put a~ay by the qni~kening energy ot God, which flowed mto your hearts out of the nseu life of Christ. You are brought up with him objectively in his resurrection, subjectively in his application of the power of his resurrection (see homiletical hints on Eph. ii. 1). II. CONSIDER THE GROUND AND CONDITION OF THIS QUICKENING. The pardon of &in. "Having forgiven us all our trespasses." Thus spiritual life is connected with pardon, and presupposes pardon. The sins of men must be pardoned belore life could properly enter. Our Lord could not have been quickened till we, for whom he died, "·ere potentially discharged (Rom. iv. 25). So, indeed, the quickening presupposes at once pardon, the blotting out of the handwriting, and the victory over Satan. Ill. CoNSIDER THE INDISPENSABLE .ACCOMPANIMENT OF THIS PARDON. The removal of Ilic condemning power of the Lnw. "Having blotted out the hand writing in ordinances that was ag:;inst us, which was coutrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross." 1. The 'l'lature and effects of this handwriti'l'lg in O'l"dinances. (1) It is not the mere ceremonial law, though its ritual observances were symbols of deserved punishment or an acknowledgment of guilt.. We cannot limit it to this law, though the ontward observances of ver. 20 were specially in view; for the apostle is not here distinguishing between Jews and Gentiles. (2) It is the whole Law, moral and ceremonial-" the Law of commandments contained in ordinances "-which fastens upon us the charge of guilt, and is the great barrier against forgiveness. It was immcJiatcly against the Jews, mediately against the Gentiles. It is the Law, in the full compass of its requirements. (3) The hostility of this Law to us. It was "against us; it was contrary to us." (a) Not that the Law was in itself offensive, for it was" holy and just and good" (Rom. vii. 12); but (b) because our inability to fulfil it or satisfy its righteous demands exposed us to the penalty attached to an undischarged obligation. It was, in a word, a bill of indictment against us. 2. The blotting out of the handwriting. It was blotted out, so far as it was an accusing witness against us, by Christ wiping it out, takiog it "out of the way, and nailing it to his cross." It was not done by an arbitrary abolition of the Law; moral obligations cannot be removed in this manner; but by the just satisfaction which Christ rendered by his "obedience unto death." It was nailed to his cross, and thus its condemnatory power was brought to nn end. Strictly speaking, there was nothing but Christ's body nailed to the cross; but, as he ,ras made sin, taking the very place of sin, "bearing our sins in his own body on the tree," the handwriting, with the curse involved in it, was identified with him, and thus God condemned sin in Christ's flesh (Rom. viii. 3). Christ exchanged places with us, and thus was cancelled the bill of indiclment which involved us in guilt and condemnation. IV. CoNBIDEil THE RELATION OF THE ATONEMENT TO TBE VICTORY OVER SATAN. " l!aviug put off from himself the principalities and the powers, he made o. show of them openly, triumphing over them in it." It was the cross thnt gave the victory' over the principalities and powers of darkness, because sin was the ground of their dominion over man and the secret of their strength. llut no sooner had Christ die<l. and extinguished the guilt lying on us, than the ground of their successful ~gency was undermined and, instead of beina at liberty to ravage and destroy, their weapons of warfare 'perished, Christ on the cross, as the wo~d signific~, reft from. him and from his people those powers of darkness who could afflict humamty by pressing home the consequences of their sin. He cast them off like baffled foes (John xii. :-11), i,iac\,) rnch a 6how of them openly as angels, if not men, coufu probably apprehend. OIi, II, 1-23.) THE EPISTLE '1'0 THE COLOSSIANS. 115

entries.title: COL 2:16
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0ondemnation of rilu,alislic observances and ascetic severities. The npostlo draws a practical inference from the view he had just given of the work of Obrist. "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of a sabbath <lay: which things are a shatlow of tho things to come; but the body is Christ's." I. THE rROHIDITION. It is twofold, re~pecting first the distinction of meats and drinks, and then the observance of times. 1. 'l.'he distinction of meats and drinks. (1) This distinction was made in the Mosaic Law as to things clean and unclean. '!'here was no prohibition as to drinl,s, except in regard to .Nazarites and priests during their ministration (Lev. x. 9; Numb. vi. 3). It is probable that the Colossian crrorists, like the Essenes, forbade wine and animal food altogether; for they imposed a rigorous asceticism upon their disciples. (2) The distinction is abolished by the gospel. (a) Our Lord hinted at the approaching abolition (Mark vii. 14, 19). (b) 'l'here was a formal annulment of the distinction in Peter's vision (Acts x.11, etc.), where the distinction between those within and those without the covenant was being done away. (c) The abolition is implied in Heb. ix. 10, where the rule as "to meats and drinks" is said to Lave been" imposed until the time of reformation." (d) It is also implied in the action of the Council of Jerusalem, and in the language of Peter respecting "the yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear" (Acts xv. 10). (3) The attitude of Ohristia11s towards this distinction. "Let no man ... judge you in respect of" them, (a) Christians are not justified now in making such a distinction or in imposing it upon others. 'l'hus the Roman Catholics are condemned for their distinction of meats: "Commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving" (1 Tim. iv. 3). It is not "that which goeth into the mouth that defileth the man" (Matt. xv. 2, 11). (b) Christians in apostolic times had a liberty in these matters which they were to exercise for edification. (u) It was allowable for a believer neither "to eat flesh" nor to drink wine" so long as the world standeth" (1 Cor. viii. 13). (13) It was allowable in the transition state of the Church, while it consisted of two diverse elements-Jews and ~ntiles-for liberty to be exercised in these matters, with a due regard to the rights of conscience (Rom. xiv. 2). (c) But we in our different circumstances must resist any attempt to impose upon us a distinction of meats. " Let no man ... judge you in meat, or in drink." It is not in mari's power to make that a sin which God has not forbidden. "It is a very small thing that I should be judged of you or of man's judgment" (1 Cor. iv. 3). "Why dost thou judge thy brother?" (Rom. xiv. 3, 10), Besides, we must remember the spiritual nature of Christianity: "The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost" (Rom, xiv. 17). We must "stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ bath made his people free" (Gal. v. 1). 2. The observance of times and seasons. "Or in respect of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of a sabbath day." The apostle said to the Galatians, "Yo observe days, and months, and times, and years" (Gal. iv. 10). (1) 'l'hcre was a provisionnl and temporary discretion allowed likewise in the matter of days. " One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in bis own mind" (Rom. xiv. 5, 6). The apostle leaves the matter of days an open question. (2) Yet no man was to be taken to task for refusing to observe them, 'l'he times were entirely Jewish. (a) The "feast day" referred to the annual festivals, like Pentecost and Passover. (b) The" new moon" referred to the monthly festival, (c) The" sabbath day" referred to the Jewish sabbath, which was always observed on the Saturday. "But does the apostle not seem to strike at the obligation of maintaining the observance of one day in seven for the worship of God, and sunder the connection that exists between the Jewish sabbath and the Christian Sunday?" We answer that: (u) The observance of the Lord's day never came into question in apostolic times. It was universally observed from the beginning both by Jews and Gentiles, It cannot, therefore, be affected by anything said as to" days" in Rom. xiv.1-6 or in this passage. (9) The devotion of a seventh part of our time to God rests on consideraLions as old as creation, for the sabbath was made for man even before sin entered the world. (-y) The sabbath of the 116 '.L'HE EPISTLE '1'0 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [ CH, II, 1-23,

Jews ,rns typical, and therefore was abolished in Christ, and therefore, as well as for other rea~ons, the Lord's day, which took its place from the beginning of the gospel dispensatwn, was changed from ~he last_ to the first day of the week. The sabbath day "·as so long and so deeply associated with the stated feasts, the sabbatical year, and the jubilee year of Juda_ism? th~t it partool~ of their tyJ?ical character, and thus passed away with the other mstitut10ns of Judaism. Ilut tlus was not the original aspect of (he sabbath, which bad nothing in it typical of redemption, for it began while there was no sin and no need of salvation. Thus, just as baptism is the Lord's circumcision according to ver. 11, the Lord's day is the sabbath of Christian times. II. THE REASON FOR THE PROHIBITION, ",vhich things are a shadow of the tbin"s to come; but the body is Christ's.'' They were useful as shadows before the Subst~nce came, but after it they were useless. l. The shadow. The word implies: (1) The dimness, the unsubstantiality of these Jewish ordinances or institutions. 'l'he light they proj~cted forward into Christian times was obscure. (2) Their temporary nature, The shadow disappears when the substance is come. 2. The substance. "The body L, Christ's;" that is, belongs to Christ. 'l'he reality is verified in Christ and the benefits or the new dispensation. 'l'be blefsings they prefigured are to be realized by union with Christ.-T. C.

(c) But we in our different circumstances must resist any attempt to impose upon us a distinction of meats. " Let no man ... judge you in meat, or in drink." It is not in mari's power to make that a sin which God has not forbidden. "It is a very small thing that I should be judged of you or of man's judgment" (1 Cor. iv. 3). "Why dost thou judge thy brother?" (Rom. xiv. 3, 10), Besides, we must remember the spiritual nature of Christianity: "The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost" (Rom, xiv. 17). We must "stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ bath made his people free" (Gal. v. 1). 2. The observance of times and seasons. "Or in respect of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of a sabbath day." The apostle said to the Galatians, "Yo observe days, and months, and times, and years" (Gal. iv. 10). (1) 'l'hcre was a provisionnl and temporary discretion allowed likewise in the matter of days. " One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in bis own mind" (Rom. xiv. 5, 6). The apostle leaves the matter of days an open question. (2) Yet no man was to be taken to task for refusing to observe them, 'l'he times were entirely Jewish. (a) The "feast day" referred to the annual festivals, like Pentecost and Passover. (b) The" new moon" referred to the monthly festival, (c) The" sabbath day" referred to the Jewish sabbath, which was always observed on the Saturday. "But does the apostle not seem to strike at the obligation of maintaining the observance of one day in seven for the worship of God, and sunder the connection that exists between the Jewish sabbath and the Christian Sunday?" We answer that: (u) The observance of the Lord's day never came into question in apostolic times. It was universally observed from the beginning both by Jews and Gentiles, It cannot, therefore, be affected by anything said as to" days" in Rom. xiv.1-6 or in this passage. (9) The devotion of a seventh part of our time to God rests on consideraLions as old as creation, for the sabbath was made for man even before sin entered the world. (-y) The sabbath of the 116 '.L'HE EPISTLE '1'0 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [ CH, II, 1-23,

Jews ,rns typical, and therefore was abolished in Christ, and therefore, as well as for other rea~ons, the Lord's day, which took its place from the beginning of the gospel dispensatwn, was changed from ~he last_ to the first day of the week. The sabbath day "·as so long and so deeply associated with the stated feasts, the sabbatical year, and the jubilee year of Juda_ism? th~t it partool~ of their tyJ?ical character, and thus passed away with the other mstitut10ns of Judaism. Ilut tlus was not the original aspect of (he sabbath, which bad nothing in it typical of redemption, for it began while there was no sin and no need of salvation. Thus, just as baptism is the Lord's circumcision according to ver. 11, the Lord's day is the sabbath of Christian times. II. THE REASON FOR THE PROHIBITION, ",vhich things are a shadow of the tbin"s to come; but the body is Christ's.'' They were useful as shadows before the Subst~nce came, but after it they were useless. l. The shadow. The word implies: (1) The dimness, the unsubstantiality of these Jewish ordinances or institutions. 'l'he light they proj~cted forward into Christian times was obscure. (2) Their temporary nature, The shadow disappears when the substance is come. 2. The substance. "The body L, Christ's;" that is, belongs to Christ. 'l'he reality is verified in Christ and the benefits or the new dispensation. 'l'be blefsings they prefigured are to be realized by union with Christ.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 2:18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.A warning against angel-worship. The apostle now notices the theological error of the false teachers, which was the interposition of angelic mediators between God and man. "Let no man rob you of your prize by a voluntary humility and worsbipping of angels, dwelling in the things he bath seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind." L ANGEL-WORSHIP rs CLEARLY CONDEMNED. 1. The angel whom John would have worshipped, said, "See tbou do it not, for I am thy fellow-servant .•. worship God" (Rev. :uii. 9). 2. God wal not share his rights with another. "I the Lord thy God am a jealous God_" The first commandment forbids all other worship. 3. There is but one mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. ii. 5, 6). Papists say that the apostle merely condemns such worship of angels as excludes Christ, but the condemnation is most absolute and simple. Desides, Christ is declared to be the one single and only way to the Father, to the exclusion of all angelic mediators. "No man cometh unto the Father but by me;" "If ye shall ask anything in my Name, I will do it" (John xiv. 6, 14). "We offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God, by Jesus Christ" (1 Pet. ii. 5). 4. The worship of angels implies an omniscience on their part which belong.~ only to God. God only knows the hearts of men (2 Chron. vi. 30). 5. Our Lord'ss1iperiority to all angels, as asserted in Heb. i. and ii., implies the same condemnation; for they are merely "ministering spirits, se11t to minister to the heirs of salvation." IL '.l'H..E MOTIVE OF THIS ANGEL-WORSHIP. "A voluntary humility.'' The idea of the false teachers, like that of modem Papists, was that God was so high and inaccessible that he could only be approached through the mediation of inferior beings. It was remembered that the Law was given "by the ministration of angels" (Acts vii. 53), and that angels exercised a certain tutelary guardianship (Dan. x. 10-21). But it was, after all, a mere parade of humility to approach God through the merliation of such inferior creatures. It implied, besides, a serious misrepresentation of the fitness of the one Mediator, of whom it was said," It behoved him to be made like to his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful High Priest in things pertaining to God" (Heb. ii. 17). He surely can sympathize with us even more closely than angels, for he shared our human nature. It was, therefore, a false and perverted humility that sought the intercession of angels. ill THE SPIRIT THAT SHAPED TBIB DOCTRINE OF ANGEL-WORSHIP. "Dwelling in the tlti □ gs he bath seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind." 1. The falae teachers claimed to have visions of the heavenly world and a knowledge of angela wliich they could not possibly possess. They claimed to know the secrets of a region which they l,ad never seen. 2. They were filled with great self-conceit, notwithstanding their purade of excessive humility. "Vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind.'' The Gnostic tendcDcy was a1'1,ays associated with an assumption of superior knowledge, but it was a~ l!ttcrly grouudless ass~mptiop. Jt was "in vain." It was without reason or OH. II. 1~23.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 117

ground. God would resist it (Jas. iv. 7); men would not regard it (Prov. xi. 2); and they themselves would inherit nothing by it but folly (Prov. xiv. 8; 1 Tim. vi. 4). Even where real visions a.re vouchsafed, there is a temptation to self-elation, as in the case of the Apostle Paul (2 Cor. xii. 7). But, in the case of false visions, the tendency would be still more manifest. The mind would be" the mind of the flesh," as it is literally; not "the mind of the Spirit." It was "the carnal mind that is enmity with God." Let us rather seek to become "fools that we may be wise'' (1 Cor. iii. 18), and not be "puffed up one against another." It is knowledge that puffeth up (1 Cor. viii. 1); it is only love that edifieth. IV. THE NEGATIVE SOURCE OF THE HERESY OF ANGEL-WORSHIP. "Not holding the Head from whom the whole body, being supplied and knit together thro □ gh the joints and bands, increaseth with the increase of God." The Colossian: errorists invented angel-worship because they did not see in Christ the true and only Mediator who was to bridge the chasm between God and men. They put inferior beings in the place of him who is the only Source of spiritual life. They did not "hold the headship" doctrinally; they had no individual or vital adherence to the Head as the Source of life to them. 1. Jesus Ghrist, as the Head, is the true Source of spiritual life and energy. He who is "at once the lowest and the highest," who is "the Word made flesh," "raises up man to God, and brings God down to man." 'l'he fulness of the Godhead resides in him bodily, and out of that fulness he communicates freely to us. 2. The ,·elation of the body to the Head. "From whom the whole body, being supplied and knit together through the joints and bands." (1) The care of Christ extends to every member of the body. We must likewise learn to extend our love to all the saints. (2) There is a double effect produced by the relation of Head and members. (a) The supply of nutriment. Christ is the sole Source of supply to our souls-" through the joints." God calls us "to this fellowship with his Son" (1 John i. 7). (11) We can have no spiritual nutriment from Christ till we have believed in him, (.B) The joints through which our supply of grace comes cannot be broken. " Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" (Rom. viii. 39). ('Y) It is through these joints we receive Christ's "unsearchable riches" (Eph. iii. 9); "all spiritual blessings in heavenly places" (Eph. i. 3); so that we come behind in no spiritual gift. (b) The compacting of the frame into a perfect unity-" knit together by bands." Christ is the Source of the Church's unity. "He bath made both one n (Eph. ii. 14). There is a unity of faith, a unity of spiritual life, a unity of ordinance, a unity of love, a uuity of final destiny, in the Church, by virtue of her connection with her Head. 3. The end of this relation. "Increaseth with the increase of God;" that is, with the increase which he supplies. (1) The body grows extensively, by the addition of new members; it grows intensively in grace, knowledge, and the practice of all holy duties. (2) 'l'he First Cause of nil this growth is God. Paul may plant, and Apollos water, but "it is God who gave the increase" (1 Cor. iii. 6). Thus through Christ, God aud man are linked together; the finite and the Infinite are l'econciled; the great problem of speculation has been nt last practica1ly solved. V. 'l'HE DANGER OF ANGEL-WORSIDP. "Let no man rob you of your prize." The apostle implies that the prize of eternal life-" the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus "-would be lost by turning aside from the Head to angelic mediators. We must not" lose what we have wrought" in this way (2 John 10). "Let no man take thy crown" (Rev. iii. 11). Let us, therefore, avoi,l "profane babblin~s and oppositions of science falsely so called " (1 Tim. vi. 20), and hold fast " the faith once delivered to the saints" (Jude 4).-T. C.

entries.title: COL 2:20–23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.A warning against asceticism. The apostle now proceeds to de<iuce the practical consequences of our fellowship in the death of Christ. "If ye died with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, do ye subject yourselves to ordinances, Handle not, nor taste, nor touch (all which things are to perish with the using) after the precepts and doctrines of men?" l. MARI{ THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES OF OUR SHA!lING IN THE DEATH OF CRRIST. l. Fellowship in Christ's death. "Wo are buried with him by baptism unto death" (Ilom. vi. 3-9). We are united with Christ in his death. Community in death in 1·o!l·cs community in life, and tins our death with Christ invol ns nut ouiy (1) li8 TUE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'IIE COLOSSlANS. [c:n. u. 1-23.

death ~ sin (Rom. vi. 2)? (2) death to self (2 Cor. v. 14, 15); but (3) death to the ~aw (Rom. vu: 6; Gal. u. 14), (4?, dcat~ to the world (Gal. vi. 14), and (5) death ~rom _the rudime1;1ts o_f ~he ~o:ld (eh. 11. 20) .. 2._ '.!'he _inconsistency of thisfellow- shiJ! u,ith a mere "!t1taluttc nlzgion. (1) Such a re~1g1on 1~ rudimeutary, disciplinary, deszgned for the infancy of the Church, not for ltll period of adult experience and privilege. Christ by his death wiped out these rudiments which have their sphere in the visible life of the world. They are but" weak and beggarly elements" from which we are for ever separated by tho death of Christ. In him all things hav~ become new. Christians cannot, therefore, live in th:1t which Christ died to take away. Besides Christians are living no longer iu the world. "'l'hey are not of the world ; " yet if they submitted to its ordinances, they were "as though living in the world." They had been called out of the world to be of another body, of which Christ is the Head. Therefo:e t~eY: we~e _not. to be conform~d to the fashion o_f_ the_ W?rld (Rom. xii. 2). (2) A rituahst1c religion 1s usually negative rather than positive m its character being i;trong in the element of prohibition: "Handle not, nor taste, nor touch.': The apostle repeats the prohibitions of the false teachers in their own words. They believing that matter wall essentially evil, resolved upon reducing our contact with it in its most familiar forms to a minimum. The prohibitions here referred to go far beyond the Leviticsl enactments, which had no ascetic tendency. 'rhe Essenes, who wero iorerunners of the Colossian errorists, shunned oil, wine, flesh, meat, and contact with a stranger. Mark how rigorous and precise these errorists were in their outward observances. They were like the Pharisees of old, who cared not for the weightier matters of the Law, but tithed mint and anise and cummin. They attributed an intrinsic Yalue to things that were fleeting : "All which things perish in the using ; " leaving no spiritual result: "For meat commendeth us not to God; for neither if we eat arc we the better; neither if we eat not, are we the worse" (1 Cor. viii. 8). Our Lord himself said it was not that which" entereth the mouth which defileth a man" (Matt. xv.16, 17). (3) A ritnalistic religion is always marked by " the precepts and doctrines of men.'' Many of the Jewish ordinances were handed down by tradition and bnd no warrant in the written Word of God, Therefore our Lord said, " They tea.eh for doctrines the commandments of men" (Matt. xv. 9). II. THE PRETENTIOUS WORTHLESSNESS OF THIS ASCETIC RITUALISM. "Which things, indeed, have a show of wisdom in will-worship, and humility, and severity to the body, but are not of any value against the indulgence of the flesh." 1. Its reputation/or wisdom. It had a show of wisdom wit,hout the reality, for it affected an air of extreme piety, of profound regard for God, and of deep knowledge in Divine things. All its ritualistic observances would be recommended by the plea that they tended to promote piety. The repute of wisdom was manifest~d in three things. (1) Will-worship, or service beyond what God requires-in a word, superstition. This is the origin of penances and pilgrimages and festivals in Romanism. They are supposed to promote piety, but they have" a mere show of wisdom." They charge God with folly, us if Le did not know what was most conducive to piety, and they involve a tacit claim to amend God's ordinances. But God loves obedience better than sacrifice (1 Sam. xv. 22), and may well ask such ritualists, "Who bath required this at your hands?" (Tsn. L 12). Will-worship has been the great corrupter of pure religion. (2) Humility. It is a studied and affected humility, not resting on a basis of faith and love, but consciously cultivated, and therefore not inconsistent with spiritual pride. "Pride mny be pampered while the flesh grows lean." (3) Severity to the body. (a) There seems a show of wisdom in this habit, because an apostle found it wise "to keep his body nnder" (1 Cor. ix. 27), and the Colossian ascetics might have pleaded that they coul<l thus enhance their spiritual insight. (b) But such severity to th.e body is expressly condemned. (11) Religion belongs to the body as well as the soul. The body, "so fearfully and wonderfully made," becomes "a temple of the Holy Ghost" (1 Cor. vi. 19). Its members are to be "yielded as instruments of righteousness unto God" (Rom. vi. 13). We are to offer our bodies as " living sacrifices," not dead or mutilated or maimed sacrifices. There is, therefore, nothing religious in whipping the body, like the Flagellants, or in denying it necessary food, or in arraying it in dirty or rngged clothing. "'l'he sacrifice of God is a broken spirit," not a macerated body. We must keep up our bodily vigour for the discharge of the duties of life, so that the body may on. u. 1--23.] TUE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. ll!J

eer_v~ tho Spirit. (/3) There ma;y be a corrupt heart under an ascetic habit of body. Spmtual pnde may dwell there m power. 2. Its failure to aCCtYmplish it, chief end. ". But ~re no_t of any value against the inclulgence of the flesh." (1) This ascetic rigour 111 designed e.s a check upon sensual indulgence. There seems "a show of wisdom" in such a method. (2) Bnt it is no check to such self-indul~ence, as the history of asceticism proves. 'l'he monastic life, while it seemed hostile to self-indulgence, made way, e.s by a sort of back door, to all sorts of sensual extravagance.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 2:1–7
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The Trinity as the source of Ohristian love and consolation. It would appear that Paul had not only the iuterests of the Colossians and Laodicean3 at heart, but also as many as had not seen his face in the flesh. He did not act on the worldly principle," Out of ~ight, out of mind;" bnt on the gospel principle, "Though out of sight, though never yet seen, yet kept in mind." We are thus brought at once to- I. PAUL'S COSMOPOLITAN SPIRIT. (Ver. 1.) The selfish soul leaves out of consideration all but his own little circle; the Christian leaves out of consideration none but his own little circle. The gospel made a cosmopolitan of Paul the Pharisee. He who had been of the straitest sect becomes the man of broadest spirit. Besides, the problem of the world produced a "conflict" within him. He was in an agony of earnestness for unseen, uncounted millions. His great soul throbbed at Rome in sympathy for all who were under Cresa.r's sceptre. .A.s the "apostle of the Gentiles" he magnified his office by making all mankind his spiritual care. II. HIS DESIRE WAS THAT THROUGH CHnIST THEY MIGHT ALL UNDERSTAND THE MYSTERY OF THE TRIUNE GoD. (Ver. 2.) For the gospel does not commit the care of the universe to a" lonely God," but to a Triune Jehovah, who, as Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, has the elements of social happiness within himself. .A. social Trinity presides over the universe. Now, so practical a truth is this of the Trinity that, as Paul here puts it, the consolation of the heart and Christian unity depend upon it. It is sometimes insinuated that the doctrine of the Trinity is a profitless and unpractical speculation. Any one who thinks so woulcl do well to read such an essay as Mr. Button's on 'The Incarnation and Principles of Evidence.' It will be seen from such a line of thought that there are deep longings of our nature which only an incarnation, and by consequence only a Trinity, can supply. But even apart from such subtle disquisition we may see in the sociality of the 'l'rinity as distinguished from the awful loneliness of the Socinian hypothesis an element of consolation ann of union. If God be a lonely being, and Martineau is driven to the term "lonely God;" if he is satisfied in his loneliness,-then there gathers round him that repellent element which we associate with the unsocial among men. I am not encouraged to come to this lonely and infinite One. He cau do without me, and it repels me to think he can. But when I learn that God is not a lonely One, but has been, so to speak, a" family Being" from all eternity, rejoicing as Father, Son, o.nd Holy Ghost in the satisfaction of his social qualities, then I am encouraged to come to him and to satisfy in him the longings of my heart. It will be found, then, that consolation is promoted by the realized truth of the Trinity in a way that cannot be secured by rival hypotheses. No unitarian abstraction can do for men what the social 'l'rinity can. It will be found also that unity among Christians is promoted by this mighty truth. God as our Father gathers around him through the mediation of his Son Christ Jesus, and through the gift of his Spirit, the scattered members of the human family, and they feel united in a sense of sonship and sociality. A social Trinity secures a united society. Hence we find such a great thinker as John Howe preaching from ver. 2, a fine discourse for "union among Protestants." Now, it is when Christ is preached in a.II his fnlncss that "the treasury of wisdom and knowledge" to be found in him is opened up e.ud the mystery of the Triune God becomes plain. It is in this full preaching of Christ that the present and eternal interests of the human race lie. Ill. HE REES THAT THIS PREACHING WILL ALSO SECURE A PROl'Elt CHRISTIAN WALK. (Vers. 4-7.) He tolls the Colossians that ho is with them in spirit, taking notice of their order and conversation. He calls upon them, therefore, to walk in Christ Jesus the Lord as they have received him. This brings before us the fact that Jesus Christ, when received by faith, becomes the tenant of the human heart. He becomes the recognized Lord of the comcicncc-, and to his sovcrci.gnty all things aro submitted. 'l'he morality 120 'I'IIE EPISTLE TO TlIE COLOSSIANS.

secured by the gospel is th~refore the simple morality of pleasing the indwelling Obrist. We mlly here follow the sainted Henry Martyn, who thus describes what the Christian walk is.. It is (1) to co~tinue to apply his ~lood for the cleansing of our consciences from guilt; ~2) to live _m ~epen~ence on lus _grace; (~) to follow his example; and (4) to walk m fellowsl11p with him. And this morahty will be pervaded constantly by the grateful 8pirit. _In truth, gratitude _is the spirit and morality is the form assumed by the gospel as 1t lays hold of the mmds of men. God having in his gospel done so much for us, we feel that we ought to do all we can for him. We consequently walk before him in love and strive gratefully to do the things which please him.-R. M. E.

entries.title: COL 2:8–15
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0hrist our .All. Having laid down the troth about the Trinity as the great want of the race, Paul proceeds to warn the Colossians aaainst the so-called philosophers. "There are certain men," it has been well observed, c;, who, because they possess somewhat more learning than others, think, when they become converts to the gospel, that they are great acquisitions to the cause; they officiously extend the shield of their learning over their more unlearned brethren, and try to prove where others believe; but, while they think they promote the cause, they generally spoil what they touch." Against such philosophers God's people in all ages require to be warned. I. THE PHILOSOPHY IS TO BE SUSPECTED WfilCH LEADS MEN AWAY FROM CHRIST. (Ver. 8.) Paul warns the Colossians against a philosophy which led men back to rudimentary forms and ceremonies instead of forward to Christ. Now, every argument which leads to a ceremony for hope instead of to Christ has some flaw in it. It may be a subtle flaw, not easily detected, but we may be quite sure it is there. '!'here is no better rule, then, than this. Christ is the embodied truth, and we have missed the road if we are not led to him (John xiv. 6). !I. As THE EMBODIMENT OF THE DIVINE FULNESS, IIE IS THE FOUNTAIN-BEAD OF ALL TRUTH ..U'D PERFECTION. (Ver. 9.) In Jesus Christ Divinity has expressed itself in human form. We can see, hear, and handle the Divine Being in the person of Christ. The Incarnation gives to men the true philosophy they long after. Christ is all and in alL Hence we are resistlessly drawn to him for the solution of our doubts and difficulties as well as for the salvation of our souls. No wonder that an acute writer entitled one of his volumes 'The Know ledge of Jesus the Most Excellent of the Sciencea.' Ill. CHTIIST AFFORDS us ALL PIIOVISION FOR OUR ACCEPTANCE. (Ver. 10.) The great question which man must ask is, "How can sinful man be accepted with God?" Philosophy replies, "By certain solemn ceremonies, by sacrifices, by circumcision, by baptism," etc. The gospel replies, "Acceptance is secured in Christ; we are complete in him," or, as the Revised Version has it, "In him are ye made full." Now, it has been insinuated that merit cannot in the nature of things pass from one person to another. The fact is, however, that we are constantly being kindly treated/or the sake of others. Children, for example, receive consideration for the sake of respected parents; individuals receive consideration for the sake of respected friends; and the whole array of letters of introduction, vicarious influence, and the like, is based up?n the recognition ?f the fact that the merit of others can overshadow and benefit those m whom they are mterested. The acceptance which we receive from the Father for the sake of Jesus is on the line, therefore, of natural law. It is the application of a principle upon which men are acting every day. IV. FnoM CHRIST WE RECEIVE THE TRUE CIRCUMCISION. (Ver. 11.) Circumcision was among the false teachers the initial ceremony which secured a Jewish standing for the Gentile proselyte. Their insinuation was that Gentiles who remained uncircumcised could not possibly be saved. It was this which Paul combatted constantly. Hence he shows, in this eleventh verse, that the real circumcision is secured in Christ for all who trust in him. It is a circumcision not made with hands, a circumcision of the heart, a circumcision which secured "the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh." If the Gentile converts realized this, then they need not concern themselves about the outward circumcision. It surely teaches us that, not by mec'.oanical, but by i;piritual means we may vanquish the power of siu within us. It is said that circum- Oli, II. 1--23,) 'l'HE EPIS'l'LE 'l'O THE COLOSSIAKS. 121

cision circumscribes lustful tendencies ancl keeps them within mechanical bounds. Whatever truth may be in this, it is certain that Jesus can so restrain uR by his indwelling and grace as to deliver us from the whole body of the sins of the flesh. V. OnnIST HAS ALSO OANCELLED THE OEREMONIES UPON 'l'HE CROSS, so THAT WHEN WE RISE WITH HIM INTO NEWNESS OF LIFE WE ARE FREED FROM 'l'HEIR OBLIGATION. (Vers. 12-15.) '!'he ritual of Judaism typified in its various aspects the atoning work of Jesus Christ. The sacrifices pointed to the ono great sacrifice on Calvary. '!'he long list of ordinances, therefore, conducted the intelligent mind to Christ's cross and received their fulfilment there. Hence it was that those who by faith passed through resurrection with Christ became as free from the obligation of these ceremonies as the risen Jesus was himself. Could any one have gone to Jesus after his resurrection ancl asked from him, with any show of reason, a fulfilment of the ceremonial Law? Is it not felt by every intelligent thinker that Jesus had so fulfilled the ceremonies in tho actualities of atonement that more ceremony from him would be unmeaning? A similar emancipation, Paul here insists, from the obligation of ceremonies is the property of Christ's believing people. A careful study of the cross is the great protection, therefore, against improper emphasis being laid on ceremonials.-R. M. E.

entries.title: COL 2:16–23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Legalism exposed. The apostle, having shown in the last section how much Christ is to the believer, proceeds in the verses now before us to expose the false use of ceremonies, or, in modem phraseology, ritualism. The false teachers were anxious to entangle the Gentile converts in a tedious round of ceremonies-to make them, in fact, Old 'l'estament ritualists. They could even adduce what seemed to them philosophic reasons for such practice. But Paul scatters their false philosophy to the winds by the magic power of bis Redeemer's cross. I. LEGALISM ANCIENT OR MODERN IS THE PRACTICE OF CEREMONIES WITHOUT TREIB TRUE MEANING BEING APPRECIATED. (Ver. 16.) 'l'he Judaizers insi~ted on the Gentiles entering into the scrupulosity of the Jews about meat and drink, about holy days and new moons, and about the seventh-day sabbath, for the word is singular as the Revised Version has it, and not plural as in the Authorized Version. Now, it was quite possible for Jews and Gentiles to enter upon the keeping of these ceremonies without ever considering their signification. A ceremony may be kept just to be able to congratulate ourselves upon the keeping of it; that is to say, a ceremony may be kept in a selfrighteous spirit instead of intelligently. When ceremonies minister to self-righteousness, when they lead to pride, when they are entertained iu order to furnish a fancied claim, they are mere superstitions. It is to be feared that no other rationale can be given of a large proportion of modern ceremonial. Jt is a mere blind and leads souls away from Christ to self-righteousness. It may, indeed, have the appear:i.nce of great humility. There may be apparent awe and regard for the angels, and the visible may seem to so impress the soul as to secure deepest humiliation; but when the issue of the ritual is self-congratulation and a fancied independence of Christ's merits for acceptance, the whole process is simply a deceptive superstition. It matters not how rustbetic the ritual may seem: the Jew of the apostolic age could ban pleaded restheticisrn like his modern counterpart; but the true analysis of the whole process is that it is selfrighteousness cultivating superstition. 11. THE LORD JESUS CHRIST MUST TEST THE MEANING OF ALL CEREMONIES, AS THE SUBSTANCE DETERMINES 'l'IIE SIIADOW. (Ver. 17.) If ceremonies cease to lea,l souls to Jesus, then they are meaningless and condemned. '!'he ceremonial laws of Moses were so constructed as to lead the thoughtful worshi]Jper on to the promised Messiah. Meat must be bloodless, because blood was to be the atonement for sin, when Messiah came. The blood was forbidden, because the blood of Jesus Christ was to be shed in clue season. The regulations about drink and holy days and new moons pointed, as may easily be shown, in some way or other to ChriGt. The seventh-day sabbath was the type of the spiritual rest to which Jesus conducts us (Heb. iv. 9-12). Christ is the Substance, and these ceremonies simply shadowed forth some aspect of his mission. But when men kept the ceremonies without ever thinking of their relation to Christ, when they kept them and made saviours of them instead of seeing in Jesus their only So.viour, they became not only meaningless but prejudicial to the interests of souls. Let Christ, then, be our test for every ceremony to which men summon us. If it is a TIIE EPISTLE TO 'l'IIE COLOSSIANS. [en. 11. 1-23.

substitute for Christ, or if it bas no relation to Christ then we aro bound to dismiss it from our thoughts as simple superstition. ' llI. FELLOWSHIP wrrn CHRIST IN ORU0IFIXION MAKES MEN FREE FROM TilE ODLIGA• TJON oF THE OLD TESTAMENT CEREMONIES, (Vers. 20-23.) Wheu Jesus died upon the cross every ceremony was fulfilled. The ceremonial La\V had no further claim upon him. In the same way, when the Gentile converts so appreciated the Crucifixion that they were able to say they were "crucified with Christ" and so "dead with Christ.," then the ceremonies of circumcision and the like were no lon"er obliua.tory upon them. They had fulfilled them in their Substitute and so were fr~e from "them. It "Was this lib~1ty for which Paul so earnestly contended. IV. Arm BELIEVERS IN CONSEQUENCE TO RENOUNCE ALL CEREMONY AND TURN Cams- TUNITY INTO QUAKERISM? Certainly not. The Gentile converts were not encouraued by the apostles to set all ceremony at defiance. Thouuh taught that the ceremonie; of Judaism were fulfilled in Christ, they were directed nit to eat blood, not to eat things strangled; they were directed to celebrate baptism and the Lord's Supper, and to keep tl,e Lord's day. But what kept them right in these ceremonies was what will keep us right in ceremonies-the simple determination whether or no they foster reverence for and deepen our interest in the atoning work of our blessed Lord. What really con- ducts the soul to Jesus is safe; but what only nominally does so and really ministers to self-righteousness is dangerous and deadly error. Let Jesus be our test continually, :md we shall be kept safc.-R. M. E.

Vers. I-7.-Introduction to the polemical part of the Epistle. I. PERSONAL CON• rnnN. 1. Paul:s st1·iving. "For I would have you know how greatly I strive for you, aud for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh." There is an advantage in the Revised translation, in carrying forward the word "strive" from the preceding verse. Having declared his striving in general, the apostle now shows ("for") how his striving was specially directed. (1) His striving was remarlc- al;/e as directed toward those who lv1d not seen his face in the flesh. Among these are 1,lainly included the Colossians. With them are associated their neighbours the Lao- ,.Lceans. The Hierapolitans (to whom there is reCerence at the close of the Epistle) are nol mentioned. But it is added generally, "as many as have not seen my face in the flesh." Spiritually present he had been (as he tells us in the fifth verse), and he must have had indirect modes of intercourse with them, yet they wanted the impression of his presence in the flesh-they wanted the impression of his personal ministry among them. It can be made out that in none of his journeys before this time did his route naturally lie by the valley of the Lycus. It is difficult to have an interest in those, whose faces we have not seen. There is something in the expression of tho countenance, as al,o in the touch of the hand, the sound of the voice. We like these, not as substitutes for the spirit, but rather as helps to our getting at and fixing our impressions of the spirit. Paul, in the quickness of his sympathy, got over this difficulty.
