He had associations in many cases with countenance, with hand, with voice. But he reserved a portion of his sympathy for those, like the Colossians, with whom he had no such associations. His concern was simply founded on the fact that they had been rescued from heathenism, that they were exposed to perils, and on the information which he received from time to time regarding their condition. (2) Eis difficulty in the circumstances in giving them any right imp1·ession of the greatness of his strivin9.. "How greatly I strive." There was no ordinary conflict in his mind. '!'here was the vehemence belonging to an intensely earnest nature. But how could he convey- the impression of what his striving was (the moral fulcrum on which he depended for moving them) to persons in the position of the Colossians? If they had had nn impres• sion of his personal ministry, then he might have revived that wherewith to oppose the heretical teachers; but he had never been at Colossm. If he had been ablo then to go to the rescue, he might have given them an impression of his intensity in tho way in wliich (like a good athlete) he !!rappled with those teachers. But he was in nn imprisoned condition in Rome; and his conflict would be none the less because he was imprisoned and far away from them. Was he, then, like a bird beating its wearied breast against the wires of its cage? No; there was outlet for the struggle within. He could relin·e himself at the thruuc of grace, and there, by his earnest pleading, move OJI, II, 1-23,] 'l'Hffi EPISTLE TO 'l'IIE COLOSSIANS. 123

the ho.nd that could move them. But that was not enough; he wished to have influ- ence with them in impressing on them what his striving was, and so he writes; and, as he writes, feeling the difficulty that ar0se from their not having seen him in the flesh, he exclaims, "I would that ye knew how greatly I strive for you." 2. The end of his striving. "That their hearts may be comforted," There are positions in which Churches and individuals stand in need of heart-comfort. Our English word" comforted" is etymologically " being made strong." "Fortified " belongs to the same root. And the one meaning passes into the other. If our hearts are sad, we feel unnerved f.Jr work. But if, amid our trials, we have comfort, we feel strong for work. (1) Com- fo1·ted in the way of having unity of feeling. "They beiug knit together in love." It is no ordinary union of Christians that is pointed to here. It is such a welding of them together as is not easily torn asunder. What an uncomfortable thing is di vision! How much to be desired in the way of comfort when, however assailed, Christians can present a united front I And the union which is not easily broken up can only subsist in love. And the love must not be a mere negative, or pretence; but must be a neep, pervading feeling. It is only when love avails to break down selfishness, to excite mutual interest between the members of a Christian society, that there is knitting together or the strong bond that is referred to in the third chapter. (2) Comforted in the way of having unity of sentiment. "And unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding." Unity of feeling he desired for them; but as the cause (not the consequence) of unity of sentiment. When there is unity of feeling in a high degree, thesCl questions can be calmly, patiently looked at without risk of a rupture. 1Ne have to aim at a right state of the understanding. "Give me understanding" is the repeated prayer of the psalmist.. Our understanding is given us to examine into facts, to plan aright for our conduct, to avoid mistakes, to detect errors. And we are constituted so that we can not only judge, but have the assurnnce that we are judging correctly. There is an assurance which is begotten of ignorance, of self-conceit. That is very different from the assurance which is the result of patient investigation, of steady contemplation. There is a self-evidencing power of the truth. The words of God, when we closely examine them, shine in their own light. There is a peculiar satisfaction in our being sure of our seeing the truth. When our eyes have been enlightened by the Spirit, we can say with confidence," One thing I know, that whereas I was bliud, now I see." It is this certainty extending over a wide range that is here represented as being the wealth of the understo.nding. This is of far more value than material riches which men heap up and know not who shall gather them. What a man gains in the way of clear convincing perception of things he can never lose. He who engages in the pursuit of these riches shall gather them in his own everlasting being. And, having begun to have an assuring view of truth, he shall go on to all riches of the full assurance of understanding. "That they may know [unto the thorough knowledge of] the Mystery of God, even Christ, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden." This is parallel to the foregoing, and points to the Christian state of the understanding. All things are dark to us at first; we have, by reflection, to clear away the do.rkness. '!'here is one thing which is pre-eminently dark, which we could never have found out for ourselves; it is here called " the mystery," and is explained to be Christ. He is the Mystery of God in this sense-that in him lay hidden all the thought and purpose of God. The theosophists ~poke of hidden things, and made much of wisdom in general and also of a special insight. The apostle declares that all the treasures that they pretended by their sophia and gnosis to discover arc hidden in Christ, and that it is by coming to the thorough knowledge of him that we get possession of the hidden treasures. The object, then, of the apostle's striving for the Colossians, as for others, was (in view of what follows) this, that, unitedly, in the use of their understanding, they might come to such an appreciation of Christ as would lay open to them all the hidden tre,,sures. If they had that, then they would be carried away by no false sophia and gnosis. II. RELATION TO THE SITUATION. 1. .J,,'xposure of the Colossians. "Tl.Jis I say, that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech." He directs himself specially to the Colossians. He has been telling them about his great striving for theru, aud about the key to the hidden treasmes, in order to put them ou their guard. 'l'hcy were in the presence of danger. There wero teachers (of whom we sl1,,\l hear more) that hacl designs on them. '!'hey used a persuasive form of speech (in a bad sense). Tht'Y h,,ll 124 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [en. rt. 1-23.

not the persuasiveness that comes from the truth. They were conscious of no basis of reality for their speech .. They tau$ht a system fo~ which there were not proors. They pretended b~ their sophm and ~osis to ?pen up hidden. things; but it was only pre- tence: Their_ fine phrases, the1_r plaus1~le representations, their large promises, wero delusive, leadmg away from reality, lcadmg away from Christ in whom alone are the hidden treasures. 2. Spfritua), presence with them. " For though I am absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stead- fastness _of your ~a)th in Christ." The spi~it is freer than t~e body. 'l'he apostle was present m the spmt, where he was absent in the flesh. This spoke to a certain cocrni- zance of them, from all that he had heard of them, and especially from the intensity of his sympathy with them. Transferred, as it were, to Colossm, his feelings (and to this prominence is given) were those of joy. He was not repelled (as from whe.t we.s dis- agreeable), but was rather enchained. It especially gave him joy to observe two points which were important in reference to his purpose. (1) Their order. They were (to take one of the associations of the word) like a well-appointed regiment. They were well organized as a community. They were organized for the advancement of the cause of Christ among themselves and beyond themselves. Hitherto they had been free from divisions. There was no disorderliness, such as there was in the Church of Corinth. (2) TM steadfastness of their faith in Ghrist. Their outward state ( which was one of order) was conditioned inwardly by faith. They had an immovable object for their faith. "If we are faithless, he abideth fait.hful; for he cannot deny himself." Their faith in some degree corresponded. It had such a hold on Christ that it was, as the word is, something firm, like a piece of solid masonry (in a fortification) not easily battered down. It would stand, he hoped, the assaults made on it by the false teachers. III. EXHORTATION TO REMAIN TRUE TO THEIR STARTING-POINT. He does not bestow praise withont giving exhortation (in view of the danger). The spirit of the exhortation is given in the words of the Lord to the Church of Smyrna (where danger, however, had not been well met)," Remember therefore how thou hast received, and didst hear." In the force of the apostle's thought there is a certain disregard of metaphor (walle, tree, building). It is, therefore, necessary to present the thought (in our division) without keepiug to metaphor. 1. We a1·e to think and act from day to day in accurdance with our first reception r,f Ghrist. "As therefore ye received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him." There is an emphatic specification of the object. 'l'hey received Christ (the person of Christ being in dispute). Whom did they receive as Christ? 'l'he historical Jesus (partaker of humanity). This Jesus they received and worshipped as the Lord (with supreme power over the universe and the Church). And the apostle holds rightly that they were bound by their past action. Having thus received Christ, they were not to cast him off. 'l'hey were not to think and act according to their pleasure or according to the suggestion of heretical teachers. But their thoughts and actions (specially the former in the present instance) were to be controlled by Christ and his laws. 2. What is added in our development is to be in accordance with its beginnings. " Rooted and builded up in him." 'l'he change of tense is not brought out in the translation. It is literally, "Raving been rooted and being builded up in him." They got a rooting in Christ at the beginni?g, viz. under Epaphras, who presented. Christ plainly to them, giving them line upon lme and precept upon precept, until they came to a clear conception of the truth. This rooting was effectual in the subsequent development. To change the figure with the apostle, they got a grounding in Christ (as we get a grounding in a language or science). Every successive layer was to be in accordance with their grounding. 'l'he building was to rise up in, and to take form from, that Christ in whom they had been so well grounded. 8. Our faith is to be established in accordance with our early teaching. "And stablished in your faith, even as ye were taught." .All early teaching is not good, and the development is often hindered by imperfect or faulty grounding. 'l'he early teaching enjoy~d by i~e ,Colossians was proved to be good by the subsequent development. There IS a m1ssmg of the thought by Meyer and Ellicott, who interpret, "'l'augh! to become established in [or,• by') the faith." The idea rather is that, under the teachrng of Epaphras, they got a nght hold. of Christ. From him thus laid bold of by them they were not to be moved away. The whole carrying forward of their faith in the way of stability was to bo OJI, IL 1-23.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSTANS. 125

toward no folse Christ, but toward Christ Jesus the Lord. Su~joined exhortation to thanksgiving. "Abounding in thanksgiving." This comes in with a certain abruptness. But the duty of thanksgiving is so frequently (five times) introduced as to form a subordinate feature of the Epistle. An overflowing of thanksgiving to God for the faith by which they came in their early teaching, and for all the blessing opened uo to them by faith (the hidden treasures in Christ), would be helpful to their faith bein"'0 stablished in view of present danger.-R. F.

entries.title: COL 2:8–15
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Philosophy. I. FALSE PllILOSOPIIY. "Take heed lest there shall be any one that maketh spoil of you through his philosophy and vain deceit." It was a real danger (as the expression bears) against which the apostle warns tbe Colossians. He refers indefinitely to the teachers (any one), but he strikingly describes what their work would be. The work of the Christian teachers on them in their heathen state, as described in eh. i. 13, 14, had been a deliverance, a redemption; the work of those teachers on them in their Christian state would be a leading them into captivity, a making a booty of them. He does not define what this teaching was, but he characterizes the substance of it (as distinguished from the form, which is characterized in the fourth verse) as a philosophy which was a vain deceit. This is not a characterization of all philosophy, but only of the philosophy with which these teachers would have made spoil of the Colossians. A philosopher is literally a lover of wisdom, and in that sense a Christian is a philosopher. The origin of the name, as given by Cicero, is as follows: Pythagoras once upon a time, having come to Phlius, a city of Peloponnesus, displayed in a conversation which he had with Leon, who then governed that city, a range of knowledge so extensive that the prince, admiring bis eloquence and ability, inquired to what art he had principally devoted himself. Pythagoras answered that he professed no art and was simply a phi1osopher. Leon, struck by the novelty of the name, again inquired who were the philosophers, and in what they differed from other men. Pythagoras replied that human life seemed to resemble the great fair held on occasion of those solemn games which all Greece met to celebrate. For some, exercised in athletic contests, resorted thither in quest of glory and the crown of victory; while a greater number flocked to them in order to buy and sell, attracted by the love of gain. There were a few, however-and they were those distinguished by their liberality and intelligrncc-who came from no motive of glory or of gain, but simply to look about them, and to take note of what was done and in what manner. "So, likewise," continued Pythagoras, "we men all make our entrance into this life on our departure from another. Soma are here occupied in the pursnit of honours, others in tho search of riches; a few there are who, indifferent to all else, devote themselves to an inquiry into the nature of things. These, then, are they whom I call students of wisdom, for such is meant by philosopher." The philosophy in question in Colossro was no humble endeavour to ascertain the nature of things, but a pretentious system without any basis in observed facts, or in reason applied to them (certainly without any basis in revelation), and therefore only vain. It had two marks of a false system. I. It was purely traditional. "After the tradition of men." Our sacred books have been handed down to us, but we do not rest their authority on mere tradition. There is evidence (to which we make our appeal) that tbey do not owe their origin to men, that they aro a Divine revelation, that they have been first handod to men by God. 'l'radition has been a frequent device in connection with systems that have imposed on the human mind. 'l'he answer to questionings has been that it was so handed down from remote antiquity (occultly, for the traditional and occult generally go together). A remarkable instance was a later development named cabbala, or tradition. The mystic elements in this were not essentially different from those which were operating around the Colossian Church. The primary substance, the Cabbalists said, is an ocean of light. There was a primitive emanation, named Adam tadmon, from which proceed decreasing stages of emana_tions, named Sephiroth. Matter is nothing but the obscuration of the Divine rays when arrived at the last stage of emanation. This (and much besides) was to bo received on the ground that it had been secretly handed down from Moses. But it is no sufficient evidence of a system being true that it has been handed down; we must submit it to further examination, atld such examination the philosophy at Colossre could not stand. 2. If was purely 12G THE EPISTLE TO 'l'IlE COLOSSIANS. [cn. II. 1-23.

m11nda11e. "After the rudiments of the \l'Or!d." \Vhat was handed down had no high gcnPsis. YC'ry crudo were the first attempts to solve tho riddlo of the universe. Empcdocles taught that all things were formed out of the four elements fire air C'nrth, _an? water, by a process of mingling a_nd of _separation, set in moti~n by th~ two pn_nc1ples of love and hato. The postulation of mtermediato agents in a descend- mg series down to one who could crente matter. was v~rr rudimentary. Tho apostle was sorry that such meagre and earth-born plulosoph1zrngs should bo palmed upon men as all that was needed to make them perfect. The standard of condemnation. "And not nfter Christ." \Vhat is tradition when we lmve Christ to give form to our !hought.s? What are the rudiments of the world (all that earth can produce of a rhilosophy) when we haYo the perfect revelation from heaven? . II. '1';1ffi TnUE r~ILO~OPHY. There are two cardinal points. (1) The fulness of God 1n Christ. "For m him dwelle!h all the fulness of the Godhead bodily." By the ple:roma of the Godhead we are to understand the totality of the Divine attributes the sum of the Divine perfections. We are to think of the pleroma as residing first in God and then in Christ (just as we think first of Father and then of Son first of original and then of copy). The pleroma resides iu the Second Person necess;rily and eternally, but nineteen hundred years ago (such is our creed) it began to reside in him bodily wise, that is to say, a connection was mysteriously formed between the pleroma in him and (what was far removed) a human body. In the body he took to himself he tabernncled on earth, and not only so, but in it now glorified he permanently resides (such is the force of the Greek word), that is to say, the time will never come when there will be a separation of the pleroma in him from our humanity. Such is the apostolic teaching, but on it reverence forbids that we should dwell. (2) ThefulneSB of Christ in us. "And in him ye are made full." It is an advantage in the Revised translation that "full" is carried forward from the preceding thought (not "fulness" and then "complete," when the word is the same). The pleroma in Christ is com- municated to us. Out of his pleroma have all we received. Christians collectively are called the pleroma of Christ. This is 110 mere refinement of thought. The comfort of it is that Christ in his redemptive work, in the fulness of his atoning merits, has made it possible for us to have more than mere beginnings or husks. There must be allowance for difference of essence, but, allowance being made for that, then all that is in Christ can be communicated to us. We can think out the Divine thought. We can be under the irnpuls:i of the Divine love. We can have strength to perform the Divine purpose. We cau come out into the Divine liberty. 1t is only Christ actually working in us that can remove all moral impediments, and educe to the full the God-given tendencies of our being. .And, therefore, the truest philosophy is to preserve a state of openness towards him. This philosophy is all-sufficient. I. It enables us to dispense with what intermediate agents may be supposed to do for us. "Who is the Head of all principality and power." Christ is not only placed over all that can be called principality and power, but he is the Source of all the vital force that belongs to them. What of the pleroma may be dispersed, fragmentary in them, is undis- persed, unbroken in him. Thero is no need, therefore, of supplementing what he can supply. 2. It enables us to dispr.nse with circumcision. It would seem that in the false philosophy with which the Church at Colossro was threatened, there was e. Jude.istic as well as a mystic element. The combination of the two was called Essenism. (1) Circumcised with Christ in /;is circumcision. "In whom ye were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of tbe flesh, in the circumcision of Christ." They bad no need of the circumcision made with hands (the material circumcision); they had been circumcised with e. circumcision not made with hands (a spiritual circumcision). 'l'hey had got the inward reality corresponding to the outward rite. This is presented here as the putting off of the Lody of the flesh. There was the putting off as of e. garment. 'fhe word in the ori"inal, being intensive, points to a complete putting off. The putting off applied to the body as a whole. 'fhe body of the flesh points to our old impure condition (in which the flesh is the dominating principle).• It could only be ideally thl\t we were thus circumcised, for there is still actual impurity in our condition that needs to be put off. When in the past a.re we to understand this circumcision as timed? 'l'he general opiuio'.I is that we are to take the time from the baptism referred to in the noxt verse. OU, U, 1-23.] 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 127

It seems moro natt1ml to interpret the circumcision of Christ ns the circumcision undergone by Christ, and to take the time from that event. It is not unnatural to pass from tho spiritual circumcision described to tho circumcision of Christ so understood, unless its spiritual significance is left out. That event was more than a mere honouring of the Mosaic rite, it pointed to (though it did not actually effect) its fulfilment. Did it uot point to Christ putting off in his death the body with which our sin wa.s associated? It could be said then that when Christ was circumcised we were spiritually circumcised in his circumcision. A cognate thought is added for the purpose of further ducidation. (2) Baptized with Ghrist in his baptism. As we interpret the circumcision of Christ of the circumcision undergone by Christ, so we interpret baptism here of the baptism undergone by Christ (not their baptism). It could be said that when he was baptized we were baptized in his baptism. There are two sides of baptism. (a) A going down into the water. "Having been buried with him in baptism." There is ~imi:ar language employed in Rom. vi. 4. We were buried with him throngh baptism into death. 'l'he language is evidently taken from immersion. It is said of Jesus that he came up out of tbo water, so we nre to understand that be went down into the water. 'rhere was, as it were, a burial under the waves. And as the coming up out of the water is connected in what follows with the resurrection of Christ, so we are to un<lerstarnl that the burial in baptism is connected with the burial of Christ. In baptism we arc represented as burying what Christ may be said to have put away in his grave-the old state of sin. 'l'be language employed here tells in fo,our of immersion as a scriptural mode. There is every reason to believe that it was the mode followed in Palestine in our Lord's day. It has an advantage over sp1inkling in pointing so strikingly to the burial of the old nature as in the grave of Christ. The only reason !hat can be urged against it is that it is not suitable in a cold climate. 'l'he use of water being all that is essential, the mode may be accommodated to altered conditions. On the other band, there is an identification of baptism with circumcision. What is the putting off and laying aside of the body of the flesh in the one, is the burial in tho other. And thus the language of the apostle seems to tell in favour of infant baptism. (b) A coming up out of the water. "Wherein ye were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead." The language is taken from the comin~ up out of the water which is associated with our Lord's baptism, but none the less truly does it 1ioint to !he fact of Christ's resurrection, which is clearly referred to. Christ went down into the grave, but came up again. So the belie,er disappears under the waters of baptism, but comes up to sight again. '!'his is a si,lo that is not presented in circumcision. In baptism there is an impressive exhibition of the fact that we nre regenerated. This uew lifo we get in union with Christ. 'l'he working of God was sigcally displayed in raising Christ from the dead. But that was more than a display of omnipotence. It is to be taken in connection with the remornl of the cause that operated in Christ's death and burial, viz. sin. Christ rose from tho dead the possessor of a new and endless life. And if we take as the object of our faith the working which raised Obrist from the dead, we shall become sharers with him in the same new and endless life. 3. Pa1·enthetical application of the being raised with Olirist to the Oolossians and to the Ge11tiles generally. "And you, being dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, you, I say, did be quicken together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses." There is a difficulty started here regarding the subject of the remainder of the paragraph. Meyer, Alford, ancl. Eadie make God the subject; Ellicott makes it Christ. Lightfoot makes it a case of a sudden change of subject. It can be said in favour of Christ being "subject," that he has been prominent iu the apostle's thought in the context as in the Epistle as a whole. It can also be said that the putting off from himself the principalities and powers is language which cau only be applied to Christ. On the other band, it is unnaturnl, with Ellicott, to pass from the thought of Christ being raised by God to the thought of Christ quickening himself. Nor is it satisfactory simply to say that there is a. sudden change of subject. 'l'he most natural solution of the difficulty seems to be to regard this verse ruJ parenthetical. The apostle 11pplies the thought of being roiseu with Christ, and, having done so, he proceeds with Christ as the subject as though the application had not beeu interjected. 'l'he Colossians had been in a. state of deadness. '!'heir deadness ,ms caused by their trespasses. '!'here is nothing of the p:rnthci~tic 128 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [on, n.1-23.

element here that was so _prevalent in the East. They had committed personal trespass against a personal Lawgiver, and. thus were thrown into a stato of deadness. Their deadness thro~gh tres_Pal!ses )s. associated with the uncircumcision of their flesh. The_y had not the sign of c1rcumc1s1on on them. .And so they had that deadness which in circumcisio:n is r~presented as being p~t awaJ>:, !:lei?~ dead, God quickened them together with Christ, gave them the reality of cu·curnc1s1on or the reality correspond- ing to the coming up out of the waters of baptism. 'l'his presupposed the oxercise of forgiveness toward them. They (and not only they) had been forgiven their trespasses. And thus, the cause of deadness being removed, they could be quickened. (1) How cirCttmcision can be dispensed with. "Having blotted out the bond written in ordinances th~~ Wll;> against us, ';,hich was ~on~rary to us: and he bath taken it out of the way, nailmg 1t to the cross. Our obhgat1on to keep the Law of God (so we are constituted) is compared to a bond. It is as though we bad subscribed it with our own band. The word is handwriting. Jn the case of the Jews it was in the form of well-known ordinances (of which circumcision was one). In the case of the Gentiles the public sense of right also found expression in ordinances. The bond was against us in this sense, that it contained obligation which had to be met by us. It was not only against us in that sense (which it was from its very nature), but in its actual incidence on us in our fallen condition it was contrary to us. It could, as it were, be brought into a court of law to effect our conviction. There it was with our autograph. We had not met our obligation and had no manner of meeting it. What Christ did with the bond was to cancel it. His pen, as it were, was drawn through it. Or the writing was erased that it could never again be brought as evidence against us. To make it moro emphatic, it is added that he took it out of the way (so that it could never again be fo11ncl). "He took it out of the midst," it is literally, so that it could never be produced between us and God. .And to make it still more emphatic, it is added that he nailed it to bis cross. It was so affixed to the cross that when he was crucified it was treated similariy and completely made an end of. His crucifixion was a meeting the bond, discharging all onr obligations to the broken Law. There is thus, therefore, no bond that can be produced for our conviction, but there is a discharged bond which can be produced for our julitification. (2) How the hel,p of intermediate agents can be dispensed with. "Having put off from himself the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it." The principalities and powers were those that sought to thwart Christ in his great undertaking, to prevent the salvation•of men. They began to gather around him at his temptation. Especially at the close did they obtain power. These evil principalities and powers clung to him like a garment. It was only by his thus allowing them to come into close contact with him that they could for ever be put off from men, It is said, regarding Hercules, the most celebrated of all heroes of mythology, that he came by his end by putting on a robe that had been steeped in the blood of Nessus, whom he himself had shot with a poisoned arrow. When it became warm round him the poison penetrated into his system. He attempted to wrench it off, but it tore away his flesh. .And he hastened his end by placing himself on a burning pile. It was sin that made the principalities and the powers like a poisoned clinging robe. But he put them off from himself. So complete was his victory that he held them up publicly to view as spoils. This triumph he obtained on the cross. It was there that the principalities and the powers bad him at a terrible disadvantage. They had, as it were, powor given them against him. But he, trusting in God, threw them off. And thus the symbol of weakness became the symbol of triumph.-H. F.

entries.title: COL 2:16–23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-T,liree errors. I. LEGALISM. "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day or a new moon or a sabbath day: which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ's." There is a detailed reference here to Jewish institutions. Eating ( rather than meat) was encompassed with regulatior.s. There was a distinction drawn between clean and unclean animals. Certain parts of animals (the fat, the blood) were not to be eaten. God's rights (firstborn, por~ione of the priests) were not to be _infringed in eating. There was not so much binding down in regard to drinking. Priests were forbidden the use of wine before ministering in the tabernacle; and the Nazaritc vow included entire absti•

ncnce frum the use of wine. The sacred times are classed according to their frequency. There were the thrco great annual feasts (extendincr each over a week) of the Passover Pentecost, 1111d Tabernacles. Every month comme;ced with a. celebration. And th~ weelcly sabbath (older than Jewish institutions) had its special services. The false teachers who sought to impose these institutions on the Colossi an Christians were Essenes. These went far beyond the Pharisees. They ate no animal food, drank no wine. They would not light a fire, move a. vessel, perform the most ordinary functions of life on the sabba.th. Everything material was inherently evil and was not to be touched more than was absolutely necessary. The apostle claims, against these teachers, on behalf of the Colossians, that they were not to be judged in respect of their nonobservance of Jewish institutions. And the ground on which he docs so is this. These institutions (in their purity, and not as exaggerated in Essenism) were only shadows of the things to come. They were connected with what was substantiril (and therefore were channels of blessing so long as they lasted), but Christians, having got the substantial in Christ, arc necessarily freed from the shadowy in the Law. No conclusion i~ to be drawn from this adverse to gospel institutions. "We may observe," says Alfonl, commenting on this passage, "that, if the ordinance of the sabbath had been in any form of lasting obligation on the Christian Church, it would have been quite impossible for the apostle to have used this language." This carried out would take the ground from under all gospel institutions. '!'here would be no sign whatever now, connected with our religion, the reality having come. Liberation frum all form is not certainly the New Testament idea. An argument may be drawn from the context. Circumcision was a shadow of the coming reality, viz. tbe putting off of the body of the flesh (death to the old). 'Ibis reality we have now in Christ, but it does not therefore follow that it is disconnected from all positive institution. On the other hand, it is the teaching of the apostle that the same reality has been pnt into the gospel institution of baptism. Another argument may be drawn from the text itself. One of the feasts referred to is the Passover. The Paschal lamb was a shadow of the coming reality, viz. the sacrifice of Christ. But that great gospel reality has not been disenshrined. On the contrary, it has been put into au institution, which is to last till the close of the earthly order of things. So with the sabbath. It foreshadowed the reality of rest in Christ. We have now got the substance, but still the substance has been put into the institution of the Lord's day, in which it will remain till all earthly institutions are done away. Only there is this to be remembered, in connection with our use of gospel institutions. We are not to be legalistic in the use of them. We are not to feel as though baptism, or the Lord's Supper, or the Lord's day had any magical power in them. They simply serve to hold up gospel realities for our faith to grasp. And there is a freedom (as of sons) which belongs to us in the use ot them, such as there was not connected with the Law. II. ANGEL-WORSHIP. "Lot no man rob yon of your prize." The Colossian Christians are here compared to the contenders in the Grecian games. The prize for which they were contending, and which they were in the way of obtaining, was eternal life. 'l'ho word translated "rob" might seem to point to the false teachers as showing hostility in tbo character of judges. But that is not in accordance with the Pauline conception, in which Christ is Judge. Uather are we to think of them as showing their hostility in interlering with them in one form or another, so as to bring it about that they, the Colossians, did not receive the prize from the judge. And this is required by the connection. For the false teachers are represented as putting an obstacle in the way of the Colossians to trip them up so that they Jose the prize. '!'he obstacle :s angel-worship. l. Its spurious humility. "By a voluntary humility and worshipping of the angels, dwelling in the things which be bath seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind." Wo have already described the Eastern doctrine of successive emanations. These the Esscnes (with their Jewish tendencies) identified with the successive orders of angels. These orders at intervals filled up the distance between God and men. They were so familiarly known as to be named. '!'here was an appearance of humility in that. For it went on the supposition of the unapproachableness of God. We are such insignificant beings that it is not for us to worship so great a being as God. It only becomes us to worship the beings that lie nearer to us (the angel~), and who have had more immediately to do with our creation. Regarding this humility the apostle asserts that it had its ground COLOSSI ANS. g: 130 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSI.A.NS. [cu. 11. 1-23.

in their own will, not iie reality. The way in which he makes it out is this: 'rhe angel-worshipper "dwells in the things which he bath seen." This must be held to be a ~eat ~lot o~ the ~evised translation. The mea~ing suggested is that the angel- "-orslupper 1s an mhab1tant of the world of sense. This is nothin" less than "rotesque, For the angel-worshipper shows the spuriousness of his humility°by confide;tly goine1 across the boundary line or sense. "Dwelling in" is a most objectionable translatio;, The word is literally to step on, to step off one place on to another. The exact sense depends on the retention or non-retention of "not" in the text. The former makes the better sense, well brought out in the old translaUon, "intrudin" into those thin"S which he bath not seen." The latter has a slight preponderance ~f authority in its favour, and may be understood as giving the sense-stepping on to the domain of the visio":?-ry. The ge~eral meaning is u1;1doubtedly this-that, w~ile p~ofessing (in his humility) that he 1s only fit to worslnp angels, he penetrates 1llee1it1mately into the in"l'isiblc world, i.e. not in the way of faith and revelation. He mak~s the large assertion that the Divine Being does not care for our worship. And he names (as though be had actually seen) the different orders of angels. And so the apostle makes it out to be not humility at all. It is (when unb,ued) inflation. It is inflation with what is baseless, wnreal. It is inflation from a bad principle,-the mind of the flesh (as distinguished from the mind of the Spirit). That is to say, there is in it fleshly discontent with the simple contents of revelation regarding the angel-world. And there is the fleshly desire to appear to know more than is to be known. The lesson to be learned from this is that we are not to undervalue oui· humanity. We are all the greater beinas 0 that our Father in heaven is so great. "We look up in our littlenesa To thy majestic stu.te; Onr comfort is thou art so good, And that thou art so greu.t." As the angel-worshipper said that it was not for us to worship God, so the agnostic says nowadays that it is not for us to know God. If there is a God, he is not to be known, and we are not at liberty to go beyond the known. 'l'bere is an appearance of humility in that, but if there is abundant evidence against holding the existence of God in Sllspense, then it is not really an indication of humility, but rather of proud dislike of God. 2. Its renunciation of the Head. "And not holding fast the Head, from wbo:n all the body, being supplied and knit together through the joints and bands, increascth with the increase of God." The apostle puts his objection to angelworship on a strong basis of truth. The parts of the body are jointed and banded. 'l'he joints and bands serve for the body being nourished and compacted. This takes place in connection with a common centre of vital energy. The result is the increase appointed for the body by God. So Christians in their relations to one another are as joints and bands. They form lines along which communications can be sent from Christ, by which the Church is nourished and compacted and has its appointed increase. Dnt this is on condition of holding fast the Head. 'fhe angel-worship, by which the falso teachers would have tripped up the Colossians on their way to the goal, would have been a losing hold of Christ. It would have been a substituting for the mediation of Christ the mediation of inferior beings. It would have been fatal severance from him who does the whole work of mediation for men. And the same strong objection is to be taken to the regard paid to angels, to saints, especially to the Virgin Mary, in the Church of Rome. Whatever distinctions may be drawn by Roman Catholic theologians, whatever safeguards may be adopted, the practical result is whattho apostle notes here, the letting go of the all-sufficiency of the mediation of Christ and the paralyzing of tho Church's energies. III. ASCETICISM. The teaching of the apostle is that Christians are freed from mundane ordinances. "Jf ye died with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, do ye subject yourselves to ordinances?" One part of the truLh of baptism is that we arc sharers with Christ in bis death. We not only die with Christ; but there is something to or from which we die. '!'his is thought of sometimes as sin, sometimeB as self, sometimes as the Law. It is here thought of as the world in its rudiments, that is to say, its teachings and rules (the latter prominent

hero), \vhich a.re 11l1 rudimentary compared with tho perfect form of Christi:tnity. We l_ia\·e died to the worlrl (God-forsaking) and its ordinances, why then, as though livin_q in the world (ns though we had not died, as thou"h our former relations to the worlcl to wrre still maintaiued), should we snbject ourselves its ordinances? 1. These ordinances a-re prohibitory, "Handle not, nor taste, nor touch." Some, by a stmn"e blunder have supposed this to be an inculcation of abstinence by the apostle. He is, ~n the contrarv disparagingly giving tho spirit of asceticism. It saitl, "Abstain, abstain, abstain." II~ gives !he very words of asceticism, "Handle not, nor taste, nor touch." The words arc given in the correct order in the Revised translation. With a descent of langua'"'e them is an ascent of superstition, The things referred to we are not to handle, nor;; we to taste them, nor have the slightest coutad with them. The error of asceticism is that it makes prohibition (negation) the essence of religion. The counteractive thou"'lit i~ that it is not by heaping up prohibitions that man's spiritual need can be met. 2. These ordinances relate to the outward. "All which things are to perish with tho using." The things are the foods and drinlcs which were prohibited. The apostlo seems to direct a double argument against asceticism. The meats and drinks ha<l 11 good property; they had also a defect. (1) They were for use. "With the uging" is his language. That is to say, they had no inherent evil (nccordin::( to the a:;cetic idea). They were made to be handled, to bo tasted, to be touched. They were ma,lo for consumption. '!'hey ,vere made (with a certain hrartiness in the expression used) to be used up. (2) 1.'hey u:ere in the use of them fo go to corruption. They could not be used over again. Decoruposition set in which became complete (destruction). As they could not thus be the be-all for man (not being eternal), so neither, on the other hand, was religion to be placed in mere abstinence from them. 3. These ordinances are humanly imposed. "After the precepts and doctrines of men.n There wero numero,,.~ ordinances of God before the perfect religion came. These had close connection with religion as Divine helps. They were laid down authoritatively by God, and by them God taught important lessons. But the ascetics were out of date with their ordinance~ (partly Jewish they were in Essenism). 'l'hey were only (even the Jewish parts of them) the precepts and doctrines of men. There was no authority for imposin~ th~m on the consciences of men. 4. These ordinances are not in their contents entitled to b, called wisdom. "Which things have indeed II show of wisdom in will-worship, an,l humility, and severity to the body; but are not of any mlue against the indulgence ot' the flesh." Ascetic observances were thought to be wisdom. They were intimately nssociated with worship. They were supposed to be based on the two great virtues of humility and self-denial. The ascetics had the reputation of carrying theso virtuc3 e,·cn to excess. \Ve have already referred to the practices of the Essenes. As au illustration of what the apostle means by humility and severity to the body, wo may take the modern instance of Lacordaire. "Immediately after Mass, anti while his face was yet lighted up with ineffable joy, he would seek the cell of one of his brethren, kneel humbly down, and beg for the full severities of discipline. Rising from it, al 1 blecdini, he would press his lips on the feet of him who had chastised him, and overwhelm him with expressions of gratitude. Sometimes be would place himself under lho monk's feet, and remain there a quarter of au hour in silence; sometimes he woulcl not be content without the bestowal of still ruder chastisement-he must be boxed 011 the cars, be spit upon, be ordered about .like a slave, • Go, wretch, brush my shoes, brine: mo this thing or that;' he must even bo spurned like a dog. Once in the convent at 01talais, a[ter having delivered an affecting sermon on humility, he felt irresistibly impelled to follow up precept by example. Ho came down from the pulpit, begged the assembled brethren to treat him with the severity ho deserved, and, uncovering big shouldera, received from each of them twenty-five strokes. 'l'he community was a hlrgo one, and the ordeal lasted a long time. Brethren, novices, and fathers stood by iu deep emotion unlil all was over, aOLl Lacordairo rose up pa.lo and exhausted. Ouo Good Friday he mado himself a cross, raised it in a subterranean chapel, and, bound to it by cords, remained on it three hours." The apostle teaches that ascetic observance., have only a show of wisdom. (1) 7'hey are voluntary. He points to this element in thu worship with which they were ossociatccl. We aro to ha.vo soul-humiliation before Gu.I We are to havtJ humiliation for sin. Dut there is no call for om dcmc::rning oursel,e~ ~r our demeaning the humanity which Goel has given us. Aud such demeaning is nut 132 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [CH, II, 1-23,

to be taken as an indicat.ion of soul-humiliation, In the same way, we have to deny ourselve~. The apostle even notes severe treatment of his body, "I buffet my body, and bring it mto bondage." But we are not wantonly to buffet the body ae though God had gh·cn it to be a pla::;ue to the spirit, or as though it were meritorio~1s in itself to do so. ~nch s~verity is not to be take~ as a trne la,ring of _self on the altar, (2) They are rneffective. He finds no fault with the end. 'I hey are mtended to check tho indulcrence uf the fle~h. But he denies them value as means toward that end. They have o~ly a !harm for the few; the many must be repelled. And even with the few they are no proper safeguards. There are often witnessed outbreaks of the flesh, and even, where there are not such outbreak~, there is not the proper condition of the spirit, The only proper safeguard is the positive of the risen life with Christ, and especially of attraction toward him, to the consideration of which the apostle proceeds.-R. F.

entries.title: COL 2:1–3
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Three wonderful things. We have here- I. A NOBLE ANXIETY. In the words he here uses Paul pictures his eagerness as the ea-::crness of the racer and the wrestler in the then familiar national games, So far there is nothing very rare, for the spectacle of anxious men struggling with keenest eagerness to gain some purpose of their own is common. Life is an arena. crowded with such. But the elements of nobleness in Paul as here discovered are: 1. His anxiety for others. He says to the men of Colossm-My "conflict is for you." It is no self-centred life that Paul lives when he spends himself lavishly for these early Churches. 2. His anxiety for the absent. There is a counterfeit coin in current speech: "Out of siuht, 0 out of mind." It is a proverb coined in the mint of a very shallow and selfish life. It is only true of the worst men. Such a Epirit (1) limits power; (2) narrows character. "\Yhilst real care for the absent: (1) Increases the power of the mind. It gets strong enoug:h to wing its pinions over oceans and even to pierce other worlds. (2) Cultivates a spiritual habit. It delivers man from being the creature of sense. 3, His anxiety for those with whom he liad no dirut connection. He is caring for the group of Churches on the Lycus that he had not planted or even visited. It was pure, disinterested love. Such is Paul's noble anxiety. Wherein does the modem gospel of altruism excel this gospel Paul believed and practised? And where has altruism the molives with which Christianity pulsates or the examples that Christianity can cite? II. A BLESSED EXPERIENCE. Analyzing these verses, we find signs: 1. Of personal comfort. The word" comfort'' here, as in the word" Comforter," points to more than solace ; it tells of encouragement, strengthening. What better experience could he desire for the members of this young Church than that their hearts should be comforted? But to that is added the blessing: 2. Of social security. Few expressions can better describe a completer unity than this, "knit together," It means an interweaving of sympalhies, an interlinking of destinies. And this interweaving and interlinking is attained by the highest and snrest method, "in love." 3. Of firm conviction. " Full assurance." There is much more here than mere opinion; there is conviction. A conviction, too, of man's noblest faculty, the understanding, which is more tha~ the reason alone. And this complete conviction is, as to the truth, of the supremest importance, namely, the acknowledgment of the open secret about God. III. A.JS OPEN SECRET. As we have seen, Paul did not mean by "mystery" an unknowable, mystical something, but rather a truth once hidden but no longer concealed, a truth fully, freely revealed. Christianity is the open secret. T~e self-revelation of CLrist is the revelation of man, of duty, of God, of Heaven. In him were stored away all the riches of truth and love for which men cried. He is the exhaustless Storehouse uf God's supplies for man's hlgher nature. He is the still small voice, and God is in the voice, and only the listening _will hear.. Or he is a vast _min~ of thought, of_ sympa~hy, uf grace, aad only the industnous, who smk the shaft of inquiry, of fellowship, of faith, will know what the mine contains. Paul knew.-U. R. 'l'.

entries.title: COL 2:4–7
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Blessrd Christian possfbilities. 'l'hese words of apostolic desire open to us three blessed Christian possibilities-a possibility to the Church, a possibility to the individual, and a possibility to the inner life of each. I. TnE FORMIDABLE STRENGTH POSSIBLE TO A CanrSTfAN CHURCH. The apostle declares that it gave him joy to behold the condition of the Colossian Church; indeed, the words dB, II. 1-23.] 'l'HE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSI.ANS. 133

he uses describe his looking ngain and again 1,ecause of the joy it gave him. What gave him such joy? 1. Their orderly array. 2. Their solid frone, as the word " stead, fastness" here depicts. In the centre of the rr.ilitary world, and made a soldier's guard, no wonder Paul lays his hands on metaphors so vividly suggesting precision, compactness, obedience. He sees how a Church can be perfectly marMhalled for its mission-the mission of a holy war against ignorance, pride, selfi8lrness, sin. Well for a Church to have ita every member n "defender of the faith." II. THE CONSTANT GROWTH POSSIBLE TO THE CHRISTIAN CHARACTER. The growth implies life. 1. The origin of the life is here described. It is "having receivecl Christ." As Simeon took the holy infant into his arms, the true Christian receive~ Christ into bis trust, thoughts, affections. 2. The progress of life is here described. The three metaphors used, of a path, a tree, a structure, teach the same lesson of intimate and advancing union with Christ. Whether walking, or being rooted, or being built, it is all " in Christ." Ill. THE PERPETUAL THANKSGIVING POSSIBLE L'! THE CHRISTIAN LIFE, Tl,is summons to thanksgiving is a sort of refrain throughout the Epistle (eh. i. 10; iii. 15, 17; iv. 2). Faber inquires whether there can be true worship without joy. Because he asserts," Worship is not fear of God or love of God, but delight in God." This i~ Paul's exposition and doctrine, for there must be joy in thanksgiving. And perpetual thanksgiving is the true spirit of those who are (1) obJects of perpetual p,-ovidence; (2) subjects of perpetual grace. Therefore abound with than.ksgi\'ing.-U. lt. 'l'.

Vers. S-15.-Tlie complete man. Tbe one thought around which we may let the many, varied, and some of them strange ideas of this paragraph gather, is the conception of the complete man. 'l'he words teach us- I. 'l'HAT 'l'HE COMPLETE MAN IS NOT LED AWAY DY ERROR m THOUGHT OR DY EVIL IN LIFE. Any one who is so led is incomplete. And the apostle is here warning his readers to be on their guard, lest, having once been emancipated from such captivity, they should be insidiously captured a.gain an<l taken away as prey i11to such slavery. His words here show: 1. How error in thouyld und evil in lij'e are closely connected. (Vers. 8, 18.) 2. The two common causes of such error and evil. "Traditions of men," mere superstitions, are the "rudiments of the world "-mere beginnings of knowledge. All such are to be condemued when they are not" after Christ;" that is, when they are not (1) doctrines of which he is the Teacher, or (2) doctrines of which he is the ultimate 'l'heme. II. 'l.'HE COMPLETE MAN DERIVES BIB COMPLETENESS FROM CHRIST. "Ye are complete in him," or we might paraphrase it, "Ye are filled up from him." This paragraph shows what Christ has done for such a man. 1. By Christ he is separated from evil. (Vers. 11, 12.) Circumcision was the great symbol of the separation of the Jews; baptism of the separation of the Christians. The complete man is as one "circumcised without hands" by Christ, bnptized as in a burial by Christ. 2. By Christ he is mad~ alii·e to goodness and to God. (Vers. 12, 13). Such a man is "risen with Christ." llo is a man marked by pre-eminent livingness. (1) The type of his livingness is here; the risen Christ; he who was gloriously alive. (2) The means of his livingness are here: through faith in the mighty power of God, which was triumplrnntly manifested in tho raising of Jesus. 3. By Christ he is emancipated from guilt. (V crs. 14, 15.) Most vi \·icl and full arc the metaphors describing emancipation from the guilt and from the power of sin. "Illottiog out handwriting," etc. And nil this work or Christ was consurnmatc,l on Calvary. He like a conqueror nailed to his cross" the wriLiu;;s" tliat were against us; on hi8 cross he openly triumphed over evil. III. CmusT TIIUS MAKES MEN COMPLETE BECAUSE OF WHAT HE IS IN lIIMSELF. The life of God must be wafted in upon man; borne in upon him. Whence? From Christ, "in whom dwells all the fullless of the Godhead bodily." There are three thoughts here about Christ. 1. .&ll the fulness of God is in him; he is not a mere emallaLion or God; not a mere flash of the light, but it~ Brightness; not a mere tone of the truth, but tho Word. 2. All the fulness of God is permanent in Christ. In him "dwelleth." He is a reservoir whose waters never fail ; he does not say be has brca,l or h& has water to bestow, but he is the Bread of life, he is the Water of life; the lloly Ghost abo,Je ur. Lim. 3. All the fulncss of God wae incarnate -in his l,umanity. It dwelt in Lim 13-l THE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. (olI, II, 1-23, --- - ----------------------·------ " b~dil_v." 'l'he pur_ity, righteousness, wisdom, compassion, love, of God wns gathered up in that human hfe. He was Immanuel, and from his fulness thus complete last- ing, human, we are fed.-U. R. T. ' '

entries.title: COL 2:16–19
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0'liri'.stian indrpendence. Remembering the evils in the Church at Colossal, namely, the ccremonlalism, the asceticism, the appeal to angelic mediators, and at the same time recalling _the theme of the paragraph preceding the verses now before us, the complete sufficiency of Christ as man's Mediator, nature's Lord and Consecrator and the soul's Deliverer from bondage to ceremonies, we nre prepared to notice th~ result of Christ's work for man and over man, as here suggested, and to consider the great theme of Ohnstian independence. I. THAT CHnISTIAN INDEPENDENCE IS A FREEDOM FROM THE BONDAGE OF CEREMONY A:!-"'D OF SUPERSTITION. The sixteenth ver.se suggests what ceremony may bind men • the eighteenth what superstition may enslave them. We notice the Christian's inde~ p ·ndence: 1. From the bomiage of ceremonialism. The form of this bondaa-e varies but its spirit continues. The form of bond:Lge in those days was (1) bond~go as t~ food. There were restrictions as to meat and drink, which were rigid as any moral c,"lde. 'l'hey were mostly Jewish, and had wrongly been inserted in the Christian ~ystem. (2) Bondage a.s to days. These were also mostly Jewish anniversaries, or monthly or weekly celebrations. The claim of their observauce was so punctilious as to be a sore bondage. From both of these the Spirit of Christ frees men, .As to meats, "nothin;; was common or unclean;" as to days, the shadow thrown in advance had girnn way to the substance. 2. From tM bondage of superstition, .A heathen super- ~tition bad intruded in the form of the worship of angels, which led to" a voluntary J,umility,'' that is, to an artificial, self-conscious affectation of humility, leading to the 1,r,)stration of men before imaginary superior beings. I•'rom this parade of humility and morbidly fostered prostration Christ delivers by bringing each soul into conscious relationship with the Highest. That lofty relationship enjoyed, there will be no cring- inp: before any who are inferior to him. II. THA.T FALSE TEACIIERS SEEK TO DEPRIVE MEN OF THIS INDEPENDENCE, So they did in Paul's day, and so they do now. '!'hey "beguile" men, trip them up in the race, and binder their attaining the prize. 'l'wo sets of falso teachers so beguile men. ] . The sentim~ntalist-tbose who foster among their adherents a pietism under the name of unworldliness. 2. The sacerdotalist-tbose who exercise over their followers a priestism that makes the man a slave of the institution, instead of the institution being a servant of the man. III. THAT CHRISTIA.N nmEPENDENCE IS DERIVED FROM AND NOURISHED BY UNION wrrrr CHRIST. I. The right relationship with Christ gives independence because of tho strength flowing from union with the Head, the Source of,all power and cont~ol. ~- 'J'his right union with Christ gives independence because it involves healthy relat1onslnp to the body, i.e. all fello\v-Christians. 'l'here is none of the ruptured relalionship with Christ or the Chnrch that some count liberty, but which is really only licence. There is ratlier the being healthily and perfectly united to Christ and to the Church by the Ji,:,;amen~s of loving relalionship-ligarueuts these that hold all togeth~r and ~old all to Christ, and gfre him the complete control of all. Each soul bas hbc:ty, Just ns tho limbs of a Leal thy man have free play. l'lloreovcr, such a soul grows w1tb the growth cf God.-U. R. 'l'.

Vcrs. 20-23.-Tl,e O'l11"istia11's exemption from bondage to outwardness. "'l'he rudiments of the world,'' of which our text speaks, arc, according to Bishop Li;.ihtfoot, " 1he rudimcn tary elementary, ordinances and discipline of the mundane sphern;" or, according to Con;bearc, "the cl,ildish lessons ?f outward thi~gs." 'l'akin~. the two renderinp together, does it not fieem that Paul 1s rather speak1_nf of the Hpmt of out- ,rnrd thiugs, and not of outward things themselves-the spmt of outwardness as oppo>ed to thnt of inwardness? An<l if so, is it not suggested here- I. 'l'IIAT TIIE CHnIS'l'IAN IS EX!sl\lPT l'ROM DONDAGE TO OU'l'WARDNJ!.SS? He is not ordinance-ridden. ,vnat ordinances does Paul primarily speak of? Mingled and interfused Judaic, Gnostic, ERscn", and l'harisnic. Paul qnotps the word8 of some of their prescrir,Live lin,itations about wine, oil, meat, etc. And also he uhows what cmuargo OII. II, 1-23.] Tlm EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIAXS. 13.5

that spirit of outwardness placed on intercourse with persons who were (1) ceremonially un_clean, (2) r~ligiously inferior, (3) nationally alien. He adduces three reasons against bemg bound m the bondage of ordinances and regulations concerning such ontward things. 1. Tl1at such things themselves are transient and fleeting. "The fashion of the world passeth away," he says in another place; and here," which all are to perish with the using." They who guide their course by such things are as mariners who would direct their voyage rather by the clouds than by the stars. 2. That the virtues that are cultivated in care for such are artificial, virtues. They engender (1) vanity, (2) arbitrai-iness, (3) false humility, because voluntary and a!Iectcd. 3. That such bondage/ails in its obfect. "Not in any honour." !I, TIIAT IN CHRIST'S DEATH IS THE POWER AND PATTEC\N OF EXEMPTION FROl[ SUCII OUTWARDNESS? Paul is accustomed to dwell on the Christian's complete identification with Christ: "crucified," "buried," "risen," with him. Here it is identificatioa with Jesus in his death. "Make thou, 0 Christ, a dying of my life." This first and mainly describes a dying to sin, here a dying to the dominion of outwardness. It is the paradox of Christian experience, "I am truly alive because I am dead." About this insensibility to the dominion of the external, this" death to outwardness," Paul here teaches : 1. Christ's death is the power by which man dies to merely outward rule and regulation. Through meditation, sympathy, fellowship, faith in the death of Christ, not only is the soul fired with hatred to sin which slew him, and with the love of God who could love thus, but of the hollowness of all formality and the coldness of all legality in the presence of such motives. 2. <Jhrist's death is the pattern of such sxemptionfrom bondage to the outward. The unresponsiveness of his dead body on the cross is an image of the soul that through faith in him is dead to the world. '.l'hat independence to the external is (1) complete, and (2) gradually obtained. "Let no man think that sudden, in a minute, All is nccomplished an<l the work is done ; Though with thine earliest dawn thou shouldst begin it, Scarce were it ended with thy setting sun." U. R. T.

entries.title: COL 2:1–3
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-St. Paul's anxieties for the Oolossians, and how they we;·e allayed. I. ST. PAUL'S ANXIETIES FOR DRETHREN HE HAD NEVER SEEN. \Ve infer from this passage, as well as from other considerations, that the apostle had not visited Colossrn and was not acquainted with the Church. Yet he felt much interest in them and had many anxious thoughts about them. Our sympathies are not to be confined to the narrow circle of our acquaintance. If a heathen could say," Homo sum," etc., much more should a disciple of "the Son of man" respond, "I am a Christian, and consider nothing that concerns Christians a matter of indifference to me;"" For we are members one of another," and the heresies that may distract our brethren in France or the persecutions that befall the converts in China should call forth onr anxieties and our prayers. The apostle has to utter solemn warnings. Most skilfully does he attract and conciliate these unknown Christians by telling them of his cares and his prayers on their behalf. There was an l,:yrf,v in his public ministry (eh. i. 29) and in his quiet hours (ver. 1 ; eh. iv. 12). It was caused by the care of souls (2 Cor. xi. 28). Absence intensified it. (Illustrations: Caged bird hearing the cries of its young. A mother hearing of the sickness or spiritual peril of a child far from home. Cf. 2 Cor. xi. 2, 3; Gal. iv. 19.) "The pastor," says Cyprian, "is wounded by the hurt of his flock." Paul's anxiety was for the spiritual comfort and concord of the Colossians. "Comfort" in its older sense includes the ideas of help and strength as well aE of soothing nnd consolation. Error weakens as well as disturbs. '.l'ho attitude of perf'etual doubt and criticism is most unfavourable to growth and harmony. We notice three things that he was very anxious for the Colossians to enjoy as means of preserving them from the errors that encompassed and assailed them. 1. Ardent love. It is by love that we gain spiritual discernment, and are thus enabled to explore the hidden treasures of grace. 'l'he intellect is affected by the heart (Ps. xiv. I). Love to a godly father may be our snfcguard against scepticism ; how much more may love to Christ be! Like a rockit!g stone, our soul may be somewhat swayed, but not" greatly moved" (I's. lxii. 2). Like a magnet, our hearts rn,iy be liable to p~rtial dcflcctious, but slill roint towllr,I, I;)G 'l'l.It.; EPISTLE 'l'O THE COLOSSIANS. [utt. 11. 1--23.

the pole. Moreover, love will unlock many a truth. Pascal has said cc In order to love human things, it is necessary to know them; in order to know things 'that are Divine, it is necessary to love them." Jf we trust and love Christ we shall know him(" We have believed, and we ~now," etc.? John vi. 68, 69; observe the order of the words), and then all the controversies of Christendom need not shake us (2 Tim. i. 12). 2. Intelligent fai/.h. "'l'~e full assurance ?f understanding," etc.. Lo_ve a~ a mere sentiment may degenerate mto a weak toleration of any error that disguises itself in the garb of love. Or, under the plea of jealousy for truth aud love for souls, it may be depraved into an intolerant bigotry. Love must be a means to an end (John viii. 31, 32). There aro hidJ.en treasures of truth in Christ cc the Truth," which need manly intelligence inspired by childlike love and trust (Ps. xxv. 9; Matt. xi. 25). 3. Steadfast consistency. (Vera. 6 7 ; see next sketch.) We are thus reminded of three chief preservatives against enor...! a warm heart, a clear judgment, a clean conscience (Eph. iv. 14, 15). II. How ST. PAUL SOUGHT TO ALLAY HIS ANXIETIES. 1. He strives/or the Oolossians in prayer. Like his ancestors Abraham, Jacob, and Moses, and his brother Epaphras (eh. iv. 12), he knew what it was to strive, to wrestle in prayer. No doubt like his Master, he was sometimes "in an agony of prayer." Gather up Paul's referen~es to his intercessions, and illnstra_te from the lives of others who have been mighty in prayer; e.g. John Welsh, the mimster of Ayr, and son-in-law of John Knox, of whom it is sairl that he used always to sleep with a plaid upon his bed, that he might wrap it round him if he rose in the night to pray. Sometimes his weeping would awaken his wife, ancl when she asked the reason, he would reply," 0 woman, I have the souls of three thousand to answer for, and I know not how it is with many of them." 2. He points them to Christ. (Ver. 3.) With an allusion to the false teachers who boasted access to some secret knowledge and wisdom into which they could initiate their disciples, Paul assures them that all tlie richest treasures of a wisdom they had not yet attained to were concealed and could be discovered in Christ himself (like pearls at the bottom of the ocean). The truth is even wider than the application the apostle gives of it. As all things were made "by him and for him" and "consist in him," so all branches of knowlerlge have a relation to him and find their truest meaning in him. (1) He is tbe Key to history. Its treasures are not unlocked until God's education of the world in its history is connected with the advent of Christ (John i. 3, 4, 9, 10; Gal. iv. 4). (2) He is the Interpreter of science, which may reveal many of its secrets to a. godless investigator, bnt reserves its choicest treasures for those who can see in them his handywork. (3) The philosophy of mind and of morals is best understood if Christ be known. We see in him ideal human nature and the power which can recover men from that injury to human nature which philosophy no kss than theology must recognize. "\Ve learn the supremacy of conscience, the dignity and value of the soul, and the fad of a life beyond death. (4) Christ is the Essence of true theology. A knowledge of Divine things apart from Jesus Christ is, at the best, most imperfect and unsatisfactory (1 Cor. i. 20, 21). But Christ is Light, 'l'ruth, Revelation, God (Luke x. 22; John i. 18; xiv. 9). 5. Christ is the Wisdom of God and the Power of God unto salvation. In him we are made "wise unto salvation," and this pearl of great price is the most precious of all the treasures which can be found in him (1 Cor. i. 30, 31). He aloue can satisfy the hunger of the soul, and thus fortify it against the errors of thoso who would beguile with "enticing worJ.s" which are "not after Christ."-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 2:4–7
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0ongralulations and counsels. "\Ve have seen that the heresy that was threatening the Colossian Church was twofold in its character. Its propagators " had a falBe conception in theology and they bad a falso basis of morals." 'l'hcse two errors were closely connected together, and seem to have sprung from the prevalent idea that matter was the abode of evil and therefore opposed to God. It was the plausibility uf these false doctrines that made the apostle so anxious. Ilut be had the firmest couviction that the Christ be proclaimed could satisfy every reasonablo want a.nd aspiration of the inquirin" spirit. '£ho words," This I say," etc. (ver. 4) look back over vers. 1-3, and remin°d them both of his anxieties and his convictions. Ilut at ]•resent the leaven bad not spread in the Church, so that the apotltle can address to t,!,en1- l. CoNGl!ATtJLATJONS ON THEIR &TEADFABTNESS. (Ver. 5.) St. Paul thus most wisely

prepares the way for wo.rnings. He shows them how deep is his interest and sympathy. He says all he can in their favour, as our Lord does to the Churches in Asia. 'l'he recogniLion of what is good in others is one of the best means of helping them to see nnd to strive against error. All right-minded Christians at Colossre would he encouraged by the declaration that so eminent an apostle as Paul could rejoice in them while he saw them holding their present faith. (For other illustrations of commendation, see Phil. i. 3-5; ii. 22; 2 Thess. i. 3, 4; 3 John 3, etc.) Men can more easily Le encouraged in the truth than scolded into it. 'l'he terms "order" and "steadfastness" may both have been used as military figures, suggested by the apostle's familiarity with military matters in the Prretorian camp at Rome (cf. Eph. vi. 13, etc.). He saw their "orderly array a.nd solid front." 'l'hey were still loyal to the truth and steadfast in the faith. Their ranks were not yet thinned by deserters, in spite of all the seductive appeals of the emissaries of error a.round them. But cautions were not needless in the midst of congratulations. When an epidemic is in the country precautions a.re needed, though it may not yet have entered our house or even our town. A fearless, cheerful mind may in itself be one precaution, just as the encouragement in our faith which we receive from the sympathetic words of experienced Christians may be one safeguard against the epidemic of unbelief. But with these congratulations on their steadfastness, St. Paul thinks it neerlrul to blenc1.- II. CAUTIONS RESPECTING THEm DANGERS. (Ver. 4.) Note: 1. Paul does not make Ughl of erroneous teacliing. He warns against "enticing words,"" persuasiveness of speech." 'l'he tendency of many now is to n~ake light of doctdnn.l, definite teaching altogether, using the Greek term for" doctrine" (dogma) as a term of reproach-" course as childish as it is dangerous. Paul knew that doctrine had a mouldii;g power on the characters of those who carue under its influence (Rom. vi. 17). He was not indifferent even to the form of sound words (2 Tim. i. 13). The variety of meaning in good honest words may nevertheless make them instruments of error, not to say deception. (Illustrate from such words as" inspiration,"" atonement," etc.) Solemn cautions are suggested to teachers and disputants by Prov. xviii. 21; Matt. xii. 36, 37. 2. Paul nowhere charges these.false teachers with immorality or any gr&ss sin. Elsewhere he does bring such charges against other heretics (1 Tim. vi. 5; Titus i. 10-16). Here the strongest is in ver. 18. This is instructive for two reasons. (1) 'l'he errors at Colossre were as yet in the bud, and hnd not brought forth the hitter fruit that was naturai to them. Dr. Lightfoot has shown that it is probable that the more perilous heresy of Cerintbus wa.s the outgrowth of these errors at Colossre (Comm., pp. 106-113). The gradual corruption of the trnth respecting the ministry as a teaching and pastoral office, apparently harmless enough at first, led on to full-blown sacerdotalism, Romanisrn, Vaticanism. (2) We are reminded of the special danger of error:1 when held aud taught by holy men. A Tetzel and a Tom Paino are harmless compared with advocates of substantially the same doctrines whose lives are blameles,. \Ve must seek to combine charity to men with unflinching opposition to tlwir erroneoua teaching when it touches the "faith in Christ." "Obsta principiis ''(Jude 3). 3. Paul counsels them to hold fast to the gospel of Christ. (Vcrs. 6, 7.) 'l'ill you can find something better, "hold that fast which thou hast," etc. (Rev. iii. 11). They had receive,! n. definite gospel from Epaphras; Paul certifies it as his own. They bad rccei vc,l "Jesus" (a living example, a dying Saviour) ns "the Christ" (God's own Son, the anointed Priest and King of men) their "Lord" (Ilom. xiv. 9). The reception of this gospel had brought "great joy in that city," and they could still " abound in thanksgiving" (ver. 7; Rom. v. 11). 'fhey had begun well; now, says St. Paul, go on well; "Walk in him." Abide in Christ and proceed by Christ, for as be is "the Truth" wherein we are to a.bide, he is also "the Way" wherein we are to walk. But he takes for granted that holding the truth of Christ is essential to walking in the ways of Christ. Notice the connection of Phil. iii. 8-11 and 12-14. 'l'his is still further seen by the other figures which he employs. 'l'he first is that of a tree. Notice the tenses employed in the participial clauses. We are once for all to be firmly rooted in Christ. As "God's husbandry," "planted in the house of the Lord," the roots of our lire are "hidden with Christ in God." To him we must cling; around him every fibre of the soul must twine. Thus "rooted nml grounded in love" because in Christ himsdf, we shall be safe against the gales of false doctrine (Eph. iv. 14), which would uproot Ollr 138 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [on. 11. 1-23.

souls ... The second ~gurc is tl~at o~ a ~onsc, "God's building," a moro frequent fiaure (Epb. ~'.- 20; ~ Pet•• !1· 6). l:d1~~ahon 1s a gradual. ,vork, and in pro port.ion to it sliall we be established m our faith. In the West Indies we have seen trees that seemed to combine the two figures of this ver_se. I_n_ the ~agnificent silk-cotton trees (Eriode11- drum) we see enormous trunks sometnnes nsmg eigb t.y or a hundred feet before they send forth any of their huge branches. 'fhe widespreading roots secure the safety of the rnst superstructure from the wildest hurricane. But around the base of the trunk there ri~e above the roots massive buttresses whereby the tree is" built up" to still greater ~.tability. 'Ihus "rooted and built up". in Christ, the Christi~n may defy storms, may wax stronger and stronger," may bnng forth "much fruit" "abounding therein in thanksgi1·ing."-E. S. P. '

V-crs. 8-10.-Christ's f'ulness the (Jhristian's safeg=rd. While thus abidinu and walking in Christ (vers. 6, 7), the Colossiaus still needed the warning, "Be on° your gu~rd;" "Take heed," etc. In the words that follow we find- I. A SUGGESTIVE SKETCH OF THE FALSE TEACHING THAT ASSAILED THE CoLOSSIANS, 1. It came t'n the garb of philosophy. Real philosophy is nowhere condemned by the apostle. The term itself warns against its abuse. It is attributed to Pythagoras, -who taught that no man was truly wise but God only, but be claimed to be a lover of wisdom. 'l'he false teachin~ at Colossai was rnther a theosophy than a philosophy. As such it was" vain deceit" (Job xi. 7-9; 1 Cor. i. 19-21; iii. 18-20). It was part of that" knowledge which is falsely so called" (1 Tim. vi 20). 2. It claimed ,·espect because of human authority and antiquity. It was "after the tradition of men." So far us the error was of Jewish origin, we ct\n imagine something of its nature from the references to it in the Gospels (Matt. xv. 2-9; Mark vii. 3-5). 'l'hese traditions had an attraction for many religious minds (Gal. i. 14). Grafted upon the i:(enuine command- rnen ts of God, they had a semblance of authority, and some of them an undefined antiquity. The false teaching that was of Gentile origin could bring forward in its support names eminent in the philosophical world. But the authority was merely of men and could not appeal to" Scripture inspired of God." 3. It :prescribed services and ceremonies pleasing to the unspiritual mind. The rite of circumcision (ver. 11), the strict observance of feasts or fasts, and the distinction of meats (ver. 16), might form important parts of & religion which would be easy to a mind religious but not truly spiritual (Ilom. xiv. 17, 18). 4. It was probably recommended by the personal influence of one or more popular teachers in their midst. This is an inference from the words, "Take heed lest there shall be any one that maketh spoil of you through his philo- sophy," etc. (Revised Version). A devout and pure heresiarch is a source of peculiar peril. Hence the vehement warning in Gal. i. B, 9. 5. But it was alienfrom the doctrine and Spirit of Christ. "Not after Christ." Paul had absolute confidence that tl,e good news be proclaimed was Christ's own gospel, by which he was prepared to test any teaching, and if needs be to condemn it as "a different gospel which is not another gospel" (Gal. i. G). There are points of resemblance between t~c heresy ~t C~loss3:" a!1d the most prominent errors of the present day that are suggeRt1ve. Ilat1onahsm, m 1ta .-arious degree~ of anti-supernaturalism, bases itself on philosophy and science (~o~called); it speaks in tones of authority, and teaches as truths the thoughts and tra~1hons and alle:;ed discoveries of men quite irrespective of whether. we have a revelation of the thouahts of God. It is recommended by the personal mfluenco of exemplary men.
