(Vers. 9, 10.) 1. The fulness of the Godhead dwelt in the eternal Word from tl,e beginning, '!'bis is ono of the s11perh11man truths revealed by God's Spirit and which eta.nds or falls with Christianity (John i. 1; 1 John i. 2). 2. That fulness now dwells in" the Man Ghrist Jesus," "the Word made flesh," "bodily." 'l'he Incarnation is the grandest supernatural fact in the world. It is a" present tmth," for Jesus Christ still Ii ves, and the "fulness of the Godhead d welleth in him" ~till. No ,vonder that mysteries and miracles should gather around our incarnate God. '!'he transfiguration and the resurrection are natural to him. Ilis dying rather than his rising is miraculou~. 3. His sufficiency as Mediator renders us independent of all other mediation. His one sacrifice as an atonement takes the place of all the elementary lessons of Jewish symbolism, and makes the sacrifices of a so-called Christian priesthood a practical denial of his work on the cross (Heb. ix. and x.). Since he is" the Head of all principality and power," we need neither saints nor angels as intercessors (1 Tim. ii. 5; Heh. vii. 25), nor can we degrade ourselves to receive God's absolution from an intrnsive priest. 4. The fulness of blessing that flows direct from Christ can satisfy all the necessities of the human heart. Let us not make light of churches, ministries, sacraments, or other means of grace. But let us hold fast to the truth that Christ himself can immediately supply all our needs, so that we may be "in him made full." We are thus reminded of man's emptiness and need (John xv. 5; Rev. iii.17); of his capacity for receiving blessings inde.6.uitely great (" filled with all the fulness of God"); of" the exceeding abundant grace of our Lord" (John i. 16; 1 Cor. i. 30; Epb. iii. 17-21; Phil. iv. 13); and of the need of union with Christ by faith (" in him") as the necessary condition of spiritual life.-E. entries.title: COL 2:11–15
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Purity, pardon, and victory tlirough Christ. Errors in religion, when taught sincerely, are intended to secure spiritual blessings (e.g. purity by austerities; JJeacc of conscience and assurance of pardon by confession and priestly absolution). But the truth of our completeness in Christ strikes at the root of all such errors, for it assures us that all the blessings we can need may be gained direct from him. In ver. 10 we learn that the headship of Christ i~ our guarat1tce that we are not dependent upon any intermediato superhuman power. In vers. 11-15 we are remindeJ. that the personal blessings which external rites were designed. to secure are ours if we arc Christ's. I. PURITY, Judaizing teachers taught the necessity of circumcision even by Gentile converts as a means of purification and salvation. St. Paul teaches the Colossians that they have no need of this, because, by union with Christ, they receive that inward purity of which circumcision was a. type (vcr. 11; Rom. ii. 28, 29). Moses and the prophets had seen through the type (Deut. x. 16; xxx. 6; Jcr. iv. 4). 'l'he believer's circumcision is distinguished from that which was typical of it in these particulars: 1. Jn its chardctcr; spiritual, not external, wrought not by hands but by the S1,irit himself. 2. In ils extent; it puts off, not a mere morsel of the flesh, but" the body of the fl,,sh," the whole body of carnal affections. 3. Its Author; it is the circumcision, not of :Moses (Jolrn vii. 22) for a nation, but of Cl,rist for all believers (Phil. iii. 3). And as Paul speaks hero of spiritual circumcision, so docs he al,o of spiritual baptis,n. His argument is not," You need not bo circumcised because you have been baptized." Here he speaks Ligl,ly of some baptism" wherein ye wero also raiseu," etc. Elsewhere be clear!} denies the doctrine of regeneration by baptism (cf. 1 Cor. i. 13-17 with 1 Cor. iv. 15). It would be strango if here he spoke disparagingly of" hand-wrought" circ11mcision, and then passed on immediately to speak of tho spiritual efficacy of "hand-wrought" baptism. 'l'his would be to introduce the very clement of ceremonialism and ritualis:n 'which he is here denouncing. Many, never baptized with water, are now "in Christ," in glory. It is the spiritual baptism alone in which we are buried and raised with Christ (Rom. vi. 3-5). 'l'he one great. baptism of the Kew Testament is that of tbo Holy Spirit (Mark i. 8; Acts i. 5). Of that, baptism by water is a beautiful emblem. But in Paul's Epistles he generally speaks of that "one baptism" rather than of baptism with water. Here he speaks of a spiritual circumcision, a spiritual rlc,tth and lmrial and resurrection, and a spiritual h1pti,nn. The baptism by the lloly Spirit is that pnrification of the soul from the lo·,c and dominion of sin by which we are set upart, consccmtcd to a course like Christ's, to a sriiritual history of which our Lord's 140 THE EPISTLE 'l'O TUE COLOSSlANS. [ CH, II, 1-23,

earth!_~ history w,1s typical as well ns causal. By union with him we are" crucified \\"it.Ii Christ," "dead to the Law,"" <lead with Christ," "buried with !Jim," "risen with him,"" sitting with him in the hc:wenly places." If the apostle here makes nn allusion to water baptism, which was symbolic of the higher baptism, his ar.,ument does not rest ,m, but is opposed to, the supposition that" it is in that font, and when we are in it, thnt the first breath of [the new] life is drawn." Nor can we see that the lowerina of a l:ody into a bath and_ the lifting_it up aga~n is a significant aud striking symbol ir the J:..unal and resurrection of Christ, especially when we remember how ditrerent the customs of burial among Jews and Romans were from our own. However, the main truth of these ,erses is clearly that in Christ we have purity. "He is made unto us of God sanctification." Every pure motive, every good resolation, every holy impulse is from him. Our entire renunciation of sin(" the putting off of the body of the flesh") is through the power of his purifying Spirit (Gal. ii. 19, 20; vi. 14, 15). By faith in God, who by his Divine power raised the dead body of our Saviour from the tomb (Eph. i. 19, 20), we too are" raised with him," etc. (ver. 12). Whatever he who has raised us prescribes as means of attaining greater purity, we will revere and observe; but we r,,ject new-fangled methods of holiness "after the tradition of men" (Ps. cxix. 128). II. "JUSTIFICATION OF LIFE." This Pauline phrase (Rom. v. 18) sums up the bless- ings described in vcrs. 13, 14. We regard Christ as the Subject of the whole sentence. He is one with bis Father in the work of quickeuing (John v. 21 ; Epb. ii. 1-5), and of pardoning (eh. iii. 13; Eph. iv. 32). But in order to accomplish this Divine work of gidng life, there needed tbe no less Divine work of providing justification. For there \\"as wbat Paul describes as a document in existence, which was a barrier to our pardon. It w,1s God's Law, not merely for the Jews (Rom. iii. 19), but for the Gentiles (Hom. ii. 14, 15), whi~b "worketh wrath" (Rom. iv. 15). But Jesus Christ, in whom "dwelletb," etc. (ver. 9), bas removed the barrier. He had power to forgive sins "on earth" (Mark ii. 10), and bas it still (Acts v. 31). The value of Christ's obedience unto death as an atonement for sin is constantly taken for granted by the apostle. He was not sent to prove it, but to" deliver" it and testify to it (1 Cor. xv. 3; 1 Tim. ii. 6). By Christ's ,icarious sacrifice the ransom is given, the bond is cancelled, the document is annulled, and our sins may be blotted out (Isa. xliii. 25; Matt. xviii. 21-35; xx. 28). We are redeemed from the curse of the Law. As the instrument of our condemnation, it is taken out of the way; it is crucified with Christ, nailed to bis crosR. According to Paul's allegory in Rum. ii 1-4, the Law, a holy but inexorable husband, is dead, and we are joined to a no less holy but a loving Lord and Saviour. The conditions of acceptance with God and final salvation are no longer "The man that doeth these things shall live by them," but "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou sbalt be saved" (Heb. iii. 14; 1 Pet. i. 9). What need have we of other means of forgiveness? of angelic intercessors or absolving priests or eucbaristic sacrifices? "In him ye are ruade full." III. DELIVERANCE FROM OUR Th"FERNAL FOES. Christ in bis fleshly nature wao r•xposed to the assaults of sin and of the evil one throughout bis life (Matt. iv. 1-11; Luke iv. 13) till the last day of it (Luke xxii. 53; John xiv. 30). But on the cross his life of humiliation and strife came to an end (Rom. vi. 10). His cry," It is finished I,. declared that bis work of conflict, as well as his work of atonement, was ended. Ho put off from himself once for all and for ever the hostile principalities and power111 (cf. John xii. 31; IIeb. ii. 14; 1 John iii. 8). The entrance of Christ into Jerusalem, commonly called bis triumphal entry, is nowhere called his triumph in the New Testa. ment. His triumph was on the cross. The powers of darkness plotted his death, and by liis death they received their deadly blow. 1'1,e malefactor's cross became the victor's car (Rom. xiv. !:J; Phil. ii. 7-11; Rev. i. 18). This victory is for us who e.re "in Christ." ::iatan and all Lis allies (Epli. vi. 11, 12) who work through the world and the flesh are conquered foes; they know it, and we do too (Rom. vi. 14; viii. 37-39; xvi. 20; 1 Cor. xv. 55-57; Gal. vi. 14). We need no other allies in this conflict, no mystic methods of exploring the secrets or annulling the power of our spiritual foes (Phil, iv. 13).-E. S. P.

\' ds. lG-19.-Tu:o dangers to be avoided. We find here two notes of warning-" Let PO wa11 j•1dge you;" "Let no man rob you.'' 'l'wo dangers need to be guarded against, on. 11. 1-23.) THE EPISTLE TO '!'HE COLOSSIANS. 141

. I. Tm: mFLUE~<;E 01!' UNfUST ~UD!lMENTB. The aposile has here in view the prac- tical error of ~uda1zrng ntuahsts: fhey ha<l received from Moses regulations respecting meats and drinks and feast,, which they endeavoured to enforce on Gentile converts as necessary to salvation (Acts xv. 1). If they did not always proceed to this extreme, they treated others as negligent of most important means of grace. They thus brou""ht a strong pressure to bear on the consciences of new convert.~ who had received no s~cll inst111ctions from apostles or other Christian teachers who had "begotten them throu"h the gospel." It was no easy thing to resist such pressure exerted by men with all the sacred traditions of Judaism behiod them ; just as it must have been hard work for the early Reformers to resist the iofluence of the hostile opinioos of all the leaders and Fathers of the Christian world. (Illustrate from the case of Cranmer.) Thus the Colossian converts were in danger of yielding to the censorious judgmcnts of these teachers and conforming to their requiremeots. In so doing they might grasp at shadows which belonged to Moses and lose the substance which was Christ's. Neither the twelve apostles oor Paul made light of Mosaic ordioances (Acts xvi. 3 ; xviii. 18 ; xxi. 26) or sacred seasons (Acts xvi. 13; xviii. 21; xx. 16; xxiv. 11). But St. Paul earnestly protests agaiost the yoke of bondage being imposed on Gentile con vcrts. W c too must beware of yielding to similar pressure from ritualiziog Christiaos. So loog as we endeavour to observe all things which Christ has commanded, we must be preparetl to brave the judgments of those who would impose on our consciences ohservaoces aocl expedients which are oot of Divine authority; e.g. the enforcing on the couscieoec of the observance of Good Friday, or of early communion, evening communion being denounced; the forbiddiog of marriage during Lent or Advent. There is peril in regardiog any human appointments as takiog rank with Divine ordinances: "I am afraid of you" (Gal. iv. 10, 11). '!'here is positive sin in enforciog them on the conscieoces of others (Rom. xiv. 1-6, 13). II. 'l'HE LOSS OF OUR EXPECTED PRIZE. (Vcrs. 18, 19.) This danger arose from the theological errors of the advocates of a rudimeotary Goosticism. This heresy was more serious than the other, as we infer from the fact that to lose our expected priw is a far greater calamity than to endure the condemoation of narrow-minded brethren. By yielding to the temptation, even through the influence of false opioions, of robbiog Christ of his glory as sole Mediator, we may ourselves be robbed of our prize, our "crown." False doctrines may be fatal when they have their roots in moral causes and bring forth " wild grapes." The element of error here chiefly c00demued is the worship of angelic mediators. It had four sources. (1) A spurious humility, as though we could not venture to have access to God except through the medi:1tion of inferior beings. (2) A vain pretence to know more than is reve11led respecting the world of spirits (" Dwelling in the things which he hath seen," i.e. his assumed visioos). (3) Spiritual pride (which is a frequent source of heresy even in Christian men; 1 Cor. viii. 1). (4) An imperfect knowledge of or trust to Christ (" not holding the Head,' etc.) This analysis of error applies, to a larAe extent, to the modern errors of the intercession and worship of angels, saints, nnd the Virgin Mary. They arise from: (1) Spurious humility; as though a child should appeal to his father through a domestic servant, when his elder brother was appointed as his tutor and counsellor (1 Tim. ii. 5; Heb. i. 14). (2) Pretended knowledge; for whatever speculations we may iodulge as to the employments of" the dead io Christ," we know nothing to authorize us to appeal to them as intercessors. (3) Spiritual pride, which show8 itself in decliniog to be satisfied or even in settiog aside "the things which are revealetl '' respectiog worship and mediation (1 John ii. 2; Rev. xix. 10, etc.), aod exalting our own imagioatioos or the uosupported assertions of fellow-sioners to the level of the true sayiogs of God (Rev. ii. 14, 15, 20). In some respects Romanists and spiritualists are victims of similar delusions. (4) A failure in "holdiog fast the Head," etc. Unhappy men! "If thou koewest the gift of God I" God is better to you than your servile fears or false humility woultl suggest. We have an Advocate, even Christ (John xiv. 6; Eph. ii.18). We need no advocate with him. "I can speak more safely and chc~rfully to my Jesus than to any of the holy spirits of God" (Augustioe). '!'he angels have not my nature, o.od I need no redeemed sinoers as intercessors, since I have the Sinless One (Heh. vii. :.!5 26). To admit any one to share with Jesus Christ the glory of the work of m~di,tti;n is (to say the least) to" h9~d tbo llcad," not "fast," but io a m~nner that is both ' • 142 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [err. u, 1-23.

lax and perilous, If we are" holding fast the Head," we must acknowledo-e him as tho Imnge of God, in whom" ~welleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily," ;s the Author nnd tho End of all creat101:1, as the Lord of the world and the supremo Ruler of his Church, as the great Reconciler between God and man by the blood of his cross and as the believer's only Hope of glory. It is from him alone that his member; receive spiritual supplies, are knit together and grow. False teachers, who would divert our faith or affections from him, may rob us of our reward. (Illustration : Racers diverted from the straight coursz toward the umpire at tho goal, or persuaded to nealect one of the laws of the game (Gal. v. 7; Phil. iii. 12-14; 2 'l'im. ii. 5; Heh. xii, 1, 2).) '1.'o us the exhortations come homo (Eph. iv. 14-16; Heb. iii. 12-14; Rev, iiL 11).- E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 2:20–23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The worthlessness of unautho,·ized ceremonialism, The apostle hero reverts to the ethical errors of the false teachers. Combining his teaching here and elsewhere respecting what he calls "the rudiments of tho world," we learn the follow- ing truths : - I. " THE RUDIMENTS OF THE WORLD " WERE USEFUL IN TREIB OWN TIME AND PLACE. The difficult expression, "rudiments of the world," seems to mean elementary teaching on the religious life which was no part of the teaching of Jesus Christ. It was not necessarily opposed to Christianity; for it included much of the Mosaic legislation under which the Jews were treated as children and pupils (Gal. iv. 3), 'l'hese rudimentary lessons were both disciplinary and typical. Paul respected the prejudices of Jews and of Jewish converts in their favour (Acts xvi. 3 ; xxi. 23-26). He allowed tender consciences to be bound by such rudiments as were not either of Jewish or Christian obligation (Rom. xiv. 2, 3, 14). So in the present day, among heathens just emerging from darkness but not yet "risen with Christ," certain elementary precepts and restrictions may be valuable as temporary educational expedients. And more stringent rules of Church discipline than the New Testament enforces may be expedient for a time in the training of converts from heathenism who have just come out from a worse than Egyptiau bondage. (Illustrate from Exod. xxiii, 13, and similar requirements in Polynesia or other mission fields.) II. THE CHDISTIAN IS EMANCIPATED FROM D0NDAGE TO THESJI! RUDIMENTS. "If yo died with Christ," etc. "This deatll has many aspects in St. Paul's teaching, It is not only a dying with Christ (2 Tim. ii. 11), but it is also a dying to or from something. This is sometimes represented as sin (Rom. vi. 2); sometimes as self; sometimes as the Law (Rom. vii. 6 ; Gal. ii. 19) ; sometimes still more widely as the world," as here and in eh. iii. 3. Our Lord, by his teaching and example, set his disciples free from the tradition~ of men (Matt. xii. 1-13; xv. 1-9) and from some of the ceremonial laws of Moses (Mark vii. 14-19, "This he said making all meats clean;" cf. Acts x; 15). Dy his death as the Sacrifice he fulfilled all that was typical in tho ceremonial Law, so that by union with him" we have been discharged from the Law" (Rom. vii. 6). By his power as the risen Saviour, the supreme Head and Lawgiver of his Church, he replaces the precepts of Moses by his "I say unto you." He thus introduces all believers into a new sphere of life and liberty (Heb. xii. 18-25). We experience what Christ can do for us apart from "the rudiments of the world," and therefore need not go back to them. Having pardon, peace, purity, through the death and resurrection of Christ, it would be as unreasonable to seek those blessings in rudiments, as it would be for a cultured literary man to be constantly practising in elementary rending and spelling hooks. 'J'o "subject ourselves" to such restrictions would boas though a slave on the free soil of Britain should still crouch before his oh! master (Gal. v, 1). Ill. THESE RUDIMENTS HA VE NO POWEil TO PROMOTE THE ODJECT FOR WIDCB THEY ARl!l nECOMMENDED. (Ver. 23.) So far as they were Mosaic they had no longer the value which belongs to even the most "positive" precept8 as a test of obedience. In tho Christian Church even the laws of Moses are merely "the precepts of men;" Jesu~ only is Lord. The rudiments respecting fasting, etc., which originated in asceticism, never had any spiritual value, but were for the most past the result of fundamental error (1 'l'irn. iv. 1-5). Self-denial for our own good or that of others is commended by Paul (1 Cor. viii. 13; ix. 27); but the asceticism of Colossre which was enforced 011 Christian converts is condemned as fostering pri<lc and powerless to suppress sin.

"Pride mny be po.mpered while the flesh grows lean" (Wordsworth). Thus the axe is laid at the root of those unscriptural austerities which are glorified in the Church of Home; e.g. even the saintly Pascal "wore beneath bis clothes a girdle of iron with sharp points affixed to it, and when be found bis mind disposed to wander from religious subjects or take delight in things around him, he struck the girdle with his elbow ancl forced the points into bis side." Men notorious for filth have been canonized (for an illustration, see Eadie on Colossians, p. 211). How absurd to think that hair shirts an,! "thongs and whip-cord arc means of grace"! But as Dr. South has said," The truth is, if men's religion lies no deeper than their skin, it is possible they may scourge them- selves into very great improvements." Occasional fasts may be of value, but a religion of asceticism is "a libel upon Providence, a surly and superstitious refusal of Divine benignity." The safeguard against such e1Tors is a clear view of our salvation by Christ, our union with him, our submission to him, and our fulness in him.-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 2:3
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-0hrist the Treasury of wisrlom. I. WISDOM Is A TREASURE FOR THE GREATEST TREASURY. St. Paul agrees with Solomon. Both exalt wisdom. It is a mistake to suppose that the gospel discourages knowledge and sets a premium on folly. It dis- regards worldly wisdom just because it brings a higher wisdom. It uses what the world calls the foolishness of preaching in order that it may confound the worldly wise and enlighten the ignoraut with the true wisdom of God. 1. The treasury of wisdom is a ;'ewel-chamber. Knowledge is good in itself. It is a treasure worth possessing for its own sake. The truly wise man would rather lose bis money than his knowledge. Knowledge bas these advantages over other possessions: (I) it cannot be stolen; (2) it is not lessened by being shared by many; (3) it does not suffer corruption; (4) it is a pure, calm, and elevating source of delight. 2. This treasury is a granary. Knowledge is good for the soul. 'fhe mind lives and grows upon ideas. 'fbe soul is nourished by the Word of God, which is the revelation of his wisdom. To know God is eternal life. 3. This treasury is a bank. True knowledge is like money. It is the means for procuring many other good things. It has a far larger purchasing • power than gold and silver. Knowledge is power,just because it shows us how to use many things which are useless to ignorance. The knowledge of Divine truth helps us to the use of Divine grace and the performance of Divine Law. II. CnnIST IS THE 'fnEASURY OF WISDOM. The Gnostics looked elsewhere. St. Paul says that, not only some wisdom, but all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, aro in Christ. They are part of the unsearchable riches of Christ. Nature is a mine in which science discovers numberless treasures of knowledge, but it is knowledge about Nature herself, not about the supernatural, the Divine, and the spiritual. Speculation soars in search of knowledge. But what it flatters itself to have discovered as moun- tain heights of knowledge often turns out to be but the shadows of cloudland. All the highest and best knowledg«tis in Christ. 1. The knowledge is in Ohrist himself. It is not simply in his teaching, much less is it in doctrines about him. To know him in his life and character and nature is to have the treasure of the best wisdom. 2. 'fhe knowledge covers the most important subfects of inquinJ. We may includo these in three questions. (1) 'l'heolo:;::ical: What is God? Christ says, "He that hath seen me bath seen the Jt'ather." 'l'o know Christ is to know God. (2) Anthropo- logical : What are man and his destiny ? In his earthly life Christ revealed the true nature and glory of humanity, and in bis resurrection its great destiny. (3) ·what is duty? The example of Christ is the answer to this question. Our duty is to follow him. III. LOVE IS THE KEY.TO TIIIS TREASURY OF WISDOM. 1. '!'he treasure is hidden. A superficial glance at Christ will not reveal it. The merchantm(ln seeks for goodly pearls; the purchaser of the field digs for the bidden treasure. 2. Nothing but love will open up the treasury. Gnostics thought intellectual enlightenment would do this; theologians in all ages have tried various keys-the rusty key of old-world le(lrning, tho ponderous key of argumentation with its intricate W(lrds; too often they have forgotten the golden key of love. 3. Love opens up the tre(lsury of wisdom in Christ. St. Paul desires the Colossians to be" kuit together in love" (ver. 2) in order that they may "know the Mystery of God, even Christ," etc. (1) 'l'hiR lovo must be love to Christ, that we may be in sympathy with man nod so know him; and (2) love to one anothc~, that we may be in sympathy with Chrisi's way of regarding God and mau.-W. 1''. A. IH THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [ell, II, 1-23.

Ycrs. 6, 7.-Growth in Christ. St. Paul is anxious lest tho invasion of n now philosophy should lead the Colossians away from their earlier Jifo in Christ. Rccocrniz- ing how rightly they had at first received the gospel, he desires them to contin~o in the faith as they had _be~n taught.. But ~hile he is most e:i-rnest in deprecating nny departure from_th_e prim1te fo11ndat10:n, he 1~ equally car?e~t m _wishing for progress in a continued bmldmg on that foundat10n. The true Christian hfe is neither a so-called progress that carries us away from Christ to newer masters, nor a dogged and stupid obstinacy that will not budge from the past and stagnates in its immobility, but a growth in Christ. 1. G1:wwrH IN CHRIST IMPLms CONTINUANCE IN CHRIST. Any other change, even though it may seem to involve an advance, is a retrogression from Christ. The Culus,ians arc exhorted to walk in Christ as they had received him. They had received him as Christ Jesus the Lord. 1. As Jesu.•. They had begun by recognizing the true human nature of Christ. The Gnost.ics were persuading them to give this faith up for the idea of a phantom Christ. We are not troubled with these Docetic notions. But practically we are tempted to lose our hold upon the human brotherliness of Christ in our doctrinal systems of divinity and our elaborate solemnities of devotion. 2. As the Lord. He was not only a Teacher, a mystic Mediator such as the Gnostics regarded him, but a Master. To regard Christ as Lord is not merely to have an abstract con- viction of his divinity, not simply to offer him worship; it is to submit to his kingly rule. 'l'o grow in Christ, then, we must, first of all, continue in brotherly sympathy with him, and also in dutiful submission to him. II. GROWTH IN CHRIST CONSISTS IN A CONTINUOUS ADVANCE IN THE CHRISTIAN LIFE, 1. We must be rooted. As the root derives nourishment from the soil for the increase of the tree, so are we to send out the deepest efforts of our soul to Christ and to draw from him ever more and more of spiritual vigour. 2. We must be built up. This is a gradual progress. It does not abolish the past in making the future, but, on the contrary, it erects the latter on the former. It produces· a compact and harmonious structure. So the temple of the Christian life should be rising in solid strength and grace and beauty, based on Christ as the Foundation, to be finished with Christ as the chief Corner-stone, and consecrated for the indwelling of the Spirit of Christ. Ilf. GROWTH IN CHRIST RESULTS IN ENLARGED FAITH AND GRATITUDE. 1. Enlarged faith. "Stablished in your faith." Faith, which is the means of growing iu the Christian life, is itself enlarged and strengthened by the process. 2. Great gratitude. "Aboundincr in thanks~ving." An advanced Christian will always be a thankful one, for be will know more ;f the !!Ood.ness of God in Christ, and his own heart will be more full of lore. Therefore also the joy of Christianity will increase with the growth of the Christian life.-W. F. A.

entries.title: COL 2:9
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Thefull divinity of <Jltrist. The Gnostic error which St. Paul seems to be opposing was twofold. It dcuicd that all the fulness of the Go~hea~ resided in Christ, teachi.no- that, while the bicrhest effluence of that fulness was Ill him, other effluences which ~ompleted it were distributed through the angels, in descendfog gradations of being. At the same time, in itR abhcrrence of matter, it refused to believe that so much divinity as it allowed to Uhrist coul<I dwell in a human earthly body, and, accordingly, it favoured tbe absurd idea that what men saw of Christ was a phantom appearance, not a real man. In reply to this twofold error, St. Paul teaches that all the fulness of the Godhead is in Christ, and that this dwells in him bodily. I. CHllIST IB FULLY DIVINE. The fulness of the Godhead is in Christ. Wherein thi8 fulness consists is an infinite mystery. We must be omniscient to measure and sound its contents. But we see glimpses of parts of it, rays of divinity breaking out liere and there. And all that we see is in Christ. There is no known characteristic of divi!iity which is not ascribed to Christ in the New Testament, from creation (eh. i. 16) to judgment (Acts x. 42) and the final restitution of all things (Eph. i. 10). 1. In tLiM fact is the essential difference between the divinity of Christ and God's dwelling in the temple of the heart of good men. In men be dwells partially. They can hold but a small part of God's nature, and they do not give up the whole of their hearts for 1that. Christ is wholly filled with the whole of God. 2. 'l'his fact helps us to escape froll.i tLe id,_-a of two or three S<;pt1rate gods. It is the one infinite God who works in (Jff,11, 1-23.J THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 145

cte~tio~, and rules i!1 _heaven, and pleads with our spirits, and dwells fully in Christ, Chnst 1s perfectly D1vrno, because the one God dwells perfectly in him. 'fhus when we worship God and Christ we are not worshipping two beinl7s but the one God in Christ. Therefore, also, all that we see and know of Christ i; ~o much revelation of God. To be in sympathy with Christ is to be reconciled to God. II. GoD IB INCARNATE IN CHRIST. The fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ in a bodily way. "Tbo Word was made flesh." Some have thought to make this fact seem impossible by absurd representations, which go on the assumption that an infinite God cannot enter a finite being without ceasing to be infinite. How he can do so wo cannot understand. This is not a subject that admits of being rationalized. But dogmatic objectors may be reminded that it is their teaching which sets a limit to the infinite by proclaiming its inability to enter fully a finite being. Docs not the infinity of God involve, not the distribution of innumerable parts through all space, but presence of him wholly in every region of the universe? Why, then, cannot he manirest his presence in a peculiar way in one being? Moreover, if God, who is always infinite, can dwell in man at all, that fact is a mystery which seems to foreshado\v the greater mystery of his full dwelling in Christ. The humanity of Christ is real and pure and perfect humanity, and God who dwells in him is still perfect God. This is very different from the metamorphosis of a God into a man that is described in heathen mythologies. It is to be practically learnt from this Christian mystery (1) that Go, is now very near to us in a brother man; (2) that we can be raised to God and become one with Christ and God through Christ's oneness with us and God (John xvii. 23).-W. entries.title: COL 2:10
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Thefulness of humanity. I. WHERF.IN TIIE FULNESS OF HUMANITY CON- SISTS. St. Paul has been writing of the fnlness of the Godhead. He now turns hi~ thoughts to our poor, naked, hungry humanity, and he shows how thero is a complet.ion and a satisfaction that may be called our fulness, in some way corresponding t•> the fulness of God. 1. The full satisfaction of our wants. We are empty, hungry, and needy. We require pardon for sin; strength for trouble, temptation, and toil; light in darkness; innumerable graces for innumerable distresses. Our fulness must be tho quenching of the soul's thirst, the satisfaction of the aching void within. 2. The/all attainment of the pe1fection of humanity. We may have every known desire satisfied and may be full up to the measure of our present capacity, am! yet not have attaineJ to the fulness of humanity. Our capacity may be enlarged, new aspirations may bo inspired in us. To attain to the stature of the perfect m,rn, to be quite like Christ, is to reach our spirit's prime and to have onr human fulness. This will be a folness of knowledge, of goodness, of power for spiritual service. II. FROM WHAT THE FULNESS OF HUMANITY IS DERIVED. By the word .. fulness" St. Paul m~ans that which fills as well as that which is perfected in itself. Christ alone can fill and perfect us. 1. We must find the fztlness in Ghrist. Because he is filled with the fnlness of God ho is himself a perfected Man and the Source of the same grace for us. We have to learn, then, that to reach our fulucss we must have what is in Christ. Perfect humanity is not possible without God. When we become possessed by the Spirit of God we become true men. This true religious life does not make us less human; it perfects our humanity. Not by science, nor by learning, nor by energy in affairs of the world, nor by any purely human effort, though all these things have their missions, but through Christ-, we may attain the true ideal of humnnity. 2. JVe can attain to thisfulness by personal union witl1 Ghrist. \Ve :nust not simply learn the method from Christ, nor seek tho blessing as a. gift of his, but derive it from close, living fellowship with him. The secret is to be " in Christ," " rooted" as the tree by being rooted in the soil derives nourishment therefrom, an,! " builded up in him" as the temple stands firm when erected on a solid fouudation.-W. F. A.

entries.title: COL 2:16
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The righta of liberty. At first sight the advice of St. Paul to tbo Colossians, not to let any one interfere with their private judgment in regard to meats, days, etc., may seem to conflict with the principle of generosity laid down in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: "If meat maketh my brother to stumble, I will eat no flesh for evermore, that I make not my brother to stumble." Buts clo~c.r ~;,:aminat.iou 1>f the two cases will show that they differ essentially. COLOSSI ANS. L 116 THE EPISTLE TO THE CuLOSSIANS, [oH. II, 1-23,

l. C-0NSIDERATION FOR THE SCRUPLES OF THE WEAK MUST DE DISTINGUISIIED FROM YIELDING TO THE TYRANNY OF THE DIGOTED. 1. It is weak brethren whom St. Paul spares in his Epi~tle ~o the Corinthians. . Dut, when writing to the Colossians, he ~ui no such people m new, but a very different class-censorious, birroted enemies of Christian liberty. Such men should be firmly opposed. 2. In thi fol"mer case St. Paul was considering the condition of the weak hrethren whom he wished to save from. .,tumbling. In the present instance no such consideration is called for. It is not their imperfections that the Colossians are to deal gently with, but the interference of r.roublesome people who will not stumble the less because they have their own way in unlawful tyranny. 3. In the former case the concession was 1,•oluntary. St. Paul spoke of his own action, freely adopted. Here, however, it is not a case of generous concession on the part of the more liberal, but one of tyrannical assumption on that of the more bigoted. This case may be illustrated by St. Paul's vigorous resistance to the attempts that were made by certain professed Christians at Jerusalem to compel the circumcision of Titus (Gal. ii. 3-5). II. 1T IS OUR POSITIVE DUTY TO MAINTAIN THE RIGHTS OF LIBERTY, We may be tempted to yield out of love of peace, or from an unselfish feeling of generosity. But this is more than a mistake; it is a fault. Several reasons concur to forbid us to yield to the judgment of the more bigoted in these matters. 1. The claims of truth. If we believe that our position is the right one, to renounce it will be to sacrifice truth. In maintaining our own rights in this instance we are npholding great principles. 2. The honour of Christ. If we renounce the freer, larger gospel for a cramped and mutilated one, we dishonour the Name of Christ. For his sake the broad generosity and liberal spirituality of Christianity must be maintained. 3. The perfoi·mance of cur own duty. We cannot serve God so well when our liberty is fettered by the interference of the narrower-minded a.s when we follow our own conscience without such restraints. 4. The good of our fellow-men. By permitting encroachments on the liberty of the gospel, we narrow the privileges which we should be offering to our fellow-men. We are put in trust of the gospel Let us beware of traitorous efforts to rob it of its richest treasures (Gal. ii. 5). Nevertheless, let ns take home to ourselves a further lesson, and beware of judging our brother Christians in regard to eabbath observance and other external habits either way-on the one hand, for too strict formalism in our eyes; or, on the other hand, for too free behaviour, " To his own Lord he standeth or falleth" (Rom, xiv. 4).-W. F. A.

entries.title: COL 2:23
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The fai1ure of asceticism. L ASCETICISM IS FASCINATING. It is remarkable to observe how readily the severest devotees of asceticism have found followers when the performance of the simpler duties of Christian charity has been left neglected. A :-t. Simeon, scorched by the blazing sun of noonday and chilledi by the cruel frosts of night on his pillar in the desert, finds enthusiastic imitators who would be slow in following Christ's lowly work of going about to clo good to his brethren. 1. Asceticism follows the notion that since indulgence of the lower natu1·e is sinful, that nature itself must be evil. In this notion is the explanation of the inclination of many of the best men to asceticism. 2. Asceticism appears to be the readiest way of preventing sins of the flesh. It seems as though the flesh could not be tamed; therefore it is caged, chained, crushed, slain. 3. Asceticism aspires to the rare holiness of excessive purity. Thus, while professing humility, it is often guilty of great pride. 4. Asceticism is within our own power and is dependent on our own will. It is will-worship. It is not the submission of our will to the will of God, but the assertion of our will though in self-restraint. 'l'his is much easier and requires less humility and faith than opiritual obedience. 5. Asceticism is effective as a display of holiness. It would be unjust to accuse all ascetics of playing for the admiration of the world. But it is impossible to doubt that the Church has had her hypocrites, who "disfigure their faces, that they may be seen of men to fast." II. ASCETICISM FAILS IN ITS PilOFESBED OBJECT. Not only can it be accused of ~elling up a false ideal; it does not even realize that ideal. Even from its own point of view it must be regarded as a monstrous failure. It is "not of any value against the indulgPnce of the flesh." History gives horrible proofs of this fearful fact. 'l'hc,

monasteries of the Midclle Ages were hotbeds of vie<-'. No more immoral men could be found among the libertines of gay society than the celibate priests, bishops, and popes of the gre11t age of professed asceticism. Literature confirms the testimony of history. '!'he writings of ascetics are too commonly tainted with an unwholesomc flavour. Subjects which to ordinary men would call up no impurc as2ociations arc suggestive of corrupt ideas to these saints. The most sacred relations of life arc degraded by thc ascetic handling of them. Marriage is regarded only iu its lowest character, and id lowered by being so treated. 'l'he finger of tlw monk leaves an unclean mark on the purest page of domestic life. This is what might be expected. 1. Asceticism is unnatural. Outraged nature avenges herself on the insult that is put upon her in th0 distortion of her life. 2. Asceticism is opposed to the sympathies of Christ. lie sanctioned the ties of domestic life and sanctionetl its joys. 3. Asceticism does not touch the seat of sin. 'l'his is not in the body. It is in the soul. So long as the heart is corrupt, no bodily restraints will make the life holy. 'l'he ascetic, like the Pharisee, cleanses only the outside of the cup. The stream must be cleansed at the fountain. 'l'he heart must bo renewed. Then it will be found that "to the pme all things are pure."-W. F. A.
