-Sect. 7. The true Christian life. From above only can we be raised. There is no salvation in mere antipathy. Disgust at the vanities of life, repulsion from earthly things, will of itself never lift us beyond them; it needs tho superior influence of heavenly things to do that.. This the Colossian errorists did not rightly understand; or they could not have made ceremonial purifications and bodily austerities the way of holiness, the means of reaching spiritual perfection. "'!'ouch not, taste not" (eh. ii. 20, 21),-tbese were their chief commandments. The physical life was their great aversion, aud to reduce and harass it wr.s the leading object of their moral endeavours. In the last two sections of his letter (eh. ii. 8-23) the apostlo has denounced t!Jeir system as false and mischievous, to be. rejected by Christian believers, since it is not according to Christ, but is, in spite of its high pretensions, essentially base and earthly. He now proceeds, by way of command and appeal, to delineate the true Christian character, the working of Christian principles of life, as contrasted with the rnystico--ceremonial and ascetic ideal of the Gnosticizing teachers. The Christian be describes is one whose "life is Christ "-a life derived from, and animated and governed by, "the Lord from heaven," and not by" the tradition of men and the rudiments of the world"-" the things upon the earth" (comp. John vi. 31-33, 41, 42, 47-59). I. Tim HIDDEN LIFE. (Vers. 1-4.) 1. The vital spring of a practical Christian lifo is personal union with Ghrist. "Ye were raised with Ghrist; your life is hid with Ghrist; ye shall be manifested with him; Christ is your life" (vers. 1-4). (1) Not only must the principle of a perfect and all-sufficing life for men be heavenly; it must be personal. "We live by admiration, hope, and love." .All really commanding and ~overeign influences acting on human nature contain a personal element. We cannot sustain ourseh-es on abstract laws, or great universal ideas, or" streams of tendoncy;" on a " something not ourselves that makes for" this or that; on formulas or generalizations of any kind, however grand and comprehensive, however true and useful in their place. In spite of all plaw;ible argument and elegant raillery, and underneath the cbauging modes and fashions of polite or scientific thought, it yet remains a constitutional and fixed 11ecessity of the human soul to find iu that which is higher tbau itself Some Onll to reverence and to obey. .Against this necessity, ~\.lexnnclrine theosophy and :modern ~cepticism equally contend in vain. Men want a living God, Ono who lcnows, who loves and hates, who wills and acts-a just God and a Saviour; and they will not have these terms explained away. We am not to be frightcnetl or discomposed by being 011, w. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 159

told that onr GoJ is" a magnified, nou-natural Man," and that our notions are grossly "anthropomorphic." We cannot believe that the Power which is infinitely greater than ourselves is less than a Person. "That which may be known of God is" so far 'manifest in ourselves" (Rom. i. 19), that what we find there of highest aud most distinctive-in thought, in will, iu affection, in moral self-consciousness-must needs be an index, the surest and directest that reason furnishes (for it is given by the very being of reasou itself), to the nature of that Power which made and governs us. To this first principle wo are compelled to hold, notwith~tanding the metaphysical difficulties old as human thought, which surround those indications----<lifficulties which meet every interpretation of them alike. The Incarnation has confirmed, while it has corrected, this universal assumption. In the mind of Christ, in the love of Christ, in the holy will that says," Father, I will . . . nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt" (John xvii. 24; Mark xiv. 36), we behold in its pnrest and most satisfying form that which may be known of God, and the relations in which as men we stand thereto. How much God is beyond and behind all that, we cannot guess; but he is all that, he is nothing less than, nothing different from, that which we see" in the face of Jesus Christ" (eh. i. 15; 2 Cor. iv. 4; John i. 18). (2) The man whose" life is hid with Christ" is "joined in one spirit" (1 Cor. vi. 17)-in a sympathy of love and fellowship of thought and aim the most complete of which the human soul is capablo--wit.h a living Person in heaven. He is" joined to the Lord," who has" all authority in heaven and in earth" (eh. i. 13, 15, 18; Rom. xiv. 9; John xvii. 2; Matt. xxviii. 18; Rev. i. 5), with the wisdom that touches on the one side the resources of omniscience and on the other the everyday experience of human infirmity and suffering (eh. ii. 3; 1 Cor. i. 2!; John ii. 25; xvi. 30; Matt. xi. 27; Heb. ii. 17, 18; iv.15; Rev. ii. 23), and the claims on our devotion of One who "loved us and gave himself for us" (eh. i. 14-, 20---22; Eph. ii. 13, 14; Gal. ii. 20; 2 Cor. viii. 9; John x. 15; xv. 13; Rev. i. 5; v. 12). In him we recognize personal being, personal worth, and personal rights in relation to ourselves, the highest conceivable both in kind and degree. To have a life hid wit.'i Christ is to dwell in an inward communion of heart with One whom we can perfectly trust, perfectly love, and absolutely obey. (3) This is life indeed (John vi. 53; 1 John v. 12). This fellowship supplies, as nothing else can do in the nature of thing~, the means of moral culture, the influences by which men may be "redeeILed from all iniquity" (Titus ii. 14; Gal. i. 4; John xv. 3), by which a Divine character is formed in the soul (Gal. iv. 19) and it is trained for the life of heaven (eh. i. 27; Phil. i. 6). 'l'he Christian life is nothing less the.n a Divine friendship (Johu xv. 12- 15; Isa. xii. 8 ; Exod. xxxiii. 11 ; Gen. v. 24 ; xviii. 17). To gain this life one may gladly consent to die to aUthat is alien from the life of Christ (ver. 3; eh. ii. 11, 20; Phil. iii. 7-12; Rom. vi. 2, 11; vii. 4-6). 2. A true union with Christ lifts 6ur aims above this world. "Ye were raised with Christ, see!,·, mind, the things above, where Christ is, for (from the things on the earth) ye died" (vers. 1--3). Christ has gone to heaven, and he is our Life. Thither he has carried with him our desires and hopes (Phil. i. 23; 2 Cor. v. 6-8). To be where he is, is the deepest longing of the Christian heart; and its attainment is the supreme reward of faithful service (John xii. 26; xiv. 1-6; Rev. iii. 21; xiv. 4). Heaven is the Christian's home, because he is there, .And he has gone thither, not simply as to " the place where he was before" (John vi. 62), and to which he properly belongs (John iii. 13), hut as our "Fore- runner" (Heb. vi. 20), the "Firstborn among many brethreu" (eh. i. 18; Rom. viii. 29). Heaven is the goal which he has marked out for his followers, the " Father's house," the uative city of all the members of his body, the Church (Eph. i. 18-23; Phil. iii. 20; John xiv. 2; Heb. xi. 10, 13-16). "'l'he prize of our high calling" ( Tiis /iv., Kll.~u,.,s, "that calls us above ") is bestowed at " the resurrection of the dead" (Phil. iii. 9-21). (1) As workmen, as tradesmen, as citizens, our aims terminate with the thin!Js upon the earth; as Christians, we seek the things that a.re above. 'l'he present in our view is the seed-time, the training school for the immortal future; and its valtHJ lies in what it leads to rather than in ,what it is. Our present spiritual life, the knowledge of Christ and communion with him wo now enjoy, is but "the earnest of our inheritauce," "the firstfruits of the Spirit" (Eph. i. 14; Rom. viii. 23; Phil. iii. 12-14). "By" this "hope we are ~aved" (Rom. viii. 17-25); for this, most of all, do we give thanks (eh. i. 3-5, 23; Phil. i. 6; 1 Cor. i. 7, 8; 1 Pet, i. 3-7 comp. homiletics, sect, 1, 'l'HE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cu. m. 1-25,

J T. 1 (3).) (2) Yet this minding of the things above involves no dispamgement of the ,ntcre.sts_ and claims of secular life. For this pre~ent is the pathway to that future. Jlow seriously important, how carefully to bo studied and appraised how dili(Tently to he improved, are the "few things" of onr earthly stewardship, if by a right "manage- ment of them we may become "lords" of the "many things" of the everlasting habitations (Matt.. xxv. 14-30; Luke xvi. 9-12; 1 Cor. vii. 31) ! But we must keep our thoughts and aims above the world, taking care not to be overcharged ,vith "cares and plrasures of this lifo" (Luke viii. 14; xxi. 34), "declaring plainly that we seek a country" (Hcb. xi. 14), turning earth at every step into" a scale to heaven," makin"' Christ all in all in family and social life, in business and in politics. 3. The Christia~ life -is, therefore, in its essence a mystery. "Your life is hid" (ver. 3). (1) "The world knoweth us not" (1 John iii. 1). As to the life of the children of this world, and of the Christian man so far as he is a man of the world, everything is plain. Tho principles and motives of the man of business, the politician, or the scientist are easily stated and generally intelligible. And the iufluences which govern the depraved, ungodly man are all too plain; " the works of the flesh are manifest" (Gal. v. 19). Bu~ the man whose "citize1rship is in heaven," who "walks by faith, not by sight," who is" looking for and basting unto the coming or the day of God," whose life it is to love and serve a Master who was c111cified eighteen hundred years ago, and whom he expects to see only after he himself is dead,-such a person is an enigma to natural men born only of this world; he is "judged of uo man" (1-Cor. ii. 14, 15). Political economy, experimental psychology with its "analysis of the human mind," fail to account for him; and the philosopher haply will pass him by as a pretence or an abnormity. He is like a planet deflected from its course by some unknown body out of telescopic reach, whose magnitude and position it is impossible scientifically to determine. (2) Our life is hidden, because he who is our Life is hidden. "Ye see me no more," said Jesus ; and aga.in, " The world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also" (John xn. 10; xiv. 19). "Tl1erefo1·e the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not" (1 John iii. 1). Our life is wrapped up in One" whom we have not seen" (1 Pet. i 8, 9), with whom we can have no kind of sensible corn• munication; in a Ch1ist who indeed was "manifested in the flesh," but was scornfully disbelieved and put to death, "justified" only "in the Spirit," seen only" of angels" (1 Tim. iii 16). A mystery to the world, the Christian life is a mystery also to its possessor as respects the methods by which it is bestowed and sustained on God's part. "'l'be things of God none knoweth, save the Spirit of God," and though we receive this Spirit, "we know" but "in part" his operations (1 Cor. ii. 11 ; xiii. 12). "Thou hearest the mice thereof"-that is all (John iii. 8). There is a supernatural something that defies analysis and measurement in the experience of every Christian-a Divine life as distinct from the natural soul-life, as that is from mere animal vitality; and this is just the sovereign creative factor of bis religion, tho principle of his new birth and new manhood: his life is" hid in God." But while this life itself is hidden, itsfruits are not (ver. 5--ch. iv. 6; Eph. v. 8-14; Phil. ii. 15, 16; Titus ii. 11, 12; Matt. v.14-16; John xiii. 35; 1 Pet. ii. 9, 12, 15; iii. 1, 2, 15, 16). 4. But the mystery of the Christian life is to have its revelation. "When Christ shall be manifested, then shall ye also be manife.,terl with him, in glory" (ver. 4). This riddle of life must be solved (1 Cor. xiii. 12, R.V. margin); "the things shaken" must be removed," that tho things unshaken may remain" (Heb. xii. 27); appearance must give place to reality; "morlality" must be" swallowed up of life;" God has" wrought us for this very thing" (2 Cor. v. 4, 5). Fai1h is the virtue of education, and must have its reward in sight; if there is nothina to be seen, then 1hose are not" blessed," but only mistaken, "who have not seen ~nd yet have believed" (John xx. 21:i). Hope must be crowned with fruition, or it will "put us to shame" (Rom. v. 5). And love, content now _to" see him not" (1 Pet. i. 8), is only so content on the assurance that "we shall see him even as he iB" (1 John iii. 3; Acts i. 11; John xiv. 3). (1) Christ shall be manifested. He has pledged himself, both to his friends and to his foes, to return (John xiv. 3; Matt, xxvi. G:1, 64). That pledge be gave in the most public and solemn manner possible, in n~serli<m of his Dirine sonship and Mcssiahship. His second coming is tho goal of New 'l'estanwnt prophecy, and of the Church's hope and longin:.( through the ages (Matt. xxv. 19, 21; Acts iii. 21 ; xvii, 31; 1 '!'hess, i,v. 14-18; l'hil. iii. 20; 'ritus ii, 13; l:Ieb. CII, III, 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 161

ix. 28; 1 Pet, i. 7; 1 John ii. 28; Rev. i. 7; xxii. 20, etc.). It is the consnmmation of human history, the denouement of the great time-drama," the one far-off Divine event, to which the whole creation moves." But he waits till "the gospel of the kinrrdom is preached to nil the nations,"" till his enemies be made his footstool," till" the harvest of the earth is ripe," till the hour has struck appointed in the Father's eternal counsels (Mar1!: xiii. 10, 32; Heb. x. 12, 13; Rev. xiv. 15, 18). Then be will appear in that glory (Matt. xxv. 31; xxvi. 64; 'l'itus ii. 13), something of which the three saw "in the holy mount" (2 Pet. i. 16-18), which dying Stephen beheld as he fell asleep, and Saul of Tarsus as he journeyed to Damascus, and John in Patmos (Acts vii. 56; ix. 3-6; Rev. i. 13-18); of which in entering upon his earthly estate he had "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" (Phil. ii. 6, 7). " We shall see him even as he is-the Lord of glory" (1 John iii. 3; Jas. ii.1). (2) Christ's glory his mints will share. They, too, will be man,;fested. 'rhere will be an "unveiling of the sons of God" (Ilom. viii. 18-25). "In this tabernacle we do gro,rn, being burdened" (2 Cor. v. 4), Our life is "cribbed, cabined, and confined." The body, virtually "clead because of sin," oppresses and conceals, while it contains, the immortal "spirit, which is life because of righteousness" (Rom. viii. 10, 11). "Now we see through a glass, darkly" (1 Cor. xiii. 12). We move about as if under a heavy, muffling cloak. "We are spirits in prison, able only to make signals to each other." But we shall then enjoy "the liberty of the glory of the children of God" (Rom. viii. 21). This "natural body" will become a "spiritual body," in which the spirit will be perfectly expressed and for ever at home, (3) Then Christ's glory will be manifest in us. He will be" glorified in his saints," and they glorified in him (2 Thess. i.10; Ps. xc. 16, 17). Like some sculptor's work, prepared in concealment and with long labour, carved out of the rough, unshapely block by many a painful stroke of hammer and of chisel, till the artist's glorious ideal is wrought out, and on some public day the finished master-piece is at last unveiled; so the man, perfect fo Ohrist, will be "presented faultless before the pre• sence of bis glory with exceeding joy" (eh. i. 22, 28; Jude 24). II. 'l'HE DEATH OF 'l'HE OLD SELF. (Vers. 5-9.) lmpurity, greed, malir.e, falsehood,- these are the leading features of the former life of sin which the apostle represents his readers as having followed before they became Christians. He does not, of course, charge all of them equally and alike with these offences. But then, as now, these four types of vice were prevalent amongst the great mass of ungodly men (ver. 7; 1 C.:.r. vi. 9-11). Such statements, when applied to men living under the influences of Christian society, must be applied with discrimination, and in the light of our Lord'8 teaching addressed to the moral Jews in Matt. v. 17--48, etc. These vices are native to the soil of the human . heart (Mark vii. 20-23). By habitual practice they take possession of the man, so that his "members" are made "slaves to uncleanness and iniquity" (Rom. vi. 19; John viii. 34), and his body becomes a "body of sin" and "of death" (Rom. vi. 6; vii. 23-25; eh. ii. 11). 'l'hey become virtually his "members that are upon the earth" (ver. 5). Under tho sway of sensual appetite and worldly desire, ungoverned by any influence from "the things above," hi~ person becomes more and more completely an incarnation of sin (Hom. vii. Ii, 20, 23). These "members," then, individually and collectively, must be" put to death;" this" body of the flesh," as a" body of sin," must be" stripped off" and" done away" (eh. ii. 11; Rom, vi. 6). Christ cannot dwell in the soul whilo "sin reigns in the mortal body'' (Rom. vi. 12). He bas no "concord with Belia!," or with Mammon (2 Cor. vi. 15; Matt. vi. 24). "The old man" must be "so buried, that tho new man may be raised up" in us (comp. Epb. iv.17-24). 1. Unchast-ity was the most conspicuous sin of the Gentile world in which St. Paul moved. There it prevailed in the groijsest and most Hhameless forms; and its prevalence is a fearful warning, as ho points out (Rom. i. 18-27), of the outcome of a godless civilization, The society of the populous Greek cities of that day was one in which "fornication, uncleanness, lustful passion, evil desire" (var. 5), had free course, and its moral condition was only less abandoned than the "reeking rottenness" of Sodom and Gomorrha. Adultery, indeed, was condemned as a civil crime by pagan moralists; but fornication they held, as a rnle, to bo an innocent and almost a necessary thing. It was in writing to Corinth, perhaps the most licentious city in that licentious age, that the apostle launched his sternest and most vehement interdict against this crime, which is a moral leprosy an,l 1w~Li- OOLOSSIANB~ I:; 1G2 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [orr. m. 1-25.

lc,nce. There he marks it out as peculiar from all other sins in being a sin against a man's own body, and an especial insult and outrage to the Holy Spirit who claims the lrnman body for his temple (1 Cor. vi. 13-20: comp. 1 'l'hess. iv. 2-8). Thero are too many evidences in the state of modern society, both in high quarters and in low, that as Christian sentiment grows weak and religious faith dies down, in the same proportion the perversion of the sexual passions follows, with its invariable result in the relaxation of moral fibre, the destruction of social confidence, and the physical decay of the corrupted race. Man begins by denying his Maker, and ends by degrading himself, '!'here aro times and places where plain speaking on this subject is needful, and no prudery or sentimental delicacy should prevent it. The tempted must bo warned; the guilty rebuked; bodily self-respect must be taught in good time. 'fho pure will know how to do this, like the apostle himself and like his Master, "in all purity." When once inward chastity has been lost and uncleanness spots the soul, the stain is not easily effaced. Evils of this kind flourish in the dark and love to be ignored. 2. Covetous- ness is idolatry. (Ver. 5.) It is, obviously nnd directly, "worshipping and serving the creature" (Rom. i 25). While it appears to be self-love, it is really the sacrifice of lSelf to the world, offered at the shrine of wealth, or fame, or pleasure. The man seeks to gain power over other men or things; but if this becomes hi8 supreme desire, or if he seeks to attain it by evil means, then from that moment the object of his guilty 1mrsuit gains power over hiin, and begins to entangle and enslave him (John viii. 34; Hom. vii. 23). His passion becomes his tyrant, his ambition an insanity, his pursuit of pleasure an infatuation. Even the thirst for knowledge, tho noblest of natural desires, may grow into a selfish greed, jealous and grasping, eating out the best affections, and producing an accomplished scholar, a master of science, void of all goodness of heart and human worth. All creaturely things, regarded out of God, are but" passing shows" (,i'5.. ~ci, idols) of the absolute and enduring goodness that belongs to him (Matt. xix. 17). The homage rendered to them-whether by the savage to his fetish, by the civilized worldling to his wealth or rank, or by the scientist to his laws and furces of nature-is idolatry, the worshipping of shams and shows, in so far as it is a departing from the living God (Heb. iii. 12; Exod. xx. 3; Isa. xliii. 10; 1 Cor. viii 4--6). .And with life thus perverted at its fountain-bead, it becomes a. mere vanity and vexation of spirit. 3. Malice is universally denounced. Moralists of all schools and all ages agree in proscribing this vice, though in little else. 'l'he malicious man is instinctively dreaded; he is a peril to every one. Sins of malice and of falsehood strike directly at the existence of society, while the two former classes of offence threaten it more gradu..1.lly and indirectly. (1) Yet it can scarcely be denied thnt unger, wrath, malice, railing, shameful speaking, are, to a large extent, congenital to human nature. It is true tbat there is an instinctive benevolence, a fellow-feeling for one's kind, only exceptionally wanting; but at the same time there exists a proclivity, that is often terribly strong even in its earliest manifcstntions, in the opposite direction. "Cain was of that wicked one, nnd slew his brother; . . . because his own works were cvi~ and his brother's 1ighteous" (1 John iii. 12). It is a. weak and fatal delusion to rely on natural benevolence as an effective and commanding moral force, a stable foundation for a system of practical ethics. Nor is it possible in the naturo of things that cnliahtened self-interest or any combination of prudential or utilitarian considera.- 1 ions sho~ld ever tench men to love their neighbours as themselves, or should succeed in suppressin"0 ra(Te and jealousy and the murderous passions slumberiug in the blood of the race. W e° must be "taught of God to love one another" (1 'l'hess. iv. 9; see 1 John ii 7-11; iii. 13-24; iv. 7-21). (2) The love of Christ will at last subdue the fratricidal passions of ma.nkind, will "make wars to cease unto the ends of the earth ; ~ and one day will brin~ men of the most distant climes and hostile i~t.erests to clasp each other's hands and look into each other's eyes and say," Beloved, 1I God so loved us, we ought also to love one another!" Hero lies the only hope of the fraternization of mankind. 4. If impurity dishonours the body, falsehood dishonours the mind. This ~in at once decrrades the man, wrongs by deceiving his fellow, and insults his God, the ever-present \Vitness and Guardian of truth (Acts v. 4; Rom. iL 1; 1 'l'hess. ii. 5; Ps. cxx.xix. 4; Jer. v. 3). Here the apostle points out (1) its inconsistency with the Chrislian character of the man (vers. 9, 10); and (2) its contradiction to the Christian view of society (ver. 11). Similarly in Epb, iv. 25; ".l<'o,r we are ~embers one of OH, III, 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 163

11nother." For II man to deceive his neighbour by word or deed, is as if the eyes should conspire to trick the ear or misguide the band. The ancients condemned falsehood between men of the same community, but generally regarded it as a lawful weapon to use against enemies or strangers; although the Stoics, with their wider views of humanity, taught on this point, as on others, a higher morality. The "Greek" might deceive the "barbarian," the "bondman" might lie to his master, and have no sense of moral wrong. And so it bas been too commonly in the dealing of servants or schoolboys with their masters, of civilized men with savages, of libertines in their conduct towards the other sex. Witness the immoral maxim, "All's fair in love and war." One chief cause of deceit would be removed if men would understand that the instinct of honour which bids them be truthful to their equals and comrades, require~ the same honesty in dealing with every man as man. The Christian acts on this principle; he will not in any sense "hold the faith of our Lord Jesus with respect o' persons" (Jas. ii. 1). (a) Many men who would resist the temptation to utter a lie in so many words, will silently act it; especially iu a continued course of action, where the deception lies not in any single definite act, but in the general construction which they lead others to put on their proceedings. Such deception is no less culpable in itself, and as a rule still more disastrous in its effects, than a palpable lie. (b) And again, men find it easy to lie collectively who would not do so singly. Though men of probity in their private affairs, they will put their hands to documents, they will consent with others to acls, which they know to bo misleading, or, at least, which they do not know to be true. And now that business is becoming more anu more a matter of "limited liability," the perils of divided respousibility in this direction should be well understood. 5. "Because of all these things God's anger is coming on the sons of disobedience" (ver. 6). Every act or thought of any of these kinds is a disobeaience, a breach of "the holy and just and good Law" under which man was first created in his Maker•~ image (ver. 10). This "Law worketh out wrath," inexorably and perpetually, against "every soul of man that doeth evil" (Rom. ii. 9; iv. 15). And that unger of God is coming (Isa. xxx. 27, 28). 'l'here is a day appointed for its "revelation" (Rom. ii. 5, 16; Mai. iv. 1), even as for "the manifestation of the sons of God" (ver. 4; Rom. viii. 19). It is already "revealed from heaven" (Rom. i. 18), aud ~ives forewarning of its advent in many a personal and public calamity (Isa. xxvi. D; :Mai. iii. 5; Mntt. xxiv. 3-42; 1 Cor. v. 3-5; xi. 30-32). On every account, the Christian must have done with the old lifo of sin. He sees it to bo incompatible with fellowship with Christ, to be hateful to God, to be ruinous to himself and tu his fellowmen. No return to it, no renewal of it, no dallying or temporizing with it in any kind or degree, can be tolerated. It must die if lie is to live. III. Till!: UNITY OF MANKIND IN CHRIST. (Vers.10, 11.) This truth belonged, at least in St. Paul's time, to the more advanced Christian knowledge, "unto which" the believer was "being renewed" (ver. 10); and the Church still comes far short of its full apprehension. 1. The gospel of Christ reveals the spiritual unity of mankind. 'l'o make this known was a part of the apostle's mission, and of the special "mystery Goel" entrusted to him ( eh. i. 25-28; Eph. iii. 1-G; Rom. iii. D-30; xv. 5- 12). Its manifestation, and the consequent "breaking down of tho middle wall of pnrtition" (Eph. ii. 14), were necessary to II complete Christian virtue, the propel' virtue of man as man, caJTied out in all his relations to God ancl to his fellows; and fur tue regeneration of human society, t.he salvation of the world. There was a preparation for this belief in the breaking down of the old nations into tho unity of the Roman empire, in the decay of local and ancestral relil!:ions, nnd in the advance of philosophy from the narrower and more political ethics of Plato and Aristotle to the moral system of tho Stoics, which wns at once more inward and more humane. But there was wantincr that conception of a living, Divine centre of the human race, given in Christ, which alone could make the sentiment of universal humanity a creative, organic force. 2. This unity has been realized in the Christian Church. It appears in the beautiful 8implicity of its childlike beginning, in the communism of the infant Church ot' Jerusalem (Acts ii, 44-47). It was eet forth in e. larger and fuller way by tho Apostle Pa.ul in addressing the mixod Churches of the great cities where ho laboured; aud was actually put into practice there in a goou degree. Jew and Greek (Gal. ii. 12), rich anu poo1· (1 Cur. xi, 20-22; the exception prov/!6 the rule: comp. Jas. ii. 1-4), 164 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [oH. III, 1-25.

master and slave (Phi\em. 16, 17), met at the same table of the Lord, mingled as eqnale in the same Christian society, distinguished only by the measure of\, grace" and "spiritual gifts" bestowed on each (Roru. xii. 6; 1 Cor. xii. 7-11). And the records of the :first three Christian centuries show bow faithfully, on the whole, this principle was maintained, and how nobly the Church held herself superior to temporal distinctioue of wealth and rank. Far indeed has she subsequently departed from this rule; and 'lost bow much thereby in spiritual dignity and power I We admire it now as a ; proof of special humility if the titled or cultured man forgets amongst Christian brethren his worldly eminence; if the employer of labour is glad to sit at the feet of his workman, when that workman, as may often be the case, is his spiritual superior; if the wealthy contributor to a Church fund does not expect, on that account, to dictate in its management. 3. The Church is destined to gather mankind into a spiritual commonwealth. In it there is to be no" strife as to who shall be greatest;" but in humility and self-for~ctfulness "the greater shall be as the younger, and the chief as he that doth serve" (Luke xxii. 24-26). There "all arc brethren, with one Master even Christ" (Matt. xxiii. 8-12). All authority and office are derived from him, and attested by bis Spirit in his people (1 Cor. xii. 1-11; Acts i. 24; xiii. 1-4; Gal. i. 1; John xx. 21). The Church is his body, complete in him-a unity in itself and in its action, because in every limb it draws its life and gets its direction from the Head. And as the Church becomes a greater and more pervasive power in the world, the spiritual brotherhood it creates will work appeasingly on the "wars and fightings," on the aristocratic exclusiveaess and haughtiness, the democratic bitterness and jealousy, the invincible prejudices, the clashing interests, by which society is distracted and its bonds are strained almost to rending, and the nations are kept in arms and burled repeatedly against ea.eh other in deadly conflict. When mankind recovers its unity in him in whom it was created and redeemed, when it is reconciled to God and bows its every knee" at the name of Jesus,"-then at last there will be" peace on earth." Where " Christ is all and ia all " antipathy must cease. IV. 'l'HE NEW CHRlSTIAN CHARACTER. (V ers. 12-17.) We have traced the principle of the Christian life in its inner ground and aim, as "bid with Christ" and seekiag its J,ome in heaven (vers. 1-4); in its uncompromising and mortal warfare with the old life of sin (vers. 5-9); in its prnpose to form a new humanity in the individual soul, and in the world at large (vers. 10, 11). We are now to follow its practical working, w see how the "new man " is to show himself in a new habit and style of living, how the" hidden life" is to blossom out into its fragrance and beauty, and its" celestial fruit" to "grow on earthly ground." We note that the Christian character is one deriv~d from God and that refers to God in everything. It is as " God's elect, his J,oly and beloved ones" (ver. 12), that we are called to assume the new habits of Christian grace and goodaess. Knowing what the Divine Father is, and what he has done for us (eh. i. 12-14), and what be intends us to be (Epb. i. 4-6), sensible of our filial relation to him (Rom. viii. 15-17; Gal. iv. 1-7; 1 John iii. 1, 2), loyally embracing his will (Rom. vi. 22) and seeking to be conformed to his nature as that is translated for us into" the image of bis Son" (Rom. viii. 29; 2 Pet. i. 4; 1 John iv. 17), we shall be "holy in all manner of conversation." But God is known to us through Christ. And. therefore, in the formation of the Christian character "Christ is all and in all" (ver. 13; 1 Cor. xi. 1; Rom. xv. 3; Phil. ii. 5; 1 Pet. ii. 22; 1 John ii. 6; John xiii. 15). It is nothing else than Ghrist formed in us (Gal, iv, 19). In the perfect Christian character, then: 1. Christ'sloverules. (Vers. 13, 14; 2 Cor. v.14; 1 John iii. i3; John xiii. 34-.) The tender heart of compassion, the gentle, sympathetic kindliness, the lowliness of mind, the uncomplaining meekness, the patient long-suffering, the forbearance and forgivingness (vers. 12, 13) of the Christian nature,-these centre in the all-perfect and all-perfecting grace of Christ-like love (1 Cor. xiii.; 1 John iv. 7- :n ; Rom. xiii. 9, 10). He in whose heart dwells the love of Christ cannot " shut up his compassion" from any within reach of help who need it (1 John iii.17); cannot be rude an<l ungracious, or hard and unforgiving (Eph. iv. 31, 32; 2 Cor. ii. 5-11); can- not be self-asserting, clamorous, overbearing (2 Cor. x. 1; Phil. ii. 6, R.V. margin; • Matt. xii. 19); cannot be passionate and resentful, irritable and fault-finding, obstinate in prejudice, intolerant of opposition. The love of Christ will assimilate his whole disposition and make it sweet, gracious, unselfish, loving, and lovable as that of an Oil, m. 1-25.) THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. 1G5

innocent child (Matt. xviii. 1-4). And the Christian man who in the spirit of this love can" possess his soul in patience" through all the strenuous endeavours and painful collisions and vexing wrongs of life, wears" the girdle of perfectness," and has attained the perfect Christian temper. 2, Christ's peace guards. (Ver. 15.) The Christian's faith and hope are assailed by a thousand enemies, Sometimes amid the common incidents of lire, sometimes in "the heavenly places" of his richest experience ancl most exalted communion with spiritual things (Eph. vi. 12)-sometimes brought about by open and palpable causes, sometimes by strange influences shadowing the inner life and coming we know not whence or how-sometimes through the ruggedness and gloom of his providential path, sometimes through mental perplexities and the chilling and confused intellectual atmosphere around him,-in any or in all of these ways "the trial or his faith" comes-comes, in one shape or other, to every man who has a faith worth trial. And then, whatever be the form which the assault takes or the quarter from which it is directed, he may find in " the peace of Christ" his strong tower of defence and harbour of refuge, His difficulties may Bot disappear under this influence; his doubts may not be at once dispelled; the conflict may still rage furiously around and within him; but he will be kept, the fortress of his heart will not be surrendered (1 Pet. i. 5; Phil. iv. 7). So long as "we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ," and" his love is shed abroad in our hearts" (Rom. v. 1-5), nothing can shake our essential faith or rob us of our immortal hope (Ps. xxvii.; xlvi. ; Luke xii. 32 ; Rev. i. 17). Neither sophistry (eh. ii. 4) nor threatening (eh. ii. 18) will take from us "the prize of our high calling." "One thing," at any rate," we know" (John ix. 25); and to it" we hani the witness in ourselves" (1 John v. 10), in" the peace of God, which passeth all understanding," "to which we were called," in the "new heart and right spirit" he has" put within" us, in the moral victory attained over selfand the world (1 John v. 4, 5): "we lcnow that we have passed from death unto life" (1 John iii. 14). And we safely infer that he " who has begun a good work in us" will carry it through (Phil. i. 6); that be will keep that which we commit to him, and "none shall pluck us out of his hand" (2 Tim. i. 12; John x. 27-29; Rom. viii. 31-39). So, uoitedly and thankfully, we "hold fast the beginning of our confidence, and tbe glorying of our hope, firm unto the end" (Heb. iii. 6, 14). 3. Christ's word inspires. (Ver. 16.) It is to" dwell in the heart richly "-to be the welcome visitant and constant inhabitant of the mind; to be listened to and diligently learned; to be cherished and pondered in inward meditation, not as an object of theoretic study only, but as the power which is to shape the character and guide the life of the Christian (Dent. vL 6-9; Ps. cxix. 105; John xvii. 17), as the soul's daily nutriment-the bread of God, "which strengtheneth man's heart,"" the word of eternal life" (Deut. viii. 3; Jer. xv.16; Matt. iv. 4; John vi. 63, 68). (1) This word gives all wisdom-best of God's gifts to man, which instructs the mind ancl prompts the tongue and guides the action of its possessor (eh. ii. 2, 3; iv. 5, 6). So furnished, every Christian (eh. i. 28) is able to minister something to his fellows of that which God has taught him by his own study of the Word and its practice in his experience of life (Matt. xiii. 52; Rom. xv. 14; 1 Cor. xiv. 31). Thus the members of the Church are able," in the meekness of wisdom," to" teach and admonish one another," "being knit together in love, and led into all the riches of the full assurance of the understanding, into the knowledge of the mystery of God" (eh. ii. 2). (2) And it stirs iu the heart an ardour of holy feeling that finds expression in Christian song. "The word of Christ," cherished in thought, kindles the emotions and wakens all the music of the soul. The early Christians were a singing people, for they were a cheerful and tha!Jkfu.l people. And subsequent revivals of religious life, as a rule, have been attended with fresh outbursts of sacred song (Ps. xl. 3). The singing of a people-its heartiness, and simplicity, and the care and pains taken in its cultivation, are a good test of their spiritual state. "Psalms, hymns, spiritual songs "-hymns old and new, narrative, didactic lyrical; in every measure and every tone or expression-songs of praise, of confcssio'n of wailin"' sorrow, of ecstatic joy; for the congregation, the household, or the private cha~ber ;-all find e. place in the diapason of the Church's music. 4. Christ's name hallows evei·ytldng. (Ver. 17.) Our eating and drinking-acts which seem the most ordinary aud purely physical, and quite remote from the interests and sentiments of the spiritual life-these are to be "sanctified by the word of God and prayer" (1 Tim. iv. 5), by the mention of Christ's name in thanksgiving to the Father, who through him sends 166 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [cu. m. 1-26.

us all life's blessings.. And _if o:ur me:e anim~l necessities or lifo nre capable of being t.hi~s hall?wcd, ~here 1s notlnng 1~ family relations, or secular employments, or social or crr1l duties, which may not receive and does not demand the same conseomtion. We may associate Christ with everything we do, doing all as his servants and under his eye, and in such a way that, by every part of our work, he may be glorified in us. And this will be a safeguard to the Christian man. Ir he is to do everythina in Christ's name, he must do nothing unworthy of that name, nothing with which he cannot ::ssociate it. Nowhere, in any company or on any business, must ho forget "either in word or deed," that this "worthy name" is the name which he bears, and whose honour is in his keeping. This is the seal that marks the true Church of Christ which every Christian wears upon his heart: " Let every one that nameth the na~ of the Lord depart from unrighteousness" (2 Tim. ii. 19).

entries.title: COL 3:18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
considerations bearing on the famlly and social constitution of life mlly be drawn from the teaching of this section. 1. We note that the apostle brings each of the three primary relationships of which he speaks into connection with "the Lord." The 'natural order of human life is grounded in C!hrist. If" all things were created and do consist in him " ( eh. i 16, 17), then, amongst the rest, this also and in chief. For man in his relation to the world around him is "the image of God," even as Christ is to the whole universe (1 Cor. :ri. 7; Jas. iii. 9; Gen. i. 26; Ps. viii.), And man is not a solitary individual; he is a social being, a race-unity. And those relations which are essential and fundamental to human society-marriage, sonship, service-have, most of nil, their spiritual type and creative ground in Christ. 'l'his is obvious in the case of the two latter relations; as to the first, see Eph. v. 22-32. 2. The intrinsic fitness of a right discharge of natural duties is affirmed in the first case (ver. 18), and implied in the other two. The apostle recognizes and appeals more than once to the sense of ethical propriety, that which "nature itself teaches" (1 Cor. xi. 14), which belongs to the universal conscience surviving in our nature though fallen and debased. All true sentiments of natural morality the Christian revelation reaffirms and supports with its dfectual sanctions, "as is fit in the Lord" (comp. Phil. iv. 8). Their consciousness of the right as the beautiful (.,.o 1<aJ\ov) was a sound and valuable element in the teaching· of the best Greek moralists. They regarded conduct as a work of art, in which graco and fitness were to be studied, and the perfection of an ideal beauty to be the aim of life, \Vhile men may have, as a rule, a stronger sense of the right, women better understand the fitting; and it is in regard to the place and duties of woman that St. Paul appeals to convictions of moral fitness and decorum (comp. 1 Cor. xi. 13; 1 Tim. ii. 10). 3. \Ve are taught, indirectly, to cherish a pleasant and cheerful temper in domestic life. Bitterness (ver. 19) and harshness, with the distrust and timidity which they engender ( ,·er. 21), and a sullen or constrained obedience (ver. 23), are forbidden; and these are the common elements of domestic unhappiness. \Vhere the husband is gentle, ancl the father tender though strict, and the master considerate, and the servants willing and honestly .1.nxious to please, there all goes well. Whatever storms may beat upon that house from without, there is peace and sunshine within, And this is "well-pleasin~ in the Lord." 4. The principle of authority is steadfastly maintained throughout, (Vers, 18, 20, :.:!2.) In every house that is not to be "divided against itself," there must be a single bead, a ruling will, a definite centre of power and direction. And that power God has placed, as a solemn trust, in the hands of the husband, father, mnster, who is in his prerogative within his own house an image of Christ in the Church (Eph. v. 23; eh. iv. 1), of God himself, the Father of men (Heb. xii. 9). This principle is the comer-stone of order in human society. Here is "pure religion breathing household laws" (\Vordsworth). L HusnAND AND WIFE. (Vera. 18, 19.) The marriage relation stands first, being 1he basis of the family, which again is the basis of society and of the community of mankind. "Ile which made them from the beginning, made them male and female" (Matt. xix. 4-6). Marriage is to be" had in honour among all" (Heb. xiii, 4; 1 Tim, iv. 1-3); and not merely the criminal act, but any impure word, thought, or look wbich offends against its sanctity, "defiles the man" from whom it proceeds, offends in an espc-2hl vay the Holy Spirit of God, and brings down his wrat.h upon the offender OH, III, 1-25,] THE EPIS'rLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. lGi

(Matt. v. 27, 28; Marie vii. 20-23; 1 Thess. iv. 3-8; 1 Gor. vi. U-20). 'l'hc degree of honour and reverence in which it is held in any society largely dete1mincs the clegree of soundness in its moral condition. Where the opposite vices prevail, whether secretly or openly practised, genern\ moral corruption and decay set in (see homiletics, sect. 7, II. 1). 1. On the one side, there is to be submission. 'l'he apostle says," Children, ... servants, obey" (vers. 20, 22); but not" Wives, obey your husbands:" "Be in subjection" (ver. 18) is a gentler and fitter term to use. Obedience implies a certain distance and inferiority that has no place here. There is something wrong on one side, or on both, when the husband gives formal orders to his wife. There should be such an intimacy of mutual understanding and sympathy between them, that they seem to have but one mind and will in all common matters. And while to that single mind the wife contributes the queenly influence of her insight and persuasion, she will feel and show that 1'esolve and direction belong to him and not to her. 'Jhe final responsibility-for the business of the house devolves on the husband, by the ordinance of God and by the nature of things, which are but two expressions of the snrne fact (1 Cor. xi. 3-15). It is his part to "rule well his own house" (1 Tim. iii. 4). 2. It was not so needful to say," "\Vives, love your husbands;" though the apostle once enjoins this, in speaking of "the younger women" in Titus ii. 4-. For failure on the wife's side in this respect is comparatively rare. But the man, full of business, often absent, and with his more exacting natnre, is more liable to fall into son:e disloyalty. He allows other company to become more agreeable to him; seeks amusements an,\ pursuits in which his wife cannot join; no longer makes her hiR confidante and the sharer of his inner life; and allows home to become little more to him than a selfish convenience. And with this selfishness and the uneasiness of conscience that attends it, there supervenes often an irritableness of temper that chafes over every domestic c,1ro or trouble, and makes no allowance for infirmities in others; that magnifies every trifling mistake or mishap into an injury, and ignores the wifo's patient affection and eagerness to please. How different is all this from the exalted ideal that St. Paul hold8 up to the Christian husband!-" Love your wife even as Christ loved the Church, a1,d gave himself for her" (Eph. v. 25). Bengel's shrewd and caustic remark on this rassa:re is too often verified: "There are many, who out of doors are civil and kind to all; when at home, towards their wives and children whom they have no need to fear, they freely practise secret bitterness." II. F ATRER AND CHILD. (Vers. 20, 21,) 1. From children, obedience to their parent~ in all things is required, and therefore in many things contrary to their inclination and opinions. Childhood means dependence and ignorance. H is only under the shelter of parental oversight that the incipient faculti€s and plastic nature of the child can be formed to the strength of judgment and firmness of character which will enable him to meet the tasks and the verils of adult life. And for this discipline to be cffcctivE', tho submission of the child must be absolute. Only when a parental commancl plainl_y contradicts the Law of God and violates the child's conscience, can any kind of disobedience bo justifiecl. In that case, obedience cannot be " well-pleasing in tho Lord." But even the worst of parents will rarely be found to have so little respect for the conscience of childhood as to enforce such nn injunction. The requirement addressed to the child presumes that the pn.rent exacts obedience. This is his inalien•• able prerogative. Instant, unmurmuring obedience should be macle the habit of the child's lifo, and as a law of nature to it. To have this understood from the first is tho simplest and easiest course. If the child be allowed, through passion or persistence, once successfully to rebel, a mischief is done not easily to be repaired. His own self-mastery, ancl tho senso of law and of duty which are to attend him through the whole of life, laro-ely rest on this basis of ingrnined obedience. For this purpose, children shoulrl. \Jo in their earliest years as much as possible under the direct influence of their parent,' presence and authority. The parental offico cannot be dischnrged by proxy. And there must be unity of parental administration, as well as h:umony between precept and practice, if a true nnd reverent obedience is to be possible. In no State was tho authority of the father (patria potestas) so strict and absolute as in ancient Ronw. Aud there can be little doubt that this stern maintenance of family discipline lar~dy helped to form the Roman character with its extraordinary vigour aud tenacity, and to !'reserve that rigid, firmly knit order anu devoted loyalty which were the secret of lGS TIIE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [en. 1u. 1-25.

Home's in,incible strength. 2. On the other hand, the father must beware lest his authority should wear a nredless aspect of severity. His ri.,.hteous clesire to "command his children and his household after him" (Gen. xviii. 19), and his anxious sense of responsibility, may occasion this, if not relieved by more genial influences. The inno- cent liveliness and the many unintended offences of childbood must not provoke him to ill temper. lie must learn by patience and tenderness to win the child's affection and open-hearted trust, without impairing its submissive reverence. A mechanical, unsym- pathetic ~trictness, or an angry and unequal discipline, will fatally alienate the sensitive heart of the child, which in that case either sinks down into a dull, spiritless apathy, or prepaT'!'.s for a passionate revolt when the hour of its strength shall come. Too often those most anxious to commend religion to their children have made it odious by presenting it in forms unintelligible to the young mind, and associating it with tasks unsuited to its powers, and burdens that it found "grievous to be borne." As the child should find in the child Jesus its pattern, and model (Luke ii. 40-52). so the parent should seek to be to his children an image of" our Father in heaven." UL MASTEn A1''T> sEnVANT. (Ver. 22-ch. iv. 1.) This third relationship is one which we may be sure will continue to exist, however varied the forms it may take, so long as the world stands. And what the apostle says here is of universal application, though slavery has happily given place to free service. Even when our lower classes sl,all have become so far raised in intelligence an<l independence that co-operation in industrial labour will become the rule instead of the exception, still there must be some to command, others to obey; Indeed, the more extended and complicatecl the operations of trade and manufacture become, the more thoroughly labour needs to be organized and authority graduated, and the more entirely success depends on manage- ment and discipline and on a right adjustment of the relations of master and servant. 1. From servant.~ Christianity demands, what conscience demands, an honest obedience, that serves as well behind the master's back as to his face (ver. 22). As a mere matter of commercial a,lvantage, the uniform presence of this quality would be an incalculable econorny and enrichment of the community. And religion secures this, directly and of necessity. The man who does his work in God's sight-" as ever in his great Taskmaster's eye "-and as for the judgment-day, cannot scamp any part of it. He is serving, not a man like himself, but a heavenly Lord, whose searching eye is always upon him, who Wlderstands and can judge every man's work (ver. 24; 1 Pet. i. 17), and who bas promised infinite rewards for faithfulness in the "few things" of our earthly probation (Matt. xxv. 21, 23). 'l'hese convictions form the best guarantee, with the mass of men the only sufficient and effectual guarantee, for good work and thorough workmanship in every department of life. "A servant with this clause, Makes drudgery divine; Who sweeps a room as for thy laws, Makes tlmt and the actiou fine." (George Herbert.) 2. And the Christian master whether at the head of a farm or a factory, of a commercial house or a private raO:ily, will remember t~at he lias ~1is dutie~ along with his rights as a ma1Jter. He is dealing with human berngs, not with machmes. The laws of political economy arc not to be his only guide. "'l'he nexus of cash-pa;rm~nts" can never be the sole link that associates any two men together. ·woe be to him 1f he say!', with Cain, "Am I my brother's keeper?" (Gen. iv. 9). "Just dealing and fairness w (eh. iv. 1) must rule in the relations of master and man, if the)'. are to be on a mo~al and ri~hteous footing. He will not take a hard advantage of his s~rvant's necessity; or allow if he can help it his dealin.,.s with him to degenerate rnto a mere struggle hetw~n capital and Jab~ur for ever/inch of vantage. 'l'be cruel greed that g_rasps at irr,media!e gain at whatever cost of toil and poverty to ot.hers, and that" grmds the faces of the poor" (Isa. iii. 15), may enrich the individual, but in the long run is fatal to the class or the trade which practises it. And the rich oppressor will have to appear at a tribunal where" there is no respect of per~ons" (ver. 25). Political economy iLself teaches that ill-paid labour is the most expensive and wasteful. ~hi: ma~ who has want a1Hl fear g11awiu~ at his btart cannot _be~ good workman, cyen if, ID spite o~ n.trt:me wmptation, he ue an honest one. Injustice and over-reachrng on the plll'"t ol IJlI. III, 1-25.] THE EPISTLE ·ro THE COLOSSIANS. 160

the rich and governing classes, polil[cal and social institutions that favour "the fat and the strong" at the expense of the weak and poor (Ezek. xxxiv. 16-27), are sure of God's heavy judgment. They generate in the hatred excited in those subject to them an explosive force which, with a suitable train of circumstances, will burst forth, as in the French Revolution, in some volcanic upheaval that the strongest social fabric will be unable to resist. Christ's golden rule of equity (Luke vi. 31) is the only safe, as it is the only righteous, basis for the dealings of man with man, of class with class, or of nation with nation in the world's great polity.

entries.title: COL 3:1
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Theobligations of the risen life. We have here a transition to the practical part of this Epistle. "If ye then were raised with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God." I. Oua BESUllRECTION WITH CHRIST. "'We are not only "dead with Christ," but "risen with him;" "not only planted in the likeness of his death, but planted together in the likeness of bis resurrection; "-" tbat we may walk in newness of life" (Rom vi. 2-4). 'l'his translation has altered our standpoint. ,v e are "quickened together with Christ, and raised together with him" (Epb. ii. 5, G). We have now an entirely new sphere of intellectual conception and moral aspiration. "Old things have passed away ; behold, all things have become new" (2 Cor. v. 17). II. THE PltACTlCAL DUTY INVOLVED IN THIS RESURRECTION. "Seek those thing~ which are above." 1. The excellence of " the things above." Tliey are (1) satisfying, as things on earth are unsatisfying ; (2) certain, as things on earth are uncertain; (3) perpetual and everlasting, as things on earth are translent and decaying; (4) suitable, as things on earth are unsuitable to an immortal spirit. 3. They are to be sought, implying (1) our knowledge of them; (~) our longing for them ; (3) our anxious effort to realize them (Matt. vi. 33). III. AN A.RGUMENT TO INCITE AND ENCOURAGE us TO THIS DUTY. (2) His mediatorial dominion and power (Phil. ii. 10). (3) Our sitting with him-" he raised us up and made us to sit in heavenly places in Jesus Christ." These places are those he promised to prepare for his people (John xiv. 2). "He that overcometb, to him will I give to sit with me in my throne" (Rev. iii. 21).-T. C.

entries.title: COL 3:4
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The believer's fi:nal manifestation with CJhrist. "When Christ, who i~ onr Life, shall be manifested, then shall ye also with him be manifested in glory." The believer's life will not be always bidden, any more than the believer's Lord. 'l'Lerc will be a period of manifestation for both. This marks the last stage of spiritual life. I. CHRIST IS TilE ESSENCE OF OUR SPIDITUAL LIFE. This is more than saying that our life is bid with him or that he is the Author of it. "He that hath the Son bath life" (1 John v. 12; Gal. ii. 20; Phil. i. 21). We possess this life in virtue of our union with him and bis resurrection (John xiv. 19). II. WE SHALL SHARE WITH HIM IN HIS FINAL MANIFESTATION. 1. The manifestation of Christ is the "blessed hope" of the saints. ('l'itus ii. 13; 1 Tim. vi. 14; 2 'rim. i. 10; iv. 1-8.) He will then be seen as he "is (L.John iii. 2), though mockers may ask, "Where is the promise of his coming?" (2 Pet. iii. 4). He will then appear glorious in bis person, glonous in his retinue of angels, glorious in bis authority. 2. We shall 6hare in that manifestation. "It doth not yet appear what we shall be, but we know that when he shall appear, we shall be like him, for we shnll see him as he is" (1 John iii. 1, 2); "We wait for the Saviour" (Phil. iii. 21); "The glo~y tho_u hast given me I have given them" (John xvii. 22); "If so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also ulorified toa-ether" (Rom. viii. 17). We shall be manifested with Christ in the glory or"'our compl~te manhood, when the conjunction of soul nnd body shall be perfect and indissoluble. We may well set our mind on things above in view of such a glorious prospect.-'!'. C.

entries.title: COL 3:5–7
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The duty of mortifying tlte old man. The apostle proceeds to deduce tl,e practical consequences of our "death in Christ" in the mortifying of tendencies to impurity, covetousness, rnal:ce, and falsehood. "Mortify therefore your members orr. m. 1-26.] THE EPISTLE TO 'rHE COLOSSIANS. ]71

which are upon the cnrth; fornicntion, uncleanness, lustfulness, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry." I. Tim NATURE AND DUTY OF M0ilTJFI0ATION. 1. Its nature. It is to resist the solicitations of sin, to suppress its first motions, to weaken its power. (1) It is a ~radual process-it is" to crucify the flesh," implying a lingering process; it is a destruction that goes on daily, for the remains of the old life still abide, thongh not in power, in the believer. (2) 'l'he word "mortify" implies that sin is not to be allowed to die out of itself; we must kill it. (3) It is a painful process. 2. 'l'he duly of mO'l'tijication. (1) It is commanded. We are to show no more mercy to the "old man" than to the" right eyo "or the" right hand" that offends ns (Matt. v. 2!l). (2) It is done in • the power of the Spirit. "For if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live" (Rom. viii. 13). Therefore it becomes not only possible, but actual. Thus "our instruments of unrighteousness" are turned into "instruments of ri-J1teousness unto God" (Rom. vi. 13). (3) It is the true conseqnence of our "death in Uhrist;" for the apostle says, "Mortify therefore your members," in allusio:1 to this death (eh. ii. 20; iii. 3). We must carry out this principle of death to sin, to the flesh, to the world. II. 'l'HE SPHERE OF THIS M0RTIFI0ATI0N. "Your members which are upon the earth." He refers: 1. 'J.'o the instruments of sinfulness. '!.'hey are called members in allusion to the apostle's figure of sin, asa body of sin (eh. ii. 11), and in allusion to the necessity of the bodily organization to their action. They aro" upon the earth," because they belong to our body or our earthly condition, or tend to mere earthly ~tification. But they are to be turned into" instruments of righteousness unto God." 2. To the various manifestations of this sinfulnees. (1) Sins affecting our personal life. (a) Sins of impurity. (a) Fornication. (i.) It is God's _will we should abstain from it (1 Thess. iv. 3, 4). (ii.) It is one of the works of tho flesh (Gal. v. 19). (iii.) It ought not once to be nnmed among Christians (Eph. v. 12). (iv.) It takes away the heart (Hos. iv. 11). (,·.) It brings dishonour and shipwreck of character (Prov. vi. 27-29; xxiii. 28). (vi.) The body was made, not for a harlot, but for the Lord (1 Car. vi. 15, 16). It is a sin against our own bodies. (vii.) The promises of the gospel ought to engage us to "cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God" (2 Car. vii. 1). (fJ) Uncleanness. This is a generic product, as fornication i8 a specific product, of" the earthly members." The observations in the one apply to the other. Those who commit such sins are "alienated from the life of God through their ignorance and hardness of heart" (Eph. iv. 17), and are "delivered up to a reprobate mind" (Rom. i. 24, 26). ('y) Lustfulness and evil desire. 'l'he~e point to" the lust of concupiscence" (1 Thes~. iv. 5), which is of the devil (John viii. 44), which wars against the soul (1 Pet. ii. 11), which dro,vns men in destruction and perdition (l Tim. vi. 9), and keeps men from" coming to the knowledge of the truth" (2 Tim. iii. 7). These Yarious sins of impurity are to be mortified: how? (a) We can only cleanse our hearts by taking heed to the Word (Ps. cxix. 9). (fJ) By prayer, as the apostle did with the thorn in his flesh (2 Cor. xii. 9). (-y) By watchfulness (Prov. xxiii. 26, 27). We ought to guard against idleness (Ezek. xlvi. 49), fulness of bread, evil company (Prov. i. ~0). (a) We must not "fulfil the lusts of the flesh," but" put on Christ" (Rom. xiii. 14). (b) The sin of covetousness. Tho apostle here introduces a new type of sin by the uso of the definite article, as if he thus exhausted the full catalogue of sin in the world. It is curious to find it linked with sins of impurity. Yet it is so elsewhere (1 Cor. v. 11; Eph. v. 3; 2 Pet. ii. 14). There is a likeness between these two classes of sins. They both imply an unlawful direction of desires not in themselves unlawful, and. they both grow by indulgence. Covetousness: (a) Issues, as a defiling thing:, "out of the heart of man" (Mark vii. 22). (fJ) It implies a greedy and distracting care (Lnko xii. 15). ('Y) It exposes to many a piercing sorrow (1 Tim. vi. 10). (6) It is a trouble to a man's own hous((Prov. xv. 27). (•) It argues little dependence or faith in the Lord (Luke xii. 30). Therefore "let us have our conversation without covetousness and be content with such things as we have" (Heb. xiii. 6). (0 Its heinousness -" seein" it is idolatry." It sets up another object of worship besides God. We cannot "~erve both God ancl rnammon" (Matt. vi. 24). Covetousness i~ base, because it sets up self in the heart. lt is odious to God (Ps. x. 3), turns our hearts away from him (1 John ii. 15), and grudges lho time spent in God's worship (Amos 172 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [OH, m, 1-25.

viii. 5). Sins of impurity are the sins of youth as the sin of covetousness is the sin of old age. III. ARGUMENTS TO ENCOURAGE UB TO THIS DCTY OP lllORTIPIOATION. u For which things' sake cometh the wrath of God upon the sons of disobedience: in the which ye nlso walked aforetime, when ye lived iu these things." 1. J.'he consideration of the u-rath of God. (1) There is wrath in God against all sin. It is the displeasure of a personal ~o~, the mo~al Goyerno_r, aga!nst sin, an~ the movin_g cause of the punishment he rnfhcts. It 1s not 1dent1cal with the pun1shment, which is only the effect of it.. It is a first principle in natural theology (Rom. i. 32); it has its root in the moral excellence of God; and is inseparable from the attitude of God toward moral evil (Heb. iii. 11; Rom. ix. 22). (2) It is an enduring fact of God's moral government-" the \\Tath of God doth come." Nothing has occurred to break the connection between sin aud God's anger, except in the case of those whom Christ has" delivered from the wrath to come" (1 Tbess. i. 10). (3) It is directed against the sons of disobedience, who disregard alike the plinciples of Law and gospel. 2. .A consideration of the former state of tlie Colossians. "In the which ye also walked aforetime, when ye lived in these things." It is good to be reminded of our past sin, (1) because it recalls the misery and guilt of our former state and makes us shrink from the thought of a return to it; (2) because it humbles us under a sense of our personal unworthiness; (3) because it quickens our sense of God's mercy that drew us out of it.-T. C.

But the anger here condemned is sinful. It is a settled feeling of hatred as distinguished from wrath, which is more passionate and transient. (1) We are warned against both. "Cease from anger, leave off wrath, fret not thyseU to do evil" (Ps. xxxvii. 8). We are not to give place to them (Rom. :xii. 19). "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry" (Eccles, vii. 11). entries.title: COL 3:9
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Tlie ground nf these practical precepts. "Seeing th~t Y?U h~ve put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man, which 1s bemg re1,ewed unto knowledge after the image of bill' who created him." We ha.ve hcni OH, m. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 173

the negative and the positive aspects of the great spiritual change effected in conversion. I. TnE NEGATIVE ABPE0T OP C0NVEBBION, "Ye have put off the old man with his <leeds." 1. The old man is the old unconverted self, strong in his deeds of sin. His deeds are catalogued among the " works of the flesh" (Gal. v. 22, 23), as well as in the context. He is to be discerned, indeed, by his works like a tree by its fruits. 2. The putting off of the old man is twofold, namely, at conversion and in tl,e gradual process of sanctification. Some teach that the old man is an unchanged and unchancreable bein", and that, as he has been crucified in Christ (Rom. vi. 6), we have nothing more to d°o with him. In that case, if we have put on the new man, we are perfectly sinless. (1) There is a putting off of the old man at our justification. (2) 'rhere is a gradual puttin\!; 6ff likewise-a " mortifying your members which are upon the earth," which is to continue till we get rid of all his deed~. The counsel, therefore, to put off the old man and put on the new man is like the similar counsel," Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom. xiii. 14), addressed to those who had already "put on Christ" (Gal. iii. 27). II. TnE POSl'rIVE ASPECT OF CONVERSION. "And have put on the new man." This is the regenerate man. He is a" new creation" (2 Cor. v. 17; Gal. vi. 15). 1. The nature of this newness. (1) He has a new nature-" born from above" (John iii. 3). He has "a new heart.." (2) He has a new obedience, both as to its spirit, its matter, and its end (Rom. xii. 1). (3) He has a new citizenship (Phil. iii, 20). (4) He hl\s new desires (Ps. Ii. 2; Matt. v. 6; 1 Tim. iv. 8). 2. It is a nature constantly renewed unto full knowledge. "Which is being renewed unto knowledge." It is not at once complete, but in a state of constant development by the Holy Spirit. Knowleuge is a principal part of the new grace of the believer. (1) It is the beginning of eternal life (John xvii. 3). (2) It has trausforming power (2 Cor. vii. 18). (3) It is necessary to our understanding the wiles of the devil and resisting the temptations of the world (1 Pet. v. 9). 3. Its renewal is after a Divine pattern. "After the image of him who created him." The allusion is to Gen. i. 26. The image of Christ in the believer is analogous to that of the image of God in the original man, but will be far more glorious, as the second Man is more glorious than the first man. Thus wo see the process of putting on the new man in its beginning (Gal. iii. 27), in its continuance (Rom. xiii._l•l), and in its completeness (1 Cor. xv. 53, 54).-T. C.

entries.title: COL 3:10
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Tlie ground nf these practical precepts. "Seeing th~t Y?U h~ve put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man, which 1s bemg re1,ewed unto knowledge after the image of bill' who created him." We ha.ve hcni OH, m. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 173

the negative and the positive aspects of the great spiritual change effected in conversion. I. TnE NEGATIVE ABPE0T OP C0NVEBBION, "Ye have put off the old man with his <leeds." 1. The old man is the old unconverted self, strong in his deeds of sin. His deeds are catalogued among the " works of the flesh" (Gal. v. 22, 23), as well as in the context. He is to be discerned, indeed, by his works like a tree by its fruits. 2. The putting off of the old man is twofold, namely, at conversion and in tl,e gradual process of sanctification. Some teach that the old man is an unchanged and unchancreable bein", and that, as he has been crucified in Christ (Rom. vi. 6), we have nothing more to d°o with him. In that case, if we have put on the new man, we are perfectly sinless. (1) There is a putting off of the old man at our justification. (2) 'rhere is a gradual puttin\!; 6ff likewise-a " mortifying your members which are upon the earth," which is to continue till we get rid of all his deed~. The counsel, therefore, to put off the old man and put on the new man is like the similar counsel," Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom. xiii. 14), addressed to those who had already "put on Christ" (Gal. iii. 27). II. TnE POSl'rIVE ASPECT OF CONVERSION. "And have put on the new man." This is the regenerate man. He is a" new creation" (2 Cor. v. 17; Gal. vi. 15). 1. The nature of this newness. (1) He has a new nature-" born from above" (John iii. 3). He has "a new heart.." (2) He has a new obedience, both as to its spirit, its matter, and its end (Rom. xii. 1). (3) He has a new citizenship (Phil. iii, 20). (4) He hl\s new desires (Ps. Ii. 2; Matt. v. 6; 1 Tim. iv. 8). 2. It is a nature constantly renewed unto full knowledge. "Which is being renewed unto knowledge." It is not at once complete, but in a state of constant development by the Holy Spirit. Knowleuge is a principal part of the new grace of the believer. (1) It is the beginning of eternal life (John xvii. 3). (2) It has trausforming power (2 Cor. vii. 18). (3) It is necessary to our understanding the wiles of the devil and resisting the temptations of the world (1 Pet. v. 9). 3. Its renewal is after a Divine pattern. "After the image of him who created him." The allusion is to Gen. i. 26. The image of Christ in the believer is analogous to that of the image of God in the original man, but will be far more glorious, as the second Man is more glorious than the first man. Thus wo see the process of putting on the new man in its beginning (Gal. iii. 27), in its continuance (Rom. xiii._l•l), and in its completeness (1 Cor. xv. 53, 54).-T. C.

entries.title: COL 3:11
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.All distinctions obliterated in <Jhrist. " Where there cannot be Greek and ,Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondman, freeman: but Christ is all, and in all." The old distinctions which separated man from man can have no existence in the new spiritual life. I. NATIONAL DISTINCTIONS ARE ADOLISilED IN CHRIST. 11 Greek 11nd Jew." The peculiar privilege of Abraham's natural seed is gone. Mercy is shown on exactly similar terms to Jew and to Gonti!e. Thus is manifest that catholicity of the gospel which the Gnostics repudiated. II. RITUALISTI0 DISTINCTIONS ARE AnOLISHED. .. Circumcision and uncircumcision." The errorists in Galatia would have imposed circumcision on the Gentile Christians, but neither circumcision nor the want of it availed 11nything in Christ's kingdom, but "a new creation " (Gal. vi. 15). Thus, while it was an ad vantage to be born a Jew rather than a Gentile, it was none to become as a Jew by conforming to its ritual (l Cor. vii. 19). III. No DISTINCTION IB RECOGNIZED AS TO CIVILIZATION on REFINEMENT. "Barbarian, Scythian." The barbarian was the foreigner, the 8cytbian the savage. 'l'ho gospel turns the barbarian into a brother, and lifts even the Scythians-the lowest type of barbarians-into the dignity of Christian fellowship. IV. SoOUL DISTINCTIONS ARE ADOLIBHED. "Boutlman, freeman." The gospel has placed them on one level ofreligious privilege. V. CnBIST BAB 0DLITERATED ALL TilEBE DIBTINCTIONS. .. Ilut Christ ii:; all, and in all," He has absorbed them all into himself, tilling the whole sphere of human life in its widrst varieties of development. He dwells in all, their true Centre; for the lifo of all believers is "hid with Christ in God." This fact places the Sl\ints under immense obligations. They must consecrate all to Christ and resign all to his wise and loving will.-T. 0. li4 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [en. m. 1-26.

.' ers. 12-14.-~he duty of put~i1:7.on all ~he chamctel'istic qualities of the new man. "e must not only cease to do enl m puttmg off the old man we" must learn to do well." "Put on therefore, as God's elect, holy and beloved ~ heart of compassion kindness, humility, meekness, long-suffering." ' ' I. 'l'HE ODLIGA.TIONS OF THE CHRISTIAN POSITION. "As God's elect holy and beloved." They are chosen unto holiness that they should be without bl~me before him in love" (Eph. i. 4). The saints are: 1. The elect ones of God. 'l'bey are chosen to final salvation (1.fatt. xxiv. 22, 24, 31; Rev. xvii. 14; Titus i. 1; Rom. viii. 33). 2. 'I71e elect are (1) holy-:(a) _consecrated to _God, (b) subjectively holy (2 Cor. vii. 1); (2) beloved-(_a) the elect10n 1s connected with God's love (Rom. xi. 28); (b) it is a free love (Hos. xiv. 5), a tender love (Joel ii. 13), e.n everlastina 0 love (Ze1Jh. iii. 17). II. THE DISCHARGE OF THESE CHRISTIAN OBLIGATIONS. we· are to put on: 1. A heart nf compassion; not a bead of high knowledge, after Gnostic perception. The aposlle hep.ins with the natural and universal instinct of pity, which is here more an act of grace than of nature, for it springs from love to God. We ought to cultivate it, (1) because the Father of mercies is merciful (Luke vi. 33); (2) because those who need it are our own flesh (Isa. lviii. 7); (3) because it will attest the reality and worth of our religion (Jas. i. 27); (4) because we shall reap after the measw·e of mercies both here and hereafter (Hos. x. 12). 2. Kindness. This is the temper of mind which produces a sweet and happy intercourse with others. Our English word is derived from'' kin," and thus a kind man is a kinned man; we ought to rogard the saints as kinsfolk, for they arc children of God and brethren in Christ. 3. Humility. 'l'his is the temper of mind wbich affects our estimate of ourselves. It is closely allied to kindness, for it takes an unselfish view of personal interests. We ought to "seek lowliness" (Zeph. ii. 3), because: (1) It is one of Christ's own graces (Matt. xi. 29). (2) God regards it as a grace eminently worthy of our vocation (Epb. iv. 1, 2). (3) He loves to dwell in e. Jowly soul (Isa. lvii. 15). He giveth grace to the Jowly (1 Pet. v. 5, 6). (4) He does not despise their prayers (Ps. cii. 7). 4. .Meelcness, long-suffering. They affect onr outward bearing towards others, especially in the case of injury or insult. They are linked together e.s companion graces in Gal. v. 22. They are eminently illustrated in the life of Christ, and are both fruits of the Spirit (Gal. v. 22). _God will guide the meek in judgment and teach them his way (Ps. xxv. 9). It is tbo praise of Christian love that it suffers long (1 Cor. xiii. 4). 5. Forbearance and mutual forgiveness. "Forbearing one another, and forgiving each other, if any man have n complaint against any." This temper is eminently conducive to peaceful relations and diminishes the 1Jatural friction of life. It implies (1) a bearing with the infirmities of others (Gal vi. 2); (2) a disposition to take wrong rather than stand upon the last jot of our rights (1 Cor. vi. 7); (3) a. pleasing of our neighbour for his good to edification (Rom. x:v. 1, 2); (4) a frank forgiveness of our neighbour in case of a fault,-jars and discords may arise even among saints. (5) It is a temper which is illustrated and euforced by the example of Cb1ist: "Even as the Lord forgave you, so also do ye." His example is decisive both as to the act and the manner of it. He forgave bis enemies: be for"ave freely; be forgave finally, for salvation. 6. Love. ".And abovo all these-things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness."· This love to the brethren is to be put on as the cincture to bind the other graces together. (L) The necessity of this love. (a) It is the proof of faith (Gal. v. 6). (b) It tends to the increase of the mystical body (Epb. iv. 17). (c) It makes us like God himself (1 John iv. 16). (d) It is a demonstration of the reality of religion to a godless world (John xv. 8; Mntt. v. 16). (2) The dignity of this love; it is "the bond of perfectness." It holds together all the graces which make up perfection. The Judreo-Gnostics found their perfection in knowledge· the apostle finds it in love. "Knowledge puffeth up, charity edifieth" (1 Cor. viii'. 1). Love binds believerij together, and looks to their final perfection in God.-T.C.

-Peace and thanksgiving. "And let the peace of Christ rule in your bear ls, to the which also ye were called in one body; and be ye thankful." I. CHRISTIAN PEACE. 1. Its .Lfothor. The word, in its substantive and verbal forms, occurs thirty-seven times in his Epistles. \Ve must be iu a constant mood of thanksgiving for his mercies, for his grace, for his comforts, and for his ordinances.-T.
