entries.title: COL 3:16
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The use of the Word for spiritual edification. The apostle, in -view or th11 right exercise of the foregoing graces, counsels the Colossians to make the Word of Christ the subject of experimental study. "Let the Word of Christ cl well in you richly in all wisdom." 1. THE EFFIC.AOY OF CHRIST'S Wo1m. 1. The Scriptures are (Jhrisfs Word. They have Christ for their Author, for their Subject, for their Eud. This is the Word that is "sounded forth" everywhere (1 Thess. i. 8), that "runs " everywhere, to be glorified in its success. It is Christ, too, who gives power to this Word. 2. This Word ouglit to dwell in u,. Not come and go, but tarry as in a fixed abode, It ought to be an abiding power within us. "'l'he Word of God abideth in you" (1 J obn ii. 14). 3. The place of its indwelling is the heart; not the memory or the head, but the heart. "'l'hy Word have I hid in my heart" (Ps. cxix. 11). 4. The manner of its indwelling. "Richly in all wisdom." (1) Not" with a scanty foothold, but with a large and liberal occupancy." (2) It implies (a) receiving the Word with all meekness and humility (Jas. i. 21); (b) dividing it aright (2 'l'im. ii. 15); (c) trying all thiugs so as to keep that which is good (1 Thess. v. 21). II. 'l'HE USE OR END OF CIIRIST's WORD. "Teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." There iR a double function here assigucd to t.he Word: one making its iufluenco felt upon the mind-" teaching;" the other upon the heart--" sin:;(iog" with thanksgiviug. 1. 'The Wo,-d is useful for teaching and for warning. Tbese represent tho 11ositivc and the negative sides of instruction. (1) Teaching. (a) This implies that the Word is to be used by every Christian for the purposes of instruction (Es:od. xxiv. 12). When we have received the "ingrafted Word" into our hearts, we must spreatl it abroad. (b) It deepens our sense of the value of the Word to impart it to others, (c) It is a test of the sincerity of our attachment to make it known. (d) It is by the efforts of all Christians in this way that the Word will eventually reach the ends of the earth. (2) .Admonition. (a) It must be grounded on the Word (Titus i. 6). (b) It mnst bo douc in lo\'e and meekness (2 Thess. iii. 1; Gal. vi. 1). (c) With a reasonable secrecy (Matt. xviii. 15). (d) With compassion and tenderness (2 Cor. ii. 4). (e) With perseverance (Prov. xiii. 19). 2. The Word is useful for the purpose of sacred song. entries.title: COL 3:17
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The principle of a godly life. This is the practical lesson that flows from the theology of the Epistle. "And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the :Kame of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him." I. THE WHOLE EXTENT OF CHRISTIAN LIFE IS CONSECRATED TO THE Lonn. Every- tl,ing falls under the two heads of words and deeds. 1. Words. (1) We must avoid words that would dishonour Christ-vain words (Eph. v. 6), bitter words (Job vi. 3), deceitful words (Ps. xxxvi. 3), idle words (Matt. xii. 36). James tells us the sins of the tongue (Jas. iii. 2). (2) We must use words of wisdom (Book of Proverbs), wordi, of truth and soberness (Acts xxiii. 25), words of righteousness (Job vi. 25), wholesome words (2 Tim. i. 13), words of eternal life (John vi. 68). 2. Deeds. These must be done (1) in faith, for "whatsoever is not of faith is sin;" (2) in prayer (Ps. ix. 1); (3) with warrant from God's Word (Isa. viii. 20); (4) with perseverance (Gal. vi. 9). 3. All, both wo;·ds and deeds, must be done in the Name of the Lord. They must have supreme reference to him (1 Cor. x. 31); they must be done under his warrant or authority, in the.strength of his grace, after his own glorious eumple, and with ultimate regard to his glory. 4. Christian obedience must all the while be mingled with thanlcs- _qiving to God the Father. We thank him (1) for the ability to do all our works in the Lord's Name; (2) for our liberty in Christ; (3) for our victory over sin; (4) for our manifold blessings in Christ. II. REA.SONS FOR THE CONSECRATION OF OUR WHOLE LIFE TO THE LORD. We ought to be more circumspect than others in our words and deeds: 1. Because "we live and die to the Lord." (Rom. xiv. 8.) We are "the Lord's." 2. Because we are entrusted with such blessings. " Because God bath bestowed upon them more blessings, and therefore as he gives more wages, requires more work." 3. Because we are more observed than others. Therefore we must "walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise" (Eph. v. 15). 4. Because we have the prospect of an abundant reward according to our works. -T.C.

entries.title: COL 3:18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The duties of wives. The apostle next proceeds to enjoin family duties, not in the spirit of those errorists, who imagined that such duties were vulgar and inconsistent with the contemplative aspect of the Christian life. His first practical exhortation is to wives, and is summed up in the single duty-" submit yourselves." I. THE DUTY OF SUllMIBSION. "Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands." This duty includes: 1. Honour. They must honour their husbands as their head (1 Cor. xi. ::I ; 1 Pet. iii. 6). 2. Trutl,fulness. (Prov. ii. 17.) 3. Obedience. (Eph. v. 23; 1 Cor. vii. 34.) 4. Co-operation with their husbands in all family affairs. 'l'hey must "guide the house with discretion" (Titus ii. 5). 5. 'l'hey must not assume authority over their husbands, either in ecclesiastical or in domestic affairs (1 Tim. ii. 11). 11. REASONS FOR THIS DOTY. ".AB it is fit in the Lord." In Oriental countries, woman was the slave rather than the companion of man, but iu the Greci1.ed communities of Asia Minor, woman held a higher position, and her new position under the gospel may have led her to carry her freedom to the point of licence. It was, therefore, necessary to define her position accurately. Her subjection to man is "fit in the Lord" on Eeveral grounds. 1. From man's priority of creation. (1 Tim. ii. 13.) 2. The woman was made for man, not the man for the woman. (1 Cor. ii. 9.) 3. The woman's priority in the original tramgression. (1 Tim. ii. 14.) 4. The man's headship over the woman. (1 Cor. xi. 3.) 6. Her weakness. She is "the weaker vessel" (1 Pet. iii. 7), and therefore stands in need of his greater strength and protection. 6. 7'he subjection to man is placed on the same basis as the subjection of the Ohwrch to Christ. (Epb. v. 22-24.) 7. But the apostle's language in the text implies a limitation upon her submission; for bhe is to be subject to him "in the Lord." Both husband and wife must have a due consideration for each other's position, because they are "heirs of the grace of life," and they must see that "their prayers are not hindered" (1 Pet. iii. 7).-'f. C.

I. THE DU'rY O\I' LOVE. ThiR love, which is con~istent with his he:vlship over her implies: 1. That he is to delight in her (Prov. v. 18, 19), and plcnse her (1 Cor. vii. 33)'. 2. (l~ph. v. 25-28.)-T. C.

entries.title: COL 3:20
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Tlie duties of children. "Children, obey your parents in all things: fur this is well-pleasing to the Lord." I. TIIE DUTY OF CHILDREN IS OBEDIENCE. This includes: 1. Reverence. (Lev. xix. 3; Eph. vi. 1, 2.) 2. Readiness to receive instruction from parents. (Prov. i. 8.) 3. Submissfon to their rebulces. (Prov. xiii. 1.) 4. Gratitude. (1 Tiro. v. 4.) 5. Submission tu their J°ust commands. '!'hey are to obey "in all things," that is, in all lawful things, for it must be done "in the Lord " (Eph. vi. 1). II. Tm: GROUNDS OF THIS DUTY. "For this is well-pleasing to the Lord." This i~, in itself, a suflicicnt reason for filial obedience. But it is well-pleasing to the Lord for several reasons. It is not enough to serve God, but we must serve him so as to please him (Heb. xiL 28). 1. It is agreeable to his Law. (Exod. xx. 12.) 2. It is right in itself. (Eph. vi. 1.) 3. Christ was obedient to his parents. (Luke ii. 51.) 4. It is necessary to the good order of family life. 5. The welfare of the child depends upon its obedience, especially at a time when it cannot reason upon what is right.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 3:21
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The duties of fathers. "Fathers, provukc not your chi!<lrca, lest tlwy be discouraged." I. 'l'HE DUTY OF PARENTS. It is l1ere exhibited on its negative shle. They are not to abuse their authority over their children by too great severity either in words or deed~. Some parents spoil their children by indulg,mce; others, by unwise severitie~. Bitter words are used, unreasonable commands are given, immoderate co1Tec1 ion is administere,1. Parents are to behave lovingly to their children, e\'en whilo maintaining their just authority over them. II. 'l'BE DANGER 0\1' NEEDLESS HARSH~"ESS. "Lest th~y be discour~getl." '!'hey m:iy lose heart; their spirit may be broken; they may become morose, sullen, nn·l reckless. Thus they may be turned aside from the service of Goel, lose the capacity to do great things, become pusillanimous, and eventually become a sa<l disappointment to their parcnts.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 3:22–25
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The duties of servants. The arostle enters into fuller detail in his injunctions to servants, because his intercourse with Onesimns, a Colossi:m slave now returning to his master Philemon in a new clmractcr, had turned his tl1011ghts to tho condition and difficulties of the whole cla!'S of dependants. His injunctions to them imply that they had a right to bo instructed out of the Word, and that if men have less consideration for their interests, the Lord redoubles his concern for them. There wa:1 a danger that slaves in the Roman empire might rcpndiato their relation to their masters, and accordingly the apostle enjoins the duty of obedience to masters, while he annouuce:1 principles destined ultimately to destroy the unnatural relation. I. 'l'HE FAULTS OF SEUVANTS. He specifics five of them. 1. Eye-service. '!'here was l\ temptation to this fault where the master's authority was regarded M unjust an,l cruel. 2. Hypocritical service, arisin~ out or a divided interest an(l the abs,·nce of singleness of heart. 3. Half-service. Scrvnnts might not please their masters "in all things," but in such thiug:1 ns pleased themsclv .. s. 4. Godlessness. 'l'bcy chose to please mtr1 rather than the Divine Master. 5. .A base and discouraged .•pirit, wl.i0h wa.s to be banished by prospects of hol\vcnly reward. CDL0SSlA)':S, N li8 THE EPISTLE TO '1.'B.E COLOSSIANS. [011. m. 1-25.

II. THE DUTIES OF SERVA?-Ts. These are all summed up in the one word "obedience." But this obedience must be becomingly rendered in several important respects. 1. "Not ·u•i'.t~ ,:y_e-serv_ice, as men-pleasers; but in sin_qleness of heart,fearing God." (1) Eyo- sc1-v1ce 1s designed to plc.nse man. ,vork will bo dona only so long as the master's eye is on the sen•ant, There is no thought of pleasing aught but man. (2) 'l.'here must be sindeness of heart, that is, simplicity and sincerity of spirit, that will lead to an undivided de'l"otion to work, arising from "the fear of God," because they realizo that the eye of the Di'l"ine Ma~ter is ever upon them. Dissimulation, duplicity, pretence, deceit, must be far from Clmst1an servants. 2. It mu.~t be hearty ser1Jice. "And whatsoever ~-e do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not to men." Servants, in obeying their masters, ~,·r,e the Lord. They do the will of God from the heart, not grudgingly or murmuringly, hut with a truly hearty obedience. 3. It must be obedience "in all things;" that is, in all things lawfol. entries.title: COL 3:12–17
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
The new life of love. We have turned over a new leaf, sc, to speak, in Lhese versts. The old life we have to mortify gives place to a new life of love which we have to develop. Now, the moment wo speak of love, we are brought into l'ehtiu11s with others. It is the social Christian life, therefore, of which Paul hern CU. IU. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 181

Rpeaks. As nlre11dy seen, be is aiming at the unity of the Church. Here we have the means by which it is secured. Let us briefly analyze this life of love. I. IT HAS A HEART OF COMPASSION. (Ver. 12, Revised Version.) All the emotion which misfortune evokes in the heart of God is to have its counterpart in the heart of bis people. "Kindness, humility, meekness, and long-suffering'' are to be in exercise within us continually. '!'be apparent drawbacks in others are thus transfiCJ'ured by our kindly spirit into helps to unity. II. IT HAS A FORGIVINGNESS LIKE THAT OF Go». (Ver. 13.) Church members and those outside the Church will, from time to time, be guilty of injustice towards us; we may have just ground of complaint. But how our brother's offences clwincllc into utter insignificance when compared with the offences we have ourselve, committed against God I It will not do to be severe on our debtors after God has been so forgiving towards ourselves (Matt. xviii. 21-35). If we cultivate a God-like forgivin"ncss, then we shall be promoting constantly the unity of the Church. " III. LOVE IS ITS noND OF PERFECTNESS, (Ver.14.) We need only study 1 Cor. xiii. to see bow love is the all-important matter. It is what brings the whole life into harmony. For love expresses the willingness of the person to give himself to the gootl of others. It is the principle of the new life, without which it cannot exist. IV. Go»'s PEACE RULES AND EVOKES MAN'S GRATITUDE. (Ver. 15.) For when we are God-like in our compassion, forgiveness, and love, we find a peaceful temper laying hold of us, We cannot war with others, but must follow the things that make for peace. To the unity of peace we feel that God has called us. lie has been our Peacemaker and the Peacemaker of many more, and so we dwell in the uuity of the one3 mystical body. And surely such a state of mind and heart is something to be thankful for. A grateful spirit for our personal peace and for the peace which permeates through the Church of God. V. GoD's WoRD IS TnANSLATED INTO HEARTFELT PRAISE. (Ver. 16.) For we can only sustain the new life by the reception of God's quickening Word. It must dwell within us richly. And if it do, it will evoke praise from our grateful hearts. We will sing in our social gatherings one to another, and be mutually helpful. '!'he meetings of the saints shall be of a most joyful character. And wliat a unifying element is always found in social praise I How it blends our hearts into unity as we praise the one Lord. The very harmony of the music catches our souls autl blends them into something like the harmony of heaven. VI. ALL LIFE BECOMES SACRAMENTAL, (Ver. 17.) There can be no idle words nor random deeds in the new life. All is consecrated to the Lord. His Name is our banner, and under it all is done. God bas thus come and made " the comrnou " clean, and the life on earth is like the great sheet of the Apostle Peter, in which the fourfooted beasts and creeping things were pure. Into every nook and cranny of the new life the consecrated spirit is carried: The meanest matters are thus lifted into heaveuly light, and God reigns over all. Tbus it is that the sacramental element is carried into all things, and we feel that "the communion of the Lord's Supper is meant to be o. sample of, and not an exception to, our common days; and in the rite there lies a mighty power to make the whole of the rest of life like itself." Arnold has a curious sermon on this text, in which be advocates the consecration in the making of "wills." But this is only an illustration of a universal principle which God requires in the Christian life. There is to be 110 exception to· consecration. In a grateful spirit we nre to do all in Christ's Name. May it be our single ambition !-R. M. E.

Ver.18--cb. iv. 1.-0hristianity remodelling the ancient household. The unity of the Church, which Paul has in view, is to have its counterpart and model in tbe unity of the Christian household. '!'be Church is only an enlarged family. Hence Church officers are to serve their apprenticeship in the matter of rule in the family. It they are not able to rule their own families well, they have no business to take office in tho Church of God (1 Tim. iii. 2, 12). Of necessity, therefore, Christianity takes up the household and sanctifies it. The relation of Christianity to family life is most important. In the present section Paul takes up tbreo relations and shows how love is to regulate them all. L THI!: RELATIONS Oli' IIUSBANDS AND WIVES. (Vers. 18, 19.) Now, it is woll kuown 182 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [en. ur. 1-25.

that women did not get justice under the ancient regime, and yet the npost.lo exhorts the wi~cs to be in subjection to their husbands, as is fittin.,. in the Lord (Revised Version). Christianity has emphasized the pa.~sive vil'tues; it .,.lorifies woman there- fore, by showing to the world how glorious a. thing it is to be subject and even ~ suffer for love. _Apparently thi~ is to n~glect "wo!11en's rights," but really it bas secured them. It 1s m woma°: lovingly filling her s~t1on that she secures, not only her rights, but absolutely her reign, Husbands, agam, aro exhorted to give up all bitterness against their wives and to love them. Elsewhere he shows that the measure of thG husband's love is to be the love of Christ for his Church; that is, a love which cnn be self-sacrificing if need lie, and which will be considerate at all times (Eph. v. 22--33). In such a case, bow harmonious family life proves! The stroncrer and the weaker natures are blended by love into one. Each has its sphere, and th~re need be no collision amid the responsibilities of love. II. THE RELATIONS OF PARENTS TO CHILDREN. Here, again, the apostle appeals first to the weaker side. He wishes children to think bow pleasing to the Father in heaven obedience is, and, as he has put their parents over them to be obeyed, the children should obey them in all things. There is to be strict obedience in all thin"s to the natural authority. On the other hand, the fathers are exhorted not to pro~oke the children by their tyranny, lest the little ones be discouraged. Paul saw no such danger from the mother's rule. A mother comes with o. tenderness and sympathy snch a.s the harder nature of the father cannot always command. 'l'his exhortation to fathers is surely a great triumph for the mother. III. Till!: RELATIONS OF lUSTERS TO BLA VES. And here, again, Paul appeals first to the slaves. He does not encourage revolt, but the conquest which comes through loving obedience. Let the slave simply obey in the fear and love of God; let him do his work, not in a. spirit of eye-service as a pleaser of men, but in a spirit of conscientious- ness a.s a slave of Christ, and he may rest assured of compensation from his Master in due season. This is liberty-the liberty of love, even though be is still nominally a lave. It is this Christian spirit which has made its mark and won the sympathy of -be world, and issued in the emancipation of the slaves. Although Christianity ,pparently neglected the slaves, it has really been their deliverer. For what has it msisted on among the masters? On justice. Above them it has pointed out a heavenly Master, with whom there is no respect of persons, and who will do right by slave as well as by freeman, and give all their due. Tbc gospel has contended for justice as between man and man, and the world is gradually coming to it. This freedom from respect of persons which characterizes God is a terror at once to the evil-doing slave and to the evil-doing master. If we could bring the world to this, men's wrongs would soon be righted. We are coming to it, blessed be God, steadily. The Christianized household is thus seen to be a unity. Husbands and wives are united in love's best bonds. Pa.rents and children a.re united in beautiful authorities and subordinations. .And masters and servants are united as subjects and servants of the one Master in heaven. It is the one God of love, who, as he overshadows all, unifies them in a lifo of love, which is the greatest witness he can have on earth. Let us sec to it that the Christian spirit in all its beautiful and unifying power reigns in our households antl fulfils within them the work of God.-R. M. E.

-0ur risen life. "If then ye were raised together with Christ.'' At this point the apostle leaves the polemical and begins foe practical. Doctrine again forms the foundation for exhortation. As in combating asceticism he proceeded upon the fact that we were sharers with Christ in bis death, so in presenting o. substitute for asceticism, he proceeds upon the fact that we were sharers with him in bis resurrection. Our being baptized with him extended, not only to our dying with him, but also to our rising with him. I. lTs HEAVENWARD DIRECTION. 1. In its connection with Christ. "Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God." It was when we were raised with Christ that we were introduced to the things that o.re above. There, henceforth, we found our proper sphere. Our being must now ever, o.nd increasingly, tend tbitherward. '!'ho things that are above we are to seelc supremely. 'l'hey am the only things which are worthy of being Bonght in the fullest sense. Of on. m. 1-25.J THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 181

the heavenly sphcro Obrist is the Llessctl and glorious Centn'. Ilc is, in a word, the things that are above. Ho is here mentioned with a local reforence. The time was when he was on earth and mingled with men. He was seen by the eleven disciples going up into heaven. He was seen by the dying Stephen standin~ on the ricrht hand of God. And we are to think of him as still stationed(" seated," it is here, and accord- ing to the usual conception) on the right hand of God. To him, then, must our beino now and ever tend. lie has gone into heaven to draw our desires and affections afte~ him and up toward him. We are to turn to him with our whole desire. "\Ve are to turn to him for all that we neen. Our spiritual life cannot be maintained without the things that are above in the shape of heavenly blessings descending on us, and we must turn to him for their bestowal (in regal manner, seeing that he occupies the sent of rule). We must turn to him with the whole a/Jecti(J11, of our being. For he is a Person (the Manifester of God, and Author of onr salvation), and is pronounced "the altogether lovely." And to be: powe1fully drawn toward him is the only way to be delivered from that in regard to which o.sceticism is pronounced ineffective, viz. the temptations of the flesh. Drawn toward him, we are drawn away from nil that should be below us, and we are drawn up to the things which are high. We have thus, though on earth, a great elevation for our being. And, in accordance with it, we should loolc hi_qh, even up to him who is seated on the right hand of God. 2. In its contrast with an earthu·ard direction. "Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth." '!'here is a word employed here with a slightly different meaning from "seek." The idea is that we are to be so drawn to the things that are above as that they are to occupy our thoughts. There is not only the sphere of the things that aro above, but there is the sphere of the things that arc upon the earth, to which also we are related. "\Ve are not to think of the latter with n sinfnl association. The things upon the earth have been made by God, and are, therefore, good in themselves. But they are evidently placed in a certain subordination. They are things upon the earth, in contrast with the things that are above. It is implied that they are not to be sought supremely, but (if they would be sought truly according to their nature and purpose) with a dne subordination and subservience to the things that are above. \Ve are not to allow them to occupy our thoughts. And the reason is obvious. 'l'bey cannot so fill up our being as to bring about our perfection and happiness. De Quincey thus concludes his apostrophe to opium: "Thoa only givest these gifts to men; and thou hast the keys of Paradise, 0 just, subtle, and mighty opium I" But the opium-eater's Paradise easily changes into its opposite. '!'here is a fluctuation connected with all things that are upon the earth. .And we know that soon our whole earthly prospect will dissolve. 'l'hat is intended to tench us this lesson, that we are not to set our mind on earthly things. We are not to feel toward them as though they were essential to our being. llut, feeling them to be limited in quality :md duration, we are to set our mind on that which is unlimited in quality and duration. II. ITs BIDDEN NATURE. 1. We are dead to the ootwardness of the worldly life. " For yo died." There is a hiddenness connected with tho worldly life which is not to be spoken of. "My soul, come not thou into their secret." But the worldly lifo is chnrncteristicnlly a life in the outward. It iB a life within the sphero of the li\·c eenses. lt is a lifo of communion n.ud commerce with earthly things. It is n. life which has its 1·001s in the world. It is a life the highest ambition of which is to appear well to the world, and to continue to appear well. Now, ns Christians, we nro dead, so far as going after the outward is concerned. We occupy a different standpoint altogether. We are dead where men of the world are alive. And the course we have to take, in obedience to Christ, may even bring us into collision with tbo world. 2. It is a life liidden with Christ in God. "And your life is hid with Christ in God." (1) Jt is hidden from the world. We are in a position to comprehend the worldly life from our experience of what sin is. But the Christian life is beyond the compre- hension of men of the world, for they have had no experience of it. They have no affinities to it, and, therefore, it is an enigma to them, as nature nnd art are to tho~o who have no appreciation of the beautiful. They see the manifestations of the Christian life but they cannot appreciate the motives by which we aro actuated, the principles by ~hich we are guided. (2) It is partly hidden from ourselv~s. '!'here is a mystery 1'-'+ TIII~ EPISTLE TO THE COL08SIANS. [en. m. 1-25.

ii; ,ill life \\-c cnt. into a 1,hnt. lo find what life is, hut it eludes the finest perception. Cl11·i,, inn~, t.hcn, cannot be cxpcckd to understand the mystery of the lifo of God in tl,e snul. And, npnrt from that, we can only imperfectly understand our experiences. Our life goes forw:nd Recording to tha thought and ,vorking of One unseen. (3) It is a l{f't of l,iddcnfdlow.sliip with Clwist. It commanced in that region of the soul which ;, penl'lrated only by our owo eye and by the eye of God. 'l.'here with Christ we dcdi~;1ted ourseh·es to him. 'l.'here we lmva fellowship with Christ, in our joys, ,·\'en in onr earthly j,,ys. There we hava fellowship with Christ in our sorrows even our so1-ro11·s of rep,·utance and painful struggles after virtue. And there he is with us to ':nc~urage ~sin nll ~l)e efforts we \mt fort~ for the ~dvancement of his cause. (4) It 1.s 111.dden in Goel. l he worldly life bas its roots III the world. The life which con,i~ts in fdlo\l·s1,ip with Christ is hidden because itis lived in God. He is essentially l,idden-the invisible God; he is called in this Epistle, elsewhere, a God that bideth l1ims,·lf. Our life, then, has its roots hi<lden in him, in his eternal purpose and inexhaustible goo,1ness. JU. IT~ FUTURE MANIFESTATIO~. "When Christ, who is our Life, shall be manifested, tlien shall ye also with him be manifested iu glory." The Christian life is to be mnnifcst.ed to men. ,ve are to 1111\ke our light so shiue before men that others, seeing our good works, may glorify our Father which is in heaven. Dut the manifestation referred to here is that to which we are to look forward as the crown of our being. 1. It results from our relation to Christ. Our life is not only with him, but he is ow· J,ife. He is the life of our life. The essential thing iu the relation here is that, thus Ii l'ing within us, he gives type and form to our life. 2. It results from his manifestation. 'J'l,ere is a manifestation yet before him. "When Christ . . . shall be manifested." It is irnpliccl tl,at at present he is in a condition of concealment. He is concealed from the world. Many think that he and his cause arc under a cloud. He is, to a certain extent, manifested in heaven; but he is not manifested in the full meaning of his work, in his full glory as Saviour. His .manifestation will be our manifestation. We shall be completely vindicated before men. It will be made completely manifest that we are sons of Gud and friends of Christ. Christ within us will work out till we are made glorious in body and in soul with his glory.-R. F.

Vers. fi-11.-Dying before rising. There is an alternating between dying and rising. llaving carried out the idea of rising, the apostle goes back to the idea of dying ; and, before this paragraph is concluded, he goes back to the idea of rising. I. MORTIFYING OF OUR MEMBERS WITII REFERENCE TO TWO SINS. "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth." It is not a ground of condemnation that our members are upon the earth. The idea is simply the members through which we J,old corre~pondence with earth. Of these members, collectively, the apostle says," I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sncrifice." Our members may be instruments of righteousness or instruments of unrig:hteousneiis. We are to mortify them by refusing to use them as instruments of •mrigl.iteousness. 1. Sensuality. "Fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire." There are four words used to describe this sin. 'l.'he first describes a special form of uncleanness. The second is wider, and includes all forms of uncleanness. The third is wider still, and describes such heated desire as may lead to uncleanness, The fourth is widest of all, and includes all such desire as implies want of purity of feeling. 2. Covetousness. "And covetousness, the which is idolatry." The article being used with "covetousness" (not with the other four words) indicates the introduction of a. new class. 'l'he,e four form one class; and this fifth is a class by itself. The fact that it i~ associakd (as in Ephesians) with forms of sensuality marks the sense which tho apostle had of its evil character. There is not here tho thou11:ht that it is to be among the tbini;s which aro not to be named. Dut there is the thought, which follows in Ephesian-s, that covltousness is idolatry; that is to say, idolatry by pre-eminence. Sensuality is al~o idolatry. It is making au i<lol of self in the form of lower and momentary enjoyment. Covetuusness has a certain aspect of unselfishness. It is a giving up of J,re8ent enjoyment; it is e. giving up even of future enjoyment. But when unveiled it is really a more systematic form of selfishness. It is making an idol of self, not in the fonn of future enjoyment, but ,which is no better) in tho form of the means of

future enjoyment. And experience shows that. the one it\ol is less rea<lily ,lethronecl than the other. The next thought (which also follows in Ephesians) is that for these sins God deals with men. "]'or which thingi sake cometh the wrath of God upon the sons of disobedience." They disobey, for the first commandment is "Thou shalt havo no other gods before me." They transgress the laws of the body; they transgress also the laws of the spiritual nature. 'l'hey not only disobey, but they persist in courses of disobedience. They are the sons of duobedience. They are as though they had disobedience as their father; so vile is their parentage. They refuse the gospel, by which they could be delivered from their evil courses. Aud therefore it is that the wrath of God cometh upon them. It cometh upon them incipiently now. It cometh upon them in the shape of a. materializing of the spirit. It cometh upon them in the shape of inward dispeace. It cometh upon them in the shape of distui·bance from without (bodily malady, loss of tstate, loss of respect, complications). God bas many ways of showing his displeasure against men for these sins even now, and his displeasure will yet be more decidedly manifested, The next thow;ht (which also follows, though not under the same figure, i II Ephesians) is that tliey were. to remember their former participation in these sins. "In the which ye also walked aforetime, when ye lived in these things." In heathenism they lived in an atmosphere which was pollution. And then they participated in these sins. If in this fact there was danger of their being decoyed hack to their former ways under false representations, on the other hand there was strength to be got from realizing how much they had benefited by the change from heathenism to Christianity. ln their present joys aucl habits (for which they were indebted to Christ) they had wherewith to oppose temptations from their past. II. THESE AND OTHER SINS TO BE PUT Aw AY. " But now put ye also [as well as others rescued from heathenism] away all these." There seems to be a retrospective as well as a prospective reference in the injunction. 'l'he other sins are in two classes. 1. Sins of temper. "Anger, wrath, malice." The first describes a more settled, tho second a more eruptive, state of onr feeling against others. They are to be conclemned (l) when they are accompanied with want of self-possession; (2) when they are accompanied with want of reasonable ground; (3) when they are accompaniecl with malice or anything like delight in the evil condition of others. When these elements are wanting, they are not to be condemned, but need to be carefully watched. 2. ,',ins of speech. "Railing, shameful speaking out of your mouth." Railing is speaking nbnsively (it may not be clamorously) against others. This is to be condemned when it is accompanied with foulness of speech (shameful speaking). The mouth should not be prostituted to such uses, "Lie not one to another." \Ve are not even to lie to ourselves. We are not to make ourselves believe that we a.re other (even wor8e) than we really are. \Ve are not to see things other than they really a.re. We are not to lie to others. \Ve are not to make it appear to them that we are other than we really arc. \Ve ore not to make them out to be other ( even better) than they re.lily are. \Vo are not to stnte things to be other than they really a.re. Wo are to put away all falsehood from our intercourse with others. Reason given for pulling away the last a11d all the sins that have been named. "Seeing that ye have put off the oltl ma.u with his doings." Our ol,\ condiLion is personified as "the ol<l. man." His doings have been pointed to, In baptism we put off the old man with his doings. We must not be o.s though unregenerate. We must have nothing to do with practices the time of which is past. 111. Tm: PUTTING ON rn THE NEW LIFE. "A.nd have put on the new man." Our recent condition is personified as "I.he new mo.n." There is u prefacing with two important stateme11ts. l. There u a distinctly defined renew,1l constantly going on. " Which is being renewed uuto knowledge after t.he imnge of him that created him." It may be said that Christ perfected the now condition fur us. As appropriated by us, it is in the way of a constant renewal of our life. A.s in a tree, so with us, with repeated cndoavours there ever results fresh accession of life. 'l'he eud of the renewal is !Jore said to be knowledge, 'rhe false teachers claimed wisuom, claimed by their philosophy to give the power to know. The apostle shows how knowledge was to be come to. Ho thinks of it as the terminus of a long process of renewal. It is the wortl which means tlwrough knowle,lgo, i.e. of God nnd redotnption. There is thus accordance 186 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [011, III, l-2G. ------. ---------------------------- with the grcnt stntc~ent, "And this. is lire eternal, that they should know thee the onl_Y true God, and h11u whom thon didst send, even Jesus Christ." There is nothino foreign to our nature in this renewal. God made us in his owu imarre, He <lcsi.,ned a renewal to go forward in us nccording to a God-liko type. Ho designed in° our renewal that we should come to the thorough knowledge of himself. And this is what redemption effects for us. 2. In respect of this renewal earthly distinctions are of no imp,•·tance. "Where there cannot be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircum- ci~ion, bnrbnrian, Scythian, bondman, freeman : but Christ is all, and in all." There is a parallel passage in Gal. iii, 28. The first distinction there (" neither Jew nor Greek") may be said to cover the first three distinctions here, Distinction is denied as to nationality(" Greek and Jew"). Distinction is denied as to religious position ("circum- cision and nncircumcision "). Distinction is denied as to culture; and here the apostle docs not take the extremes of culture; but more strikingly takes those who to the cultured Greeks were barbarians, and to them opposes the Scythians who were barbarians to the barbarians. Distinction is denied as to social sto.tus (" bond man, freeman"), which distinction had significance in the early Christian Churches, from the number of slaves connected with them, and had special significance in the Colossio.n Church, from the conversion of a Colossian slave still with the apostle at Rome. There is not, and cannot be, any of these distiuctions. In Galatians the apostle teaches that there are no distinctions on the ground of our sonship in Christ. Here he teaches that there are no distinctions (in keeping with the thought of the pre-eminence of Christ) on the ground of Christ being all o.nd in all in the great renewal. (l) Christ is all in the renewed. The great need of our nature is to be renewed, o.nd Uhrist fully meets that need. He gives the whole contents and form to our renewal. United to Christ by faith, we become receptacles of Christ. 'Ihe pleroma dwells in him, and that pleroma floods our being with light, with strengtb, with purity, with all things. Renewed only from Christ, our life manifests itself only in Christio.n forms. (2) Ghrist is all in all the renewed. Men were broken up into classes, castes. The Jew drew back from the uncircumcised; the Greek despised the barbo.rian; the barbarian despised the Scytbian ; the freeman despised the bondman. The apostle points to the fact that the great renewal takes place in all alike. Alike in being creo.ted in the image of God, they are also alike in tbe renewal tho.t takes place on that ground o.nd according to tho.t fact. The poor Scythian can be filled full and beautified in the possession of Christ as well as the Greek, the bondman as well as the freeman. Jn view of this essential identity, all these earthly distinctions become of no account.-R. F.

entries.title: COL 3:12–17
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
- Wnat particularly we are to put on. How we are addressed. "Put on therefore, as God's elect, holy and beloved." The Colossinn Christians had been elected by God out of a state of heathenism. By arrangements over which they hacl exercised no control, the gospel had been brought to them and had been the means of their conversion. As elected by God, they were consecro.ted to God and ~ere in the e11joyment of the Divine love. The Colossian Christians were not except10nal. We ha,·e been elected by God out of the ungodly state of our own hearts and out of the ungodly influences tliat more or less prevail in a semi-Christian state of society.. ~'hus brono-ht into a true Christian state, and in that. sto.te devoted to God, and the recipients ,,f ~ny tokens of the Divine favour, it becomes us to feel the force of it in reference to our duty. I. 'l'rrE CHRISTIAN FOP.MB oF LOVE. The concluding representation is that all are bound together by love. 1. "A heart of compassion." In the ?rigi~al there is indicated the supposed seat of the sympathetic feelings. In heathemsm 1t was rather a heart of cruelty that was worn. 'l'he weak were down-tr9dden and neglected._ The soCtening influence of Chri,tianity appeo.rs in our hospitals _and asylums, ~~ our a bborrence of oppression, in the missiono.ry enterprise. '£here 1s a fine sens1 b1h ty to the miseries of others in those who have felt the Divine cornpnssions toward them. Especially are we to feel the sorrows of our fellow-Christians. 2. "Kindness." We rnay show kiudness where there is nothing to draw forth compassion. Under all circumstances are we to be kinO', There is nothing which we can wear outwardly to be compared with kindness. "Kind hearts are more than coronets." Kindness is tho disposition to think about others. It adds greatly to the joy of their existence to let

them ~eo (even in Jitlle ways) that we arc not forgetting them, but are giving them a place in our thoughts. As God's holy and beloved, we a.re to be the vehicles of thn Divine thoughtfulnes.q, 3. "Humility." As a Christian grace, humility is founded upon the fact of our having humbled ourselves before God as sinners. As a form of love, it is the disposition which forbids us to exalt ourselves over others. It is a. form of selfishness simply to wish to give others a sense of our importance and of their unimportance. Rather does love impel us to sink our own importance and to prefer them. 4. "Meekness." This is founded on the fact of God being the First Cause of the provocation received from others. As a form of love, it is the disposition which prompts us to endure rather than retaliate on those who have wronged us. 5. "Longsujfering." This is founded on the fact of God having suffered loop: and much with u~. As a form of love, it is the disposition which forb:ds us to weary of the good of others. It is enduring in hope. 6. " Forbearing one another." Forbearance seems to be the practical exhibition of the last disposition. It is implied that we all need to have forbearance exercised toward us, as well as to exercise forbearance ourselves. 7. "And forgiving each other, if any man have a complaint against any." It is here "each olher," with a look forward to the thought of our being all first forgiven by Christ. Just, cause of complaint has already been supposed. How are we, as just complainants against a brother, to act? We are not merely to endu~e and to endure for his good, but we are to advance to positive forgiveness. That is to say, in love we are to remove the complaint, so that it is as though it had never been. The highest example of forgiveness. "Even as the Lord forgave you, so also do ye." The Lord had just complaint against us; who shall estimate what it was? But he carried out a work for us the purport of which was the removal of the complaint. That we have appropriated, and now we are in the position of those from whom complaint has been removed. Forgiveness is usually associated with God, but in this Epistle, in which prominence is given to the Person of Christ, it is associated with him. The fact of Christ being called here "the Lord" points to the fact that, as his servants, we are bound by his example. lf the Lord has so acted, servants must not nurse their wrath. The seven graces bound together by love. "And above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectaess." '!'here is the perfect number, and they are bound in the bond of perfectness. Love is thought of as the girdle which binds the garments which have been put on. i.Ne have seen its presence in all the seven. 'l'hey are simply love in seven different relations. 'l'here is thus no looseness a.boat them, but they constitute a perfect whole. II. THE CamSTIA..'I FORllI OF CONCORD. "And let the peace of Christ rule in yonr hearts, to the which also ye were called in one body." The peace which i~ the l)rinciple of concord is distinctively the peace of Christ. That is to say, it is the peace which Christ possessed and which he lclt as a legacy to his disciples. He possessed 1\ holy feeling of tranquillity in view of death and under the wrongs which were heaped upon him, in the enjoyment of his Father's Jove and in the conscious and complete c,urying out of his Father's purposes of love toward mrn. And this holy feeling of tranquility it is intended that wo too should have, in nil circumstances (in our case based on the atonement), in the enjoyment of our Father's love and in the conscious endeavour to carry out his pmposes of love. The peace of Christ is to rule in our hearts. In the margin it is "arbitrate." And some have thought the menninp: to be that, between contending feelings, the peace of Christ is to act as umpire. But the meaning seems simply to be that it is to rule so as to put down all disquictinp: feeling, nnd so that we have it toward God and toward all around us. 'l'he one body is hem thought of as a society in which all are called to a holy feeling of satisl'action. It is, therefore, n society in which concord (out of a Christian ground) reigns. "And be ye thankful." 'l'his is the recurrence of what has been noticed as a subordinate fcatnre in the Epistle. What we are to bo thankful for is the trnnquility which makes concord. III. 'l'HE CHnISTIAN FORMS OF RELIGIOUS EXERCISE. 1. The reception of the Word. "Let the Word of Christ dwell in yon richly in all wisdom." 'l'he Word also is <l.is- tinctively the Wor<l. of Christ. That is to say, it is the Word which Christ spake a1Hl which he caused to be proclaimed. It may be taken as including inspired additions. 'l.'here is a great richness in tho Word of Christ. It contnins all the thoughts that aro needed to give us peace, guidnnce, strengthening, heartening, umlcr earthly conditions. "\Vo arc to receive it to bo our l'C'rmanent possession. Wo arc to receive it, not scant, ly, 188 THE EPISTLE 'l'O TIIE COLOSSIANS. [en. m. 1-25.

but in all ,'ts richness. We are to receive it in all wisdom, that is, in all wise appre- hension of its meaning, and not in the way of false interpretation. 2. Christian song. In Ephesians this is introduced as a counteractive of false excitement as one of the manifestations of a true excitement of the Spirit. Here it is introduced 'as the result of the indwellin2; of the Word of Christ. It was out of no cold heart, but out of a heart of summer gladness, that the \Vord of Christ came, and, received into us it wells up in all joyful feelings which find expression in song. (1) Re11ponsive song. ' "Teachino- and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual son"s." 'l'h~ historic psalms and other compositions used in the service of praise which"are called hymns, fall under the head of" spiritual songs." In Ephesians the idea of responsivenesH was brought out in the words" speaking one to another." Here it is said more definitely "teaching and admonishing one another." The principal purpose of song is to enliven. Ilnt the apostle here teaches, that it is not aside from its principal purpose to teach and admonish. And this subsidi~ry didactic, monitory purpose it is fitted to serve from its being the outcome of the Word of Christ. (2) Silent song. "Sin.,ino- with grace in your hearts unto God." This singing is only in the ear of God. Our ~tLer exercises arc heard by God too. For it is said, "Then they that feared the Lord spake often one to another: and the Lord hearkened, and heard it." But this is for self-edification, with God as the only listener. It is singing with grace, not with gracefulness, but with the grace that preserves from vanity, from extravagance, and enriches with all Christian elements. IV. THE CnRrsTIAN FORM OF SPEAKING AND ACTING. "And whatsoever ye do, in word or in deed, do all in the Name of the Lord Jesus." '!'his, like the others, is associated with Christ. His being called "Jesus" points to his having been a sp<iaker and doer in human nature himself. The meaning is, not that we are formally to invoke the Name of Christ in connection with our speaking and doing. But they are to be according to the rules laid down by Christ and as unto Christ. They will thus be redeemed from all mere naturalness and all sinful elements that mix with them, and will have a richness as from the Word of Christ. "Giving thanks to God the Father through him." 'l'his is again the refrain of the Epistle, with a certain prominence. Our thanksgivings are ·to be unto the Father. We are to give thanks through Christ as Mediator. It is only through him that we have leave to thank God. It is only through him that we have anything to thank God for. It is through him that all the blessings of salvation come to us; and so it is through him that we are to thank God for them.-R. F.

Ver. 18--ch. iv. !.-Relative duties. The two considerations on which the apostle's treatment of the relative duties here seems to be based are these: 1. The position of authority is also rel,a,tively, by Divine constitution, the stronger position. 2. Christ is to be regarded as represented in the position of authority. 'l'hroughout the paragrnph he is designated in respect of his authority. That there may be no doubt about the reference, it is expressly stated, in the twenty-fourth verse, that Christ is Lord. I. WIVES A?rn nusBANDS. 1. Wives. "Wives, be in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord." The wife has the weaker position. "The weaker vessel" is the language used by Peter. She is more delicately constituted, and is not so fitted t-0 fi"lit her way in the world. She is made to lean upon her husband, and therefore it is fittin"' that in her duty she should fall into a certain subordination to him. This is not o~ly fitting in itself, but it is fitting in the Lord. That is to say, it is Christ who is over her in her husband. If, then, she is a Christian wife, she has more than her husband to regard in the relation. She will be willing to be directed by Christ in her ]rnsband. 2. Husbands. "Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them." The husband (" band of the house") has the stronger position. He is more robustly c0netituted. He has a bolder judgment. And so the controlling power has been placed in him. Dut that does not point to his using it for selfish ends. Christ, as the Head of the Clrnrch, as is brought out in Ephesians, used his position only to love the Church :,nd to give himself up for it.a deliverance. So it !B t~e duty of the husband, as the represeutative of Christ in the relation, to love his wife and to protect her weakness with his strength. lie is not to be a despot, putting bitterness into his strength against his wife ;-that would be utterly inconsistent with acting in the Name of CbrM. orr. m. 1-25.J THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 189

II. CIIILDREN AND PARENTS. 1. Children. "Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well-pleasing in the Lord." Children are at first utterly helpless. And for a long time they are dependent on their parents. Especially, in their inexperience, are they dependent on the experience of their parents. That points to their being obedient to their parents. The principle is, as stated here, obedience ir. all thing.•, there being no exception to it in the mere pleasure of the child. In Ephesians the rule is grounded on its being right. The rule for the wife, we have seen, is grounded on its being.filling. The rule for children here is grounded on its being well-pleasing. That is to say, it is a beautiful thing to see children subjecting their impulses, their wishes, their plans, to the better judgment, riper experience, of their parents. It is a beautiful thing to see them rendering prompt and universal obedience. This is not only beautiful in itself, but it is beautiful in the Lord. That snproses that they have given them• selves to the Lord. In that case they will regard their parents as given them by the Lord. And not only so, but they will regard them as in the place of the Lord lo them. It is pre-eminently a beautiful thing when children learn to reverence and obey their parents, not simply as their parents, but as placed over them by Christ. 2. Parents. "Fathers, provoke not your children, that they be not discouraged." Parents (for we are to think of the whole ruling power relative to the children) have the stronger position. There is great disparity at first for purposes of rule. But they are not to use their position to provoke their children. That is the coarse way of ruling. The ro<l, though necessary at times, is not to be the substitute for reason. It is also generally the selfish way. Parents cannot take pains with their children. They cannot bear with their dulness. They have not the patience to deal with their self-will so as to have it overcome. They cannot bear to have their liberty curtailed, their comfort disturbed, by their children. And so they passionately, tyrannically, carry out their pleasure on their children. That is not only to be condemned in itself, but it is especially to be condemned in those who should regard themselves as the representatives of Christ to their children. Christ does not act harshly to men. He does not act harshly to them. And therefore they should not act harshly to their children. 'l'he effects are, as might be expected, bad. The children are discooraged. Youth is the time of hopefulness. With the wakening of the powers hopes spring forth. And parents have carefully to watch over the calling forth of the powers of their children. It is allimportant that these be directed in a Christian way. But children ,1,re easily discouraged. 'l'hey lose heart before the difficulties connected with following out useful and Christian aims. And they need to have many words of encouragement spoken to them. 'l'hey need to be shown what they can do. But to give them no encouragement, to treat them as though they were incapable of anything great, to heap reproaches on them, to punish them harshly, is to crush the life out of them. The breaking of the spirit is said to be the bane of youth. III. SERVANTS AND MASTERS. 1. Servants. (1) Rule. "Servants, obey in nll things them that are your masters according to the flesh." The slave was entirely at the mercy of his master. God never intended any one to be in thnt position. The servant with whom we have now to do occupies a very different position--still, however, the weaker position in the relation. And as for childrcu, so for servants, the rule is obedience in all things. 'l'hat is to say, within the proper sphere of work there is no exception founded on the mere pleasuro of the servant. When it is said that obedienco is to be rendered to them that are masters according to the flesh, there is I\ suggestion, though yet only a suggestion, of a relation to a higher Master. (2) Principle. "Not with eye-service as men-pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing the Lord." The principle is not men-pleasing, or regard simply for the human master. 'l'hat is not fitted to be a principle, for it proceeds on a variable element. It requires no more than eye-service, or as it is here (:s distinguished from Ephesians), acts of eye-service. The eye of the master cannot always be on the servant. If, then, the servant is regulated by the eye of the mast~r, his work must vary accordingly, being sometimes well done, sometimes ill done, and sometimes not done at all. The principle is fearing tho Lord, or regard for the Divine Master. We are not to understand regard for the authority of Christ in general, but regard for the authority of Christ as rei'resented in the master, even in the slave-master. 'l'his is fitted to be law universal. For the eye of Christ, being all-seeing, is always on the servant. There is thus cxcluu.ed duplicity; thore is 190 TilE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [ea. m. 1-25.

rcqnir~d singleness of service, or the eye always on Christ in the work done. (3) Quality. "\Vhatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord,and not unto men." If tbe slarn looked away to the Lord beyond his master, then, whatsoever he did, whether it ,ms work great or small, oppressive or not oppressive, he could do it not only with a. sense of freedom, but co~d~ally. C~rist regarding his work and entering thoroughly into 1t, he could do 1t from his 10most bemg. And so when a. Christian servant falls in with a ba~ master,_he is not at liberty,_as ui:ught here, to do his work grudgingly. He has lh1s reason 10 :my case for heart10ess 10 the work, that he is rendering it to One who is worthy. (4) Encouragement. "Knowing that from tho Lord ye shali receive the rcc0rr:pcnse of the inheritance: ye serve the Lord Christ." This was a new .order of things, a new field of thought, for the slave. A serv:mt rightly considers himself entitled to payment for his labour. The slave was entitled too; but he was not accus- tomed to look for payment. Certainly he never thought of being recompensed with an inheritance. In the eye of the law he could not hold an inheritance. He was only property himself. And yet here, as a freeman in Christ Jesus, it is promised that he "·ould have an inheritance. This was nothing less than the inheritance promised down the ages to tha people of God-the inheritance without any subtraction from it-. This he would receive at the hands of the Rewarder of his servants. He was defrauded all his days of the just reward of his labour; but the Lord would see to bis beina recom- pensed, and in better kind. The Lord whom he served was no tyrant, but th~ Christ who had died for bondman as well as for freeman. And so the Christian servant can make sure of being recompensed. It should be a. pleasure to serve the Lord Christ now. It should be a pleasure to serve him even without thought of reward. But the Lord Christ is of liberal mind, and will see to all hearty work being rewarded. And if the heartiness has been overlooked on earth, the reward will only be the greater in heaven. (5) Warning. " For he that doeth wrong shall receive again for the wrong that he bath done : and there is no respect of persons." If a. servant gives eye-service to his master, or in any form wrongs him, it is not to be supposed that the Lord Christ will overlook the wrong. There will be a receiving again for the wrong that he hath done, It will be so much taken from the final reward. Christ is partial neither to servant nor to master, and, in the final righting that is to take place between the two, it will be seen that bis face is set only against wrong-doing. 2. Masters. "Masters, render unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven." The master has the stronger position; but that is only that he may use his position for the sake of the weaker. He is to render to his servant that which is just, that which does not depend on his pleasure, but is grounded on the eternal order of thiogs. .And beyond the just he is to render to him that which is equal. In Ephesians it is said that he is to do the same thiQgs. The meaning seems to be that, as the servant is required to give him hearty work, so he is required; on his part, to give considerate treatment. Such equality is becoming in a Christian master. For he also has a Master in heaven. The servant is to give hearty work out of regard to that Master. Out of regard to the same Master he is to give considerate treatment. 'J'hat Master is considerate toward him; he is to be considerate toward him who has been JJbced by Christ under him as a servant.-R. F.

entries.title: COL 3:1–4
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The Christian's higher life. Our text gives us a magnificent picture of the higher life of man, indicating the means of its beginning, the signs of its progress, and the hope of its perpetuity. I. Tm~ EXPERIENCES OF THE BEGINNING OF THE HIGHER LIFE. These initial experiences are spoken of under the three allied figures of death, the hiding as of burial, and resurrection. There is an experience: 1. .As of death. "Ye have died." The soul as it becomes Christian passes through a death with Christ-(1) a death to sin, (2) a death to the bondage of outwardness. Dead, yet alive !-the ryaradox that finds its counterpart in the gardener's insertion of_ t~e vi~e shoot, that va~ ~ut off an~ so d~nd to its old stock under the bark of the living vine. 2. .As ri/ hiding away m burial. "llid." That 'may mean (1) what is concealed now will °Jo revealed by-and-by; or (2) it may denote a lifo of much blessed solitude, and ·,o of sacred seclusion; or (3) it may IJ1ean a life of fellowship with the hidden Chr:st; or ( 4) it may tell of a life whos1: i,urposes and inspirntiuus arc bid iu Go<l. ~. As of resurrection, "Risen.'' OH, m, 1-25.] TtlE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 101

'l'hat must indicate (1) a living life, such a life as Ezekiel portmys, " I will open your graves, and give you a new heart, a heart of flesh;" and (2) an elevated life. No more of the carth......earthy, no more grave-clothes, sepulchre, and earth-worms, bnt such beauty and activity and blessedness as belong to the scenes of Christ's forty days' risen life. II. THE DUTY OF THE HIGHER LIFE. The duty is twofold, and the way of obeying is twofold also. 1. 'l'he twofold duty of the higher life. (1) The withdrawal of chief concern from inferior things. "Set not your affections," etc. Does not this mean, cease to entwine your affections round the things of time, cease to concentrate your energies on the things of this world? So far we have only the negative aspect of dnty; but, there is: (2) 'l'hc fixing of chief interest on superior things. They arc twice spoken of here as" things above;" and may they not-denote what is above socia,ly, intellect-ually, spiritually? 2. The twofold method of attaining the performance of this duty. (1) "Seek the things that are above." Let the hi 6her things be the object of pursuit. What higher things? Plato would have said, "The true, the beautiful, the good." Most modem Christians, meaning the same, would have said, "Heaven." And Paul, meaning the same, would have said, "Christ." For surely Christ is heaven and heaven is Christ. Well, therefore, does Bishop Pearson urge, "Rise to Christ with the wings of your meditation and in the chariot of your affections." (2) " Set your affections on things that are above," Not only seek heaven, but think heaven; not only think heaven, but love heaven. Our life cannot rise into I\ higher realm of itself any more than a bar of iron can lift itself. Both have capacity of response, Christ is the magnet to uplift our natures. Love him, and the love of him lifts up. III. THE DESTINY OF THE HIGHER LIFE. In the fourth verse we have the onwanl aspect of the higher life, 1. There is to be a complete manifestation of this higher life. Paul has said now it is "hid," then it will be unveiled; now it is buried, then it will be "risen." Because of misunderstandings, and misconceptions, and harsh judgments of others, the "higher life" is now often hid; then all will be explained, interpreter!, rectified. Because now that life is so often in itself distorted, confused, it is partially "hid;" then in ease and naturalness and grace it will gloriously "appear." 2. 1'he perfect revelation of this life will be in perfect m1ion with (Jhrist. (1) How? Because he is the Origin and Sustenance, the Life of man's own inner higher life. (2) When'? No calendar can fix the date. It will be the time of his appearing; and that will be to the ages ns his incarnation was-" the fulness of the times." (3) What? The glory we shall have will be his glory. That is the glory of purity, simplicity, victory, sacri- fice, love. The paragraph we have thus considered names Christ four times. Our model is Christ's death; our strength is Christ's risen life; our heaven is Christ's glory ; our hope is Christ's coming. "Yea, thro' life, death, thro' sorrow nnd thro' sinning He ehe.11 suffice me, for he he.th sufficed • Christ is the End, for Christ was the Beginning; Christ the Beginning, for the End is Christ," U. R. T. Vere, li-11.-Death to evil. 'l'he centml thought around which the strange and striking ideas of these sentences gather is" Death to evil." St. P,rnl e:,;horts us to put evil to death, to make n corpse of it. Here we have truly "More janua vitro." \Ve inquire- !. IN WHAT THIS DEATH CONSISTS. "Put to death your members which are upon the earth." The meaning seems to be the same as Christ's command, "If thine eye offend thee, pluck it out," etc. Neither Christ's nor Paul's injunction can mean hack, hew, maim, the limbs and organs of the body. For that is contradicted by such other teaching as" Yield your members as the instruments of righteousness;" aud such disablina of limbs aud organs would be useless, for the dumb can be profane, and tho blind h~stful, and the crippled dishonest. "Out of the heart proceeds evil." TI.to fiaure in the injunction of our te:,;t may be that which the whole context suggests, n~mely, put these members to death, so far as evil practices are concerned; be as dead to them. Or the figure may have reference to that which describes the entire sinful chara.cter as "the old man "-an olu man having limbs, organs, etc., here calle,I member$. 192 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [ml. JJI. 1-25.

So thcs!' physical members are but symbols of the morn!. Anyhow, there is olenrly cnjoin<'d here: 1. Death to corrupt livi11g. This corrupt living is diYidcd her11 into t~rn classes-impurity nnd covetousness. 'l'hese divided betw!'en them include the whole domain of sin and 8el_fishness. Covetousne~s,. wl)ich. is cherished by mnny who ha Ye the repute of respectab1!1ty and even of Chnst1amty, 1s so base, so loathsome so irreligious, that it is here linked with hideous uncleanness, and is distinctly decl;red to be idolatrous. Avarice becomes the worldling's religion; greed of gain the miser's worsl1ip. Evils such as these, and on which the apostle says God's wrath rC'sts, must be slain. 2. Death to w,-ong conversation. Paul deals with the sins of speech which sceme,l, like C'Chocs of the past, to linger on the lips of the Colossians. 'l'hey nre to Jl'.lt off (1) "an_ger,"_i.e. se~tl!'d hatrecl; (2) "wrath," i.e. tumultuous outburst of pass10n; (3) "mahcc," i.e. mal1gn1ty, spitefulness; (4) "blasphemy" i.e. slanderin" • (5) "foul-mouthed abuse," i.e. all such rough speech as now is know~ a.s the Billin"~~ gate of social, political, or theological controversy ; (6) "falsehood," a word, alas! that needs no description. All these six evils of speech are to be slaiu. 3. Death to con- ventional distinctions. The special errors that we have seen were prevalent at Colossai \\"ere those that primarily led Paul to deal with this evil. Four conventional distinc- tions that, wherever they separate men's interests or destroy their mutual sympathies, must be slain, are here described. (1) National distinctions: "Greek and Jew.'' (2) C'erernonia.l : "circumcision or uncircumcision.'' (3) Distinctions of culture: "bar- barian, Scythian.'' Max Millier finely shows how, until Christianity inserted the word "brother" instead of" barbarian," as descriptive of humanity, there was no science of language. (4) Social: "bond and free.'' 'l'here seems to be special referenco here to the rnnaway slave who was going to carry to his master the apostle's letter, and who was to be received as a brother both of Philemon and Paul. II. How THIS DEATH rs TO BE EFFECTED. Evil does not die of itself, but must be slain. Nor docs it die easily; it must be strug~led with. It is to be put to death: I. By huma,n endeavour. " Put to death.'' You are wrestler in some tragic game, soldier in the momentous battle, executioner in the solemn judgment; therefore you must throw your opponent, stay your enemy, bang or gibbet the culprit. Here is abundant and righteous scope for all our fighting instincts. 2. By Divine renewal. " Which is renewed.'' The death of the old is ensured by the life ot' the new; just a.s old leaves a.re pushed off the boughs and branches by the young vegetation of spring, so the old character is displaced by the new. This power is (1) Divine; (2) constantly put forth; (3) according to Divine ideal-" after the image of him that created him.'' Christ the Ideal is Christ the Source of all. He is in the renewed man a.s the germ of life, whose outbursting, as by one blow, kills evil, and whose constant development insures all good.-U. R. T.

entries.title: COL 3:12–17
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
- 71ze marks, TMthod, and motive of the Christian life. This paragraph is part of the practical application of the great principle St. Paul has been expounding in this chapter, viz. the Christian's death to evil through the death of Christ, and life to holiness through bis life. We have here- 1 THE MARKS oF THE CHRISTIAN LIFE. When the Christian life is illustrated, as here, by a garment, the analogy must not be pressed too far, For instance, unlike a garment, the Christian ehara.cter is not (1) merely outside a man, nor (2) separable from a man. But that character is like a. garment: 1. Deca.use by it a man is known and rrxognizable. 2. Because by it a. man is adorned. Tl:crc are in Paul's description eight characteristics by which, as by a beautiful garment, the Christian man is recognizablo and is adorned. (1) "Bowels of mercies," which we may paraphrase as "a. heart of compassion." .Anthropologists largely judge what physical race a man be!ongs to Ly his skull; the Christian must judge what race a man belon~s to by his heart. T811der-hea.rtcdness is a sign of the Christian a.s certainly as truthfulness, or temperance, or honesty. (2) "Kindness:" this is the constant, steady, often noiseless, but al ways beneficent, stream flowing from such a heart. (3) " Meekness ; " for whilst the aposLle sternly condemns mock humility, which the pietistic among the Colossinns had affected, be ri~orously insists on that self-humiliation without which no roan can be reckoned a. follower of the meek and lowly Jesus. (4) ••Long-suffering:" this is a temper of life described iu the beautiful_ word "patience,'' cu,ri it indicates freedom frolJ). the OU, m.1-25.] THE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. 193

intellectual impatience which makes men proud and restive, and from the emotional impatience which makes men fretful and irritable. (5) "Forbearance and forgivingness," which need no description. (6) "Charity;" the love that girdles and holds together all the graces. (7) "Peace of Christ;" which is the peace Christ gives, and is like the peace he possesses. (8) "Thankfulness;" gratitude to God and to one another, which implies a whole catalogue of virtues. II. THE METHOD OF ATTAINING THE CHRISTIAN LIFE. The method here described is threefold. 1. Ohrist's dealing with us. "Let the Word of Christ dwell in you richly." "The Word of Christ." By this we understand: (1) The vVord that came from Christ to us. That Word is not to pass away, but to "dwell" in us. (2) 'l'he Word that spoke of him. Whether it were in Scripture prophecy, parable, or statement, it unveiicd Christ to us. That vision is not to pass away, but to "dwell" in us. (3) The Word that Christ himself speaks. He communes with us in the secret chambers of our soul, and what his still, small voice says to us there about pardon, duty, God, must not pass away; it must dwell there. (4) 'l'he Word is indeed Christ himself. He is theuttere<l thought, the expressed love from God to our soul. He must dwell in us. 2. Our words to one another. We only gain ourselves as we help others. vVe must communicate what we have received if we are to become strong. ( l) We are to tench. (2) vV e arc to admonish. Of this there are many ways. One is here described by" psalms and hymn~ and spiritual songs." 3. Our word to God. "Singing with grace in your hearts to tho Lord." '!'here must be the outpouring of the heart to God. III. THE MOTIVE INSPIRING CHRISTIAN LIFE. 1. Here is the widest description of the Christian life. It covers "word and deed." 2. Here is the deepest motive of the Christian life. "The Name of the Lord Jesus." It is the Name of him who brings God near, who is the Reconciliation of all things to God, So that what is truly done in the Name of Christ brings the world near God, lifts up human nature into fellowship with God. No wonder that Paul adds, for all this let there be" giving of thanks." 'l'he Christian life ought to•he a eucharist.-U. R. 'l'.

entries.title: COL 3:18–21
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The Christian view of family life. The spirit which wa.. abroad in the early Colossian Church was at once so ascetic and so pietistic that it underval netl home, depreciated family ties, despised human relationships. We have heard Paul boldly meet this spirit with the great doctrine that Christ is the Fulness of all things, Sustainer of all, Mediator of all, King of all, End of all. Here, and in preceding paragraphs, he is meeting detailed developments of that evil spirit by detailed precepts flowing out of that great doctrine of Christ the Fulness. In our text the apostle teaches what we may group around three points. I. TRE DUTmB OF FAMILY LIFE ARE RECIPROCAL, He addresses first one and then another of the group in a home, He does not speak of them or describe them to one another, but sharply, smartly, directly, he turns to each with the summons," Ye." And thus he summons each to the task of his own duty, the fulfilment of his own obligation, As in some noble antiphon the singers take up their alternative parts, so in the music of home life the members of the family respond with their alternative duties, Between husband and wife, parent and child, the only truly Christian relllLion- ship is that of inter-dependence and of reciprocity. II. TRE PBIN0IPLEB TO GUIDE FAJIIILY LIFE ARE SIMPLE AND YET SUFFICIENT, The statement of the principles here does not seem intended to be exhaustive. Sorue parallel passages to the Ephesians are much more complete. But the principles here noted are specimens. They are moral samples of what must actuate family life. And they are simple enough. Nothing grand, romantic, or impossible. "Wives, submit." '!'his cannot mean where conscience protests. It must rather indicate where taste or opinion differ. Defer rather than strive. " Husbands, love." '!'his great king-word" love" ( which Paul explains in 1 Cor. xiii.) claims from the husband what Christ gives to the Church- his all. And one injunction of that lovo will be "Be not bitter," i.e. rough, rude. Many a courtier in society is uncouth as a hear at home. '!'hen he is not a Ghristian husband after this model. "Children, obey." Cultivate the spirit in which the chil,l Jesus went down to NazareLh, and was subject to his parents. Such a going down prepares for the true exaltation; such subjection qualities for sub,equ~nt sovereignty. "Fathers, provoke not," Avoid the harsLuc,s, aod even the though tlcs:i c::i:.actiuus from COLOSSLU\8, U THE EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [cH, III, 1-25,

your children by which their spirits will become sullen, hopeless, moody. They will want spirits that parents have helped to make buoyant, not that pa.rents have broken. III. THE MOTIVE FOR FULFILLING TllE DUTIES OF FAMILY LIFE IS DIVINE, Whilst secondary motives are thus given to fathers, etc., we find in the pa.ssa.o-e the highest motive is a.gain and ..gain pressed. "In the Lord," " Well-pleasing to the Lord " " As unto the Lord," etc. Such a life a.s Paul described can only be achieved by the force of sufficient motive. And such motive he supplies, Here is argument enough for such a course of conduct, inspiration enough for such a spirit of family life. "In the Lord." There is a wonderful fulness of meaning in that phrase, as the Greek language employed it. But not a profounder fulness than the Christian experience interprets when it shows Jesus to be the Source of motive, the Standard of duty, the ,ery Sphere of being to the Christ-loving ma.n.-U. R. T.

entries.title: COL 3:22–25
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Religious regulations for master and servant. The length of the paragraph on this topic is probably partly the result of Paul's having then and there so much to do with Onesimus, the runaway slave whom he was sending ha.ck to his master. "Bought and adopted and in Christ a brother; claimed and complete\i, and in Christ a man." But besides this personal reason, Paul must have felt -that there was, in the state of the Colossian society of the time, an urgent need for_ this lengthy and detailed description of duty. And is there not now? Are not masters and servants in England failing in their reciprocal duties very largely because they are expecting, as Dr. Chalmers said, "universal selfishness to do the work of universal love"? Therefore we may well notice-- L THE CHARACTERISTICS OF A TRUE SERVANT'S SERVICE, It is •marked by: 1. Obedience. Engaged for given duties, do them. Refusal to do them, neglect in doing thern, is immoral, irreligious, You cannot be a good Christian and a bad servant. 2. Thoroughness. Not "eye-service." This happy expression is probably the apostle's coinage. It describes obedience that is superficial, inconstant, hollow. 3, Simplicity of motive. "Singleness of heart." Not having two purposes nor secondary aims. 4. Earnestness. "Do it heartily." Whatsoever ye do, work at it. The lazy and lethargic are repulsive, the enthusiastic are noble. II. THE CIIARACTEB.ISTICS OF A TRUE MASTER'S MASTERSHIP, The duties of a master are as clearly enforced as those of the servant, "The same light attempers various colours; so the same principle regulates various duties." There is claimed from the master: 1. Justice. That is, what the law demands, what is legally right and square. There is, however, much more, 2. Equity. "What is equal." Equity is more than law, more than legal claim. It is a. liberal interpretation of justice in common matters; a response to the intuition of what is right, even though no law defined it or enforced it. It was this teaching about equity that was really the insertion of the leaven that has destroyed slavery in Christendom. What is the touchstone of this equity? Surely this golden rule, "Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even the same to them likewise." ill THE MOTIVES BOTH OF TBUE SERVICE AND OF TRUE MABTERBHIP. The motives put before both masters and servants are two. 1. They both sustain a common relationship to Glwist. (1) All are his servants. Servants, "Ye serve the Lord Christ;" masters "Ye also have a Master in heaven," (2) All work is done .in his sight. 'l'herefo~e do it "fearing God." , (3) All may be done for his glory. "There is _no respect of per~ons." 2. Christ_ will_ 1·ightly deal out r~tribution and rew_ard. With Christ is "the reward of the inheritance." From Chnst men shall receive for "the wrong which they have done." Our conclusion is: I. Cherish a Christian ambition to serve well. 2. Cherish a Christian ambition to rule well.-U. R. T. ,,ers. I--4.-Present privileges: future glory. ~he apostle !30W proceeds to t~e application of the grand truths he has been expoundrn~. Note m what~ l~fty strain he begins.
