As in the previous section he refutes practical errors by remmdmg of the sublimest doctrines, so here, before giving exhortations_ ~n special sins a~d ?-u~ies, l~e bteeks to lift the Colossians to the heights of that new spmtual, heavenly hfe 1t 1s their pririlc;;e to live. (Like a commander encouraging his troops in tho field to u111intai.r OH, III, 1-25,] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 195

the striclest discipline by motives suggested by the purest patriotism and the dignity of their trust.) I. TaE CHRISTIAN'S PRESENT PRIVILEGES. 1. " Ye died." This figurative expression de~cribes the _c~mplet_e change ~h.ich takes pl~ce in th~se who are truly regenerated. It 1s most stnkmgly illustrated m the convers10n of an idolatrous or a profli"ate man. But eve_ry true convert dies to his former self, i.e. is separated from it as by a death and bunal. (Illustrate from Eccles. ix. 5, 6, 10.) As a Christian martyr, worn down by the sickness and pain of a long persecution, obtaias a blessed release and separation froDl this;present evil world by death, so is the Christian, by union with Christ, set free, as by a death aad burial, from two of his most formidable foes--the Law and sin. (1) We died to the Law (Rom. vii. 4, 6; Gal. ii. 19). We renounced all dependence on: works of Law and trusted for justification alone to the work of Christ. (2) W o <lied to sin. We were set free from the love of sin and are being set free from its power. Crucifixion, though fatal, was not immediately so. So our "old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away ("",,."P'Y7l8fi), that so we should no longer be in bondage to sin" (Rom. vi. 6, 14 ). "It wo.s the sight of thy dear cross First weaned my soul from earthly things," etc. 2. " Ye were raised together with Christ." (Eph. ii. 4-6; Gal. i. 4.) In the world, not of it. uWe dwell in the flesh, but do not live in the flesh" (Luther). The trne sphere of our life is "heavenly places." Does this seem mystical when spoken of tradesmen, eagine-drivers, or kitchen-maids? But if they are Christ's they have a life which is "hid with Christ in God." It is a still and secret life, hidden from the world. The Christian has a differep.t spirit (John xiv. 17) and aim (1 Cor. x. 31) and strength (Phil. iv. 13). He is like a palm tree in the desert, verdant and fruitful, because far beneath the sand the fibres of its roots are enjoying a hidden life of moisture which keeps the tree alive in spite of arid sand o.nd cloudless sky. 3. Ye may" seek" and "set your mind on the things that are above." Is not this a privilege as well as a duty? Reflect on the honour of being allowed to fix our best thoughts and our purest affections on persons and objects not at all affected by the change and disappointment aad lransitoriness of this world. (Like a sailor amid the hardships of a long winter voyage, whose thoughts and emotions are constantly turning to wife and children in his distant home. He does not need to be told," You ought to think of them; you must lovu them.") Who.t are "the things that are upon the earth"? Find tbe answer in 1 John ii. 16, 17. Thuy belong to a state from which we profess to have been conclusively delivered. Shall Lazarus take plea.sure in his grave-clothes or the healed demoniac in his fetters? Shall those who profess to b11 living a resurrection-life with Christ "mind earthly things"? Riches? (Ps. !xii. 10; Prov. xxiii. 5; 1 Tim. vi. 7). Worldly power or fame? (Ps. lxxiii. 18-20; Isa. xl. 6-8; Jo.s. i. 10, 11). Shall we cling to a sinking vessel when our home is in sight? If we find it hard to enjoy our privileges, let us take the following hiats. (1) Give more thought to "the things that are above "-to the great themes of God, Christ, heaven, eternity; and in the light of these, look down on the transitory trifles of this worhl. (2) Do more fur Christ, who, "seated on tile right hand of God," is doiag so much for us (Matt. vi. 33). (Illustrate Christ's manifold activities for his people in that heavenly world.) Recognize t.liat you have a citizenship in the heavenly places, and thereforo civic duties among them. (3) Make sacrifices for Christ and eternity. Treasure there as large a proportfon as your conscience will justify of money, time, and every talent you possess (Matt. vi. 19-21). II. THE CHRISTIAN'S FUTURE GLORY. (Ver. 4.) This follows from ver. 3. Concealment with Christ ensures safety. Our future is wrapped up with his (John xiv. 19). Our lifo is, as it were, deposited with Christ's life in the very sanctuary of the Godhead. God will not forget that trust (2 Tim. i. 12). Christ himself liveth in us and is our life. What is awaitiag Christ? A glorious mnuifestation (Titus ii. 13; cf. Acts iii. 21 and 1 Thess. i. 10). That manifestation will, by reason of tho identity of Christ and his servants, be the manifestation in glory of Christians also," the sons of God" (Rom. viii. 19). (Illustrate from contrasts suggested by lsa. Ix. H; Matt. xjii. 43; John xvii. !24.) Clirist is now conccalcrl, and it is our winlcr; his revelation Hl6 THE EPISTLE TO THE CULOSSIANS. [ou. m. 1-25.

will bring s11mmer to our souls (2 Thess. i. 10). The glory in which we shall be revealed was said by the schoolmen to consist of the robe of the soul and the robe of t.he bod;i:. }· Ther~ ~11 be glo:y for the soul. No more s~'!l. (1 John iii. 2), or sorrow (Rev. vu. l 1), or d1v1ded affections, or darkness (1 Cor. xm. 12; cf. Rev. x.xii. 3 4 • perfect service, perfect satisfaction, perfect security). 2. In that glory the body shali share (1 Cor. xv. 42-44, 53; Phil. iii. 21). "'l'he resurrection of the dead is the confidence of Christians" (Tertullian; 1 Pet. i. 13). 'l'hat "grace to be brouaht unto us" will brighten into glory. It will be his glory; that is enough for us.-E."'s. P.

entries.title: COL 3:5–7
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Sins of the flesh and the sin of rovetousness. Paul, an example to faithful preRchers, is not satisfied with general exhortations; he is pointed and personal in his allnsion to special sins. The great motive power is in the preceding truths (,·ers. 1---4, "Mortify therefore," etc.). What neither Je,vish ceremonialism nor Gnostic teaching could secure (eh. ii. 23), Christ "011r Life," our "Hope of izlory,• could effect. Note the use of similar lofty motives in Rom. vi. 1, 2; xii. 1; 1 Cor. vi. 15, 19, 20. The term "members" is used, not physically but figuratively, as is" aid man" in ver. !l, including those bodily and mental faculties which may be the occasion of sins of the flesh and sins of the spirit. We find first a list of various- !. SINS OF THE FLESH. (Ver. 5.) Contrast freedom of the apostolic speech on such subjects and the reserve of the present day, which may be excessive, seeing that sins of intemperance and unchastity are the most frequent causes of Church discipline. The conscience must be instructed as well as aroused. Hints as to Aafeguards to be throw11 around the young by Christians; their duties to their own sons and daughters, their apprentices, aud domestic servants; social customs, such as "statute-fairs" for hiring servants, "treating," crowded homes, etc. ; bad laws (young girls insufficiently pro- tected; state recognition of vice; licensing laws, etc.). The censure aud treatment of offenders of both sexes should be far more impartial, and profligate men be branded by the indignation of Christians as one faint image of "the wrath of God" (ver. 6). 'While seeking to put away these sins from our midst, we must also put to death the very roots of these prolific evils in our own hearts (Matt. v. 27, 28). Govern the thoughts. (Distin,..,cruish between a thought injected into the mind as a temptation, and indulged as a sin, Heb. iv. 15.) Guard all the avenues of temptation (cf. Job xxxi. 1; Ps. xvii. 3; Eph. v. 4): bad books; dangerous company; amusements that excite the passions; intoxicants (Matt. v. 29, 30; Rom. viii. 12, 13; Gal. v. 24). Let the body and the brain and the mind be kept in healthy exercise; this will aid us to "keep under the body" (1 Cor. iL 27). God "knoweth our frame;" Christ "our Life" has passed through our temptations. Elevation of spirit (vers. 1 and 2), uulike pride (Prov. xvi. 18), may g11ard us from debasing ourselves: "Ye were raised with Christ;" "mortify therefore," etc. II. THE SIN OF COVETOUSNESS. Covetousness (,r;\.E11ve{Ca.) has been described as" the fierce and ever-fiercer longing of the creature which has turned from God to fill itself with the inferior objects of sense." It is a wider term than "the love of money,". though that "root of all evil" is the most glaring form of it and the one we take as our illustration. It is significant that here and in Eph. v. 5 St. Paul couples covetousness with the most loath£ome sins. A covetous man is an idolater because he loves, trusts, and serves money more than God. This sin is: 1. Mult,Jorm. It is Proteuslike in its shapes: the avarice of the miser, the ostentation of the nouveau riche, or "that loudest laugh of hell, the pride of dying rich." One of its most common and yet scandalous forms is withholding "more than is meet," robbing God of "the firsifruits of all our increase,", which God claims under the gospel, though not in the form of Jewish tithe (cf. Prov. iii. 9, 10; xi. 24; 1 Cor. xvi. 1, 2; 2 Cor. viii. 12; ix. 6, 7). 'l'hiB form of covetousness among Christians may need to be mortified by repeated acts of giving, though painful at firnt, till duty becomes privilege and the les~on is learned, "It is more blessed to give than to receive." 2. It is specious. It is a subtle spirit, 1,eedina ureat discernment for iis detection and great grace for its expulsion. It trnns- 1urms its~lf into an angel of light, and calls itself "prudenco" and other deceptive 11ames. It is said tliat St. Francis de Sales received at the confessional a greater number of persons than were ever known to visit one confessor besides, but that be u:d uot rcmemLer a single iustancc in which covetousness had been confessed. .No OH, DI.1-25,] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 197

wonder, then, that Church censure for covetousness is exceedingly rare (1 Cor. v. 9). 3. It is odious to God. (Ver. 6.) 4. It is ruinous to the srnd. (Gal. vi. 7, 8; Eph. v. 6, 6; 1 Tim. vi. 9, 10.) 5. It needs ceaseless vigilance and all the powers of the heaverdy life to mortify this "member," which is so peculiarly tenacious of life. Christ's love and power alone can avail (Titus ii. 14).-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 3:8–11
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-77ie new life in Ohrist the death-warrant to old sins. The apostle still employs the most powerful motives possible in his exhortations to personal holiness. His figures and illustrations vary (" Ye died; ye were raised with Christ; therefore put your sins to death." "Ye put off your old nature and put on a new nature; therefore put away your old sins "). I. OLD SINS TO BE PUT AWAY. From the sins of the flesh Paul passes on to sins of the spirit and the tongue. There are two groups. 1. "Anger, wrath, malice." Discriminate between these. 'Op-yf, may be a right state of mind (Mark iii. 5; Eph. iv. 26), but is easily depraved into a criminal anger, or into BvµJs (wrath, passion), or ,c,uc!a. (malice which wishes or seeks to do injury). In fact, all our evil principles may be said to be good principles fallen and debased. Selfishness is fallen self-love; envy is depraved emulation; revenge is fallen resentment; sinful anger is righteous indignation degraded and debased. The lawfulness of anger must be determined by it~ direction, its degree, and its motive. In the daily struggle against various forms of sinful anger, we may give the following hints. (1) When passion rises in the soul, let it not overflow through the lips. Suppress the mutiny within the citadel (Ps. xvii. 3; :xxxix.1; Jas. i. 19). (2) Let the battle be fought in sight of the cross and in memory of the provocations we have given to God (Eph. iv. 31, 32). (3) Rely on Christ's power to save now (Titus ii. 14). 2. "Railing," "shameful speaking," lying. Among tl1tl commonest forms of these fruits of an evil heart (Matt. xii. 34) we note: "llackbiting," reckless detraction, i.e. seeking to draw a person down from the reputation he enjoys. (It is not necessary or lawful to speak all we know against a persou, thou:~h many act as though they were at perfect liberty to utter it, if only it is true.) A ttributing wrong motives-a very common form of" shameful speaking," a gross breach of "charity" (1 Cor. xiii. 7), and an arrogant claim to a "discerniug of spirits," Exaggerations; false advertisements; conventional falsehoods in business (Matt. v. 37; :.l Cor. i. 12, 17, 18; Eph. iv. 25). II. THE DEATH-WARRANT OF THESE OLD SINB. Covet not, rail not, lie not, etc., "seeing ye have put off," etc. Two truths are taught. 1. We profess to be enjoying a new life. So complete is the change it is described as a change of nature (" uld mau .. , new man"), a new creation (2 Cor. v. 17; Gal. vi. 15), a new birth, a new resurrection. Of this new life we learn: (1) It is Divine in its origin (" him that created him"). (2) Progressive in its nature (" being renewed unto knowledge"), like a statue becoming more and more like the ideal of the sculptor; or a youth maturing into manhood; or a pupil growing into intimate acquaintance with his master's deepest thoughts (John xvii. 3; Rom. xii. 2; 2 Cor. iv. 16; Eph. iii. 16-19; Phil. iii. 9-14). (3) God-like in its character(" after the image," etc., Eph. iv. 24). A reneweu saint is more God-like than an nnfallen Adam (Rom. v. 21). The issue of this progressive growth "unto knowledge" and mature Christian character is seen in Eph. iv. 13--16. Everything connected with that new life is in deadly antagonism to every kind of sin, which must be" put away," like slothful habits by the scholar, or "weight" by tbo runner. Sin is like poison to the new life we profess to enjoy, depressiug vitality if it does not extinguish life altogether. 2. Jn this life Christ claims supremacy. (Ver. ll.) Dr. Lightfoot suggests that the distinctions here said to be abolished were selected witl.t special reference to the circumstances of the Colossian Church : to the J udaizing of some, to the Gnostic pride of others who despised the unlettered; nnd that bis relation at the time he wrote to the slave Onesimus led him to add "bondman, freeman." 'l'he unity of the race and the brotherhood of men a.re distinctly Christian doctrines. "The head of every man is Christ" (1 Cor. xi. 3). Our union and subordination to him constitute our equality with one another in the world of grace (Matt.. xxiii. 8--10). For all earthly distinctions sink into insignificance compared with his supremacy antl his presence in us all. (1) "Christ is all:" he is "all" to God (eh. i. 19; cf. ha. xiii 1; Mnt.t. iii 17), as the only begotten Son, the one atoning Sacrifice (" the La rn b of 198 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [err. m. 1-25.

God"), th? o_nly_ Mediator, the appointed Judge (John v. 22, 23; Acts xvii. 31). Con- trast the hm1tat10ns attached to Abraham, the fnend of God (Gen. xviii. 18-33), and Mose\ who was "faithful as a servant," but could not redeem his brethren (Exod. xxxii. 3~, 33 J, and "the fulness" of Christ (Heb. ix. 26; x. 10-14). Being "all" to God ho is all to us; the Centre and Circumference of truth; the Alpha and Omeo-a. of our life·, "the Author and Fini~her of our faith." He is a Saviour in whom" d,~clleth all th~ fulness," etc. ( eh. ii. 9), "in whom are bid," etc. ( eh. ii. 3), ,vho is "full of grace and truth," whose love "passetl1 knowledge," whose blood "clcanseth from all sin 1" and "who of God is made unto us," etc. (1 Cor. i. 30). (2) Christ is" in all "-in all of us· for he comes to save, to conquer, to reign, to share l1is very life with us ((fal. ii. 20)'. \Vhere he comes, sin must go; he can brook no rival; for "in all things he must have the pre-eminence." And he is in all things: "He fills all things" (Eph. i. 23; i<". 10). A sense of the all-pervading presence and power of Christ should (a) abase the Christian tempted to be proud of birth, purse, or brain; (b) give dimity to the 1owliest disciple in whom the Son of God dwells; (c) pledge us to ce~seless strife against every form of sin.-E. S. P.

Ycrs. 12, 13.-The Christian's wa1·drobe. The apostle havin" bidden the Colossian converts strip off the filthy rags of their old life, takes th~m into" the Christian's ward- robe and shows them some of the robes of righteousness, the beauties of holiness the jewels of grace, with which they may decorate themselves. These are the only pri~stly vestments in which God's "royal priesthood" may appear" glorious in the eyes of the Lord." Nor should we ever dare present ourselves before the Lord unless we arc attempting to "put on" all these. (Illustrate from "court dress," or Matt. xxii. 11-13.) This spiritual investiture is urged on the Colossians by ·two considerations. I. THEIR RELATIONS TO Gon. "Elect, holy, beloved." 1. Elect. • Our outward religious privileges (1 Cor. iv. 7) and our inward spiritual state (1 Cor. xv. 10) are the result of a Divine choice. Christian experience, no less than God's Word, attributes the beginning of the new life within us to a work of God, and therefore to a purpose and choice of God (2 Tim. i. 9). But for what end has he thus chosen us? We find answers in such words as "fruit" (John xv. 16), "holy" (Eph. i. 3, 4), "sanctifica- tion" (2 Thess. ii. 13), "obedience" (1 Pet. i. 2). 2. Holy. Here is the true idea of the only Christian priesthood, viz. consecration, being set apart for service and spiritual sacrifices to God. 'l'he self-denial of the one High Priest is our pattern and our inspiration (John xvii. 19; Heb. iii. l). There are not, in the 'New Testament, two groups of virtues, one for the clergy, the other for the laity, as (Mr. Ruskin tells us) are represented by some of the medireval poetR and painters. All Christ's disciples.are called,· as priests, to be equally "saints," "holy" (1 Pet: i. 14, 15). 3. "Beloved';" enjoying that special love of complacency and delight of which Christ speaks (John xiv. 21; xvi. 27). "The order of the words admirably corresponds to the_ order of the things: eternal election precedes sanctification in time; the sanctified feel God's love and forthwith imitate it" (Bengel). • II. THE EXCELLENCE OJ<' THESE CHRISTIAN GRACES. 1, 11 .A heart of compassion" towards those who are in a worse condition than ourselves, whether caused by sin or calamity. A compassionate nature brings pain with it, yet it is "twice blesse<)." Silver is no substitute for sympathy. Money sent 'by a rich Christian who will not take the trouble to "visit the fatherless and widows" is worth less than the sympathetic words and deeds of a poor compassionate neighbour. Refer to Christ being often "moved with compassion" and putting forth a healing touch. So now Heb. iv, 15; 1 John iii. 17, 18. 2. "Kindness" to all, perhaps especially to those who arc our equals and need no special compassion (cf. Gal. vi.10; Phil. iv. 8; 1 Pet. iii. 8). A kind heart is a cheerful heart, and provides "a continual feast" (Acts xx. 35). 3. "Humility." "There are many," says Augustine, "who would more readily give all they have to feed the poor than become beggars themselves before Goe\." So humility needs to go hand-in-hand with compassion and kindness. It is fostered by a true Yiew both of our own sinfulness and the dignHy bestowed upon us. We need it in J,rosperity lest we become insolent to our neighbours (Esth. iii. 5; Luke xviii. 11), ,,r evell towarcls God (2 Cbron. xxvi. 16; Ho8. xiii. 6); and in adversity, lest we "faiut," elc. (Heb. xii. 5-9). 4. "Meelcness;" that quiet, gentle spirit which will cm. III. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE 'rO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. H):)

calmly endure disappointments or slights. It is a source or power (Eccles. vii. 8). It is not constantly vindicating itself and disputing with Msailants (Ps. xxxvii. 5, 6, 11). When we see the power which meek spirits gain over others stronger and rougher than themselves, we see the wortle fulfilled, "A little child shall lead them." 5 Longsuffering. In regard to Divine afflictioos, see on eh. i. 11. It is more difficult to exercise it towards men than towards God. In relation to our fellow-sinners we may learn from God's long-suffering towards them. (See the legend of Abraham and the fire-worshipper in Stanley's 'Jewish Church,' i. 21.) And if we are long-snfferinotowards those that sin against God, how much more towards those that offend us! Let us learn of God (Matt. v. 45; Rom. ii. 4) and of his beloved Son (1 Pet. ii. 23). 6. Forbearance and forgiveness. " Forbearing one another." This is often the first step towards frank forgiveness. It may avert a quarrel, for which two are needed. "To conquer one's self is the greatest of conquests," says Plato ( cf. Prov. xvi. 32). This victory over self aids us in the victory over the transgressor (Rom. xii. 21; e.g. David, 1 Sam. xxiv.). "Forgiving each other, if any man have a complaint against any." Our Lord has laid down the law of offences among disciples (Matt. xviii. 15--17 ; Luke xvii. 3, 4). A Christian spirit will hail the signs of incipient repentance, and will exact no unreasonable humiliation. And even towards the most impenitent offender we may exercise the most forgiving spirit, like God, "ready to forgive" (Matt. v. 44, 45). Observe the pathetic plea urged : "Even as the Lord forgave you," etc. Our Master Christ sUll has this power (Matt. ix. 6; Acts v. 31). He has used it on our behalf, first when we applied to him with the burden of all the guilty past, and since then day by day (John xiii. 10). Shall be be so prompt and free, and we be hesitating and reluctant (1 John ii. 12)? And this motive is as stringent as it is pathetic. Note the prayer taught (Luke xi. 4), the command given (Mark :xi. 25, 26), the warning uttered (Matt. xviii. 35). Imagine an unforgiving man offering the prayer (Matt. vi. 12), "As we forgive," etc., and interpret it into plain language. If we do not forgi.e, do not let us dare to pray (1 Tim. ii. 8).-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 3:14
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-.A threefold cord of grace; We have here an attractive pie ture of a loving, peaceful, thankful Christian. I. LoVE. It is compared to the girdle, put on over the other articles of attire, and helping to bind all in .their place. Christian love is no mere natural emotion or selfinterested affection. It is the fruit of the Spirit, whereby God is sincerely loved for his own sake, and one's neighbour for God's sake. To love even our fellow-Christians because they are God's children is not always easy, on account of their inconsistencies. But it is eminently a Christian grace (John xiii. 35; 1 John v. 1). It is called "the bond of perfectness," because: 1. lt is the element of all other graces, the sphere in which they are exercised. It is like the golden light in which some summer evening landscape is bathed, or the green grass on which the multicoloured flowers are blooming. Without love," knowledge puffeth up," gifts are" sounding brass," faith is idle (Gal. v. ti), zeal may be wildfire, mercy weakness, humility pride, and charity ostentation. With love, each of these may,be the Spirit's fruit. It is thus the bond of perfectness, the distinctive feature of a complete Christian character (Rom. xiii. 8; 1 Cor. xiii. 8, 13; Gal. v. 14). 2. Love is the pledge of all other graces. l!'or if we dwell in love and in God (1 John iv. 16) we enjoy increasingly the perfectious of God. 'l'he outer dress is generally the most valuable part, ancl a sign that other parts are present and in keeping with it. So thQ precious girdle of love, visible to all, is a sign that other graces are present and kept in their place by this "bond of perfectness." Cultivate it by charitable judgments, by much forbearance, by seeking to win and refine the less attractive, and to walk in the path marked out for us by Christ (John xv. 12; Eph. v. 2). II. PE.A.OE. This peace Is described by a most attractive name, "the peace of Christ" (John xiv. 27), the tranquillity of a trustful child. The term "rule" may be unucrstood in two senses. 1. Exert its power to protect. (See Phil. iv. 7, where God's peace is likened to a garrison; Ps. cxii. 7; Isa. xxvi. 3.) Peace gives strength, and strength peace (Ps. xxix. 11). 2. Sit as umpire. When in d.oubt in regai:d to business specu~ations, worldly amusements, etc., we may ask, "Which course will the peace of Christ ruling in my heart approve?" To such peace we are called, but to enjoy it we must THE EPISTLE TO THE COLO8SIANS. [ou. m.1-25.

al1ow ~his peace to rule. _We shall ~he~ be _kept fr~m falling (Ps. cxix. 165), have peace m conflict (John xvi. 33) and 111 mact1on (Ps. 1v. 8), throucrh life and iu ceath (Ps. xxxYii. 37). Peace is the faithful handmaid of love, which attends it even in the stormier days of life (Rom. xv. 13). lIT. THA~KFOLN~ss. I_f God's love _is shed abroad and Christ's peace rules in our hearts, grateful feelmgs will well up like sparkling streams. And gratitude to God will deepen Joye and preserve in peace, fosterin~ forbearance pity unselfishness and patience under those trials which a loving Father appoints ro( our dducation.-E.'S. P. Vers. 16, ]7.-The power of the Word and the Name of Christ. "Having exhorted them to be thankful, he also shows them the way" (Chrysostom). But the connection is wider than this. In ver. 16 the apostle shows how a right use of Christ's gospel may promote the graces to which he has been exhortino-; and in ver. 17 bow the rio-ht. recognition of the Name of Christ will be a comprehen~ve rule to aid us in every d~ty of life. I. THE POWER OF THE Worm OF CHRIST. 1. "Let the Word of (Jhrist ,/,well 1n you richly in all wisdom." If "every word of God is pure," and therefore both powerful and precious, this is pre-eminently so with "the word of the truth of the gospel." To exert its power it must not he a transient visitor (cf. Jer. xiv. 8), but a resident in the soul, and that "richly." We must welcome it impartially-its doctrines (Rom. i. 16, 17, etc.), precepts (Ps. cxix. 128), and promises (Rom. iv. 20, 21). We must receive it with Joy as a treasure we prize (Ps. cxix. 72; J er. xv. 16), like sweet poetry that lingers in the memory, or a friend enshrined in the heart (Prov. iv. 21, 22). We may expect it to be a power to ourselves; it will promote in us every kind of wisdom, making us "wi~e unto salvation," and enlightening the intelligence as well as the heart (Ps. xix. 7, 8; cxix. 130). entries.title: COL 3:18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Husbands and wives. Notice the honour given to marriage by Moses (Gen. ii. 23, 24), and still more by Christ (Matt. v. 31, 32; xix. 3-9) and his apostles (Eph. v. 22-33; 1 Tim. iv. 3; v. ).4.; Heb. xiii. 4, etc.). Chris~ianity a gospel of OJI. III. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 201

great joy to the world's suffering women. But blessings rest upon law. The nearer mnrriage is brought to God the more sacred its duties become. In vers. 18, 19 we have in n condensed form rules more fully set forth elsewhere (1 Cor. vii.; Eph. v.; Titus ii.; 1 Pet. iii.). We sec exhortations- !. To WIVES. Gathering together some of the precepts scattered throu!Th the Epistles, we find a fuller summary of the Christian wife's duties at home in 'ritus ii. 4, 5 (make home the happiest place in the world for both husband and children). In 1 Pet. iii. 1.,--6 a contrast is drawn between bodily and spiritual attire, between that which may please the eye of frivolous men and women 11nd that which" in the sight of God is of great price;" not the latest Paris fashions, but "the om11ment of a. meek and quiet spirit" (a lesson especially to Christian matrons to set a. safe example to their juniors). The "manner of life" prescribed in both these passages may be attained by a conscientious observance of the exhortation, "be in subjection." Every family must have one head. Though" Jove is the fulfilling of the Law," if the words "authority" and "subjection" are never to be beard in the home, it must be through a conscientious regarcl to mutual duties. This subjection is "fitting." "Doth not even nature i!self teach?" The satire poured on an imperious wife, and the sympathy felt for a. widow deprived of her stay, supply answers. Scripture teaches the pre-eminence of the husband as illustrated by various relations between the sexes: e.g. the order of creation (1 Tim. ii. 13), the derivation of woman (1 Cor. xL 8), her destiny (Gen. ii. 20; 1 Cor. xi. 7, 9), her share in the first transgression (1 'l'im. ii. 14) and penalty (Gen. iii. 16), and their relative position in the kingdom of grace (1 Cor. xi. 3). Thus submission is" fitting in the Lord." And the same words remind us of the only limit to it (Acts iv. 19; v. 29). T,l'o motives are suggested. 1. An ungodly husband may thus be won for Christ (1 Pet. iii. 1; 1 Cor. vii. 16). 2. An obedient wife is a living type of Christ'; obedient Church, and is thus a witness to the reality of Christ's authority in both tl1e family and the Church. II. To HUSBANDS. "In exhortations the scales should be equally poised" (Cbrysostom) as they are here. For what St. Paul has said to wives already suggests tu husbands: If our wh·es are to be such to us, "what manner of persons," etc. ·t (2 Pet. iii. 11). Turning to 1 Pet. iii. 7, we see some of the husband's duties. "Dwell with them" (ma.king home magnetic) "according to knowledge" (the highest wisdom you can gain for governing and guiding)," giving honour," etc. (the honour of esteem, of attention to the latest day of life, of confidence, etc.). These duties are summed ui, here in "love" (Rom. xiii. 10). St. Paul does not say, as the complement of ver. 18, "Govern them," but" Love them." The loving husband will secure the dutiful wifo. Motives are suggested both by reason and revelation. I. A wife is, by God's appointment, pa.rt of our very selves (Eph. v. 31 and 28). Marriage is e. union of souls. "Bitter against them? "-against those we have taken into the very shrine of our Ii ves ~ Plutarch tells us, "They who did sacrifice at the rites of Juno took out the gall of the victim and threw it a.way, signifying by the ceremony that it was not fit that bile aud bitterness should enter into the married state." W. Jay quotes Eph. v. 29 thus:"' Nu man ever yet hated bis own flesh,' but many a monster bas done so." 2. A wifo is the weaker vessel physically, not spiritually. Further motives, addressed to the godly, are: 3. You are" heirs together of the grace of life." Disunion will hinder prayers (Matt. xviii. 19) and progress in your pilgrimage. 4. A husband's love is to be a copy of Christ's love (Eph. v. :l5-27), self-sacrificing, purifying, winning the allegiance of the whole nature. Learn: 1. The grave responsibility of entering the marriage relation. Take no ouo as a wife for whom you cannot cherish the love of esteem; or as a busbancl whom you cannot reverence as worthy of being a. guide and a stay. 2. The duty of Christians to marry" only in the Lord" (ver.17; 1 Cor. vii. 39). 3. The preciousness of e. spiritual bond which shall survive the dissolution of the marriage tie by death (Luke x.x. 35, 36).-E. S. P. Vere. 20 2I.-Cht1dren and parent,. The family and the Church, the natural and spiritual h~me, are the two most sacred associations on earth, having as their Head" the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named" (Epb. iii. 15). The 1,trength of the nation and the welfare of the world are inseparably bound np with 202 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [err. III. 1-25

families. M:uhme de ~t~cl, asked by Bonaparte what was the greatest want or France, replied," Mothers." The gospel brings to families the blessing of Abraham (Gen. xvii. 7) !'Ind of Jesus Chtist (Matt. xix. 13-16; Act.s ii. 39). It has meesa.,.es to children and to parents. I. THE MESSAGE OF THE GOSPEL TO CHILDREN. Children have a place in the kin11dom of heaven (Mark x. 16), recognized by baptism_into the Name of Christ, the Lord ~fall (Matt. xxviii. 18-20). Hence they are addressed as called to be young disciples. The obedience of childhood to both parents (Prov. i. 8) prepares for dutiful love in moro advanced years (Prov. xxiii. 22), and teaches lessons of submission to the will of tho Di.ine Father. Three motives are suggested in these messages. 1. "For this is right." (Eph. vi. 1.) Tbere is a fine ring as of genuine metal in this motive-the supremacy of duty irrespective of reward. Obedience is but payment in part of a debt due to parents. 2. " This is will-pleasing in the Lord." Remembering the one qualification suggested by "in the Lord," children may enjoy Enoch's testimony (Heh. xi. 5). 3. It has a special promise (Eph. vi. 2, 3), which was given to Gentiles. Illustrate from the national persistence of the Chinese; from the continuance of the Rechabites (Jer; mv. 18, l 9; and see Smith's 'Dictionary of the Bible,' ii. 1008); and from the tendency of obedience and purity in youth to promote health and long life in maturity. But the corn plexity of natural laws forbids us to consider this an absolute promise to each individual. The most dutiful Child among men (Luke ii. 51; John xix. 25-27) died young under the law of obedience and sacrifice for others (John xii. 24-26). rr. THE MESSAGE OF THE GOSPEL TO PARENTS. Combining ver. 21 and Eph. vi. 4, we are reminded of the following truths. 1. The grave respO'Tl,sibility of parents towards their children: who bear on them the image of God, though marred by evil; who belong to Christ and have a place in the kingdom of God, and yet are in a world of sin; who have to be steered through the perils of youth to a Christian manhood and womanhood, which we desire to be something better than our own. 2. The privilege of recognizing their relationship to Christ. They belong to him. They n:eM_ not to be brought into, bnt to be brought up in, the nurture of the Lord. Christ (John i. 9) is nearer to them and speaks to them earlier than we can. If we are giving to them wise Christian nurture we should expect that they will grow up within the shelter of the fold, following the Shepherd's steps. 3. There is a treatment which discourages early piety. Anything calculated to provoke to anger tends to discourage children from believing they can be young disciples and seeking to live as such. Hence this caution to fathers (as heads of the honse and as more likely to abuse their authority). From which caution and the precept in Epb. vi. 4, we may gather such hints on parental duty as the following. Make the character and temperament of ea.eh child a special study, employing moral principles impartially, but adapting treatment to individual cases, Rule by love and not by fear, avoiding the perils of over-indulgence (1 Sam. iii. 13; 1 Kings i. 6) and overcommandment, never making false threats, nor hesitating to revoke a hasty command "·hich reflection will not justify; nor punishing under the influence of passion. Seek to win the confidence of the children in regard to their spiritual history. Do not propose to them tests of Christian character unsuitable to their age, or visit childish faults as though they were grave moral delinquencies. In choosing for them companions, schools, occupations, "seek first the kingdom of God," etc. (As warning illustrations, cf. Gen. xiii. 10-13; xi.x. H, 31, etc.; 2 Chron. xviii. 1; xxi. 6.) In every department of life seek to combine the needed discipline (wa•li•la.) and instruction (11iiu8urla.) with that personal influence and example which alone can make them" the chastening and admonition rf t/;e Lord." 4. Children are a most powerful and touching motive to parental piety. (Cf. John xvii. 19.)-E. S. P. Ver. 2~h. iv. !.-Servants and their masters. Many of the "servants" pf the New Testament were slaves. 'l'heir general condition was lamentable. Illustrate this from the penal code etc. (Smith's' Dictionary of Antiquities,' art. "Servus"), and from the incident that had r~cently occurred at Rome (Tacitus, 'Ann.,' xiv. 42-45, or Conybeare and Howson's •St.Paul,' ii. 468, n.). Paul's connection with Onesimus also brought the subject prominently before his mind. Christianity, by tho very divinity of its truths, tended to unsettle the mind of a convert.ed slave if his master were a Christian, and still more if he were a reckless heathen. It came like a torch of truth into an atmosphere orr. m. 1-26.] 'rHE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 203

laden with the explosive materials of falsehood and fraud. It might easily have lit up the flames of o. new servile war. But ,Jesus Christ came to effect the grandest revolution, noiselesHly, by the spread of Divine principles fatal to every wrong (Isa. xiii. 2-4, 0, 7). The precept, Matt. vii, 12, laid the axe to the root of slavery, as it also underminded the ramparts of every other ancient wrong. Christianity must crusb slavery, or it will be corrupted and vitiated by it. Meanwhile it bettered the position of converted slaves. It made them masters of their own consciences. It taught them so to prize their spiritual privileges as not to be over-anxious about their earthly lot (1 Cor. vii. 21-24). The same principles are applicable to the present conditions of Christian servants and their masters. I. THE DUTY AND DIGNITY OF CHRISTIAN SERVANTS. It is significant that some of the most impressive statements of Christian doctrine and duty are found in sections of the Epistles addressed to servants (vers. 22-25; Titus ii. 9-14; 1 Pet. ii. 18-25). In this passage we see: 1. The servant's d,,1,ty. (Ver. 22.) • We are reminded here, as in the previous exhortations, of the qualification implied in the term, "according to the flesh;" e.g. Obadiah (1 Kings xviii. 3, 4). Masters cannot command the consciences even of young apprentices (cf. Matt. x:xii. 21; Rom. xiv. 12). God only can adjust the shares of responsibility for a double sin (Job. xii. 16). Servants are especially warned against a common form of unconscientiousness-" eye-service ; " e.g. wasting a master's time, or hiding up slovenly work done in his absence. The :fidelity of Joseph (Gen. xxxix:. 3, 6, 22, 23) may be taken as a pattern, and Nehemiah's maxim (v. 15) as a motto. 2. The servant's privilege. (Ver. 23.) Being bound to do everything in the fear of Goel, he may do everything in the love of God. The great regulating principle of the Christian life may be a motive and au under-current of thought in every detail of duty (as the love of wife and children is to a father busied in commerce). As Jesus was "about his Father's business" when at the carpenter's bench, and as Paul was "serving the Lord Christ" when plying the needle or shuttle, so may Cbrist be served in the kitchen. (Illustrate from George Herbert's 'The Elixir.') Such service being "from tbe soul" will be such as can be presented to the eye of the Divine Master, who is always watching us, with that "singleness of heart" which is the strength and stay of every true disciple's character (2 Cor. i.12). 3. The serva11t's recompense. (Vers. 24, 25.) '!'he twenty-fifth verse reminds even clown-trodden slaves that the wrongs they endure will be no excuse for the wrongs they do. The law of Lev. xix. 15 is the rule of the Divine Judge. But the encouraiement precedes the warning. The reward will b.e proportionate (Eeh, vi. 8; cf. 1 Cor. iii. 8). It will consist of an inheritance (Matt. xxv. 34; 1 Pet. i. 4), the chief glory of which will be its sinless service of a Master who; by giving us the honour of thus serving him (Rev. xxii. 3, 4), will be serving us ( Luke xii. 37). II. THE RESPONSIBILITY OF CHRISTIAN MASTERS, (Ch. iv. 1.) Two things nre demanded even for a slave. 1. Justice. '!'his could easily be refused; and human tribunals, if they could be appealed to, might entangle the weak, but be powerless to restrain the strong. Plato (' De Leg.,' c. 6) tells us that the noblest specimen of justice is when a man ab~tains from injuring those he may easily wrong. Christianity demands even more than this. Hence such cautions as some of the rules of feudalism suggest : "Behveen the servant and the lord there is no judge save God;" "'!.'he lord who exacts what is unjust from his servant exacts it at the peril of his soul." 2. " That which is equal." (Cf. Eph. vi. 9.) This extends to slaves the protection of our Lord's "golden rule," and places masters under this royal law. This points towards emancipation, and in most cases enforces it on the enlightened conscience. In our present circumstances the rendering of that which is equal will restrain masters from giving the lowest market price for labour such as bare justice might demand when that price involves grinding poverty; and leaving old servants to "the law of demand and supply." But servants must live under the same law, not forgetting the responsibilities and risks of capital, or nurturing an unreasonable selfishness. Some noble illustrations _of how Christianity leavens commerce in this a3pcct havo been seen m Englaud during tho "cotton famine" of 1862, and in more recent years, when, for tbo sake of the workpeople, mills have been kept running and collieries working at a very serious loss. Observe the motive: "Ye have a Master in heaven,"" higher than the highest," before whom earthly distinctions arc but trifles; who delights to observo every generous act; 204 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [ou. III. 1-26.

""ho nt any time may call master or servant to give an account of his stewardship; from whom we shall need to receive, not rigid justice, but unmerited ruercy, through his own generous gift of grace in Christ Jesus (Matt. v, 7; vii. 2).-E. S. P.

A husband's love is to be a copy of Christ's love (Eph. v. :l5-27), self-sacrificing, purifying, winning the allegiance of the whole nature. Learn: 1. The grave responsibility of entering the marriage relation. Take no ouo as a wife for whom you cannot cherish the love of esteem; or as a busbancl whom you cannot reverence as worthy of being a. guide and a stay. 2. The duty of Christians to marry" only in the Lord" (ver.17; 1 Cor. vii. 39). 3. The preciousness of e. spiritual bond which shall survive the dissolution of the marriage tie by death (Luke x.x. 35, 36).-E. S. P. Vere. 20 2I.-Cht1dren and parent,. The family and the Church, the natural and spiritual h~me, are the two most sacred associations on earth, having as their Head" the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named" (Epb. iii. 15). The 1,trength of the nation and the welfare of the world are inseparably bound np with 202 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [err. III. 1-25

families. M:uhme de ~t~cl, asked by Bonaparte what was the greatest want or France, replied," Mothers." The gospel brings to families the blessing of Abraham (Gen. xvii. 7) !'Ind of Jesus Chtist (Matt. xix. 13-16; Act.s ii. 39). It has meesa.,.es to children and to parents. I. THE MESSAGE OF THE GOSPEL TO CHILDREN. Children have a place in the kin11dom of heaven (Mark x. 16), recognized by baptism_into the Name of Christ, the Lord ~fall (Matt. xxviii. 18-20). Hence they are addressed as called to be young disciples. The obedience of childhood to both parents (Prov. i. 8) prepares for dutiful love in moro advanced years (Prov. xxiii. 22), and teaches lessons of submission to the will of tho Di.ine Father. Three motives are suggested in these messages. 1. "For this is right." (Eph. vi. 1.) Tbere is a fine ring as of genuine metal in this motive-the supremacy of duty irrespective of reward. Obedience is but payment in part of a debt due to parents. 2. " This is will-pleasing in the Lord." Remembering the one qualification suggested by "in the Lord," children may enjoy Enoch's testimony (Heh. xi. 5). 3. It has a special promise (Eph. vi. 2, 3), which was given to Gentiles. Illustrate from the national persistence of the Chinese; from the continuance of the Rechabites (Jer; mv. 18, l 9; and see Smith's 'Dictionary of the Bible,' ii. 1008); and from the tendency of obedience and purity in youth to promote health and long life in maturity. But the corn plexity of natural laws forbids us to consider this an absolute promise to each individual. The most dutiful Child among men (Luke ii. 51; John xix. 25-27) died young under the law of obedience and sacrifice for others (John xii. 24-26). rr. THE MESSAGE OF THE GOSPEL TO PARENTS. Combining ver. 21 and Eph. vi. 4, we are reminded of the following truths. 1. The grave respO'Tl,sibility of parents towards their children: who bear on them the image of God, though marred by evil; who belong to Christ and have a place in the kingdom of God, and yet are in a world of sin; who have to be steered through the perils of youth to a Christian manhood and womanhood, which we desire to be something better than our own. 2. The privilege of recognizing their relationship to Christ. They belong to him. They n:eM_ not to be brought into, bnt to be brought up in, the nurture of the Lord. Christ (John i. 9) is nearer to them and speaks to them earlier than we can. If we are giving to them wise Christian nurture we should expect that they will grow up within the shelter of the fold, following the Shepherd's steps. 3. There is a treatment which discourages early piety. Anything calculated to provoke to anger tends to discourage children from believing they can be young disciples and seeking to live as such. Hence this caution to fathers (as heads of the honse and as more likely to abuse their authority). From which caution and the precept in Epb. vi. 4, we may gather such hints on parental duty as the following. Make the character and temperament of ea.eh child a special study, employing moral principles impartially, but adapting treatment to individual cases, Rule by love and not by fear, avoiding the perils of over-indulgence (1 Sam. iii. 13; 1 Kings i. 6) and overcommandment, never making false threats, nor hesitating to revoke a hasty command "·hich reflection will not justify; nor punishing under the influence of passion. Seek to win the confidence of the children in regard to their spiritual history. Do not propose to them tests of Christian character unsuitable to their age, or visit childish faults as though they were grave moral delinquencies. In choosing for them companions, schools, occupations, "seek first the kingdom of God," etc. (As warning illustrations, cf. Gen. xiii. 10-13; xi.x. H, 31, etc.; 2 Chron. xviii. 1; xxi. 6.) In every department of life seek to combine the needed discipline (wa•li•la.) and instruction (11iiu8urla.) with that personal influence and example which alone can make them" the chastening and admonition rf t/;e Lord." 4. Children are a most powerful and touching motive to parental piety. (Cf. John xvii. 19.)-E. S. P. Ver. 2~h. iv. !.-Servants and their masters. Many of the "servants" pf the New Testament were slaves. 'l'heir general condition was lamentable. Illustrate this from the penal code etc. (Smith's' Dictionary of Antiquities,' art. "Servus"), and from the incident that had r~cently occurred at Rome (Tacitus, 'Ann.,' xiv. 42-45, or Conybeare and Howson's •St.Paul,' ii. 468, n.). Paul's connection with Onesimus also brought the subject prominently before his mind. Christianity, by tho very divinity of its truths, tended to unsettle the mind of a convert.ed slave if his master were a Christian, and still more if he were a reckless heathen. It came like a torch of truth into an atmosphere orr. m. 1-26.] 'rHE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 203

laden with the explosive materials of falsehood and fraud. It might easily have lit up the flames of o. new servile war. But ,Jesus Christ came to effect the grandest revolution, noiselesHly, by the spread of Divine principles fatal to every wrong (Isa. xiii. 2-4, 0, 7). The precept, Matt. vii, 12, laid the axe to the root of slavery, as it also underminded the ramparts of every other ancient wrong. Christianity must crusb slavery, or it will be corrupted and vitiated by it. Meanwhile it bettered the position of converted slaves. It made them masters of their own consciences. It taught them so to prize their spiritual privileges as not to be over-anxious about their earthly lot (1 Cor. vii. 21-24). The same principles are applicable to the present conditions of Christian servants and their masters. I. THE DUTY AND DIGNITY OF CHRISTIAN SERVANTS. It is significant that some of the most impressive statements of Christian doctrine and duty are found in sections of the Epistles addressed to servants (vers. 22-25; Titus ii. 9-14; 1 Pet. ii. 18-25). In this passage we see: 1. The servant's d,,1,ty. (Ver. 22.) • We are reminded here, as in the previous exhortations, of the qualification implied in the term, "according to the flesh;" e.g. Obadiah (1 Kings xviii. 3, 4). Masters cannot command the consciences even of young apprentices (cf. Matt. x:xii. 21; Rom. xiv. 12). God only can adjust the shares of responsibility for a double sin (Job. xii. 16). Servants are especially warned against a common form of unconscientiousness-" eye-service ; " e.g. wasting a master's time, or hiding up slovenly work done in his absence. The :fidelity of Joseph (Gen. xxxix:. 3, 6, 22, 23) may be taken as a pattern, and Nehemiah's maxim (v. 15) as a motto. 2. The servant's privilege. (Ver. 23.) Being bound to do everything in the fear of Goel, he may do everything in the love of God. The great regulating principle of the Christian life may be a motive and au under-current of thought in every detail of duty (as the love of wife and children is to a father busied in commerce). As Jesus was "about his Father's business" when at the carpenter's bench, and as Paul was "serving the Lord Christ" when plying the needle or shuttle, so may Cbrist be served in the kitchen. (Illustrate from George Herbert's 'The Elixir.') Such service being "from tbe soul" will be such as can be presented to the eye of the Divine Master, who is always watching us, with that "singleness of heart" which is the strength and stay of every true disciple's character (2 Cor. i.12). 3. The serva11t's recompense. (Vers. 24, 25.) '!'he twenty-fifth verse reminds even clown-trodden slaves that the wrongs they endure will be no excuse for the wrongs they do. The law of Lev. xix. 15 is the rule of the Divine Judge. But the encouraiement precedes the warning. The reward will b.e proportionate (Eeh, vi. 8; cf. 1 Cor. iii. 8). It will consist of an inheritance (Matt. xxv. 34; 1 Pet. i. 4), the chief glory of which will be its sinless service of a Master who; by giving us the honour of thus serving him (Rev. xxii. 3, 4), will be serving us ( Luke xii. 37). II. THE RESPONSIBILITY OF CHRISTIAN MASTERS, (Ch. iv. 1.) Two things nre demanded even for a slave. 1. Justice. '!'his could easily be refused; and human tribunals, if they could be appealed to, might entangle the weak, but be powerless to restrain the strong. Plato (' De Leg.,' c. 6) tells us that the noblest specimen of justice is when a man ab~tains from injuring those he may easily wrong. Christianity demands even more than this. Hence such cautions as some of the rules of feudalism suggest : "Behveen the servant and the lord there is no judge save God;" "'!.'he lord who exacts what is unjust from his servant exacts it at the peril of his soul." 2. " That which is equal." (Cf. Eph. vi. 9.) This extends to slaves the protection of our Lord's "golden rule," and places masters under this royal law. This points towards emancipation, and in most cases enforces it on the enlightened conscience. In our present circumstances the rendering of that which is equal will restrain masters from giving the lowest market price for labour such as bare justice might demand when that price involves grinding poverty; and leaving old servants to "the law of demand and supply." But servants must live under the same law, not forgetting the responsibilities and risks of capital, or nurturing an unreasonable selfishness. Some noble illustrations _of how Christianity leavens commerce in this a3pcct havo been seen m Englaud during tho "cotton famine" of 1862, and in more recent years, when, for tbo sake of the workpeople, mills have been kept running and collieries working at a very serious loss. Observe the motive: "Ye have a Master in heaven,"" higher than the highest," before whom earthly distinctions arc but trifles; who delights to observo every generous act; 204 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [ou. III. 1-26.

""ho nt any time may call master or servant to give an account of his stewardship; from whom we shall need to receive, not rigid justice, but unmerited ruercy, through his own generous gift of grace in Christ Jesus (Matt. v, 7; vii. 2).-E. S. P.

entries.title: COL 3:1
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Christian aspiration. IC we would understand St. Paul we must often remind ourselves of his view of the Christian life as a union and identification with the life of Christ in its several stages. 1'he apostle teaches that the Christian has to live spiritually the same life that Christ lived both spiritually and visibly. He must lrnmble himself like Christ, his old self must be crucified, he must be buried to the world and then rise again in a new life. Now, we are to see how the .Ascension follows the Resurrection; how, as it was in the human experience of Christ, so spiritually to us there must be a rising to the things above after we have come from the death of sin to the new Christian life. I. CHRISTIAN ASPIRATION SPRINGS FROM THE EXPEDIENOE OF A NEW SPIBITUAL LIFE, The resurrection must precede the ascension. Chriit rose from the dead before he was received up into heaven. We have our resurrection. Without it we vainly strive to aspire to higher things. So long; as the soul is dead in trespasses and sins it can have no power to rise to the heights of celestial experience. But this resurrection has taken place in every true Christian. Christianity docs not satisfy itself with the death of the old life of sin. It is itself a new resurrection-life. 1'he destruction of old habits, evil pleasures, a wicked will, etc., are but the first process. The very purpose of this killing of the old is to make way for the awakening of the new life. Christ could not have risen if he had not died. He died that he might rise again. We die to sin that we may thereby rise into newness of life. The Christian lives with the energies, faculties, l1opes, and aims of a new life. All is not done in the act of tbe new birth. 1'his, like natural birth, is the beginning of greater things. 1'he aspect of the new life must be onward and upward. IL Cmw;TIAN .ASPIBATION AIMS AT THE TIIINGS THAT .ARE ABOVE. It must soar above the sinful pleasures and habits of the past. It would be undoing all the work of redemption if the freed soul were to let itself be agaiu taken captive by sin. The death-agonies of-repentance and the birth-throes of the new life would be endured in vain if, like a sow returning to its wallowing in the mire, the soul went back again to grovel in the low and evil things of its old life. What is the use of the beautiful wings of the moth if it continues to crawl over the garbage on which the caterpillar fed? :Moreover, the Christian aspiration must carry him away from the old narrow restraints and formal methods and la.ws of the old life. 1t is not for him to go back to "ordinances" (eh. ii 20). Observe, however, that the aspiration is to be to. that which is above, not merely to that which is future. The mere longing for heaven as a home of the future may degenerate into an idle sentiment. 'l'he true Christian aspiration looks upward rather tban forward. It seeks tbe heavenly things that may be had already in some degree. Its aims are for those things which are spiritually higher and better than the things at present experienced. The Christian should prefer heavenly treasure to earthly riches; the smile of God to the favour of man; truth, purity, anu love to any things that are seen and temporal. III. CHRISTI.AN ABPIBATION IB SUPPORTED BY FELLOWSHIP WITH CHRIST. Nothing is more difficult than active aspiration. 1'he aspiration of sentiment that looks up may be easy. But the aspiration of life that seeks the things tbat are above is beyond our common endeavours. The wings of the soul are foeble. We lose ourselves in the clouds of our lower atmosphere before we have a glimpse of the stars above. Storms beat us back again to earth, weak and weary and sad. We can only safely aspire in Christ. .As we die with him and rise from the grave of our old selves with him, BO we ascend by continued fellowship with him. We may hold it true "That men may rise on stepping-stones Of their dead selves to higher things.'' But we find ln experience that the process is slow and toilsome. We want a hand above to draw us up. Now, as Christ is already in glory, when we seek to be near to Christ we approach his high estate. Two important lessons llow from this truth. 1. We caimot remain in fellowship with Christ if we grovel among the things of earth, on. III. 1-25.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 205

Christ ascending to heavenly pl~ces will leave us behind a~d beneath his companionship unless v:e ~scend to heavenly mmiledness. The worldly mmded Christian is the Christless Christian. 2. But close fellowship with Christ is the ooo way by means of which wo may ascend to the things which are above.-W. 1". A.

entries.title: COL 3:3
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-'.ffie hiddffl life. After Christ died ho was seen no more by the world. It is true that for forty days he appeared repeatedly on earth, but only to his own disciples. The world never saw him after the stone was rolled against the entrance of the sepulchre in Joseph's garden on the night of the Crucifixion. And soon he ascended to heaven to bo with God, and was no longer visible even to hia own followers. But be will come again, when "every eye shall behold him. 1 Now, a similar experience is that of the true life of the Christian. He has died to the old life in the world which the world fully understood. He has risen to a new life which the world does not unrierstand-a secret, internal, spiritual life united to the life of Christ and hidden in God. But this life will be revealed when Christ appears again. I. THE CHRISTIAN LIFE IS HIDDEN. 1. Its source of supply is hidden. Its origin is mysterious; for "the wind bloweth where it listeth," etc. And its continue,! stbtenance is mysterious. The same Spirit which feeds it gives its birth. 'l'be world sees the fire in the front, and they wonder that the waters of adversity no not quench it: but not behind, where One is constantly pouring on the oil of spiritual grace. 2. Its true 71ature is hidden. 'fhe fruits are manifest. The hidden nature of the spiritual life is no excuse for fruitlessness in the outer lifo. But the life itself is not the less secret. The stream flows underground, thou~h it proves its presence by the fresh verdure above. It is known only to the soul and to God; known perfectly only to God, for we are mysteries to ourselves. 3. Its destiny is hidden. 'vVe may hear the deep murmur of the water of life. But we cannot trace the course of the river, nor see where it flows into the ocean of God's being. The world does not understancl the aim3 and aspirations of the Christian. Thus he may be much maligned. Let him mercifully refrain from judging those who in their opposition know not what they do. II. Tms LIFE IS WITH CHRIST IN GoD. 1. It is with Christ. That is the essential characteristic of it. Union with Christ is the cause of all the glorious and mysterious results of Christian experience. Christ is now biclden in God. Therefore his people are spiritually hidclen with him. Better be hidden with Christ than famous without him. There are secrets that are delicious in their very secrecy. What can be more happy than the secret relation of Christ to the soul? 2. It is in God. This fact accounts for the secret character of the life. God is unseen, and all relations with him aro invisible. To he deep and spiritual our life must go out into the darkness that it may find its home in God. If there is no mystery in our Christian experience, this must be shallow and altogether earthly. It can have no living relation to God. III. THE HIDDEN LIFE WILL BE MANIFESTED IN 'l'HE FUTURE. We talk too exclusively of the revelation of evil experiences in the great future. But many good and glorious secrets will also be declared. '1.'he despised faithful servant of Christ will h~ honoured, the misjudged character will be clearecl, the bidden life will reveal itself iu glory. '1.'he idea of a "spiritual body" seems to imply tho visible appearance of the spiritual life. The manifestation of Christ will bring with it this manifestation of hi,; people (1 John iii. 2). Note, the doctrine of the bidden Christian life is placed between two practical exhortations: (1) that we should set our mind on the things that am above (ver. 2); and (2) that we should mortify what remains of the evil life (ver. 5). -W.F.A. Ver. 11 (last clause).-Christ all, and in all. I. THE FACT. 1. Ghrist is everything to the Christicin. All other interests sink into insignificance bef0re him, as the stars fac.e at the rising of the sun. (1) Christ is the whole price of redemption. We need no additional 0o-race to that of bis gospel. We have not to supplement that gospel by the Law, or to eke out the store of grace with onr goo1 works, or to add the intercession of saints to that of Christ, or to offer any fresh sacrifices to complete the atonement. Christ cried on the cross, "It is finished." He, and he alone, is sufifoieut to bring full Ralvation. (2) Ghrist is the one Lord of our lives. He will nccP.pt uo divided dev11- tion. He, aud he alone, has a claim to rule over our hearts. There is but one Kiug of 206 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [ OB, W, 1-26.

the kingdom of heaven that is set up in our midst. Any priestly protension, any dogma.tic teaching, or any political coercion that interferes with the authority of Christ, is treason against Heaven. (3) In Christ are all our requirement8, To be in him now is the deepest peace; to be with him hereafter is the joy of heaven. All sympathy for all kinds of men, in all possible conditions of sorrow or of joy, may be found in him, All truth of the highest Divine things may be seen in him, the "Word" of God. 2. Christ fills everything for the Chi·istian. He is in all, (1) Christ is in the whole heart. All the true Christian's thought and affection are filled with Christ. It is true that Christ does not exclude natural human affections. It was the fantastic mistake of the Church that a St. Catherine, in order to be the bride of Christ, must be exclnded from human love. On the contrary, Christ enters our human affections,and pervades them. In regard to social intercourse we may say- " Let not my heart within me bum Except in all I thee discern." (2) Christ is in the whole of life. He does not belong to a small consecrated section of it, a temple of holiness, shut off from the busy haunts of commerce and pleasure. He comes into our business, our pleasure, our mundane affairs generally. He is as much in the office and the workshop as in the Church. He claims the six days as much as the Sunday. (3) Christ is in each and all of his people. He is not only in apos- tolic leaders and pattern saints; he is in little children, the ignorant, the insi"nificant the imperfect, the latest converts of a mission to degraded heathen. '

II. THE OOKSEQUENOES OF THIS FACT. I. lt is a motive for holiness. If we are new men in Christ, all life belongs to him. 'l'here is no room for the indulgence of sin. Any unclean spot is a desecration of his temple. 2. This fact breaks down the separati711l barrier between man and man. Political distinctions(" Greek and Jew"), religiou11 distinctions apart from Christ(" circumcision and uncircumcision ''), distinctions of civilization ("barbarian, Scythian ''), social distinctions ("bondman,freeman"), all melt before the unifying influence of the common presence of Christ. 3. This fact is a motive for Christi-an charity. (V ers.12, 13.) It should lead to wider sympathy and warmer compassion; to greater gentleness, forbearance, and meekness; to a. more forgiving spirit among Christians. Remember that a.s you treat your fellow-Christian so you a.re treating Christ (Matt. :x.xv. 45). If it is difficult to love him for his own sake, love him for the sake of Christ. 1f there is little of beauty in his soul and much to repel and annoy ns, still coosider that, though the temple is not attractive, there dwells within it One who is altogether lovely. Love the Christ who may he found even in the uncouth Christian.-W. F . .A.

entries.title: COL 3:14
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The bond of perfectness. I. No CrrnIBTIAN CHARACTER IS PERFECT WITHOUT LOVE. There may be wide knowledge, stainless purity, and fiery zeal. But the character wiil be broken and unfinished if the golden grace is missing. This has been singularly forgotten by the Church. Anything but Christian charity has been sought after, ln the very zeal for other excellences this one has been trampled underfoot. II. LoVE IS THE CROWNING CHRISTIAN GBACE, ".Above all these things put on love." 1. Love is the highest pinnacle of the Christian temple. 'l'oo often the supremacy has oeen given to orthodoxy, to negative purity, or to rigorous devotion. It has to be learnt that it is better to be heterodox and to love o.ur brethren, than to be sound in doctrine and selfish in heart. It needs also to be more understood that he who denies himself most for his brother stands higher than he who is simply irreproachable in behaviour. 2. Love is thus supreme (1) hecanse it is of the essential nature of God, who is love; (2) because it is the source of all other graces; (3) because in itself it is better than anything else. IIL Lovr,; BINDS 'l'OGETHEB ALL OTHER CHRioTfAK GRACES. Without it the character is not only imperfect, it lacks unity and cohesion. Love is like the keystone of the arch, which both completes the structure and holds all the other stones together. l. Love should surround every other grace as the bond surrounds the bundle. Purity, truth, justice, coura~c, kwi,~rnuce, etc., should all be exercised in love. 2. Love sliou]J bring all other graces 1,earer together. 'l'hrough love we should realize the rclaLion 11ctween gcnero~ity and justice, purity and liberty, meekness and cow·age. 3. OII. III, 1-26.] 'l'llE EfIS'l'LE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 2-0~

Love should make a harmonious whole of the character. The separate sticks become one bundle when tied up together. Love should give unity of spirit and purpose to the whole life. 4. Love should perfect the strength of the Christian character. When all _the graces are bound by the bond of love they mutually etron"then one another. Selfishness distracts, divides, and weakens life. The soul that is p~ssessed by love is strong,-W. F. A. •

Ver. 15,-Peace the umpire. St. Paul is not exactly desiring that the peace of Christ may have a large place in the hearts of his readers, that it may be unfettered and dominant, that it may govern all the affections and passions of the soul, as the trans- lation in our Authorized Version would lead us to read his words, and as they arc commonly quoted. Instead of the word "rule" we should read "arbitrate." The apostle would have this peace arbitrating among the conflicting claims of variou~ interests and the mutually opposing forces of various thoughts and feelings. In fact, it is to bo an umpire. l. WE NEED AN UMPIRE IN OUB HEARTS. The conditions of our troublesome inner life prove this necessity. 1. The war of passions. Earthly desire fights against heavenly aspiration, bodily appetite against spiritual hunger, selfish greed against generous love, wild passion against pure emotion. 2. The conflict of claims. Public claims conflict with private claims. Future interests do not agree with temporary advantages. We are drawn hither and thither by cross attractions, confused by a babel of contradictory voice~, urged by the force of a tempest of impulses. 3. The distrartion of doubts. Our thoughts will not harmonize. One idea clashes with another. We hear no music of the spheres in the circling doubts of our troubled minds. W c need an umpire to help us to discover what are true among so many prophet-voices. II. PEACE IS THE UMPmE NEEDED BY OUR HEARTS, \,Vhen we possess our souls in quietness we are able to see the right and the truly desirable as we never can while we are distracted by exciting influences. 1. Peace arbitrates between the pas&ions. Like a runaway horse who bas taken the bit in his teeth and rushes on blindly to destruction, passion sees nothing, and the soul possessed by passion wrecks its highest interests. We must be calm to know what feelings may be indulged and what must be curbed. 2. Peace arbitrates between conflicting claims. When all claimants shout together it is impossible to discover the rights of any. There must be quiet in the court of justice. There must be quiet in the soul, that a en.Im consideration of app:1rently opposed duties and iuterests may be made. 3. Peace arbitrates between distracting thoughts. 'While the storm rages the sea is turbid. The waters must be calm if we are to look down to the pearls that may lie in their depths. We must think quietly if we would think truly. Ill. lN CHRIST WE FIND THE PEACE WHIOH WILL BE THE UMPIRE NEEL>En BY OUR SOULS. It is vain simply to exhort the heart to beat more calmly. The very effort to do so only increases the perturbation. It would be cruel mockery for a man to say to one in distress and tumult, "Let peace arbitrate in your heart." You may as well command the wild waves of the sea to hush themselves to rest. 1. Christ gives peace. He who said, " Peace, be still I " to the waters and there was a great calm, speaks peace to the troubled soul: "Come unto me, . . . and I will give you rest." 2. Christ gives his own peace. The peace of Christ is that which dwells in him. As he desired that hie joy might be in his disciples, so he also blessed them by leaving his own peace as a legacy when he departed. "My peace I give unto you" (John xiv. 27). Nothing is ·more wonderful, nothing is more beautiful, than the calmness of J csus among tho storms of human foes and diabolical temptations that beat upon him. Like the steady beams of the lighthouse shining calmly over a wild waste of howling waters, Christ, the Light of the world, shone in quietness of soul over all storms and tumults. Now he gives this his peace to his people.-W. F. A.

entries.title: COL 3:16
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Psalmody. Psalmody held a very prominent position in Jewish worship, and there are evidences from the apostolic writings that it was not less honoured in the Christian Church. Certainly a dispensation which was ushered in by angel-anthem,, and which surpassed all that went before it in gladness, should not be wanting i~ scopo for praise and adorntion. The Church that neglects psalmody neglects a most unpor- :?08 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [on. m. 1-25.

tant element of its life and work, and will assuredly suffer in consequence. Let us especially beware of the absurd notion that good music is essentially allied to any particular kind of teaching, and the most foolish, suicidal policy of degrading the ~ervice ?f song ~ecause 'l\'e. ~ay not agree with the doctrines of those people who develop 1t most richly. Tins 1s to leave to them a monopoly of a pleasing attracUon and of a function of the Christian life which all Christians have a right and a duty to cm ploy. If it was wise not to " let the devil have all the best tunes," it must be 11nwise to permit those people whose religious teaching we think erroneous to have all th9 good music. Consider some of the leading characteristics of good psalmody. I. IT SHOULD BE BEAUTIFUL. This is but an external condition, and worthless without higher qualifications. But it is not unimportant. 1. We should offer our best tu God. It is unworthy to cultivate good music in our homes and to seek the best music for our entertainments, and to yet offer our praises to God in slovenly, unmusical tones. 2. We should help the expression of our own devotion by all means in our power. Good psalmody will not create devotion in an undevout heart, but it will assist it in one that is devout, while wearisome dulness and jarring discords will greatly hinder it. 3. We should attrae,t others to our religion. It is not only lawful, it is our duty, to use all means that we may win some. No means are more effective than good psahnody. Now, this beauty of psalmody is evidently contemplated by St. Paul. "Psalms" represent what is sung to musical accompaniments; "songs," what is rendered in poetry. Poetry and music constitute the external beauty of psalmody. II. IT SHOULD DE HEARTFELT. "Singing with grace in your hearts." 1. The first condition is the enjoyment of Divine grace. Psalmody should be .the expression of adoration and praise in response to the grace of God. If we have not the grace we cannot truly take our part in the Church's song of praise. But let us not distress ourselves with the narrow notion that none who are not clearly spiritual Christians can take part in Christian psalmody. For the grace of God is so wide and various that every man has tasted some, and they who have not the highest grace have still enough for devout thankfulness. 2. The praise must come from the heart. Whether we have received much or little grace we must be consciously thankful, and must sing God's praises in our 8ouls if we are really to praise him at all. After all, the music of the heart, even if it be sounded forth by a very harsh voice, is what God most values. !II. IT SHOULD BE OFFERED TO Gon, THOUGH ALSO AIMED AT OUB OWN MUTUAL INSTRUCTION. 1. The first great object of psalmody is "singing . . . unto God." This gives to it its peculiar solemn interest. Worship is expressed by it, and worship is the noblest act of the soul. 2. Nevertheless, indirectly we teach and admonish one another by the,e songs. Strictly didactic poetry is uot, perhapg, either very interesting or very instructive. But the experience of one soul when breathed forth in song may be helpful to another soul. Hence the supreme value of the Hebrew psalms, those inimitable expressions of universal religious experience. We may receive in song what we would not heed or feel when offered in formal instruction.-W. F. A.

Tho Church ie not an almshouse for the indolent ; it ie a hive of industry. Christ i~ Master ae well as Saviour. The first act of faith is to receive the grace of Christ in order that the second may be to obey his commandments (John xiv. 15). II. THE BEBVI0E OF CIIBIBT EXTENDS TO THE WHOLE OF LIFE. It is not simply a matter of what we call religious affairs, the devotions of the sanctuary, etc. It is not merely the doing of work that is called spiritual, such as preaching, teaching, etc. The bond-servants are bidden to serve Christ in their daily work. They are exhorted to work heartily as unto the Lord, in whatsoever they do (ver. 23). We must serve Christ in our daily business. III. THE SERVICE OF CHRIST MUST BE SINCERE. 1. It must not decrenerate into eye-service. Our work is not to please men, but to serve Christ. His eye is ever on us. It matters little whether men admire or neglect our work. 2. It must be done in singleness of heart. Christ will take no divided devotion. We must not be covertly seeking our own interests as distinct from the interests of Christ, so as to have a double, distracting, and often conflicting series of ends to be pursued. \Ve shall gain our own blessedness in the single-eyed service of Christ, and not as a side issue. 3. It must be done from the heart. It must be no mechanical work. \Ve must think about it and put our heart and soul into it. There is a world of difference between the obedience that simply follows the word of command as the signal rises or falls when the lever is moved, and the obedience that considers, feels, and adopts the wishes of the master, and carries them out intelligently and voluntarily, as the signalman interprets and follows the code of directions. IV. Suca SERVICE OF CHRIST ENNOBLES ALL WORK. Work is noble or mean, not so much because of the kind of things done, as on account of the motives that inspire it. A surgeon has to do things which would be disgusting in themselves, but which are refined by the humane motives that prompt them. No task undertaken for a pure purpose can be degrading. The most menial work done for Christ's sake is elevated to the level of the devotion of the angels. V. CaRISTWILL RECOMPENSE HIS SERVANTS ACCORDING TO THEIR SERVICE. "We shall all appear before the judgrnent-seat of Christ." This is the judgment of Christians. We are inclined to forget this while warning publicans and sinners of their coming juclgment. Christians will have to p:ive an account of the use of their talent. 1. Then deceitful eye-service will be exposed and punished, 2. Then/uithful, obscure devotioi• will be revealed and rewarded.-W.
