entries.title: COL 4:7–18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Sect. 10. Personal messages and greetings. The last section of thiR letter is of a more purely epistolary character, and is not, therefore, so directly available, as the foregoing sections for public instruction, belonging to its framework or setting as a piece of Christian teaching. Nevertheless, these closing verses have their own peculiar interest and value-great value for historical and critical purposes, connectin,; the Epistle as they do by the most authentic notes of circumstantial association with the narrative of the Acts of the Apostles, and bracing it firmly into the whole coherent structure of the history of the apostolic Church. Moreover, in the brief but pointed and striking notices here given us, aided by what we know from other sources of the persons mentioned, we may find not a little of indirect and incidental I)rofit "for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for discipline in righteousness" (2 Tim. iii. 16). I. ST. PAUL'S ASSOCIATES. 1. Tychicus, the faithful messenger. (Vers. 7, 8: comp. Eph. vi. 21; Acts xx. 4; Titus iii. 12; 2 Tim. iv. 12.) His association with the apostle in his last journey to Jerusalem, attended with so many affecting circumstances and terminating in his long imprisonment, seems to have led to a devoted attachment on the part of 'l'ychicus to St. l'aul. After returning home, as we may suppose, from Jerusalem, he had journeyed again to Rome, very possibly at the request of the Ephesian Church, to assist and comfort the imprisoned apostle and to bring back news of him. And he returns with these three priceless letters in his charge (Ephesians, Colossians, and Philernon), with Onesimus whom he is to accompany as far as Colossre, and as the bearer of reassuring tidings from St. Paul. Again, some years later, when the apostle's friends were fewer and devotion to his cause still more hazardous, we find 'l'ychicus employed on similar commissions. (1) The apostle has found him to be, what every Christian should be to his fellow-Christians, "a brother beloved; " w bat every officer of the Church, whether in higher or lower capacity, must strivti to be-" a faithful minister and fellow-servant in the Lord," faithful to the Lord and faithful in all brotherly love and "good fidelity" to his fellow-servants. So Tychicus is a blessing both to the apostle and to the distant .A.';iatic Churches. (2) While the Christian depends for strength and consolation in the first place on the fellowship of Christ in the Spirit (2 Cor. i. 3-7; 2 Thess. ii. 16, 17; John xvi. 33), yet how precious and helpful is such communion as this with Christian friends at a distance (1 Thess. iii. G-10; Phil. iv. 10; 2 Car. vii. 6), with faithful sufferers in Christ's cause, with those who bring tidings and words of cheer from brethren far off in other lands ! ( 3) They arc, indeed, "brethren beloved" who, like 'l'ychicus, pass from land to land, from Church to sister Church, in honourable ambassage, as "the messengers of the Churches and the glory of Christ" (2 Car. viii. 23). 2. Onesimus, the converted slave. (Ver. 9.) His position and character will be more fully discussed under the Epistle to Philemou. (1) He is commended to the Christian circle at Colossre on accouut of his ch,iracter- " a faithfui and beloved brother." The apostle had learned to love and trust him, as "tht> child of his bonds," as "his very heart," for his goodness and proved fi<loliLy and helpful service to himself (Philem. 10-13). Greatly had he wished to retain him, but it was the servant's duty to return to bis master. The qualities the apostle marks in him deserve equal respect from us in whatever grade of lifo they appear. The master who fails to recognize in his loyal and humble Christian servant "a brother 220 THE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [en. 1v. 1-18.

beloved in the Lord," is wanting in the simplicity and elevation of the Christinn character, aud has yet to learn that "in Christ J csus there is neither bond nor free" (eh. iii. 11; Gal. iii. 28). It was, however, for Philemon and his Colossian friends II severe test of Christian conviction and of their confideuce in St. Paul to be required to take back this runaway slave as "a faithful and beloved brother." (2) He is commended to them by his Co'lossian origin. "Who is one of you." It is a natural and kindly feeling that prompts this reference. Ties of neighbourhood and early association as well as those of kindred, are providentially formed, and belong to the divinely :on- stituted framework of human life (Acts xvii. 26). This claim of Onesimus is not destroyed by his being a slave, at the very bottom of the social scale; nor was it forfeited by his misconduct. Now that he repents and returns, he is to be received by his Christian follow-townsmen as one of themselves. 3. Aristarchus, the devoted comrade. (Ver. 10.) He was a representative or the Macedonian Churches (Acts xx. 4), who were dearest t-0 the apostle of his children in the faith (1 Thess. ii. 19; Phil. i. 5) in writing to whom he laid aside his official title and was simply Paul, whom alon; he allowed to minister to his personal needs (Phil. iv. 10-18; 2 Cor. xi. 8-10). And he, along with Luke, shared the hardships of the apostle's perilous winter voyage to Rome (Acts xxvii. 2). Indeed, he had been with him before he set out from Ephesus, and was seized by the Ephesian mob at the time of the riot there, being evidently a p~rson of some note and distinction. We know nothing more of bis services to the cause of Christ, beyond this record of his assiduous and self-sacrificing attendance on St. Paul. How much the apostle, with his physical infirmities a.nd his sensitive nature, owed to such friendship, and how much the Church owes on his account, we cannot tell. Those who may not have great gifts for public usefulness may serve Christ most effectually oftentimes by serving his servants, by their private friendship and aid cheering the hearts and strengtheniug the hands of those on whom fall the l,eavier responsibilities of the Church's care and strife, and who but for such timely help might haply sink beneath their burdens. Little as we know of this man, with what a bright distinction his name is marked, and what a place of honour will he his in the book of life, whom the apostle designates," Aristarchus, my fellow-captive, who has been a comfort to me" l 4. Mark, the recoTJered friend. (Ver. 10.) He, like Onesimns to his master, had been "aforetime unprofitable" to St. Paul (Acts xiii. 13; xv. 36-41); and his unprofitableness had caused a serious breach between the two great Gentile missionaries. But now, and again at a later time, he is marked out as "useful for ministry" (2 Tim. iv. 11). St. Paul's firmness and fidelity in refusing, at whatever cost, to take with him an untrustworthy man, had, we may presume, helped to rouse in Mark a better spirit. (1) .At any rate, the position in which he now appears aud the honour which belong to his name in the Church of Christ, shows that onefalse step or unworthy act in a Christian life need not be absolutely fatal (Gal. vi. 1). The immediate result of any fapse must be evil; and it may be followed throughout life by painful consequences. Yet Mark, like Peter, rashly generous and apt to over-estimate his strength at first, when chastened and corrected by experience, becomes the trusted and honoured friend of the two chief apostles, as well as of his only less illustrious kinsman Barnabas. And to him it was given to write the priceless second Gospel, which, in its freshness and simplicity of tone, and in its vivacity and dramatic energy of style, indicates those qualities in John Mark which, i';1 spite of his early failnre, made him so much valued and beloved. (2) And St. Paul B treatment of Mark throws an interesting light on his own character. With all his uncompromising sternness and the intensity of bis passionate nature, there was no bitterness or suspiciousness, no cherishing of personal resentment in his heart. Some men will never trust again a friend or servant who once, unrler any circumstances, has failed them. But the apostle shows a more Chrii;tian and a wiser disposition. As he bids others, so he acts himself, "forbearino- a11d forgivin" if he have blame against any" (eh. iii. 13): compare the crucial instance of 2 Cor. ii. 5-11. As "the Lord forgave" Peter who denied him, so the apostle forgives Mark who _had_ deserted him. And by the way_ in which he co~- mends him to the re"ard of thlB distant Church, he shows how entirely Mark has his approval and confideice. We note also how once more he takes the opportunity of a ki11dly reference to Barnabas. 5. Jesus Justus, a Catholic-minded Jew. (Ver. 11.) lie is known to us here only; but as one of the three (with Arist11rch11s nn<l Mnrcne) oa. 1v. 1-18.] THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSI.ANS. 221

who alone "of the circumcision" were the apostle's "fellow-workers unto the kingdom of God," and "a comfort unto him." Aristarchus and Mark were old friends and associates of St. Paul, attached to him by many ties, Jesus Justus, we arefoclined to think, was a Christian Jew of Rome, and in that case was, it appears, the only member of that community-a tolerably large one, as we should gather from the Epistle to tbe Romans-who heartily supported the apostle in this hour of his need and danger. Many of the Jewish brethren at Rome openly opposed him (Phil. i. 16); others regarded him with a cold and suspicious indifference. At a later period he bas sorrowfully to say of his friends at Rome, "All forsook me" (2 'l'im. iv. 16). But, whether Jesus Justus belr,ged to Rome or not, the fact that he was found at this time by St. Paul's side says a great deal for his courage, as well as for his largeness of heart and enlightened views. The three pillar-apostles at Jerusalem rather acquiesced in St. Paul's principles ann the policy he had pursued than actively supported them (Gal. ii.); and their professed followers in the Jewish Churches denounced them and set up a counter-agitation. If for no other reason, then, it was fitting that the name of this Jesus should be honourably recorded. To the apostle who had been in so many "perils from his own countrymen" and "from false brethren" (2 Cor. xi. 26), every "fellow-labourer of the circumcision" was an especial "comfort." His cognomen Justus attests his reputation amongst his compatriots for legal strictness and uprightness; and this high character would make his attachment to St. Paul the more valuable. 6. Epaphras, the earnest ministel". (Vers. 12, 13.) With the name of Epapbras we are familiar already (see homiletics, sect. 1, II. 2). Though absent from his people, he is none the less concerned for their welfare. When he can do nothing less, he can pray for them all the more. We note: (1) The intensity of his ministerial solicitude; "always striving [ wrestling] for you in his prayers" (ver. 12); "he bath much [painfulj labour for you" (ver. 13). The critical state in which he had left his charge at Colossre, the insidious and ominous character of the errors introduced amongst them and with which he had found it so difficult to cope, were constantly weighing upon his mind, and kept him uncea~iogly active in earnest wrestlings of prayer for his people's souls. (2) The extent of his care. "For you, and for them in Laoilicea, and for them in Hierapolis." The neighbouring cities with their little Christian flocks, exposetl, or likely to be exposed, to the same perils that threatened Colossre, share bis solicitude. And the responsibility of the Christian minister cannot at any time be strictly confioed to his own immediate charge. Each member shares in the joys and griefs, the daogers and trials, which belong to the whole body of Christ. And Churches bordering on his own and connected with his people by ties of acquaintanceship aod frequent intercourse must especially attract his pastoral sympathies and intercession. (3) Tlie aim of his ministry. "'l'hat ye may stand perfect and fully assured in all the will of God" (ver. 13). This is the end of Christ's redemption and of his whole administration of the Church (eh. i. 22). This was the end of the apostle's labours (eh. i. 28, 29). Every true Christian minister will set the same mark before him, namely, the individual and collect.ive perfection of his people in all that goes to make up a complete Christian manhood (Eph. iv. 13). And, partly as resulting; from, partly as contributing to, their moral perfection, he must seek that their Christian convictions may be deepened and confirmed, may be more intelligently as well as more heartily and practically, and so in every way more surely, held (Eph. iv. 13-16). (See homiletics, sects. 1, III. 1; 3, I.; and 4, I. 2). 7. Luke, the beloved physician. (Ver. 14.) Of all the apostle's friends, none was dearer to him or more serviceable than St. Luke. He was with him to tho very last (2 Tim. iv.11). His writings, while they keep the writer's personality modestly out of sight, betray in him a man of a careful and diligent habit of mind, of considerable breadth of culture, and of a tender and sympathetic heart. 'l'he Acts of the Apostles show him to have been a warm and admiring, yet impartial, frimd of St. Paul. And his Gospel is penetrated with that Pauline universalism which both he and his master first found in Christ. The apostle probably owed not a little to Luke's medical care. And we are all indebted to this quiet and skilrul physieian, who im,\erstood so well St. Paul's peculiar temperament and the value of his life to the Church, and whose intelligence and special training rn:i.de his companionship so pleasant an,l so useful to the apos1lc. 'l'he medical profession is that which stands nearest to the ministry of Christ in the honours of sclf-sacrill~e and devotion to humanity. There is c22 THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. [OH. IV, 1-18,

no vocation that demands a higher combination of intellectual and moral powers or that puts a greater strain upon a man's best qualities. It may briug and often d~e~ bring, the physician into a sympathy with the mind and with the m'ission of Christ closer and more real in some respects than auy other work can do. Its best services aro beyond all material and earthly re,vard. Exercised by a wise and faithful Christian· man 1 it bec?~es a_ministry of u~speakable blessing t-0 soul as well as body, reaching, :is did Christ s miracles of healmg, the soul oftentimes through the body. Medical men Christ, "the good Physician," claims above other men for his followers and fellow-workers. 8. Demas, the ba,ckslider. (Ver. 14; 2 Tim. iv. 9, 10.) This man must have been valued greatly by the apostle, to be mentioned in such company, In his second imprisonment he urgently requires Timothy's presence, "because Demas l1ad forsaken him." He appears to have depended hitherto upon Demas and to have' prized his aid. Demas had chosen his lot with the persecuted apostle, and for some 'time served him steadily and well; and then at the last, when the need was greatest, he deserted him, not through fear of danger, it appears, but for the sake ofworlclly gain- " having lo'"ed this present world." Whether he was ever restored to Christian fidelity or not, we cannot tell. His case is so much worse than Mark's, in that the latter gave way to fear under sudden impulse, and in the unexpected hardships and dangers of his first probation; while Demas seems to have forsaken the apostle deliberately and heart- lessly, and when he was no mere novice in the service of Christ. He is an example of' those in whom the good seed takes root and grows through the frosts of spring to a fair summer promise, and then "the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful" (Mark iv. 19). • II. THE MESSAGE TO LAODICEA. (Vers. 15-17.) This passage assumes a peculiar interest in connection with the after history of the Laodicean Church, and the terrible rebuke addressed to it by Christ in Rev. iii. 14--22. It is the only instance in "hich the apostle salutes one Church in writing to another. If the letter received from· him by the Laodiceans was our (so-called) Epistle to the Ephesians, inasmuch as there is no particular greeting to any Church appended to it, we can understand why be should add this kindly salutation here. The Churches of the Lycus valley were so closely linked together tbat the state of one was to a large extent the state of all. We are not surprised, therefore, that the contagion of the Colossian evil spread to Laodicea. Jn that wealthy and luxurious city it bore disastrous fruit, in the corruption that Christ himself through St. John afterwards denounced in his Apocalyptic message. (1) The Colossians and Laodiceans are bidden to exchange Epistles (ver. 16), as they. share the apostle's greetings and alike excited his anxiety (eh. ii. 1). Their similar condition and co=on dangers called for the same warnings and instructions, and the two Epistles largely explain and supplement each other. And indeed, wherever lo~al circumstances permit, as in the freedom and ease of communication amongst ourselves it is so largely possible, Christian intercourse should be promoted, co~certed measures should be taken, the forces of the Church should be combined in resistance to the spread of error and the contagion of vice. "Union is strength." (2) Nympha (01· Nymph<is) is greeted by name (ver. 15), according to the apostle's custom, who loves to single out for honour those who serve the Church by the readiness by which they place their house and means at her service (1 Cor. xvi. 15, 16; Rom. xvi. 3-5, 23). (3) The most oignificant sentence of this passage is the warning addressed to Archippus (ver. 17), whom we suppose to have held an office of trust in the Church at Laodicea. He is the Hon of St. Paul's honoured friend Philemon, and had been on 8ome former occasion (probably at Ephesus) so closely associated with the apostle in circumstances of labour and danger that, ~ writing to his father, he calls him "my fellow-soldier." And yet symptoms of negligence have appeared in his conduct of affairs at Laodicea, tb!lt call forth the gentle yet serious admonition, "Take heed to the ministry that thou rcceivedst in the Lord, that thou fulfil it." How grave his responsibility if this warni,,n- failed to take effect, and if the all but apostate state of the Laodicean Church some ye~rn afterwards was in any degree due to the unfaithfulness of its first pastor I III. 'l'HE APOSTLE'S FAREWELL. (Ver. 18.) These brief, affecting word a proceed from 1he autlior's own hand, the lar;;e and difficult characters themselves a reminder of his affi;ctiuns in the [;Ospel. 1. He bids the Culo~sians remember his bonds (comp. Philcm.

10, 13; Phil, i. 7, 17; Epb. iii. I, 13; vi. 20; 2 Tim. ii. 9, 10; see homiletics, sect. 3, I. 4) -so sore a trial to him, so great an advantage and glory to them, callin,,. for their tender and prayerful sympathy, and for their most regardful heed to all that he had written. 2. He wishes them grace--grace first and last (comp. eh. i. 2, and homiletics); the grace they had received already (eh. i. 6, 12, 21, 27 ; ii. 6; iii. 12, 13 ; Eph. i. 3) being the pleiige and the earnest of all the fulne~s of tha.t "supernboun,ling grace" which reigns" through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom. v. 20, 21; 2 Uor. iL 8; Eph. i. 3; John i. 16).

entries.title: COL 4:1
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The duties of masters. "Masters, render unto your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven." I. THE DUTY OF MASTERS. It is here enforced only on its positive side. 1. Justice. Masters must give their servants what is according to contract, or according to what is just in itself, as to work, wages, food, correction, and example. 2. Equality. Masters sometimes treat servants unequally in demanding inconvenient service, an unreasonable amount of work, in withholding wages. 'l'hey ought to treat them so that they may serve them cheerfully and efficiently. II. THE BEASON TO ENFORCE THIS DUTY. "Knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven." God's majesty and man's authority stand together. The Lord in heaven is the Master of masters, and will avenge the wrongs they may inflict on their servants.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 4:2
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -Exhortation to constant prayer. The apostle then gives some special concluding exhortations: "Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching therein with thanksgivin~." I. THE DUTY OF PERSEVERANCE IN PRAYER. 1. This does not imply that we are to devote all our time to prayer; for it would be inconsistent (1) with other duties; (2) with man's mental and •moral nature; (3) with the design of prayer itself. 2. It implies that we are to be often engaged in prayer. (1) There is nothing more sanctifying and refreshing and strengthening to the soul. (2) Continuance in prayer brings larger blessings from on high. (3) 'l'he Scripture contains many examples of continuance in prayer (David, Daniel, Paul, our Lord himself). (4) The delay in the answers to prayer ought to lead us to persevere therein, because (a) it may lead to a deeper sense of want; (b) our faith and patience need to be tried; (c) the time for the answers may not have come. II.. THE DUTY OF WATCHFULNESS IN PRAYER. 1. We must be watchful as to the spirit of prayer, not indolent and remiss. 2. We must watch for arguments in prayer. a. llfe must ivatch for suitable praying seasons. 4. We must watch against watcldessness. 6. We must watch for the answers to prayer. 6. Remember Christ's example as he watched in prayer. (Matt. xiv. 23, 25.) Ill. THE DUTY OF JOINING THANKSGIVlNG WITH OUR SUPPLICATIONS AND OUR WATCII- ING. 1. We must always in prayer give thanks for mercies received. (Phil. iv. 6; 1 'l'hess. v. 16, 17.) 2. We must thank him in praises. 3. God answer, according to our gratitude for mercies received.-'!'. C.

entries.title: COL 4:3
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
.-Prayer for the apostle and his companions. "Withal praying for us also, that God may open unto us a door for the word, to speak 1.he mystery of Obrist fur which I am also in bonds; that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak." I. EVEN THE GREATEST IN THE CHURCH NEEDS THE PRAYERS o~· THE LEAST. 1. It is the duty of the people to pray for their ministers. 2. It makes prayer profitable to interest ourselves in the welfare of others by intercessions for them at a throne nf grace. 3. The progress of the gospel depends much upon the prayers of the saints. (2 'l'liess. iii. 1.) II. 'faE SUBJECT OF THE PRAYER. It was that the apostle and Timothy nnd Epaphras might have abundant opportunity of preaching the gospel, as well as liberty, power, and success. The prayer implies: 1. 'l'hat God can open a tray fur the gu.s}'el 224 'l'HE EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIA.NS. [011, IV, 1-18,

among the hearts of men. It was the Lord who opened Lydia's heart (Acts xvi. 14), and "opened the door of faith to the Gentiles" (Acts xiv. 27). 2. That God could liberate the apostle from prison as a condition of carrying on his apostolic work. 3. 7'/int the apostle's impri~onment was caused by his devotion to tl1e "mystel'y of Christ," which was the admission of the Gentiles to salvation on equal terms with the Jews, or, in other words, "Christ in them the Hope of glory" (eh. i. 27). He would not have heen in prison if he bad been preaching a gospel with Judaic restrictions. His bonds wc,re due to the strength of Jewish prejudices. But" the truth of the gospel" was so dear to him that he was content to suffer for it, and even to forego the opportunities of enlarged usefulness out of prison. 4. That he might be able to use his opportunities with boldness and success. People ought to pray that their ministers may be able to preach the Word with power (1 Thess. v. 5); with urgency (2 Tim. iv. 2, 3, 5); with patience, constancy, and fear (1 Cor. iv. 9; 2 Cor. vi. 4; iv. 8); with faithfulness (1 Cor, iv. 2); with zeal (2 Cor. v. 11; 1 Thess. ii. 12),-approving themselves in the sight of God to their hearers' consciences (2 Cor. ii. 17).-T. C.

entries.title: COL 4:5
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The behaviour of Ohristiam in the world. "Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.'' Consider- I. THE PERSO~S WHO ARE TO BE INFLUENCED BY OUR WALK. "Them that are ,,ithout.'' Christians are those who are within (1 Cor. v. 12). Unbelievers are" without "-outside the Church, without God, without Christ, without hope in the world. They are those whom "God judgeth" (1 Cor. v. 13). Believers ought to ha.ve regard to such persons, not only in their prayers, but in the wisdom of their personai walk. II. THE NATURE .A.ND IMPORTAKCE OF THE BELIEVER'S WALK DEFORE THE WORLD. " Walk in wisdom, ... redeeming the time." 1. It is a wise walk. " Be ye wise as serpents" (Ma.tt. x. 16). Zea.l is not enough. Love is not enough. Walk circumspectly, RO as to give no offence or put occasions of reproach in the wa.y of sinners. 'l'his is done by believers (1) walking in the light of God's Word (Ps. cxix. 1); (2) walking in all faithfulness of their calling (1 Thess. iv. 11, 12; 1 'l'im. vi. 1); (3) walking in love to one another, without murmurings or disputings (Phil. ii. 15, 19); (4) walking in meekness toward a.11 men (Titus iii. 1, 2; Jas. iii. 13); (5) walking in a.11 patience and constancy under rebuke or injury (1 Pet. iii. 13-16). 2. Such a walk is influential toward unbelievers. (1) A. believer ought to be more careful of his wa.lk before them than before believers. (2) Such a walk ha.s a. winning effect upon the world, which thus sees the reality of true religion. Believers are to be" living epistles of Christ, known aud read of all men" (2 Cor. iii. 3). (3) A. foolish wa.lk will ea.use the enemy to blaspheme. 3. Believers ought to seek comtant opportunities ofobeying this command. " Redeeming the time." External opportunities are to be sought for, and never to be neglected. Ministers must preach while the door is open; people must pra.y at every opportunity (Eph. vi. 18; Luke xx.i. 36). They must walk in the light before the night comes. '£he times may not always be favourable.-'!'. C.

entries.title: COL 4:6
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-The importance of seasonable speech. "Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with sa.lt, that ye ma.y know how to answer each one." 'l'?e conver- Ha.tion of believers is to have reference to "those without" as well as their personal behaviour. L TUE NATURE OF SEASONABLE SPEECH. 1. It is to be" always with grace." (1) It is to spring out of some grace of God in the !,cart, such as kuowledge,joy, love, fear; to be seasoned with the recollection of God's grace to us in Christ (Ps. xl. 11); and to minister grace to the hearers (Eph. iv. 29). 2. It is to consist of gracious words. (1) N,,t words or railing, or blasphemy, or corruption; (2) but words that are (a) seasonable (Prov. xv. 23), (b) wholesome (Eph. iv. 2!:1), (c) kindly (Prov. xxxi. 26), (d~ hopeful. ::i. The conversation of believers is to be uniformly with grace. The precept 1s always in force. Much <lepends upon the continuity of a gracious hab)t of talk. It is_ to be ,xcrcised in all places, at all times, yet with due regnrd to what 1s seasonable or timely. 4. It is to be seusorced with salt. It is not to be insipid and without point., so as to be iucapable of edifying man's spirit. It must have penetrative force, either for ~he yur- J•ose of directing the ingnirer or answering the scoffer. "'l'hc tongue of the _wise 1s ~s choice silver;" "'l'he heart of the wise teachcth liis mouth, and ad<leth learning io his OH. IV, 1-18.] THE EPISTLE '1'0 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. 225

lips" (Prov. x. 20; xvi. 23). Our Lord said," Every one must be salted with fire, ev<ory sacrifice must be salted with salt" (Mark ix. 49). The person is salted first; the salt is found in his words and deeds afterwards. II. 'l'm: END OF SEASONABLE SPEECH. "That ye may know how to answer each one." Thie implies: 1. 'l'hat the truth wal be spoken a,'}ainst. (1) It is the heritage of "the sect everywhere spoken against" ( Acts xxviii. 22). (2) It is hard for carnally minded men to understand it, and therefore they gainsay it. (3) Them are men who "hold down the truth in unrighteousness" (Rom. i. 18). 2. That believers are to learn how to give a ri,'}ht answer to objectors. We are to" give a reason of the hope that is in us with meekness and fear" (1 Pet. iii. 15). It must be done (1) prayerfully; for "the answer of the tongue," as well as "the preparation of the heart," " is from the Lordi' (Prov. xvi. 1). (2) With faith in God's promise and hope (Pd. cxix. 42; Matt. x. 19). (3) With a good conscience (1 Pet. iii.J6). Thus objectors will be put to shame who" falsely accuse our good conversation in Christ." (4) \Vith a due consideration for the circumstances of each objector, whether he be sincere or insincere, ignorant or malicious. We are "to answer each one" according to the necessities of each case (I'rov. xxv. 11; :uvi. 4, 6).-T. C.

entries.title: COL 4:7–9
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -The bearers of the Epistle to the Oolossiana. Though the apostle had but few friends at this time in Rome to comfort him in bis "bonds," he spares two ut' them to comfort the Colossians. I. THE PERSONS WHO 0ABBY THE EPISTLE TO CoLOSS&. Tycbicus and Onesirnus. 1. Tychicus. (1) His history. He was a native of Asia Minor (Acts xx. 4), and probably of Ephesus (2 Tim. iv. 12). He accompanied the apostle at the close of his thinl missionary journey (Acts xx. 4). He was now again with the apostle at Rome, near the end of the first Roman captivity; and he appears again with him at the very end of the apostle's life, when the apostle is sending him to Crete and to Ephesus (Titu~ iii. 12; 2 Tim. iv. 12). The name 'l'ycbicus appears on Roman inscriptions as well as on inscriptions in Asia Minor. (2) His character and work. He receives three titles of distinction and praise. (a) A· beloved brother, in relation to the whole Christian Church; (b) a faithful minister, in relation to bis evangelistic services to the apostle (Acts XL 4); (c) a fellow-ser,ant in the Lord, a co-operator with the a1,ostle in Christian labours. 2. Onesimus. This was doubtless the runaway slave of Phi lemon, whose conversion is recorded in the Epistle to that Colossian brother. (1) He was a native of Colossie-" who is one of you." (2) His changed character-" the faithful and beloved brother." (a) He was lately unfaithful, now he is faithful; he was lately an object of contempt and dislike, be is now an object of love. (b) The repentance of a sinner is a fact to be gratefully recorded. His former sins ought to be no disparagement to bis present standing and repute. "Where God forgives, men should not impute." (c) The apostle is not ashamed of a poor slave, and comrucnt!s him to the love of the Church. • II. 'l'HE DESIGN OF THE SENDING OF TYCHIOUB AND ONESIMUS TO CoLOSS~. "Whom I have sent unto you for this very purpose, that ye may know our estate, aud that he may comfort your hearts." There are two objects. 1. To make known tlie affairs of the apostle and of the Roman Church. It was not necessary, therefore, tha~ he should give them any information about himself or the cause of Christ in Rome. The Colossians would hear all by word of mouth. 2. To comfort the hearts of the Oolossians. 'l'hey would comfort them (1) by their very presence; (2) by bringing the Epistles from Rome; (3) by their news concerning the apostle; (4) by their practical exhortations, enforcing the doctrine of the Epistle and the duty of perseverance in faith and grace to the end.-T. C.

entries.title: COL 4:10
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Greetings from three loyal friends of the apostle. The Epistle ~llll~ with salutations, first from three Jews, and then from three Gentiles. I. 'l'mi: THREE JEWISH FRIENDS OF THE APOSTLE. 1. .Aristarchus. "Aristarchus my fellow-prisoner saluteth you." He was a native of 'l'hessalonica (Acts xx. 4), wl,o accompanied the apostle in bis third missionary journey. He was seized alon:; with the apostle at Ephesus (Acts xix. 29), and accompanied him in bis voyage to Rome (Ad:; xxvii. 2). He now shared the apostle's imprisonment at Rome. Adversity does uu~ COLOSSlANS. Q 226 THE EPISTLE 'l'O THE COLOSSIANS. [OH. IV. 1-18,

lessen his affection for the apostle. 2. Marcus. "And Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (touching -whom ye received command~ents; if he come unto you, receive him)." This ,vas the author of the second Gospel, who was associated with the apostle in his earlie,r missionary labours, and afterwards forsook him at Pamphylia, under circumstances that led to a rupture betwoen Paul and Barnabas (Acts xv. 39). He is now affectionately commended to the Colossians-for he had evidently recovered the confidence and love of the apostle-as "one useful to him for the ministry" (2 Tim. iv. 11). Mark was now resident in Rome. It is not possible to know what were the commands which the apostle had sent to the Colossians concerning him; probably they were to bespeak a hospitable reception for him, as the Pauline Churches may have suspected his fidelity. 3. Jesus. "And Jesus, which is called Justus." He is only mentioned in this place, He is not probably the same as Justus of Corinth (Acts xviii. 7). He was attached to the apostle. It is curious that a disciple who bore the name of our l.ord should have also borne his title of "·the just one." • II. THE APOSTLE'S mGH COMMENDATION OF THE THREE FRIENDS. "These only are my fellow-workers unto the kingdom of God, men that have been a comfort unto me." 1. They were Jews. "Who are of the circumcision." 2. They were exceptions to the rule of anti-Pauline animosity on the part of Christian Jews, The exception is limited, probably, to those Jews in Rome, who preached Christ "through strife and envy," hoping thus to "add affliction to his bonds" (Phil. ii. 20). But these three comforted him by hearty co-operation and their kindly sympathies. The best and greatest men need the comfort of the very humblest, who in their tum r_ebuke the conduct of those who grieve God's servants and are thorns in their sides.-T. C.
