entries.title: COL 4:7–18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Personal salutations and pastoral cares. The personal references in Paul's Epistles are valuable in several wayA. "Proper names, although they be recited alone in the Scriptures, are not to be despised" (2 'l'im. iii. 16). "For like as if any one should find dry herbs, having neither fragrance nor colour that was pleasing, arran~ed in the surgery of a doctor, however mean may be their appearance, will yet guess that some virtue or remedy is concealed in them ; so in the pharmacopceia of the t:lcriptures, if anything occurs that at first sight may seem to be despised by us, yet may we determine of a certainty that there is some spiritual utility to be found in it; because Christ, the Physician of souls, we may suppose, would place nothing insignificant or useless in his pharmacopceia" (Origen). These personal references are useful: 1. As supplying " undesigned coincidences" (Paley's 'Harm Paulinm,' eh. vi., viii., and xiv. ; and Birks' 'Harm Apostolicre,' eh. vi.). 2. As correcting errors; e.g. the alleged episcopacy of St. Peter at Rome from A.D. 42-68 is rendered incredible by the silence of St. Paul in all his Epistles from Rome (vers. 10, 11). 3. As helping us to form a vivid idea of the apostle's circumstances at different periods, and their bearing on his life's work and teaching. From these twelve verses we gather such facts as these, each of which may suggest some useful lessons. He was a prisoner, adding his autograph message "in a chain" (Eph. vi. 20); enjoying for the present considerable indulgence (Acts x.xviii. 30, 31), and hoping for a speedy release (Philem. 22). He enjoyed the company of friends both old and new. Here is Tychicus, probably from Ephesus, a tried companion in toil and peril (Acts x.x. 4; Eph. vi. 21); and Onesimus (a trophy of Divine grace, a jewel rescued as from the common sewer of the corrupt metropolis; teaching us to despair of no one). These two are being sent to tighten the bonds between the Churches in Asia and the apostle at Rome (vers. 7-10; Eph. vi. 22). Others remain to aid and cheer him. ..tl.ristarchus of Thessalonica, one of the firstfruits of Europe, now a voluntary prisoner (Acts xix. 29; x.x. 4; xxvii. 2). Mark, now 1mjoying the fullest confidence of St. Paul (2 Tim. iv. 11): an encouraging illustration of bow "patient continuance in well-doing" may cast early errors into oblivion and win back confidence once withdrawn; and a caution even to an apostle against too stern a judgment on a young brother. Jesus Justus, the only other Hebrew Christian mentioned, otherwise unknowo, yet worthy of honour in all ages, because "a comfort " (I) the apostle: an encouragement to workers little known in the annals of the Church (Matt. x. 40-42). Epaphras, probably the founder of the Colossian Church, who Lad often preached to them and now prayed much for them. Luke, the first medical missionary, a minister to the soul as well as to the body of the sorely tried apostle. Last comes Demas, mentioned without any commendation; still a fellow-labourer (Philem. 24), but in whom St. Paul may have already detected signs of that worldly-mindedness which led him afterwards to withdraw from duty and danger, if not altogether to make shipwreck of faith (2 Tim. iv. 10)-a caution against backsliding in heart (Prov. xii·. 14; 1 John ii. 15). The salutations to brethren at Colossro further remind us of the social life and limited conditions of the primitive Christians(" Nymphas, anti the Church that i~ in their house"), of the value of an earnest ministry to the Church (ver. 17), nnd of the duty of cherishing fraternal sympathy with other Churches (vers. 15, lG). 'fhis reference to the Epistle to Laodicea suggests to us that, though a letter may be lost and a Church may languish or die (Rev. iii. 14-22), the Word of the Lord in the letter and to the Church endureth for ever. Many of these references group themselves around the names of those who were pastors or evangelists, and suggest final thoughts respecting a minister's responsibilities, anxieties, and encw.rageinents. 1. Responsibilities. (Ver. ]7.) The ministry was" in the Lord." In union with and in subordination to him he was to exercise it; and only by the utmost vigilance and energy could he fulfil it. To every minister such a charge is given as 2 Tim. iv.1, 2, 5, and such promises as 1 Tim. iv. 16. Responsibility inspires zeal (2 Cor. iv. 1, 2; v. 9; vi. 3-10), anJ 240 THI<: EPISTLE TO 'l'HE COLOSSIANS. [CH. IV, 1-18,

fosters that spirit of dependence which ensures the blessing (1 Cor. iii. 7). 2. .Anooietic.~. (V<'rs. 12, 13.) A faithful minister can aim at nothing less. Ho cannot ndapt tho standard of the gospel to the maxims of the day. He has to educate tho mind and tho conscience, that bis flock may be "perfect and fully assured iu all the will of God." He must teach and warn, apv_lyin_g gencr:i,l principles to i:ractical det3ils, being bimsolf an example to the flock (1 'l m1. 1v. 12) m laboms and m prayers, so that those who know him beRt may bear such witness to him as Paul does to Epaphras. 3. Encourage- •ments from tbree sources: sympathy, such as Paul enjoyed from friends at Rome and at Coloss.-e; co-oreration from" fellow-workers unto the kingdom of Goel;" affection, such as love to the one Lord an? labours for him_promote iu men of different temperaments, so that we find Paul sprn1.krng of many of his colleagues, uot only as honoured fellowsoldicrs, but beloved _friends (ve:5- 7, D, 14; Rom. :-Vi. 12). For 111l such the apostle hreathes the concludmg prayer 1n one comprehensive term," Grace be with you."- R &~ •

entries.title: COL 4:2
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Steridfastness in prayer. I. IT IS GREATLY NEEDED. 'l'he seven deacons were chosen partly in order that the apostles might not be hindered by temporal alfairs from continuing steadfastly in prayer (Acts vi. 4). St. Paul exhorts the Reiman Christians to this same steadfastness (Rom. xii. 12). It is requisite on many accounts. 1. There are never wanting subjects that claim our prayers. 2. When we are least i11dined, to p,ay we are in most need of prayer. 3. Only constant prayer can be profoundly spiritual. It is the ever-flowing stream that wears the deep water-course. The bird that soars high must be much on the wing. 4. Steadfastness in prayer is rewarded by Divine resp011ses; e.g. Abraham's intercession for Sodom, the parable of the importunate widow, etc. IL IT 1s A SIGN OF SPIRITUAL HEALTH. After the ascension of their Lord the early Christians continued steadfastly in prayer (Acts i. 14); so did the converts of thii day of Pentecost (Acts ii. 42). 1. It shows a spiritual tone of mind. We may pray in special need without this, and we may pray at set seasons of devotion without it. But to live in an atmosphere of prayer, to pray because it is natural to us to talk with God, because we love communion with him, because prayer is our vital breath, and so to pray without ceasing from inward devotion rather than frvtn external prompting,-all this is a sign of ·true spirituality. 2. It shows spiritual vigour. S.uch prayer is .no mere listless droning of empty phrases, no sudden burst of temporary ejaculations. It implies a strong, deep energy of devotion. III. IT IS DIFFICULT TO MAINTAIN. It is easy to cry out to God in great _extremities. Prayerless men pray under such circumstances. It is easy, too, to pray when we are in :, mood of devotion. The difficulty is to continue steadfastly in prayer. The hindrances are numerons. 1. Lack of interesti11g subjects of prayer. There may be nothing that touches us as a great want or strongly appeals to our sympathies at some seasons like the dire needs and touching claims that inspire our petitions at other times. 2. External distractions. The pressure of business, the din of the world's affairs, uncon- _genial society, even too absorbing Church work, especially in this age of rich activity and meagre contemplation, check prayer. 3. Internal hindrances. We are not alway11 in the mood for prayer, Sometimes- " Hosannas le.nguieh on our lips, .And onr devotion dies." This may result from physical weariness. The spirit may be willing though the flesh is weak. We should then turn aside and rest awhile from the tiring work of the world. But it may result from sin. Sin is the greatest hindrance to prayer. IV. IT MAY BE MAINTAINED DY THE GBACE OF Gon. 1. It is not to be revived in weaknes6 by greater assiduity in formal devotioo. It is a fatal mistake to confound long prayers with steadfast prayers, and to suppose that spending more time in saying prayers will strengthen our enfeebled spirit of prayer. It will have the opposite effect. Nothing binders true prayer so much as continuing the form of devotion without th& JlOwer. 2. The recret is to seek the reviving Spirit of God. If prayer is growing faint, there may still be energy for uttering the petition, "My soul cleaveth uuto the dust: quicken thou me according to thy Word" (I's. cxb.. 25). All true prayer is an inspira- OH, IV. 1-18.) 'l'HE EPIS'l'LE TO THE COLOSSIANS. 2H

tion. The deepest prayer comes from the striving of God's Spirit within us. "Th o Spirit nlso holpeth our infirmities . . . the Spirit himself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered" (Rom. viii. 26).-W. F. A. Ver. 6 (first clause).-The wisdom of the <Jhurch in its relations to the world. J. THE CHABA0TERISTICB OF THIS WIBDOll. The Church needs wisdom. Cbristiaus must be wise as serpents as well as harm less ag cloves. We are to blame for lack of wisdom as well as for lack of other graces, for this is a gift of God (Jas. i. 5). 1. Tbis wisdom is practical. It concerns itself with behaviour rather than with speculation. 2. It must be pure. There must not be the slightest unfaithfulness to Obrist, tampering with truth, or casuistic deviation from the highest principles. II. THE OCCASIONS FOR THIS WISDOM. It was most necessary in the apostolic age, when the Christians existed only as small communities scattered about among adverse populations. But it is always more or less called for. 1. For lawful self-protection. If persecuted in one city the servant of Christ was to flee to another. He was not to court opposition. Martyrdom is only a glory when it comes in the path of duty, and never when men go out of that path to seek it. 'rheu it degenerates into little better than suicide. 2. To conqww opponents. The Church has a mission to the world, and she will fail in this mission if she cannot win her enemies over to her own side. For Christ's sake, and for the good of men who need his gospel, this wisJom must be observed in conciliating foes that they may themselves be brought into the Church. III. THE :MANNER OF EXERCISING THIS WISDOM. 1. In understanding those who are without. We often provoke oppositiou because we do not study the weaknesses and prejudices of others. On the other band, Christians have shown a needless scorn for the good in others. True charity will take note of all that is admirable, and think of wh,tsoever things are worthy in the world outside the Church. 2. In an attractive exhtbi- tion of the blessings of <Jhristianity. Souls are not saved by rating and scolding men. 'l'he world must be drawn, not driven, to Christ. A morose Church will only rerel an unsympathetic world. Wisdom towards them that are without will forbid the scandal of quarrelling among Christians.-W. F. A. ,

entries.title: COL 4:6
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content:
-Salt. Our speech is to be" seasoned with salt." The context shows that this advice is given especially in regard to the conversation of Christian people with ::nen of the world. It is part of the "wisdom towards them that are without." Instead of offensive fault-finding, haughty self-assertion, or morose indifference, our speech is to be courteous-" with grace;" and pleasant-" seasoned." Salt stands for wit in Greek references to it as seasoning speech. But with St. Paul it seems rather to mean a pleasant, kindly, interesting characteristic of speech. I. SPEECR SHOULD BE COURTEOUS. "Be courteous" is advice that comes to us from the sturdy fisherman (1 Pet. iii. 8). If we cannot agree with another there is no reason why we should treat him unkindly. If we must even oppose him, still we can do it with consideration and gentleness of manner. In general intercourse it is well that an aITability of behaviour should characterize the Christian. How courteous Christ was with all classes I St. Pau I is a model of the true Christian gentleman. The essence of courtesy is sympathy for others in small things. It is hollow if we manifest hostility or sclfisbuess in large things. The courtesy of II Chesterfield has a flavour of hypocrisy about it because it is based on selfishness. Still, if we are sympathetic in serious matters we may be much misunderstood, and we may really give much pain by a needless brusqueness of manner. II. SPEECH SHOULD m, INTERESTING. Salt is seasoning. It gives pungency. Something similar should ho found in our conversation. Dulness is an offence. It is an infliction of intolerable weariness on tbo listener. On the part of the speaker it shows either want of interest in his subject (in which case he should let it o.lone), or want of interest in his hearer (which is a direct result of lack of sympathy). Moreover, tho Christian is called to bo frequently bearing testimony for his Master. He weakens that testimony by giving it in an uninteresting manner. He should study his words. But, better than that, he should have his theme so much at heart as to speak with the eloquence of enthusiasm. IIL SPEECH snouLD DE PUilE. Salt is antiseptic. The Christian shonld not only COLOSSIANS, B TIIE EPISTLE 'l'O THE COLOSSlANS. [en. IV. 1-18.

iwoid unwholc~ome topics and styles of speech; he should bring into convol'sation a positirn, purilying influence. 'l'his does not mean that he shottld be always quotina (t•x Is and set rdil(ious rhrases, or ahrnys dragging in religious subjects out of place and season. He degrades them, provokes his hearas, and stultifies himself by so doin"'. Bnt he should seek to elcrate the tone of conversation, to guide it from unworthy suhj ects and to infuse into it a pure tone. There are Christ-like men whose very 1•rcsence in a room seems to rebuke cl"il talk and to breathe a higher atmosphere into the con 'l"ersation. How purifying was the conversation of Christ !-W. F . .A.

Ver. rn.-.4. friendly exchange. I. SCRIPTURE IS INTENDED FOR GE8ERAL READING. The two Epbtles are to be read in the Churches. 'l'hey are not to be reserved for the bishors, the more initiated or the more advanced Christians. All members of the two Churches, young and old, slaves and freemen, illiterate and cultured, imperfect and sr,iritual-minded, are to hear the two Epistles. Now, these Epistles contain about the most advanced doctrine of all writings of the Bible. They approach nearest to what is anal,,gous to the inner Gnostic doctrines of all Scripture teaching. If, therefore, any porticns of revelation should be reserved for the few, it would be these. If these are for public pen,rnl, surely the simpler Gospels and psalms must ho also public prc,perty. The Bible is a bo0k for the people. It is free to all. No man has a right to bar access to the tree of life on the pica that the ignorant do not know how to help themselves from it and mu~t have its fruits doled out by official guardians. 'J'he greatest philosopher may find unfathomable depths in Scripture; but a little child may also read clear truths therein. If it be said that the ignorant will misuc.derstand, the reply is-They will gain more truth on the whole, in spite of misunderstanding, by free access to the Bible than when only led to it by others. God can take care of his own truth; the l.lible was written for the people, and the people have a right to their own. No guardians of Scripture who are to measure it out to others at their discretion were ever appointed b_v Christ or by his apostles. II. THE ScRIPTUilE THAT IS USEFUL TO ONE CHURCH WILL BE USEFUL TO ANOTHER. Tlie two letters were written with special regard to the peculiar circumstances of the two Churches. Yet they were to be exchanged. Much more, then, should Christians \\'ho have not had any private Epistle of their own benefit by the public Scriptures. Special wants arc not primary wants. The great need of revelation is common to all. The flllldamental truths of the gospel are needed by and offered to all. '!'he highest glories of revelation are for all. Jil. Oun. READING OF SCIIIP'l'ORE SHOULD NOT DE CONFINED TO ISOLATED Fll.AGMENTS, A Church which Lad been honoured by receiving an apostolic Epistle written expressly for itself vrould be kmpted to depreciate other apostolic writings, or at least to consider that for its own use its own Epistle was of paramount if not of exclusive importance, It would be in danger of making its one Epistle its own New 'l'estament, to the disregard of all the re,t. Dut the advice of St. Paul shows that such an action would be a mistake. 1. Our n-adi11g of Scripture should be wide and varied. We must beware uf confining our attention to favourite portions. By doing so we get one-sided views uf truth, and probably, even if unconsciously, select what seems to support our own Lotions to the ne,;l,ct of what would modify them. We may most need to read those ScripLures in wl,ich we feel lea8t interest. 2. Scripture balances and interprets :.icripture. 'l'l,e doctrine of tl,e Christ which is the leading theme of the Epistle to .:.e Colossians is closely related to the doctrine of the Church which is the central suuject of the so-called Epistle to the Ephesians (that, probably, referred to by St. Paul as the Epistle to the Laodiceans). IV. 'JIIERE 6IIOULD DE INT.ERCOMMUNION DETWEEN CmllS'l'IAN CONGREGATIONS. TI.Jere is too much corporate selfishness in the Church. We should be the better for more eccl~siastical altruism, or rather communism. 1. 'l'his is most to be looked for l,etween neighbours. Laodicea was near to Coloss:e. 2. Aud it should be cultivated uetween the prominent and the obscure. Laodicea was an important city, Colossai a stnall town. Yet the Churches in the two places were to show brotherly sympathy on e'lual terms and to be mutually helpful to one another. While the strong should help t1,e weak, the: weak shculd beware of sdfishness and do their best to serve the sLrong, -W.F.A. •

entries.title: COL 4:18
entries.author: George Gillanders Findlay
entries.content: -" Remember my bonds." St. Paul's occasional references to his boncl~ nrc :r.ever thrust forward in the spirit of the histrionic martyr an<l never expressed in a murmuring tone, but they evince the irksome restraints under which he laboured, and they give a certain pathos to his entreaties. To be alw:iys chained to a soldier, possibly one of rude and coarse manners, must have been peculiarly distressing to a man of sensitive, refin~d disposition like St. Paul. Feeling the burden of his bonds, tl,e apostle prays his readers to remember them. I. REME:MDEn TnEM IN SYMPATIIY. It is something to know that friends are feeling with us, when they can do nothing directly to remove the cause of trouble. The lowliest may help the greatest by his sympathy. An apostle seeks the sympathy of obscure Christians. Christ looked for the support of his disciples' sympathy in the hour of his greatest agony, and had the last drop of his bitter cup in the failing of that sympathy (Matt. :x..xvi. 40). II. R1rnEMDER THEM IN PilAYER. When we cannot work for our brother'~ release from trouble, we m:iy pray. With all the power or Rome at his b.Lck, Nero cannnt prevent the feeble Christians from having recourse to the mighty weapon of prayer. Let us beware of a selfish narrowness of sympathy in prayer. There are always many calls for prayers of intercession. Very touching is the ancient prayer that bas come down to us from the dark ages of persecution, and is presented in the so-called 'Divine Liturgy of St. James:'" Remember, 0 Lord, Christians sailing, travelling, sojourning iu strange lands; our fathers and brethren, who are in bonds, prison, captivity, and exile; wbo are in mines, and nndcr torture, and in bitter slavery." III. REMEMBER 'l'HEM rn GRATITUDE. St. Paul was suffering for the gospel. Th-1 real cause of his imprisonment was the persecution of the Jews, who were more bitter to his liberal version of Christianity than to the more Judaistic Christianity of the other apostles. Thus he described himself, "I Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus in behalf of you Gentiles" (Eph. iii. 1). Therefore his bonds merit our grateful memory; and the sufferings of the champions of Christian liberty merit similar reverent and grateful recollections. It is well that these memories should be handed down from father to son, that the stories of the heroes of Christendom through whose toils aud sufferings we now enjoy so many privileges should be taught to our children. IV. REMEMBER THEM IN REVERENCE FOR ST. PAUL'S AUTHORITY. His bonds lend weight to his words. They prove his sincerity. They are a reason for listening to his entreaties. By bis sufferings he entreats us to walk worthily of our Christian calling. So the greater sufferings of a greater Friend give force to his persuasion when he bid~ us follow him.-W. F. A.
